The strengths of KOTOR are what I now play BioWare games for, which is the emphasis they put into writing. If I had to give my formula for what makes a good game it would be a well written story with finely tuned gameplay. With KOTOR the gameplay is decent, it’s your standard party based RPG where you can tune your character to suite your play style through various skills and feats and you can pick two members of your party to accompany you with their own skills so you conceivably conquer any obstacle. Knights of the Old Republic is probably the best Star Wars game that has been made and it can back up that statement with multiple awards and Aspyr Media porting it to Mac OS and iPad. Yes, you can play KOTOR on your iPad!
I could go on for several more paragraphs on the level of writing behind KOTOR but when good writing is basically BioWare’s identity now should they even get credit for doing what is expected of them? Instead let’s talk about something that has been slightly controversial in games: moral choice. A feature that has been popping up more and more recently, in games such as Dishonoured, Mass Effect, Infamous, The Walking Dead, et cetera. My biggest problem with the majority of moral choice systems in games is that the choices aren’t realistic enough or so obvious that you make choices to get the result you want instead of getting the result based off the choices you made. Often the choices are give an orphan a hug or murder said orphan’s cat and I realize that in 2003 and even today it probably wasn’t the easiest thing to do to make a program factor in several different choices like a choose-your-own-adventure novel. In KOTOR your moral choices are do you want to be a jedi or a sith?
Speaking of laser sword wielding samurai the whole RPG element of the game falls apart when you’re basing your game on a preexisting world meaning that the wealth of weapons, armor, and upgrades are going to go to waste since the majority of players are just going to be using lightsabers and wearing jedi robes. Sure there’s a certain amount of customization to be held there, you can use one lightsaber or two lightsabers be they normal or short or wield a Darth Maul double-ended job. Providing you have the right crystals you can change the colour of the blade and add augmentations. Of course you can always choose not to play as a jedi and go through the rigmarole of playing as the class you started out as or micromanage your party’s equipment like the weird mother who is just a little bit too involved with her children’s lives. The stats portion of all of the equipment I also find to be rather a large waste of time. Most people I know who have played KOTOR simply go into the swkotor.ini file type in EnableCheats=1 into the proper location and then in game hit the “~” key and enter the invincibility cheat.
Knights of the Old Republic is still a good game even for a Star Wars game or maybe in spite of being a Star Wars game. Of the Old Republic franchise it is my favourite and the fondness I feel towards it made me try other BioWare games with an open mind. Though playing through it this time I realized that Knights of the Old Republic can be considered a rather successful reimagining of Star Wars IV: A New Hope and in same degree the rest of the original trilogy. I think we can all agree that if you’re going to draw heavily from a Star Wars movie you might as well do it from the good ones. But seriously if you haven’t tried KOTOR yet I strongly urge that you do.

Evoland is a great example of a game that has a great concept, doesn’t know what to do with it, and then fumbles the ball at the one-yard line.

The first hour or so of Evoland is fantastic – it assaults you with nostalgia as you unlock upgrades to the game at a fast clip. Once you clear the first town, however, the flaws of the game become suffocating, and even though the game is only about three hours long, it felt like it should have only lasted for half of that.

For one thing, the randomized battles add a horrible amount of teeth-grinding fluff to the game – they appear early, and never fade away. The game’s Steam page promises fully real-time battles by the time you’ve upgraded Evoland enough, but in reality the active combat zones are few and far between. Enemy variety is very limited, and I would always try to busy myself with something else as I hammered on the “A” button during battles. There’s almost no fear of death, as your character is capable of healing and there is NO mana bar to limit the ability to do so. Enemy scaling is frustrating as well, as your character is capable of dealing damage that always seems to be about one point short of the mob’s maximum life bar, requiring multiple hits on multiple mobs for arbitrary EXP that really doesn’t seem to boost your stats in any measurable way. It’s dull and pointless.

Furthermore, the game begins to rely far too much on RPG tropes. Sure, that’s the main hook of the game, but I started to become annoyed when the main character, “Clink,” used a buster sword to fight the main villain, “Zephyros” (and guess what happened to the female protagonist, “Caris”). When I thought the story was going to deliver something at least somewhat original, or put a twist on a trope, I instead found myself wandering a field to hunt a “choboko.”

Speaking of the tropes, they don’t fully evolve the game, as I was expecting. If you get near the end of the game, after you’ve unlocked full 3D models and HD backgrounds, and you travel back to the starting village, the game automatically reverts back to SNES-era sprites. Backtracking actually becomes somewhat of an inconvenience.

In all, Evoland feels like an overpriced student game that managed to do a good job up front, when it really has no real legs to stand on. Not recommended – just watch the GiantBomb Quick Look and call it good.

I really wanted to like this game, but was ultimately disappointed with the final product as it failed to scale in size when moving up from it's humble gamejam origins.

You'll be able to see the various ways gaming has evolved while also having an enoyable gaming experience.

Enjoyed this game more than i thought i would.  Quite the throwback to many older games, almost identical to Zelda at times, although the game says it's influenced by Diablo and Final Fantasy as well, which is clearly obvious in some parts.
The game is constantly unlocking things from the history of video games suchs as upgraded graphics, sounds, names, towns, signs, movement/combat abilities, weapons, increasingly difficult puzzles, and breakable pots.
There are times when the game requires you to "go the past" where older graphic styles help you complete the game where the newwer ones dont, which is really neat.
There are some "oh come on!" moments where you're zigzagging through mazes you feel dont really need to be there, but when i think back on older games, they had those moments too so it almost felt right to have them there.
Lots of humour in the game too, some of it hard to notice though, like in the "Diablo" portion of the game, when you look in your inventory all the items you are wearing have hilarious names and abilities attatched to them.
Definately a fun game, highly recommended, i even found myself playing till i had all the achievements.  Once you beat the game there is a neat way of travel so you're not constantly stopped for combat in the open world too, which would get annoying if you're just looking for 100% completion.

The New Hotness.
I've had my eye on Blood Alloy for sometime. I've never passed on the opportunity to play it at PAX East or BostonFIG, and now I am happy to say the final product lives up to expectations. The initial tutorial is a little rough, but once the camera pulls back and the gloves come off, the game does not disappoint. You'll be dashing, slashing, running, and gunning your way through waves of enemies, with nearly reckless abandon, all while enjoying the grooves of a killer soundtrack. It's not a game that demands a lot from you and you'll be unlocking new items, levels, and music every couple rounds.
Now for the main reason why I'm posting this review: justification of cost. At $12.99, no, it's not the cheapest game ever made. It's also not the most expensive one, and I can say on good authority that the developer, Suppressive Fire, has been busting their butts for YEARS to get this game out. The results speak for themselves. It's smooth, fast, and most importantly, so far for me at least, stable. People have paid much more for games on Day 1 that can't even connect to their own servers. Blood Alloy offers a solid chunk of content with really fun gameplay for a fair price without ANY online requirements. For a game to be stable on Day 1 in 2016 shouldn't be such a shock, but it honestly is.
The game seems to be set up in such a way that if enough gamers support it, more content will follow. You may think that means waiting it out, but it's a catch 22: they can't make content unless you support it, but you don't want to support it unless they make more content. To that I say, give me a break. There's no Season Pass, there's just the game, and this is a game and a developer worth supporting. Watch this game can ramp up over time and become unstoppable. Like I said, it's a solid chunk of content built on a very solid foundation.
I would say this seems like an excellent game for streaming. With rounds being (for me at least) under 5 minutes long, and a consistent reward loop, this has the makings of a great game not only for communities to enjoy, but potentially even for competitions.
If I had any feedback, it would be that the mouse is very sensitive and is currently unresponsive in the menu; the vertical dash section of the tutorial is pretty punishing; and the menu UI could use a bit more polish and some more options like max camera distance and screenshake level, but these are HARDLY killer criticisms and the kind of stuff that can be taken care of in a patch or two. The game itself is great. G-R-E-A-T great. Pick it up and support a really cool developer who's made a really cool game.

I prefer a non spoiler review. It's a short game but you won't worry about that so much. This starts as a story driven game, which is good. Then the mechanics kick in and really draw you into the world. The idea is you are a play tester that is finishing the game thats been in dev for 20 years. . .
The favourite is the mechanics. An enemy approaches, and you capture them in your trap. Then rip out all their code (walking, hostile, teeth). Leaving a harmless little jellybean.
Then the idea is to reprogram enemies with collected attributes from other enemies. I approached the game as the sort with hundreds of attributes at the ready, so each scenario was tactically handled. There are some attribites that are difficult to consume at first due to your resources not being varied enough and your enemies being too powerful. But you eventually end up getting them. The challenge to do so was highly satisfying.
By the end I was standing on the back of a flying turtle and flying around the map with my swarm of flying machine guns. Click to direct. Done. I won't lie. I smirked a bit.

Total play time: 43 hours before I gave up in disgust.
Crashes: too many to count.
The good:
lovely graphics. (When you can see them beside the immovable overlay screens.)
The really ugly:
Worst user interface of any game I've EVER played. Confusing. Redundant. And impossible to actually FIND anything if you don't already know EXACTLY where it is.
Flight mechanics: ships in space aren't air fighters. or worse cars in mud.  Why can't SPACE simulations get this right?  If I shut off the engines, I don't just bloody stop. I keep going. But not in this game. Freelancer got it right, and it made space combat FUN. Others never seem to have learned the lesson. If I want an air-based dogfight game, I'll go get that, not a game that's theoretically based in space.
Mouse resolution seem to be hard-coded rather than depending on operating system settings, then they don't give you a means to reduce the sensitivity. So if you have a high resolution mouse, hope you like making micrometre movements to control things. Or go with a joystick, which isn't nearly as precise - and you have to be VERY precise when shooting because there's zero give.
Stupidly high learning curve, and (almost) zero tutorial. Examples:
-- In the FIRST tutorial (simulator) mission, you're told "don't forget to activate your turret" - and left with ZERO instructions on how to do that. You're on your own trying to figure out what you need. I did eventually figure it out, several hours into the game, and the answer is nowhere NEAR the weapon options panel they provide.
-- They give you a jump drive? You have to "just know" that you need lots of energy crystals for it, and where and how to get them.
-- Want to activate your jump drive? You better "just know" that it's going to make you stop in space with a big flashing "Hi, I'm a target" for a while. So although the enemy can jump as soon as they're in trouble, you trying to do so means certain death.
-- Want to buy something? Who created that interface? Wasn't anyone with any kind of user interface knowledge.
-- Want to do some trading? Well, it seems you don't have the trading interface. Except you DO have the trading interface, says so right in your ship inventory. Finally discovered that it's not the right LEVEL of trading interface, which is given a different name in the error message than it has in the inventory. Again, you just have to know.
-- The list goes on, and on, and on. Sadly, most of the online advice is written by people who HAVE that encyclopaeodic knowledge and forgot that they didn't once have it.
-- Regularly throughout the campaign you're told "meet you at XXX". Without being given ANY hints as to where it might be. Having to go to external sources just so you can actually figure out where you're supposed to next is definitely poor design.
-- Attempting to build a "factory complex" is an exercise in frustration since the positioning controls were done by someone who had never, ever used any kind of CAD program. It's what I'd expect out of a novice doing a project for a Bachelor level graphics class, and even then they probably wouldn't get a good grade. It's not something I would ever have expected out of a commercial product such as this one.
-- The list of faults goes on, and on, and on.
And, finally, the kicker: the storyline breaks. Hard. With no way to figure out how the hell to fix it. Mission 7, finding the crystals, your contact doesn't show up where they're supposed to be, which means no way to continue. Since I've spent several hours between the previous mission and this one trying to earn enough credits to get a better ship, I have NO idea where it might have gone wrong.
I might as well have started one of the "no storyline" missions, because this one is now totally hooped.
Not to mention crash after crash after crash making game (almost) unplayable. Latest one? You finish a long mission (only the 2nd or 3rd one) with zero chance of saving and... it just hangs there, staring at the piece the Talon just dropped, keyboard locked. Did I mention no chance of saving and no quick-saves so you have to repeat the whole, long, frustrating experience rather than restart from further along the mission line.  Worse, apparently there's a way to save without docking, as I was reminded by the game when it misinterpreted my "fire at the enemy" for "save this game", but I was defeated in trying to figure out where or how to purchase the necessary bits and pieces to make it possible. I'm pretty good at figuring things out usually, but this game is that obtuse.
I was REALLY looking forward to playing this game. But as it stands, it's an unplayable mash of crap that requires an encyclopaedic knowledge of the game JUST TO PLAY THE FIRST BLOODY MISSIONS!
I'm sure the game is fun for those who took the hours and hours to develop that encyclopaedic knowledge required to do even the most basic tasks in the game. For someone like me who doesn't mind some complexity, but would rather just get in and play before I'm hit with the whole enchilada, this game isn't for me. Or for anyone else who feels that it shouldn't be necessary to digest a 96 page manual, megabytes of online information, and go through several hours of online learning just to complete the first few missions.
Annoying. Very annoying.
edit: 8-Mar: yet I still intend to master this game. Yes, it's annoying in so many ways, but hopefully once I *have* acquired the required encyclopaedic knowledge (or at least a portion thereof) it gets better? Certainly has promise, I just hope it can realize that promise.
edit: 11-Mar: after trying for many hours to get this game to work, all I can say is "no, not for me". If you want a game that takes hours of research just to START the game, and many more hours of external out-of-game research to even have a hope in hell of doing anything, then you might try this game. If you want something fun, not frustrating in the extreme, and something that doesn't resemble more of an office job than a "game", stay away. Far, far away. Personally, I'm giving up in disgust.

As most of the following negative reviews of this game have already previously stated, this game even though is in stages of Early access still stands without current potential. Let me begin with the building structures, they are very confusing and expect you to build a basic nessecity by hand. This isn't the Sims! We shouldn't have to craft a restaurant or bathroom step by step. Also I heavy dislike the building mechanics, If something you placed is off by an inch then it will look dumb. The money you earn is ridiculous. It offers no challenge, you should have less money and have to earn it slowly. In JPOG your park would be shut down if you had low money. Moving forwards.
Secondly let me talk about the A.I. oh where do I begin? The human A.I. is the absolute worst, I had 20 people literally cramming into each other and not going anywhere. The dinosaur A.I. is pretty basic too, I mean it's not the worst but there are definitely rooms for improvement. They will get stuck in trees often so you need to control them to get them out. They don't move as much either.
Next are the models, now I won't complain too much about the models because I enjoy them fairly well. The dinosaur models are pretty well detailed when up close and I do find the human models to be pretty ugly. And they fade away like ghosts when you zoom out of your park, that applies to other objects as well.
Some things I thoroughly enjoy such as the world map, which is a very detailed globe where you can either send a dig site or buy from the black market. One complain I have is that its so easy to obtain a dinosaur. In JPOG you had to buy individual dinosaur DNA to increase the lifespan as well as creation. In Mesozoica, you just buy one skin per dino and you instantlly have it available. This offers no challenge at all and I hope they change it.
Next are the sounds, now you won't hear much from a dinosaur unless you control them. So far in my playing, humans have no sound either. I'd like to hear the sounds of a mighty roar from a T.rex or the hooting of a parasaurolophus. That's just my idea.
Also this game is lacking basic species such as triceratops and spinosaurus, hopefully they will be included in the next update.
Then we have the lack of terraforming. Oh boy where do I begin with this one? Every basic simulation game includes terraforming such as making lakes, rivers, mountains and I could go on. The most you can do is make a bunch of trees and rocks and all must be placed individualy. And let's say I really want a forest. That means I have to place hundreds of trees down individualy and man! Does that hurt my fingers needing to click each and every one. There needs to be an option to place multiple pieces of foliage.
My final conclusion is that this game is rather boring after the first 15-20 minutes, there is easily room for improvement. And don't even get me started on the countless bugs I have discovered in this game within minutes of starting it. I recomend waiting for improvement, or better yet wait for two other dinosaur park simulation games coming out called Prehistoric Kingdom and then there is Jurassic:World Evolution.

Certain sound effects, such as the Tarbosaurus' biting noise, also suffer from this (hurt my ears when I heard it, and I had lowered the volume). Similiar negliance goes all the way down to the details with spelling and grammar errors.The UI feels like a level editor and is confusing to navigate. There is no collision with objects (objects can be placed on top of each other, or sideways on fences). Dinosaur AI is minimal at best. Gameplay is nearly nonexistant and I spent much of my time openning boxes at the black market. The modular system is a pain; I don't understand why this system was implemented with few premade buildings (as shown in concept art). I don't object to the idea of modular building entirely, but at this point it is more a chore than a fun addition. It makes me wonder what all the delays were for, and what they were accomplishing, when frankly the demo from months ago was at about the same place as the current product. At this point, one of the only redeeming factors is that some of the skins look nice (there is a clear discrepancy between artists).
I would not recommend buying this game at this point. It's possible that it may improve in the future (which I hope it does), but at this point all it has is potential.
(Will update review in future if/when major patches occur)

Unfortunately, I cannot recommend this game, and it really sucks to say that because I had a lot of anticipation and good thoughts for Mesozoica. Yes, I have played less than an hour of the game, however in that 0.7 hours of gameplay I find the game to be extremely limiting in terms of goals and flow. After I figured out the controls (more on that soon), I went on to building enclosures, paths, and even attempted to build several of my own structures. As exciting as I found that to be I cannot, at this point, really finding anything more than sitting there and doing some designing and watching the dinosaurs walk around. This game was billed as a "next generation tycoon simulator" akin to games such as (the obvious one) Jurassic Park: Operation Genesis, Cities Skylines, and the Roller Coaster Tycoon series. However, I feel that Mesozoica lacks almost every bit of what makes those games what they are and why they are so fun to play...goals, management of the park, overseeing security for park guests, financial benefits and consequences, ability to upgrade equipment for the dinosaurs and park itself. If I remember correctly, early on the developers had three different companies for the player to choose from, each with their own pros and cons and would affect how the player would make decisions. What has happened to that? I'm not sure, but it is not shown on the Mesozoica website nor the Steam page.
Mesozoica also lacks a tutorial mode so the player is left to fend for themselves as far as what the controls are, what is in the user interface, and just having a poor guide in the "Help" box. Because of the lack of a tutorial, I found myself really having to spend time just troubleshooting my way through before actually beginning to play the game. I really hope that the developers take note of this as I am not the only one who finds this annoying and a detriment towards the overall game.
I completely understand that this game has taken a lot of time, effort, and money to be made and that it is in Early Access. Maybe at a later time when the game is at full release and more positive feedback is coming out I will give it another shot, because I had such high anticipation and good thoughts about this game. However, with that being said, for the price that the developers want and the fact the negatives far outweigh the positives at this point, I simply cannot recommend this game to anyone until major adjustments are made.

I bought this game for £1.74 in a random Steam Sale a few years ago. That means, at the time of writing this, I've spent £0.00125 an hour playing Awesomenauts (halp me!).
It has it's flaws, but I love it.
Pros:
- It's a 2D MOBA so the platforming adds an extra spin on the genre, giving you variations in characters with vertical movement, and a mix of map designs.
- Great mix of characters to play (27 as of the review, 8 of which are through DLC/Expansions)
- The art design is reminiscent of an 80's/90's Saturday morning cartoon and looks polished. The art team are gradually improving the early sprites animations, but some of the latest ones are incredible.
- Voice acting and music is awesome(nauts) with a good sense of humour that fits the idea of the game perfectly.
- The devs have updated the game with new features since launch (Custom Games, Replays, Spectator Mode), but this can take a painful amount of time to release.
- The Devs are active in all social media, forums and message boards, including dev streams and weekly dev updates on Twitch (even giving away rare skins and copies of the game to give to friends). So they are connected with their players.
- It's always no more than £6.99, which can give you the best value for money or £/hr if you like it.
Cons:
- Currently low playerbase. It's been gradually dwindling for the past year, but hopefully this will change if they can keep up with the content but much faster. This can also lead to strange matchups with players with various skills in different leaderboard positions facing each other (this is changing slightly with the new 3.3 update).
- No dedicated servers, so P2P online play, can make games frustrating against players in other countries the other side of the world. This was slightly improved with the new 3.3 matchmaking update, but is still present.
- Considering it's a 2D MOBA, there needs to be more maps (currently 5, but the latest one was the newest in 2 years). A way around this would be a custom level editor with Steam Workshop support.
- The devs try to tackle balancing the characters in the game all the time (even classic original heros), which I know can be tricky but is frustrating to keep on top of.

It's with real regret that I cannot recommend this game as I do really enjoy some aspects of it.
The problems for me though are too great to ignore and there are a few of them.
1. The game hard crashes on me once every 5-6 hours or so despite my machine easily meeting the minimum hardware requirements. Each time it has happened I've lost the progress that was made not only in terms of the results, but more importantly the tactical tweaks. It's very hard to recover any momemtun when you return to a tactical setup that you've already tweaked with succsess, not knowing exactly what it was that was changed to improve.
2. The man management aspect is too frequant and incredibly tedious. I understand that this is most of what good management is about but it's really not fun. Players will be constantly complaining about not being involved when not selected, which is fine but you then have to choose a generic response that provides a binary outcome. The press conferences and tunnel talks are so unbearable I end up turning them off. The talk of the main new feature for 2018 being more man management is already enough for me to know that I won't be purchasing it.
3. The 3D match engine is now where most of the development work seems to be occuring however, currently it is a very bad way to read the game. Overall the engine is very impressive and can be great fun but when my full back scored three belting free kicks in the same game it suggests that there is just not enough variety in the outcomes at this stage to make it worthwhile. It's actually better to analyse the game in play without the 3D engine, then watch the highlights once the game is over.
I do have more problems with the game however I should state that this is definalty not a bad game and it can be fun. It's just such a shame that most of the new features added each year more and more seem to be the parts of the game I end up turning off.
Somewhere in there is the game I want to play but it's buried under so much tedium it's really hard to actually say that I enjoy myself whilst playing.

This game sat on my wishlist for a year or so after I first played the demo, and after finally getting to play it, I am very satisfied. The Magic Circle might not be very long (I have about 4 hours of playtime on record to finish), or mind-blowing in any way, but it is, in fact, incredibly unique. The mechanics are interesting, the story was good, and there was even some puzzles in there that I didn't really expect.
Pros:
+ The story. This is a game about game devs working on a twenty-year long video game project with an "auteur" who won't allow his "vision" to get tampered with by his former pro-gamer coworker and their spunky intern. You are a playtester who starts mucking around in the code and...
+ The mechanics: ...bringing back formerly "deleted" enemies and scenery and stealing attributes like fire attacks, and adding yourself to its list of allies. I made a mushroom hop around and a key breathe fire. By the end, I had a horde of allies following me around and fighting my battles.
+ Meta-humor. Tons of references about game development hell, with things like a DOOM-esque sci-fi area that you can explore (complete with pixely goodness) from an abandoned version of the game, game devs arguing about how the player can beat the final battle without a sword, storyboards and sketches, notes from the devs about unfinished levels, etc.
+ Puzzles. There was definitely more of a puzzle aspect than I suspected after playing the demo! Pleasant surprise!
+ Secrets to find. Hidden bits of story, upgrades for your minions.
Neutral:
~ There are basically two sections to the game: 1) A big open, interconnected world with lots of different areas and unlockable upgrades, story points, enemies to edit or fight. This was the main game and it was incredibly fun, but then... 2) There's a "level designer" bit, where you have to design a level with a good difficulty level and interest curve for another character to play through in order to finish the story. This was not quite as fun for me because it felt tedious, and a definite shift in the game's mechanics. You could still edit enemies, but there wasn't any skill to it. Basically, you set up the level, have the character playtest it, then debug it so it doesn't kill or bore him.
Cons:
- Length. I could have done with a little longer gameplay, more areas to explore and more baddies. Overall, I was pretty satisfied with my play experience, but for some people (especially at full price), it might feel too short.
Overall: Very fun and unique, interesting mechanics. 9/10.

Where to begin with this game?  The long and short of it is that this is a sad conclusion to more than two years of waiting.  While I personally missed the Kickstarter in 2015, I began following only a couple short months after this campaign ended.
First off, let me say that the game is definitely pretty detailed which helps to explain why the images that are posted to the Steam page look pretty stunning.  In addition, I love the realistic globe which is used as the fossil hunting map.  And the ability to control the dinosaurs in the game is a nice concept as well.
With these positives being recognized, there is not much else going for this game.  First off, as many others have said, there is no tutorial at this time.  You are just thrown into the game and there is a lot that this game does that makes no sense.  For example, you have to go to something called core blocks to be able to select a hatchery rather than just being able to click on it.  While I am not opposed to the core block system, it makes literally no sense to not be able to click on the structure as well.  There is also the fact that it is difficult to find the exit menu.  I clicked the escape button multiple times and was unable to bring it up.
The next thing I would like to mention is the number of dinosaurs that are in this version is shockingly low.  As of this writing, there were only about 19 different types of dinosaurs.  This is pretty insane considering there was a time that they promised somewhere around 90 different types of animals, which was later scaled down to 40.  They implied that these 40 would be there at release but alas they are not.
While on the topic of animals, I will also mention that the animal AI is pretty basic.  There is still a lot that they cannot do and they just do not feel as if they are alive.  Even the dinosaurs in JPOG felt more alive than the dinosaurs in Mesozoica.  Add to this that the visitors also feel pretty fake and the models for the visitors are pretty horrendous.  Overall, the AI still needs a massive amount of work.
Adding to these issues, the building system is really odd.  It is basically a poor knockoff of Planet Coaster.  Except in this game, you have to literally design everything yourself practically and there are many really weird objects that are available for use.  While they are trying to get people to create stuff to upload, I think it's pretty sad that a lot of this was not already done.
Also, to go back to a previous point about things not feeling alive, another problem with the game is everything feels incredibly empty.  The rather small map literally has nothing but grass.  No rivers, hills, trees, nothing.  There are mountains but they are outside of the bounds of the map.  So everything looks really weird.  In addition to this, there is very little in the way of park management.  They say they are going to work on this, but it is pretty sad right now.
I could honestly go on and on but I think this is a pretty good summary of many of the major issues that this game has presently.  The larger point I am making is that these developers have been issuing delay after delay for the better part of two years and this is the embarrassing product that they have given us.  This is bad even for early accesss.  While this game may get better over time, it is an incredible distance from being a good game, let alone a sucessor to JPOG.  I would also take many of the positive reviews with a huge grain of salt.  Many of the fans of the game have a rabidly blind loyalty to the game and would likely have given this game a positive review no matter what.  My personal reccomendation is to wait for a few months.  Or, better yet, wait for the Early Access of Prehistoric Kingdom which is planning to launch in November.  Their demo right now is worlds better than this game.
And, just to end this review, I just want to say that, on a personal level, I find all of this to be deeply disappointing.  I have been waiting all this time anxiously hoping the developers would prove me wrong and release something truly incredible, but, once again, they have failed and that is a true tragedy in my books.

In short:
If you like a nice action game with beautiful cinematic presentation and a good (but not over-the-top) story, pick this one up, especially in a sale.
Detailed review:
"Ryse: Son of Rome" is a third person action game set in ancient Rome. You follow the story of Marius, a roman legionnaire, whose loyalty to Rome and a personal vendetta lead him into battle against the barbarians of Britannia.
Although the tale of Marius certainly isn't the feat of a literary genius, it is entertaining and serves its purpose of providing the foundation for a nice game, aimed at presentation.
And that is, where its greatest strength is lying. The graphics are beautiful, most sceneries are stunning and detailed, and I especially liked the cutscenes. When in a dialouge, the expression on people's faces are very nicely done, and although the main protagonists are quite the stereotypes (which suits the - a bit cliché - story), the voice-over actors did a terriffic job in my eyes (or better, ears).
The game's mechanics are simple and easy to learn, yet fighting without getting hit isn't as easy to master. Gameplay ist pretty repetitive (fighting in an area, moving on, fighting in the next area, moving on, moving on in formation, fighting and so forth...), but presentation makes all but up for it, especially the upgradeable QTE executions. Slashing through barbarian hordes while Rome is under siege is pretty impressive - and after all, I came here to slice barbarians by the hundreds.
On the other hand, that's also a bit of a downer: you have no other enemies than barbarians. At the end, you fight some rogue Romans, but they are essentially barbarians in armor. Not even the "bosses" are that hard to fight either.
It took me about 6 hours to finish the story mode in a leisurely pace, I have not yet tried the gladiator multiplayer.
While playing, I only encountered bugs three times: twice i fell through the floor when moving to another area and died , which forced me to reload (autosave points are fairly frequent), and once the aiming aid in a shooting sequence didn't seem to work (aiming fast and accurately without is quite hard on gamepad), so i switched to mouse for this sequence (the on screen button displays change instantly with the source of the input!).
To sum this up: if you like to watch movies like "Gladiator" or "Ben Hur" for their setting, or "Die Hard" for its action, and not its unexpected, Nobel Prize winning story, then this is the game for you. Especially on sale, probably also for its normal 20 bucks.

It was a fun game, had a lot of references to older games (and I do mean, a lot.) The design of the game was great, from the combat to the art styles through the ages. In the later game, a time traveling segment was a great puzzle, and switching from 2D to 3D just added so much more.
However, I would do yourself a favor and wait for it to go on sale.
I'm unsure if the creator(s) of this game were making an homage or a parody. In a genre that is so filled with tropes and cliches, I'm farily dissapointed that this game went off the way that it did. Most of the humor in the game is not subtle; extremely so at times. For example, the card game, an obvious reference to Triple Triad, was named Double Twin. Hah. I get it.
Also, the side character with the name Kaeris? Yep. Exactly what you're thinking if you've ever played FF7. The different genres of the games are more or less brushed past within the first hour of gameplay; you go through adding sound and color, and then blaze quickly through a 2D RPG into a 3D one. The rendered backgrounds are only in their retro state for a minute or so, before you get the chest to make the graphics more HD. After that point, the game doesn't change outside of a small Diablo style area, and a final boss that I was completely unprepared for since the gameplay mechanics hadn't been shown in the game until that point.
There is a sudden rush of story, and then the rest of it is given through brief exposition by the villian. Beating him, you are treated to a blade runner line drop, and then credits. I honestly feel if the bulk of the concept was done for a 48 hour challange, then the creator(s) could have done a lot more with what they had, but it still feels like a rushed game.
I had fun playing the game; I'll be honest, I enjoyed it a lot. But in the end, I still dropped ten bucks on a game for the privilage of playing it once and then never playing it again. And the sad part is, that with as extensive as the RPG genre has gotten over so many years, this game could easily have been worth much, much more.
All in all, if you see the game on sale, or don't mind dropping ten bucks on a one-off game, go for it. It's worth a playthrough, but don't be surprised if it makes you wonder what it could have been.

Evoland is an Action RPG that takes the player through the history of gaming in a thoroughly humorous and nostalgic experience. Unlike most RPGs, the game is focused less on character development and leveling up and more as a humorous experience designed to bring a smile to the faces of veteran players as they progress through the various ages of the RPG, taking in the sights and bringing up fond memories. Packed to the brim with endless references, it’s clear from the start that Evoland was made with the utmost love for games of time gone by and provides an authentic experience throughout.
Evoland is a game with a lot of charm, not least due to its sincere parodies of aspects such as the linearity of open world games like Final Fantasy, complete with a suspiciously named substitute called “Kaeris”, who specializes in magic asks our hero (and the player) politely to help her save her town.  Of course the player is forced to agree as to set into motion the events of the game. The humor makes sure that the player knows that this is clearly a game made from the heart and not once do the references feel forced or contrived. What will appeal most to gamers are the faithful replications of games like Final Fantasy and Zelda. Beginning the game with nothing more than the ability to move right and with Gameboy era graphics, the player soon, “unlocks” features such as SFX, 3D graphics and HD textures which are used uniquely as an aspect of the gameplay, becoming more advanced as the player progresses through the game. It’s hard not to raise a smile when switching from 2D to 3D within a matter of seconds and such use of visuals and sound is nothing if not innovative, helping to immerse the player into a game that reads like a history book of the gaming industry.
That’s not to say that the game is perfect by any means, as there are several flaws that stick out as surprising, considering the obvious care to detail within the game. Factors like the lack of a sprint unlock came as a surprise considering just how expected it is in line with the other unlocks, and in certain parts of the game, it comes across as a very much needed feature which lack of inclusion can only serve to puzzle players. The switch to Diablo-like gameplay for a dungeon is very much less polished than the rest of the game and it’s not rare to find yourself shouting out in frustration as you try to adapt to gameplay so clearly not replicated to the high standards of the battle systems for the Final Fantasy and Zelda sections. That’s not to say it’s bad by any means, but the high standards laid down previously by the game serve only to emphasize just how annoying it is to have to deal with the clunky controls that are introduced and the dungeon will have players pulling their hair out in frustration as they die many a death trying to come to terms with the controls.
The balance of the game also works against it as the various unlocks, arguably the most intriguing parts of the game, are largely completed within the first third. It’s hard not to feel that they should’ve been spread out further throughout the game, as you find yourself wanting to spend more time immersed within the 2D world, which is soon eliminated to make way for 3D, proceeding to make up the bulk of the rest of the game. That’s not to say the 3D sections are any less impressive, it’s just the enjoyment of the game as an interactive history of gaming is over all too quickly and leaves the player crying out for more. Such weighting to the first third of the game can also be seen in its references, which gradually decrease as the game goes on. Early in the game everything the player interacts with has a witty remark or object leading to several genuine laugh out loud moments whereas the latter stages lack interactivity leading to a loss in the charm that the game possesses as the game becomes an almost straightforward RPG.
Evoland is a unique game in that it’s impressive to see the scale of references and care to detail that is present within it. Despite several surprising flaws, it’s not often in a game where one can relive some of the greatest game-playing experiences from Final Fantasy and Zelda in a couple of hours and the combination of the two games is almost seamless in their execution. Nothing less than a love letter to the games of yesteryear, Evoland will delight players both old and new as it takes them on a journey of nostalgia through a loving send up of the best games of years past.

I found something very troubling about this game.
This game is supposed to be a SIMMULATOR, but it's not quite. One would expect that a main feature of the game would be that if u play with tactics, you can get a more favourable result. Wrong: whatever you do with your tactics, outcome is pre-established. This is a ruination of the game experience.
Why I say this? After a lot of play I got it to the perfect condition to demonstrate this.
SCENARIO: I am in the first 5 positions in april, the opposite team is AI controlled sitting on 20th place, very bad morale, very bad players. One would expect to crush them.
Now, how the simulation actually goes: you lose. you load the game wondering why? So you start tweaking tactics to understand how game works. Initially you use the 3 tactics your team is 100% familiar with. You fail. Then you let assistant play with his tactic. He fails. Then you start playing a lot with tactics during the game. you fail. You loaded and tried a lot of stuff to beat a very bad team. Result was already established, nothing you can do.
Conclusion: this is not a simulator as we would expect it to be, tactics to matter a lot, Game is configured to react differently, I don't yet know how, but I am dissapointed to know that my tactical play doesn't matter.

The Magic Circle is a first-person exploration/puzzle game. It's unique to me for a few reasons:
1) The premise of the game is subverting an in-game game. But the path isn't linear or obvious - one of my favorite moments is when a character says they won't help you so you can come up with your own creative sabotage.
2) There's a pretty rich story. Sometimes it distracted from the gameplay, but the characters are strong and you get to know them well.
3) They got the talented Stephen Russell as a primary voice actor (the gravely voice in the trailer). He's a fan-favorite from Thief 1 & 2, Skyrim, Fallout 4, and others. His performance was excellent, and I found myself playing past the ending to find more of his dialgoue. Ken Levine also has a cameo role, and it's pretty cool that they got these two in the same game.
The premise and gameplay of The Magic Circle are fresh and creative. Give it a go!

First and obvious question - is this a demo for money?
After playing it, I don't think so anymore. It does not feel, like a cut out part of something bigger.
What it actually is - not a demo, but a whole game. Not small, but rather compact.
Which, I find, is a good thing, when done properly. For example, if you have only 1-2 hours a day of free time, you can play this and even complete a mission or two, and not leave it for later.
It has a lot of stuff to do and different ways to do it. And not just stealth vs agression. Different ways within those two. Or even both at same time. And if you are trying to get that S rank on all missions or even 100% completion it will take time. Especially if you, like me, like to do things your way.
For me it took more than 40 hours to get 100%. Sure I saw some guides here and they were words of wisdom for me, but because game is going in real time and some random stuff happens, I rarely can recreate exactly what is showed in that video, for example, and just doing it differently becomes easier option.
The game has a good story and interesting ways of presenting it - through usual cinematics, through dialogues of passing soldiers; just some things, that happen before your eyes and tapes that you find on your missions. From bits and pieces, everything is coming together and creates a whole world.
Also it means that, basicly, you get as much lore and exposition as you want.
You keep playing, keep listening, keep watching and it all comes together in your head.
The story itself is rather mature and definitely deserves its M rating (minor spoiler:
). But, in the same time, there are places for some comic relief and goofaround. And, of course, some famous trademarked Kojima BS. It always been a part of Metal Gear Solid games, which is great.
By the way, absolutely no knowledge of previous games are required to understand what is going on. Game provides tons of information on that topic. There is a backstory in text form, and tapes, where you can listen what happened in Peace Walker game, after which things happen in this one.
Things, that annoyed me in this game, were technical ones.
This game uses resourse management technology called streaming (google it, if you want; gamespot's @lucyjamesgames made a reality check video about that stuff). Obviously, it is a modern game, with modern graphics and technology under the hood of that Fox Engine.
But sometimes, it shows itself in most infuriating ways.
If you played GTA3 , for example, there was a typical situation: you stand on a road, look one side - see a car - thinking "ok, that's good, what's on the another side?" - look around - "no, that previous was better" - you turn back - there is no more car - it just dumped from memory, because you wasn't watching it.
Same crap here - you tranquilise a soldier, lay him down and go for some business. Come back - he disappeared. You think "wtf?", look around, walk around for some time, look another way, then coming back - Bam! - he is here, where you left him, lying - loaded. But, at the same time, some another sleeping dude, somewhere else, probably disappeared. And it keeps happening. OMG.
Sometimes it is just gamebreaking.
Or, another example, you waiting for a dude to pass by, looking through binoculars in another direction - turning back to check if he is passed - Nope! - he unloaded when you turned away - now he is loading back on same spot you left him fifteen seconds ago and starts walking again. Sometimes you just have to watch somebody through your binoculars, through walls and obstacles (yes, you can) constantly, so they actually keep on moving. Yeeeah.
Another technical problem, for me personally, is FOV.
It's console (75 degrees, apparently, by default) and it cannot be changed by game options. I saw some modding can be done to change that, but if you don't want to mess with game files, or just don't want to do it for another reason - you have to adapt, either way.
To conclude - the game is good - worth your money (on sale - definetly). More importantly - worth your time.
PS: not a typical review, but just my thoughts, that became words, after I finished a game.

Sorry to kick a man while he's down or however the saying goes, but I really can't recommend this game now, EA or not. I'm basically repeating what everyone else said. I had actually forgot the game was still being developed until I got a random email a year later where they acknowledged how overdue they were. Did I mention the developers like ignoring genuine relevant questions from their own playerbase? Get used to that.
So nonetheless, I get my key from them and I try to be optimistic and what I gather as positives are:
-Dinosaur models are great, the skins are nice and diverse. I'm really ok with the what some will view as a limited dinosaur choice IF everything else would have been better.
-World map is a cool concept
-On it's lowest setting I feel in time this could be a rare toaster friendly game to those with lowers specs which is a nice audience to cater to since it's usually overlooked by many developers now'a'days.
But everything else is garbage. Just going to bullet point them for reading sake.
-That building interface is ridiculously awkward.
-No significant buildings (yet) other than some barebones ones such as Hatchers etc.
-Not even a tutorial from the get go?
-AI is clumsy as hell. I do mean really clumsy. Tyrannosaurs getting chased by herbivores, Baryonyx just chilling right in the corner of a fence and getting stuck. I'd put this down to bugs, but no part of the AI is enjoyable so far to me.
Final thoughts: Maybe Jurassic World Evolution scared the crap out of you all and forced you to release your game early (which in turn is already overdue), but what you've just released is what i'd consider a 2.0 version of your Demo. And to launch it at a base price of €30 (regardless of it's 10% off) when the game is barely passable to be called an EA game with the amount of time you've had to develop it in my opinion is utterly selfish.
Of course people can try it out for themselves, but money doesn't grow on trees and for that god awful price tag I wouldn't expect anyone to pay that. To anyone who was excited and may be disheartened by these negative reviews, stay optimistic but if possible be patient. As a backer waiting for this for a very long time however, i've completely run out of patience. They have a lot of work to do but this game has plenty of potential to turn things around.

If a MOBA and a brawler had a baby, this would be it. It's absolute non-stop fun.
You can get really good at it if you learn how to read your opponents and have good timing, or you can just have fun getting your butt kicked like I do. Personally, I think Awesomenauts has something for everyone: hardcore MOBA fans, or filthy casuals like me. Awesomenauts is extremely easy to play, but hard to master.
Graphics are stellar, the game has a really nice aesthetic to it that's not too cartoony or too serious.
The only problem with the game is lack of players, which can make finding two perfectly balanced teams hard, but Ronimo makes it work, especially with the new matchmaking update.
And speaking of the devs, they're awesome. Ronimo is extremely engaged with the community in a way not seen in the vast majority of games. You've got player-imained and player-created content like new nauts and skins, new bot AI, etc. all being implemented by Ronimo. They're very active on the official forums as well as /r/awesomenauts, and are very fast to respond to support emails be it regarding a game issue or issue with a toxic player. They're super dedicated, delivering updates and tweaks still very often.
If you've never played it before, at least give it a try! It's an amazing game that's still constantly evolving even years after it's release. But be warned! It's extremely addictive, you probably won't ever want to leave.

It's an okay game - a great tech-demo of the Xbone's technical skills as a console - but man, it gets tedious with its gameplay. There's only so many times I can execute the same 3-4 enemies with the same 5-7 executions (double executions, while adding another 2-3, are difficult to pull off thanks to the consolitis aspect of "the game wants to magnetically attract you to attacking the same enemy" which means that you'll likely accidentally slaughter the guy you were trying to weaken, in order to do a double execution) without getting bored. That can sum up my irritation with the game - the enemies are tedious, repetitive, and boring, and the executions are the same. The combat itself LOOKS beautiful - like a movie - but it's just dull.
However, the game is absolutely beautiful. I don't know if I've ever seen better facial animations in a video game. The cutscenes are pre-rendered video files, locked to 60fps for smoothness (which explains why the game download is like, 50GB in size) which is obnoxious if you have a super-powerful computer, but it does make the cutscenes look amazing 99% of the time (1% is pixelation motion blur in the video file).
The story is average - a bit predictable at some points (hello parents) and in other times, haunting and sad. Your final boss, for example, is really someone who I wished you formed an alliance with. And indeed, I was surprised when the game didn't go that way.
All in all, I still recommend it. But I wouldn't pay more than $10 for it, when it goes on sale. It's a beautiful tech demo with an "average" story, but the gameplay is dull enough that you might not make it to the end.

Nothing sets a new space game of possibilities like X3: Reunion. An improved version of X2: The Threat, it gains its repetition in its ability to specify AI behaviour to an even further level. In other words, X3: Reunion starts the chain of allowing players to automate their universe, letting the robots and humans do the work for you. It certainly is an upgrade to X2, especially with the types of ships and mechanics. Some of the music is directly imported from the original games, but some new ones are very attuning, especially when coupled with the stunning graphics of planets, environment, etc.
However, the other parts of the game were not as well done. The plot contains scenes that aren't exactly do-able until you retry, and sometimes forces you to improve upon your ship or amount of money just to continue. Not only that, the big complexity of mechanics, removed core stations that were essential to sustain the game economy in previous games, and the unfamiliar controls of ships (especially with the lack of a cockpit) makes this game almost unsuitable for any new players without previous experience with previous X games. Comparable to X:BTF, but even worse, on things that Egosoft could have easily improved upon.
Overall, this game is certainly a good game, for those whom have already understood the core gameplay. However, it's just not newbie-friendly, the learning curve is much too high for anyone with high patience to overcome by just playing this game, and even for people who have played all previous games still struggle to develop the edge needed to enjoy anything. As such, it rewards veterans with a sense of complexity, but starting out with X2 first is more than recommended to start advancing towards the ever-complicated X3 Series titles.

Let me start by saying that I really love this game.  It's one of the coolest games I've ever played. You can be whoever you want (within reason) in this beautiful universe.  You can be an industry mogul, managing your company on a galactic scale.  You can be a cop, hunting down bad guys for money.  You can flip that coin and be one of the bad guys, a pirate, making your living by preying on defenseless ships.  You can be a freighter pilot, transporting wares from point A to point B for profit.  You can even be a fleet commander (after you've been playing for awhile), leading enormous space battles and snapping screenshots like a lunatic.  And that's just the beginning, it's set in a living world, where every ship you see is just like you, actually doing something and going somewhere in this massive galaxy and contributing to the intricate, supply and demand based economy.  Be that as it may, it's not for everyone.  If you have a lack of patience, a desire to build a huge empire right off the bat, or you like epic space battles from the word go, then do not buy this game.  If, however, you want to feel like you accomplished something when you do get those things, you want unlimited freedom in space, and you have a RIDICULOUS amount of spare time on your hands, then you will enjoy this.  If you are a busy person with lots of important stuff to do, you probably won't have time to do much in X3: Reunion.  If you are like me, and you have no life, X3: Reunion is the game for you.
The Pros:
+Infinite freedom in space.
+Beautiful graphics that have aged really well (the game was made in 2005).
+Wide variety of ships.
+You can drop in and out of the plot any time you like.
+Realistic economy based on supply and demand.
+Build your own space stations to further populate the universe.
+Be the space trucker of your dreams.
+Buy and sell space drugs.
+Buy and sell space moonshine.
+Buy and sell other goods in a black market as large as the legit one.
+Persistent reputation that affects how you will be received by the locals.
+Trade, fight, cheat, and steal your way to the top.
The Cons:
-REEEEALLY steep learning curve, as the game comes with no tutorial.
-Boring plot, but it really doesn't matter because if you are playing an X game for the plot, you're playing for the wrong reasons.
-Starts off unbearably slow (picks up pace later).
-Atrocious voice acting (makes for a good laugh now and again).
-Confusing jargon (a jazura is a year, I think a mezura is a month, but I don't know for sure).
-Terrible writing, bad puns, etc.
-Your autopilot WANTS TO KILL YOU.
-This game is highly addictive, and you will probably lose friends over it.
In conclusion, X3: Reunion is one of the best games I've ever played, and I will probably never sleep again.  My social life as I know it is over.  It's an absolutely fantastic game, but don't take my word for it, play it yourself and make your own opinion about it.

Did you play RPGs on the NES? SNES? Playstation 1? Then you will most likely enjoy Evoland. It's a charming adventure that will make you chuckle, smile and fondly remember the eras of past gaming - although if you never experienced them or weren't alive when these eras happened I imagine you won't be having much besides a blank stare throughout the entire thing. Thats the biggest point I can make - unless you have experienced these video game eras first hand, the humor and charm will seem nonexistant. If you buy it and expect to be taught a RPG history lesson you will be disappointed.
You play as the standard everyhero named Clink - an obvious amalgamation of Link and Cloud - the everyheroes of FF7 and Pre-OoT Zelda games. The main thing you'll be doing is finding technology upgrades that will advance the tech from black and white to color, from 8bit to 16bit, adding save points, health meters and much more.
Halfway through the game the tech advances appear less and less and it becomes more of a simple action AND turn-based RPG. But even in these later sections there are some interesting uses of switching between 8bit and 3D render modes to complete puzzles. It's nothing too difficult but overall a clever way of making challenges. My personal favorite area was the "Diablo-clone, action RPG" stage complete with ridiculous loot drops. It's also the only area you can play as Kaeris(I wonder who shes based off of? /endsarcasm)
The story portion of the game only takes a few hours but there are some collectibles you can search for to extend your play time like Stars or Cards that you can use for the bonus card mini-game(more or less identical to FF8's Triple Triad). The game also has some pretty nice artwork and music - I've found myself humming tunes from the game long after completing it. Heck, I even payed for the soundtrack.
I personally enjoyed this game and I got exactly what I thought I'd get by reading the tagline - a short story about the evolution of RPGs. That said considering the short length and the simplicity of the second half, $10 is a bit steep. Buy it on sale if you can.

Worth a look, but I won't blame you if you give up after the first splendid couple of hours.

What can one say about Chowderchu? Does the Chowder make the chu or does the chu make the chowder? This game does not answer those questions, but it makes one think about the nature of things. And the nature of things is insanity. The definition of insanity, as per someone somewhere, is doing the same thing over and over again expecting a different result. I know this now, I have stared into the face of insanity and everything I knew about the world was shattered. When the pieces were put back together like a haphazard puzzle missing a few pieces, it was the face of a little wizard by the name of chowderchu.
The game plays like sisyphus on a healthy dose of DMT. Yet like sisyphus, you go on and on and you click the mouse over and over again and overtime you realize that these actions have meaning. Sisyphus may be considered a figure that has been punished in the cruelest way possible, yet to a person that understands the Chowderchu, they know that he has been given a task and while the task may never be complete - that task gives meaning. I feel strongly that Chowderchu is the same way, though I assume there is an actual ending somewhere. Seriously though, play this game and experience it first hand, you owe it to yourself and to your future clone.

This is definitely not what I was expecting.  As far as I've seen, there are no dragons like those in the pictures.  Each game lasts about 30 minutes, I think, and is extremely fast-paced.  You do not pick your engrams, you start with all of them.  Saddles are also not required, all tames are automatically equipped.  The crafting is also different, for example you don't need spoiled meat to make narcotics anymore.  Gathering and xp is also, as expected, insainely buffed.  You'll constantly hear the levelup noise and a few seconds of gathering on plants will give you a ton of fiber to deal with.  Most people seem to end up with a rex and couple mammoths when the end-game comes along, at which time it slowly closes, forcing players into the center.
I wanted to see more normalized gameplay, where you have to strategize to actually get kills and survive.  This has no real strategies, just a couple template builds you can find online.  The map is very limited in size so there's nowhere to really hide, plus the many 'drops' that occur will always spawn way above each player.  So if there's a mammoth drop (yea, seriously, 4 mammoths fall from the sky for no apparent reason lol), you'll easily see where everyone is.  It's too redundant for me and after a few games I found it quite boring.
Now if it were up to me, I'd make this thing the full map size, a few hours duration, and taming/xp/gathering to be set alot closer to normal, maybe 3x.

Dragon's Lair is a well known game glorified into what we would call a quick time event simulation.  It appeals to nostalgia thanks to the animation style and it's fame.  While I do recommend this game, there are a few precautions to point out.
Understand that this is literally QTE: The Video Game.  This isn't a bad thing pointing this out, as the animation is humorous as well as the various ways Dirk can fail.  You can literally watch the game on Youtube, and it is not long at all once you know the button inputs for each sequence (12 minutes or so).  There is no controller support, so you are stuck to using your keyboard arrow keys and spacebar.  This isn't honestly that bad, but one cannot try to use an arcade stick to relive the feeling of using that kind of controller if they wished.  Despite the 720HD upscaling, it is dated looking but I am not surprised given the age of the animation.  I understood what I was buying, and I bought this and Dragons Lair II at $4.99 each.  I knew exactly what I was buying as well, so I have no regrets about this purchase.
Dragon's Lair has been released on tons of platforms, but there isn't anything particularly special about the steam port vs others.  There are two slightly different modes and two difficulties to choose from, so the game can be replayed a few times before you will probably be done with it for a while.  You can also turn on and off hint prompts that tell you what button to press at the right time to make the game easier or harder.  Just know what you are buying, and that what you see in the steam trailer is pretty much what you get.

I am a FM17 addict, and so can you.
One of the main reasons for all of the hate towards FM17 this year is that the match engine has become really well balanced after SI developers closed off "exploits" from previous editions.
Now managers have to build a tactical system from the ground up and plug any holes they see along the way. It's a thrilling experience that is one of the least forgiving, yet most satisfying out of any video game I have played in quite some time.
In previous editions, like FM15 for instance, one's poor tactical setup could be bailed out by the long throw exploit that would achieve wins for managers who's setup never warranted it.  Or in FM16 where the short pass out of the corner kick created havock for the opposition, and therefor covered over any glaring holes in the manager's tactic.
These editions allowed wins without the work (players cried about it being too easy by the way), and now that the developers have created a FM17 that is near-perfect, these same players cry about it being too hard.  In FM17 this means that instead of using plug-and-play tactics, players are now forced to read real-life tactical theories and analysis to come up with systems for themselves.  And there are a number of FM17 specific tactical communities to help new players out along the way -- message me anytime and I'll point you in their direction.
Another reason why players leave negative reviews about FM17 is that they refuse to see the value in buying a new game year-in-year-out because they don't believe there are enough added features.  I can't tell folks how to spend their money, but I think the contract system where you get a significant discount on each new Football Manager after having owned the previous version is one way the developers have shown they keep their ears attentive to the wants and needs of their community.
But price aside, I also take exception with this complaint that each new FM doesn't offer anything new from the last.  Take a moment to search the web for articles and press regarding the scouting system SI employs to create each FM game.  Go ahead and combine the number of scouts at Bayern Munich, Real Madrid, Barcelona, Juventus, Manchester City, or any other 3-5 massive clubs and your accumulative number will still not come close to the number of scouts that SI uses.  The depth of real life knowledge available in FM17 is unbelievable, their black box of scouting reports on players from as far as Malaysia on down to a second division team in San Antonio, Texas (hell, they even include a couple dozen amateur youth clubs I grew up playing against in Texas).  I have never played a video game where the knowledge gained from having played it bleeds over so seamlessly into the real world sport that the game islooking to simulate.
In fact, a number of real life clubs (both big and small) have contractual agreements with SI to use FM's black box to scout players themselves because SI's player analysis is that damn good.
The scouting network and their reports alone are enough for me to by FM each year. And this is just one of a gang full of new features that come along with each new iteration of FM.
And I promise anyone who buys this game, and puts in enough hours to get past the learning curve, will never watch soccer the same way again.  It really opens you up to a whole new understanding of how the beautiful game is played.
This game isn't for everyone, however, and I would never tell someone that they're wrong for having bought FM17 and disliking it.  Some of my friends who love soccer the most have tried and passed on FM before, so to each their own.
But with all of these negative reviews out there I wanted to put in my two cents.
TL;DR - FM is the most enjoyable video game series I have ever played with FM17 being its best iteration yet, with more real world application and depth to its play each year, please don't listen to negative reviews and check this game out for yourself. If you do, you'll never watch real life soccer the same way again.

Keep in mind this is a very early access game. As of the time of this review, it is only day two of this game being released. There is a lot of hype about how it isn't even as polished as the demo, etc.
You'll find that the developers largely post updates on their Facebook. Explanations for setbacks, etc, have been clearly communicated on their Kickstarter. Please, if you are purchasing this game, envision it as a new game. Things change, things happen. This is what we have right now.
Which is a tycoon style game in which you build your own dinosaur theme park. Some features are missing but will arrive later once re-defined.
The UI: It is a bit confusing right now and you really need to just open a file you don't care about and click everything to learn it. Hopefully this is due to change and it's quick to learn - just a bit tedious and can be frustrating if you want to go in and just do what you want.
The Gameplay: It's interesting with how you unlock dinosaurs and skins and honestly I enjoyed the two hours I spent playing. They flew right by! I would like to see more dinosaurs, and the ability for the dinosaurs to have wants and needs - for the environment to affect them, etc. it is enjoyable, it is simply limited.
The Graphics: Stunning! However, it seems lower end computers will experience lag and frameloss with this game even with low settings as it is not yet optimized - which  makes sense, it's only second day of release. Optimization updates will likely come in the future.
Video and Audio: Both are pretty good. Sounds seem ok. Has beautiful ambient sounds. However the music on the world map is deafening. I had to turn it down to 20% to be able to hear myself talk or even be able to think clearly. Overall the sounds are good and the video settings are simple. Again, might be hard to run for lower end systems.
Lacking at the moment: The purpose of the park. You just build a park and rack up dollars to build more. There are no downsides. Dinosuars don't seem to actually need that food/water as they have no needs yet. Soon they will. The visitors also don't seem to have needs or wants. They're like zombies wandering around the park, sometimes going into the cinemarex and sitting on benches but otherwise they don't seem to care much.
My personal thoughts: It's missing some big features I was hoping for on release but I understand that the game basically is a reset of their ideas and goals. They have a lot of dinosaurs to do and a lot of work to put back into it to reintroduce some of those features we're missing. The goal of this game isn't just to place blocks and have a park, it's to build a park with your own creative mind and enjoy it. Don't like your hatchery? You can build a building all around it, select it, and make it into a blueprint to place it anywhere you like. Have a different hatchery for every kind of dinosaur! Build your own burger stands, your own museums, etc. You are not bound by the buildings they provide to you - but they are provided, and are right there to click and place into the world. Even with it being highly simplified I found i lost myself in almost 3 hours of explorative gameplay. Testing this and that, and once I had a feel for it, I had a great time just creating. That said, I am a creative person.
I absolutely DO recommend this game but I recommend also that you watch some Lets-play videos of it so that you get a feel for what it is like first. Get a feel for the game, what to expect, and whether you feel the cost is worth it right now. It will be worth it, in time, I'm betting. This is a very Early Access game - catch that? Early Access! Your goal in purchasing an early access game isn't to have a game to bang away at - but rather to have a game which you can give feedback on and help them build the game both you and the developers want to see. I love that we can unlock different skins for the dinos. That you have to do this to have variety, to have dinos at all. I like the features that are there for obtaining these dinosaurs but I don't want to ruin it for people who might see it as spoilers. I like the building aspects. That you can cuztomize absolutely anything. It's all beautiful. It just needs more.
TL;DR of course it has issues and doesn't have much content. This is day 2 and they're redoing some of their features. I look forward to a better developed and more polished game.

The lack of provided basic buildings (hatchery, visitor center and visitor kiosks) is frustrating. Not everyone likes to build from scratch. That was my least favorite part of Planet Coaster. It probably would have been better to save that function for when the steam workshop was up not before.
As for the dinosaurs themselves, they are OK. The animations are meh, models are high quality but some of them have poor design. Like the Rexes weird bump on the base of its tail. AI is entertaining how everything seeming wants to kill everything. Really, why would Hadrosaurs and the Pachyrhinos want to murder Gallis so bad? Or for that matter why would Edmonts and Pachys want to kill Paras? This goes on and on as if the AI was designed to make any dino want to kill any dino smaller than it if it isn't its own species. So much for cross species exhibits. Also, juvie carchar can kill an adult Argent in four bites?
Now, I won't talk too much about bugs because it is just released but come on. Unresponsive UI requiring frequent restarts and on reload the dinos no longer move? Might as well not have a save function as you need to restart entirely almost every time you load a save.
For now, I will refund this grossly overpriced tech demo and maybe come back in a year or so. I recommend not spending money on this game just yet.

The game is an early access game, and there is still a lot of work needed before it will be finished. I know that it has been in development for 3 years already, however I did not follow their streams at all. So I started the game without knowing what it will be like. A new dino park game, that’s all I knew.
There is no tutorial yet, so if you start the game you have to try everything yourself. The UI is a bit strange, but once you get to know how everything works its quite ok to use. The help section in the game gives you at least some answers, which was enough for me. Just a little tutorial how to get your first dino would be nice.
The building is working fine for a start. There are still some bugs, and the structure deleting is a bit inconvenient, but that’s all. I made a park today, with every dinosaur available yet, and in the end it looked quite nice.
The AI of the visitors and the dinosaurs on the other hand, is a little mess. The visitors walk around, take a seat if there is a bench and walk away again. Sometimes they start running when a dino is out, or very close to the fence. That’s all for now I guess. I hope that in the future the visitor’s behavior and satisfaction will be important as well. At the moment they simply don’t need anything. They will interact if there is something interactive available, but it doesn’t affect anything.
The dinosaur AI is quite simply as well. My dinos just ran off to the food and water and continued eating/drinking for the rest of the time. In the end most of them were stuck in the water feeding bin and in each other. What I miss here is the health and wellbeing of the dinosaurs. Something like illnesses, brutality between carnivores or fights to decide the new alpha animal.
In conclusion, I recommend the game. I know that it is still barely finished, but I started the game today and built my own park in about 7 hours, and I really had fun. I remembered my childhood Tycoon parks and just played around a bit. Of course I had some funny bugs like ghost benches and water addicted dinosaurs but I enjoyed it! It’s sad to see so many negative reviews after one day. Give the game a chance guys, it’s barely even released yet! :)
