One thing I haven't seen anyone talk about in reviews is the way you unlock dinosaurs for your park, by using dig sites or the black market. Both ways give you a means to get new skins for your dinosaurs using in-game money, like a loot box system. As it stands right now, there is no reason to ever use a dig team, because using a dig team gives you only a chance at a skin after a minor wait time, while the black market guarantees a skin with no wait time. The only downside to using the black market is the higher cost, but theres not enough things to spend money on currently, so thats really negated.

It took me just three hours to play this game from beginning to end, however it left me feeling like there's more to find. A second playthrough confirmed that I'd missed an area. It's full of parodies and inside references, and is superficially similar to DLC Quest, but very different. The boss fights are tough, but not too tough, just tough enough to be extremely rewarding to defeat. It's funny, but not overly silly, and I totally recommend it.

A lovechild between Legend of Zelda and Final Fantasy (with some Diablo kink in the bedroom) causes this game to appear. You see it grow from the state of a baby into a mature person as you pick up the upgrades and continue on in the game. A fun little idea I must say, to let the players see how the genres have grown through the years.
The biggest issue I see with this game though is the sheer length of the game, which isn't much to be quite honest. My 6 hours isn't even the minimal you need to 100% a game (which I by the way rarely every do), it's probably something like 4, maybe 3 or quite easily 2 if you know what to do. Most of the time for me was to get the Card Champion achievement, which can be troublesome if you have all of the cards since it can be all about luck with that one. The game is also very easy, there's hardly any difficulty in it at all, the most hard I had was probably the last boss, and even that was dang easy.
What is there though, as per mentioned in the first paragraph, is a fun trip down memory lane if you ever played any of those kind of games. However, to fully experience this game, I highly recommend NOT watching anyone play it, so much gets ruined if you do and I'd honestly say there won't be a reason to buy it if you do. Anyway, I'd say wait for the game to go on a sale, preferably a lot lower then usual. The game is super short and I feel the full price is a little too much for that.

I just can't recommend this. The core of a hidden object game is of course the hidden object scenes, and the resolution on these is simply horrendous, not to mention inconsistent. is a short and fast-paced hidden object adventure, where you play as Isabella, the one and only who can save the kingdom and your future prince from the hands of the evil witch,
With a simple and classic story, where you have to save your place of birth, the game is still entertaining enough, but at a fast passed rithym, due to the easy puzzles and minor changes. I would assume this is a fantastic game for anyone starting out in this genre, especially for the younger ones. Those looking for a challenge are in for a disappointment.
I also assume the engine used is a rather old one, because the resolution is very poor, and although the game graphics  aren't that bad at all, they are ruined by the poor resolution.
I still like the 3D effects on background environments, mixed with the 2D art of objects and characters, but with such low resolution, it's painful to stop and admire the scenes.
The player gets the chance to explore a fantastic and magical castle, go through every door, in every possible room, and even get a look at the nice gardens outside.
Despise being short, it's a well balanced game when comes to an almost nonexistent storyline to follow. Every action and object make perfect sense in this magical world. With an ending forcing somehow a plot twist, but not even reaching it,
released a pretty solid, simple and little adventure for anyone who enjoys simple mysteries and huge castles.
With just 3 hours, I also want to point out that the final boss fight, or I might say a duel, where the player comes face-to-face with the evil in a battle to find the most hidden objects in the shortest periods of time, was a terrific idea, and without a doubt the most thrilling point of the game!
Worth being played, especially if you have a couple of hours left to burn, or if you're looking for a relaxing game but still interesting!
4/10

I was looking for a decent strategy game that allowed me to create my own characters (ex. X:COM, Wasteland 2) and stumbled upon this magnificent specimen of a game. If you like 4X games that include exploration, resource gathering, unit and building construction, espionage, stealth, diplomacy,  trade routes, a market that reacts to supply and demand, a strong fantasy theme, very unique factions with their own backstory, quests, RPG style leveling with skill trees, and being able to outfit your units with different armor, weapons, and trinkets, then this game is for you.
Moves and combat are turn based and there is both a overall strategic element (the world map) and tactical combat that utlilizes the surrounding terrain including cliffs, forests, and grassland to provide offensive and defensive bonuses and LOS.  Units react to morale when fighting, and can inflict and receive numerous buffs and defuffs such as heals, stuns, disease, and burning fire with DoT.  You can manually control your units in battle, issue movement and combat orders and select offensive defensive, or hold stances, or let the program autoresolve the battle for you.
There only possible negative i can think of is the micromanaging of constructing units and buildings; moving the population from focusing on science, industry, food, economy (dust),  or influence, depending on what your needs are at that particular moment.   I spend a lot of time deciding on what to build next.  I'm sure as I get more familair with the game that will improve but just wanted to toss out the learning curve is quite steep.
There are a ton of great guides and videos out there and the community is one of the best I've seen as far as helping players such as answering noob questions and providing advice on well, just about everything.
It is deep, it is complicated, and a blast to play.
Highly reccomended.
EDIT:  I read the AI can control your build queue for you and if you mismanage things too bad it will even take over and start to sell off assets to get things back under control.   Although it will take some extra time to make those "what to build next" decisions, at this early stage I'm going to go ahead and make them so I can better understand what all of the different buildings, and improvements actually do.
PS... the tech tree is divided into 6 tiers and aside from having to research 9 tier 1 topics to get to tier 2, etc. you have a lot of freedom on what you want to research in whatever order you prefer.

I got pretty frustrated with CivV, and the differences in this one were intensely satisfying. The other reviews are pretty good so I'll just list some bits that stood out to me:
-Privateers (make an army anonymous and then attack your ally).
-The factions are quite different, and the game feels pretty different based on which one you pick, to the extent that you'll settle in differnet places based on your faction.
-The AI seems really good compared to CivV, in the sense that it doesn't immediately seem comically stupid. This is mostly because it just ignores you, but that can help immersion a lot more than the dumb stuff the AI does in CivV. It also makes the game pretty easy since the AI probably won't attack you unless you torpedo your economy to the point that it can just steamroll you effortlessly, though idk if that's different on high difficulties. The AI is good for picking up the game, but try to find humans to play with eventually.
-The earlygame is really well realized, lategame and the victory conditions are kinda bland. I consider this a good choice, since in 4Xs the games are basically decided by the time lategame rolls around anyway, so they might as well allocate resources to the parts that people are always engaged with. Maybe this is just my bias because I always end up with an enormous lead by the last few eras though.
-Custom factions are a thing, and they're fun to mess around with.
-You can put the cities on autopilot instead of queueing up the same 20 buildings for each new city. Sorta wish you could do this with the hero levelling tree but oh well.
Great 4x game, vanilla is totally functional but the expansions are certainly worth it.
I'm not very good at 4X games, and I'm not very good at this game, but I'm having fun, so that's good.

As a huge 4X fan I'd love to recommend this game and it does look and feel like a quality game. However, it consistently fails to keep me entertained when I try to play it. It's too slow and cumbersome; too by-the-numbers treadmill-like.
I can recommend this only to people who just love 4X games and have already exhausted the long list of strategy games that are better than Endless Legend.

To be honest the only reason I bought this game was because 4 days had gone by and there still wasn't a review on the store page. I was kinda hoping for a quirky underrated gem, I guess. I was half-right; boy it sure is quirky. I mean, when the dev popped into the corner of the screen in the form of a youtube-esque facecam in a lazy costume in a poorly-lit environment recorded on a below-average quality webcam, I knew I was in for something at least DIFFERENT, and I'll admit, the gag made me laugh. The music isn't bad either, it's a bit short so the loops gets old quickly but it's nothing too unbearable.
Unlike the graphics. I don't think I've ever purchased a game on Steam with artwork this terrible. 90% of the time, I have no ♥♥♥♥ing clue what the hell I'm looking at. Now to be fair, if I tried to make a game and do the artwork myself, it would probably look just as bad or worse, which is why I would stick to what I'm good at, and find people who are good at what I'm bad at to do the rest. The environment is a total clustercuss of indistinguishable assets and the characters themselves might actually make you vomit. I've seen better character concepts on the average 14 year olds Deviant Art page. Water tiles are literally nothing more than 4 lines made with the pencil tool in a couple different shades of blue, it's aMAZing. The games sense of humor seems to revolve around the idea that it doesn't actually care, at least I think that's what it's going for, I couldn't tell how sincere it was to be honest, so its okay to be ugly as long as it plays nice, right? but it doesn't.
The controls, oh my god, the controls. So basically it's a non-traditional platformer. Your basic jump ability is a little weak so you have to draw a line from your character to the spot you want to jump and he flings in that direction, which sounds easy, but you don't get a great sense of exactly where you're going and you have to correct your course once you're in the air, but it's so hard to control because your character flies through the air so quick that it's really difficult to process what's going on. You really have to plan ahead before each jump, it's so disorienting. You'll probably be stuck in the intro for a little while before you adjust to simply jumping from platform to platform, and even though I did get the hang of it, it never actually felt natural, merely understood. You also have this teleport ability that can teleport you a short distance, but it doesn't seem to make any sense to me. It's supposed to go where your cursor is, but sometimes it would work and sometimes it wouldn't and I couldn't make heads or tails on how the mechanic functioned. Eventually I figured out which parts of the level wanted me to teleport and to where, but that was just from looking at the level design, I never actually understood it. It's like someone saying "press this button" without being told what the button does.
There's combat too, if you can call it that. You have this tiiiiiny little white line called the chow-blade, or something to that effect, which is kinda ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t when virtually every enemy has ranged attacks and you practically have to hump their face to damage them. It was clear to me that this was not a combat-oriented game so I avoided the monsters, but the platforming was frustrating and didn't make sense to me so I avoided that too and got a refund instead.

This is a game.  It looks like a game, it acts like a game, it even plays like a game.  You press buttons to move, you press buttons to shoot, you can even press buttons to do other stuff and there's lots of stuff to do. You can build stuff, you can build stuff that builds stuff AND you can build stuff that blows stuff up.  You can attach stuff that blows stuff up to stuff that moves, and you can make stuff that moves move around stuff that doesn't. Ryse: Son of Rome, this is a tough decision.
First of all let me say, I loved this game. I am not a big fan of multiplayer in general, so I played this game entirely for the campaign. The campaign is short but it is just amazing. I consider it one of my favorite stories that I ever came across in a game.
The graphics are obviously amazing and I was also a huge fan of the combat system. I actually really enjoyed it.
So why the thumbs down?
When I was in the middle of chapter 7 (out of 8) the game decided to delete my character stats for no reason whatsoever. The next time I started the game, I could still continue the campaign from the point where I had stopped, but my character was back to Level 1, which makes it extremely difficult to beat the enemies the game throws at you in chapter 7 and 8.
Obviously I checked the forums and I saw a lot of people complaining about the exact same problem. Some of these posts were over a year old, but there was no solution at all. It seems clear to me that the developers decided to simply ignore this problem, which is something that obviously should've been fixed immediately, since it's basicly a game breaking bug.
I loved the game so much, I actually replayed a bunch of the earlier chapters to level up my character again and then finished the game. The ending is awesome!
So yeah, it is a short but fantastic game, but I just have to give the game a thumbs down when the developers don't fix such a severe problem that a lot of people seem to have encountered.

I would call this game "Internet Argument Simulator" but unlike Internet Arguments, this game has classy and respectable insults such as "Your mother looks like your father." and "A pigsty dances like a hamster and smells of your hat, and I have proof!"
But in seriousness it's an interesting and fun game, especially for the price. You can quickly boot it up, have a few rounds and walk away with a smile on your face.
The game simply works on you try to string together a soul crushing insult, hoping to take advantage of any insecurities the character your opponent chose while trying to prevent them from doing the same. It requires some wit and planning to try and make sure you prevent your opponent from getting phrases they'd want.
There's a few modes to pick from, ranging from simply doing a 1v1 insult sling fest with a bot, a "tournament" mode where you face bot after bot to try and complete a campaign (and in turn unlock new characters), and then there's PvP (both on one machine AND online). It makes it an interesting party game where you can still play it single player and feel satisfied.
It's not a fancy game, but it's artstyle is pretty interesting, and gives it the quircky charm it needs to pull off this kind of game, plus the pre and post-game dialogue settle the whacky nature of the world.
I only hold a couple issues with it: One is that it feels that I can't sit down for extended periods of time with this game, otherwise I start getting burnt out fast since a lot of "insults" tend to be built from the same parts.
The other is that sometimes it feels you lose simply because you had no choice (you'll get a board where you can't make a good insult where your opponent can string it forever). However this rarely happens so I don't mind.
Lastly, that they don't have full voice lines for all phrases (Though this is slightly fixed by the fact they have some silly "placeholder" lines such as a character going "Your mother BLAH BLAH BLAH your father").
Definetley worth $2.00... Literally so fun with your friends. The only con is that it should've been called "Roast Simulator 2016"

For the moment I wouldn't suggest getting the game unless you want to access a game that is early access and therefore not fully operational yet. With the consideration of it's current price, I wouldn't recommend buying this game just yet. I've backed his game from the beginning however and was thrilled to give the game a go. While it's not currently up to the level of JPOG, it ceraintly has potential to do that and more, so long as the current issues get worked out.
Pros;
+The amount of different dinosaurs currently available
+Amount of different skins available for each dinosaur allows for plenty of customization
+There is a potential to make your own buildings within the game
+The game has the potential to do everything JPOG allowed for and much more.
Cons;
-The AI is still quite buggy with people getting stuck on objects such as benches, and dinosaurs not interacting with each other properly. I quite often end with different species of herbivores attacking each other for no reason.
-There is a lack of buildings that are typically found in theme park builders such as drink stalls, etc.
-Some buildings don't work fully yet, such as the helicopter pad.
-The background noise has a tendancy to cut out and some dinosaur noises don't play correctly at times.
-There is currently no tutorial in the game, which was initially frustrating.

Even though the demo actually had the audacity to unironically call the zoo "Harambe Park" I'd much rather play that than this version.
Content which worked reasonably well back then is either broken or completely missing and they also managed to make the animations look worse than they originally were.
Instead of adding a lootbox system, which is completely unnecessary for this genre, maybe the people behind this masterpiece should have invested their time in playing JPOG or Zoo Tycoon 1 and 2, so that they actually know how a management game needs to work.
What also disturbed me is how the UI, menu screens and handling of the game look and feel like they were made for a console game.
Early Access may be an excuse for an unstable framerate, bugs and glitches but not for bad design decisions. And there are plenty of those to be found in the current state of Mesozoica.
Maybe this will get better in the future but as of now I'm requesting a refund.

I have been watching the progress of this game for a long time now and have been looking forward to it since it's announcement. There are a lot of things for me to say about this game, so I am going to split it in two sections: good and needs improvement/presence.
The Good:
When opening Mesozoica, I was greeted with a beautifully designed start menu. It was clear as to what gamemode did what and gave me the option from the get-go to have a "Site B." I really liked the option to explore the game as a whole instead of me diving into the deep end and using all my money on things that aren't important to start out with.
The Game features many different dinosaurs ranging from the famous Tyrannosaurus Rex to, a dinosaur that I didn't even know existed, Mamenchisaurus, who all have many skins to give the park more soul. All the dinosaurs are beautifully crafted making your park as realistic and immersive as possible.
I absolutely love the building blocks. The game provides the ability to create your own buildings for your guests to interact with. This feature quite literally make the possibilities endless for the player to have a park that is truly theirs. This leads me to the next part: the custom blueprints.
The custom blueprints is quite a genius idea. It allows you to save the building that the player created with the building blocks and put a copy in another part of the park or in a completely separate park. And if this feature wasn't cool enough, you can export the file of the player's custom blueprint and send it to your friends and vice versa.
That being said there are many things that need improvement
The needs improvement/presence:
Needs improvement:
Since this game was released not even 24 hours after this review is posted and it is still in early access, I will not be going into too much detail in this portion of the review. The Mesozoica team has brought an amazing game from what I understand is a small team. I have faith in their ability to make the game better as the year(s) progress.
The dinosaur AI needs a lot of improvement. As I am writing this review, I have been watching two Gallimimus's walking intoi the same stack of hay and the only way they are going to get out is if I control them and walk them out of it myself. Adding onto the AI, the dinosaurs that I have seen don't have a herding ability, at least from what I've seen. The dinosaurs walk aimlessly around and don't interact with one another, and when they do, it's because they are killing a dinosaur of a diffent species. This includes herbivors killing other herbivors (which is something that I found to be quite dissapointing and irritating).
The available building that your guests can interact with are a burger kiosk, a movie theatre, and the main entrance. That's it. To all onto that, there is no customization to the buildings. They just exist and guests stand in front of them. It would be nice to have a similar UI that is seen in Jurassic Park: Operation Genesis where you can choose what is being sold at each establishment and setting a price for the product. Also, I have yet to discover any vehicle. There is nothing on the helipad; it just exists for the purpose of looking pretty at the moment.
As for things that I would like to see in the game:
Steam workshop integration so that players can upload building that they create for others to use.
Clipping of the building blocks. This is something that I was shocked wasn't in the game. If you have the ability to make your own custom buildings, I would think that the final product at least looks like something that was made by the game devs and not a four year old's Lego building.
Along with the Steam workshop integration, I would love the ability to visit other people's parks. If that could somehow be possible, then I would be very happy.
All in all, Mesozoica has many things good and bad about it. It has A LOT of potential and should be something that you keep your eye on. This game is still in early access, so expect this game to be better than it currently is.

-The dinosaurs for the most part are either quite ugly compared to other games out there or are just off, and god are most of the animal animations horrendous.
-The dinosaur control system is very unique for a tycoon game, but it's practically pointless and extremely buggy.
-The graphics are ok imo but the render distance is terrible.
-The dinosaur digup system: easily the worst part of this game. Not only is it♥♥♥♥♥♥easy to get dinosaurs but you also get them from LOOTBOXES. First of all, the devs claimed no microtransactions or lootboxes for the game, but I call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. It's blatantly obvious das what they're doing. Why else would there be a popularity system based on crate rarities? Hell, even if they decided that its a completely free no microtransactions lootbox system (which is pretty dumb, that really defeats the point of the lootbox system in general), then how immersion breaking is it the dinosaurs just plop out of a crate? You don't see any dinosaur bones, you don't extract DNA, you don't even see any embryoes or eggs. Keep in mind I'm perfectly ok with lootboxes, I love Depth to death for example. However, it as a base game mechanic is something I'm easily against to the max.
-The game itself doesn't even work as a game, making it feel like a demo rather than an early access game. Looking at other people's videos and my own experience (I was in sandbox but my money still counted it seemed), it's pretty much no consequences to anything. People will come regardless of how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ your park is and the only thing you can do is just make and look at dinosaurs.
Mesozoica in general is also pointless. Now that the REAL JPOG sequal has arrived, it has 0 purpose. It's literally just asking for a fight it can't win. Mesozoica will only get lasting attention because it came out first, but the minute JW: Evo comes out it will just be known as the worse JW: Evo. Keep in mind that we don't know whether JW: Evo will actually be good, but that doesn't change the fact that this is AAA+ Published Game vs Indie Game, and we all know who's going to win that fight.
So yeah, hope yall enjoy that kinda in-depth review. If you want to see the full livestream of my first impressions and then review, happily click on the video down below.

Review in early access, will update as the game gets closer to release.
First thing first: I backed the game on kickstarter a few years back. I have been eargerly waiting for it to be released, and signed up for what i knew would be a comparatively small game (at 20$, you can't expect a HUGE triple A game). As everything on kickstarter, i even wondered if the game were to be released at all. The fact that we got something is a good indicatioon there is hope for the game.
On with the review.
The Good:
* Beautifull graphics, the dino models are very realistic, the texture are gorgeous and the animations fluid. The visitors also look good, and the different buildings, while rather generic, looks ok. The plant life and smaller details (fences, grass etc) also are quite convincing.
* The game run very smoothly. I got an I5 4690 with a gtx 950 2go and i am experiencing buttery smooth framerates. For an early access game, it's very nice to see optimization already being implemented (*cough* ARK *cough*)
* Dynamic Dino Growth. The creatures start as baby and grow to adult size as time goes. Pretty neat!
The bad:
* Not exactly what we were promised at first. There is basically only 2 pre-build venues, and very little in the way of variety to create your own. This is early access tho, and I am fairly confident more things will come with upcoming updates (fences, more blocks etc)
*The Ugly:
* The game is completly barebone. No management, no staff, no way to track guest need/wants etc. Dino A.I. is implemented (they move as herds, herbivores will kill baby carnivors, Carnivores will hunt herbivores...) but is rather rudimentary so far.
*UI. It doesn't need to be redesign, it needs to be implemented. Period.
Overall, I'd say that as is, the game is more of a tech demo or Alpha than a beta/early access. Their is potential for greatness here, and you can easely see the passion that went into creating the dino; but everything else have been overlooked (so far) Here is to hope the developpers will see their project to the end and deliver a great Tycoon experience.
In conclusion, this is a very rough first draft of the game. If you go in expecting a AAA title, polished and finished, in the same vein as Planet Coaster right off the gate, you will be sorely disapointed. If you go in expecting the fondation of a game showing a whole lot of potential, and are ready to wait for the game to grow. You will find an interresting little dino simulator. Just keep your expectation in check and/or wait for the game to be further along in development.

After 1,500 hours and counting of gameplay, here are a few thoughts.
Immediately upon purchase, I was very happy with the overal design, UI and look of the game. Sports Interactive have really gone a long way in recent years in this field. Contrary to many other opinion and reviews, I find the UI intuitive, and once acquainted with very well thought out. Many believe some screens hard to find and access - but I do not notice this much.
Improvements on the Game Engine are nice, but were expected fixes to previous versions rather than ground-breaking novelties. This is an area that must, must be improved upon, but in such a way that the game remains playable for the huge majority of customers who play on laptops. The next iteration of the game needs to work on this hugely.
Tactics. Still very hard, like previous versions, to install a clear philosophy into your team - and instructions that should distinguish your team hugely from another - short passes vs direct passes - are actually hardly noticeable on the pitch. The next iteration should add to the tactical possibilities but most importantly make a team like Stoke City FC distinguishable from Barcelona FC. Tactical tweaks should result in visible, on-pitch differences in the way a team plays.
Secondly, the extremely rigid tactics 'board' where one assigns player a position should be made much more malleable, and instead of a set of positions one should be able to fluidly place a player wherever one wishes to place him.
Improvements in contract negotiations are hugely noted and lauded. Extra-realism in these due to contractual clause additions and the like. Work to be done on the AI transfer system and the personalities of a club's board. As recent events have shown - a board can take the decision to sell a player without a managers' consent. Would be a 'sweet' feature.
Pep Guardiola moving to Man City whilst Pellegrini was still manager was very interesting, and one should as such be able to negotiate contractual terms with a club whilst another manager is still in the job - albeit reaching the end of his tenure there.
Training. Hugely controversial, although most agree the current system is restrictive and not well thought-out. Individual training is fine - but team training needs to be revamped somehow. Care must be taken here because the game is already very slow-paced and adding huge amounts of detail to training can make it arduous to proceed in your virtual game. Extra detail to the current system without hugely changing it needed.
Extra financial options. Clubs are now money-making and money-oriented. Extra control and importance on issues such as pre-season tours/tournaments and shirt-sales/ticket prices would be great.
Sports Interactive, although this review has been highlighting for the most areas for improvement, the current iteration of the game is already fantastic and your work must be aplauded. Thank you for your devotion and hope you can take into consideration some of these reasonable proposals.

Evoland is a trip through some of the worst features of games past, and reminds you why developers have since moved on to better mechanics.  Here are a few of them that the game indulges:
1. One-hit game overs - You're in this mode at the beginning of the game.  Add to it that you're on a grid and so are the randomly-moving enemies, and it's a recipe for disaster.  I died at least 3 or 4 times, starting the whole game over every time, before I could reach the first save point.
2. Really annoying low-health sounds - I get it that we're supposed to be careful, but come on.  It sounds like the alarm clock from hell, and I had to actually shut off the sound when it came on.  Don't believe me?  Search for it on YouTube and listen for yourself.
3. Backtracking - Notice that chest that seems impossible to get to?  That's right, if you want to get 100% completion, you're going to have to backtrack a LOT.  You only get certain skills later in the game, and will have to head back to earlier areas to use them to get all the collectables.  The game world isn't massive, but the random encounters will be fighting you every step of the way.
4. Loading screens - Yeah, yeah, reading data from disks on the PS1 was a tad slow, I get it.  But don't give us artificial loading screens at every one of the four area transitions in a town, and especially not in a town with...
5. Multi-layered fetch quests - We need bombs!  That guy probably has some! "Well I used to, but not anymore.  Go talk to that gal."  ...and you finally get the bombs FIVE PEOPLE (and even more loading screens) later.
6. A lack of mid-boss checkpoints - Figure out the boss's first stage, only to get stomped flat on the second?  Too bad!  You get to fight the entire thing all over again.  (I normally wouldn't complain, but the second stage is essentially random and requires a lot more luck than skill.)
While interesting at least in concept, it doesn't stand up in practice.  Aside from the interesting time travel puzzle and the surprisingly functional Diablo section, it's all incredibly boring and tedious.  You're much better off playing the games it borrows from (2D Zeldas, Final Fantasy VII, Diablo), than this mess.

Bear in mind this is a review of the game as released on the 2nd January 2018
Ok, let's start with the good. The dinosaur models are of a consistently high quality, with a variety of choices for skins for them. The animations, while a little clunky, are passable. The system by which you obtain new dinosaurs and skins is pretty decent.
Now.. the bad. No easy way to go about this, so here we go. Firstly, the building system is fiddly and difficult to use properly, with a lack of preset blueprints to save you time. Fences and paths both work on a grid system, which would be fine but for the fact they're both operating on different grids, making it a lot more work than it should be to make fences and paths line up properly. If you build too close to the edge of the map, your fences and paths start to miss sections, effectively rendering the edges of the map unusable for anything. It took me asking on the discussion how to actually delete sections of fences and paths, as the ingame help section doesn't mention it. Turns out you have to go into the build fences and paths menu, then select the fence or path you want gone, then delete it. Go figure. Also, buildings occasionally don't realize they're connected to a path. The dinosaurs like to get stuck on the water supply, as well as each other, and as they move so does their tooltip menu, making it far, far more difficult than it should be to select a dinosaur then pilot it yourself to get it unstuck from it's companions. Terraforming is nonexistent, as is dinosaur AI. All they do after hatching is go eat then spend the rest of their lives glitched into the water feeder. Menu navigation is needlessly fiddly as well, with "minimizing" an option in the building menu leaving you unable to do anything else till you un-minimize it, and exit the menu properly.
Now, I understand that this game is Early Access and will be hopefully improving as time goes on. However, this release is of alpha demo quality. I have no intentions on giving up on this however, and will be more than happy to update my review as time goes on. I do not regret paying for this game, on the condition that it recieves the fixing it needs to be playable. However, to those without the desire to be a part of what is essentially an open alpha program, I cannot in good faith suggest a purchase at this time. If you want to be able to play a spiritual sequel to JPOG, you have some more waiting until that void in the market will be satisfied in full.
If, however, you're the kind of person that enjoys providing feedback, is happy to deal with bugs and won't♥♥♥♥♥♥♥out at the devs at the drop of a hat, I do recommend getting in on this game and helping ensure it is successful. Remember, there's two other titles (that I will not name for politeness' sake, but I'm sure you know what games I'm talking about here) on the horizon that, if released in a more playable state, will easily beat this game in it's current form, so the clock is ticking. One of those games is a movie licensed game, with a full studio behind it, and if Mesozoica wants to be a success it needs to be in a playable state before this game hits.
As for concrete suggestions, the number one thing the devs need to work on is the building system (especially fences and paths), dinosaur AI and menu navigation. I've noticed a trend on the Mesozoica Facebook page, where the devs offer new skins or dinosaur species as apology for delays or bugs. This is if anything counterproductive. I'd suggest putting a stop to new species releases entirely, with the sole focus being on the gameplay itself, fixing the three main problems I just mentioned. I do want to see this project succeed, and I have high hopes for it if the devs take these criticisms on board and work to address them.

I'm writing this review with an open mind as it is only day 2 of the EA. I'm also writing this having played JPOG and it being one of my favorite games to this day. Now, Mesozoica has a lot of potential, but there is still much that must be done to it for it to reach that point. As many have stated, the UI is not that great, to put it lightly, the AI of both dinos and guests can use much improvement as the dinos barely react, if at all, to others of the same species and the guests simply walk around without seeming to notice anything.
I played sandbox mode and my dinos would walk around a bit, but then they would drink water. Either the dinos in my game will die as soon as they stop drinking, or they just get stuck in the drinking animation and do nothing else. Eventually I moved to the actual campaign mode and when I made dinos there (I only made two, the carchardontosaurus and baryonyx) neither would walk on their own accord. I could control them and move them around, but when I stopped controlling them they stopped all movement and acted like statues.
Those were the main issues I had with the game, I didn't hit much on the AI and UI as everyone else seems to be doing that, and for the most part I agree with what they're saying, along with the lack of campaigning in campaign mode.
With all that being said, I found myself enjoying the game. Maybe it's because it's the first game of it's kind that I've played since JPOG. Maybe not. The dinosaur skins are beautiful. The animations, when present, seem to be fluid, all that I've noticed. Could use some more premade buildings as in souveneir shops, restaurants etc... but I don't really mind that. Yet. Because I know that it's still early in the EA phase.
I'm hoping that the Devs will release patches to fix the bugs and release more content for campaign, buildings, AI, UI, etc... All in all, I will continue to play and see how this game progresses.

I bougth Ryse: Son of Rome for 5€ during a sale, finished the whole campaign on normal difficulty (called Soldier), tested the first chapter of the campaign on very difficult (called Legendary) and tried "Multiplayer", where I finished one level and tried another. To accomplish this it took me about 6,5 hours using a XBOX One GamePad.
As you have already guessed: Ryse:SoR is a rather short game. The story is pretty simple and very foreseeable, so it isn't much of a loss there. The bigger problem by far are the controlls. They too, are very simple and unfortunately sometimes not as precise and predictable as one migth wish. This results in many failed attempts to evade attacks and overall lacks depth and actuall satisfaction for the nice executions. You basicly press Y and X until the opponent is reade for the execution (to which you are urged as it gives extra experience or refills your health) and then press RT. In between you block with A or try to evade attacks with B. That's it. No combos, no influence on which execution will be performed.
While trying "Multiplayer" no match could be found so the only possibility was to play the missions solo. And if you are wondering why I use "" on "Multiplayer": there is no real multiplayer mode, only Co-Op for only two players.
Though admittedly the game is absolutly beautiful it has not much to offer besides the graphics Especially when you compare it to games like the Devil May Cry series or Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance it is clear that more development time should have been spend on a vivid combat system and diverse enemies. Therefore I cannot recommend Ryse:SoR.

Princess Isabella is a well done HOG with surprisingly decent voice acting, music and art. You play as Isabella trying to restore the castle by clearing rooms of curses. To do this you’ll have to solve simple puzzles, find shattered mirror pieces and collect items to solve puzzles you may have seen earlier. This also has the classic HO static screens where you need to find various items.
You’ll fly through the game quickly as it’s very easy. My completion time was a little over 2 hours. The puzzles are easy and the game shows you where the mirror shards are at. Due to the low resolution, I’m almost glad it showed the mirror shards as some of them I just couldn’t make out.
There is a great progress tracking system in this game. It will tell you when a room is clear, your mirror shard progress and an overview of the mansion (which also lets you fast travel to any room). Even further, after you collect all the shards for one person, it asks you if you want to travel right back to the hall with the mirrors. It’s a nice touch and was unexpected.
One odd negative about this game. Not sure if it's Steam or the game, but Steam doesn't detect when you exit the game. It will remain "running" until you kill Steam via the task manager.
+Good, simple story
+Classic HOG screens
+Fast travel
+Great progress tracking
+Music and art are well done
+Must kill Steam process or else it's always "running"
+Short! (2 hours)
+Too easy
+Low resolution can hinder finding mirror shards and hidden objects
Above average

Ah, KOTOR.
You would think there would be more Star Wars RPGs.  I mean, they sell Star Wars themed everything.  They sell Star Wars brand clothes and bed sheets, toys, board games, FPS games, flight sims, toothepaste,  even dirigibles (ok, maybe not dirigibles).  But there is only one franchise RPG for Star Wars fans and that is KOTOR.
Bioware standard fare at this point, but at the time it was relatively new and not quite as old hat as it is now.  Three person party, pseudo turn based combat (an early predecessor to real time with pause), an inventory so large you would need your own hyperspace lane to store it in, and a myopic good/bad morality system that is a little bit silly.  Still, it's a Star Wars RPG.  You can make your own JEDI, with lightsabers!  The story line is campy Star Wars silliness, and I love it. Also, lightsabers.  Bioware standard cast voice actors.  Some memorable characters that I really enjoyed (plus stupid whiney, debbie downer Carth Onasi).  Of course, there has to be some abstractions to the combat: namely  PCs and NPCs (as well as mobs) can take a blaster to the face or a lightsaber to the gut and not, you know, instantly die.  But hey, thats an RPG for you.  Did I mention that there are lightsabers?
Seriously, this game defines "Bioware Game" from 2003-2010 just like Baldur's Gate did between 1998-2003,  If you've played any Bioware game between KOTOR and DAO:Awakenings you know what to expect.  If that satisfies you, I encourage you to play it.  If it doesn't, you probably won't enjoy the game.
This game is my gamer comfort food.  It never tries to be anything but what it is, and it lets you (just for a moment) escape to the Star Wars universe.  If it did nothing else but that, it would get my recommendation.  The fact that it still holds up 10+ years later as a pretty fun game closes the deal for me.

Yet another unfinished, buggy, poorly-made Early Access game which will likely never be finished... this is not. However, it is still presetning itself as one.
This may be the story of a broken, unfinished game. But the game which you play, the game about that game, is most certainly neither of these things.
Instead, it is a clever, charming puzzle game, in which every puzzle has no solution. No formal solution, at least, because the in-game dev characters haven't gotten around to finishing them.
However, with the tools you have at your disposal, it is possible to MacGyver yourself not just one, but a number of potential solutions to each obstacle. And that, in my opinion, paves the way for the greatest part of this game: the social aspect.
Sure, it feels great to come up with a clever way of traversing one of the puzzles. But it feels even better to then tell a friend your solution, only to find out that they never thought of using that method, and instead used some elaborate ticks of their own which you had never thought of.
And even without a friend who also plays this game, I can guarantee that anyone going through this game's story a second time will likely solve a number of puzzles a different way the second time around than they did the first.

Let's start with saying that this game is great. They start you off with a tutorial on the basics of the game, which are complicated enough as it is, but they don't tell you how to exactly win the game. There are several ways of winning, you just have to be faster than your opponents. Also to note, usually there is a semi-clear strategy as to how to win/beat an RTS game, but since your win conditions are several in options, the strategy of how you go about winning is really up to you... which makes it difficult when you first start off. BUT, don't be discouraged, after about 4-5 hours I started to understand how to play better and the payoff is totally there. It's a very satisfying game when you start off with nothing and you work your way up to dominate.
I've played my fair share of RTS games and this is confusing on a different scale, perhaps if you have played this developpers other RTS games then it might not be so bad. For me, my background is in SC, SC2, and the C&C series with a bit of Age of Empires. In this game, combat with your enemy could possibly not occur until like 2 hours into a game. I find with my playstyle I go for more of a expansion/scientific victory, even though my background denotes going for action more than just building up.
Overall I enjoyed this game enough to write a review about it, which is rare in any case.

Garbage game with a garbage monetization system.
Don't be fooled by the slick presentation.
Currently the game's "tactics" are terrible.  It's basically to set up the most possible buffs on 1 char and let that char kill everything.
But the game is actually heavily gated by upgrades which come either extremely slow.  Silver chests and gold chests.  Gold chests come with at least 2 items and often high rarity ones, while silver chests come with 1 item, often low rarity. Silver chests cost 50 gems or whatever, gold cost 500 or $$.  The upgrades can have massive effect on a character, much more than 100% increased damage.  Every "new" campaign or variant you complete you get 100 gems and each boss (every 5 levels) gives you between 5-12 gems and a chance at a silver chest (in 100 bosses I got I think 4?).
Very quickly to "finish" a mission you have to get into the massive damage numbers.
And not only that but there is basically no tactical variance or differentiation between the quests/levels.  They are all functionally the same.  Enemies spawn, walk at your party and the party kills them.  It's not clear if certain enemy types have more hp than others, and if so it doesn't feel that way (they all drop the same amount of gold and seem to take the same number of hits on the same level).  Some variants spice things up by making some enemies harder but  that's it.
And the party comp stuff is really dumb.  You basically get 9 heroes, and it ends up being 7-8 heroes buffing and 1 to 3
heroes dealing damage basically, depending on which heroes you might choose to deal damage.
Overall just a terrible game that plays itself (the only interesting aspect), wrapped in a skin that takes the worst microtransaction system as a way to progress.
Not worth the download even though it's free.

Clocking about 7 hours of play time yesterday starting from scratch I found X3: Reunion to have quite a steep learning curve. I had chosen the Normal/storyline-on difficulty.
Maybe I'm getting too old (42!) to remember countless hours in my youth trying to figure out how to handle misjumps in "Elite", battles in "Wing Commander: Privateer" and similar games "Frontier" etc. but I had expected it to be a piece of cake to swoop in and save the day in this one...
Man was I wrong!
This game puts you in battle from minute 1! I was still trying to figure out the viewscreen, icons, menus... let alone how to throttle up/down when the bogies came at me. Concentrating at battle at hand everything less important had to wait (unimportant like: do I have different types of guns on this boat, how do I target enemies, fire missiles...).
Finally came the part where I took control of turret guns and I could "relax" a little and let the action just happen.
It was not until the "track the Marauder" mission that I got some spare time to investigate the menus and found information about the ship, keybindings for this and that. I had to visit a few game wikis to figure out why I could not repair the hull of my ship... I simply did not understand the pricetag was too high for my wallets contents. On my to do list is still to read the manual - this is very unlike the trend in modern games where you learn throughthe first couple of missions.
Why am I even playing this game? The answer is simple: pure nostalgia!
The games from my youth mentioned earlier had me spellbound then. Around the end of last millenium a demo for "X: beyond the frontier" came out with references to the same games I loved. I think it was only one ot two short storydriven missions... but the trading system was also revealed and I was hooked.
The best thing, as I remember that demo, was a lot of speach. And it was in german! Now, my german was nowhere near fluent but I could understand quite a lot. And what I did not understand only build up the sense of mystery and being in an alien world. It was perfect!
So of couse I bought the game when it came out... and played quite a bit before I realised that some of the spell of the demo had vanished. And in that realisation it came to me that I had been playing the game in english... I was missing the mystery of a german speeking world. Now I may remember wrong, but the game disk did not include german language files so it was not until much later that I found that it could be downloaded through some patches... tried it, but by then I was way too deep into the game to make the switch permanent... the spell had gone.
When I started playing X3 this all came back to me when I was examined the different goods to trade.
The voice said "Teladianium" and I was back in the german world.
Something about this word has so much of the german language in it.
Enough flashbacking!
The future:
I expect to spend yet countless hours in the X3 universe, with both "Albion Prelude" and "Terran Conlict" in my steam library I predict I will not run out of missions in a while.
The though of building a trading empire, setting up my own Ore mines, programming flight patterns... everything that was not possible in the first game "X: beyond the frontier"... I wanna do!
I recommend this game to anyone with a passion for space opera storylines, open sandbox worlds, and vast options for customising your role.
Of course based on only 7 hours of play time :-)

For example I have snuck in undetected with out being seen or touching a single Marine, saved the hostage, shot may way out of the tunnel, stole a jeep by killing the driver, called for extract, drove to the LZ as the chopper was showing up, and laid suppressive fire till he got low enough to board. These endless on the fly options make even my 10th play through feel drastically different.
The control options are amazing. Leaning out from cover to fire, grabbing people up and interrogating them, or choking them out, or cutting their throat, or using them as a shield to fire over their shoulder. All of it a fluid and ridiculously easy to do. While easier to perform actions than MGS4 was there are some moves I miss like rolling on my back and firing up, leaning out to look instead of just to fire, and being able to use the weapon selector switch to swap between single, burst, and full auto.
The game is ridiculously well optimize even on the highest setting.
Cons-
Play this with an official X-Box Remote! The game is picky on what remote you are using and while it does support Keyboard and mouse it is a console port with K+M is an absolute struggle to use. You have to be able to press in the direction of the wall to lean on it, issue is as you spin the camera to look around forward becomes left then back then right then forward again. The problem stems from the fact analog stick was 45 degree angles, keyboards do not. So when you are spinning the camera you tend to jump from cover.
Price,
$60 is outrageous for this game with such little content, even $20 is kinda steep. I got it on sale for $7 and this game is well worth $7. Put it on your wish list and grab it on sale.
TL;DR
Pros
Ridiculous amount of in game options, from on the fly interacting with the environment, to tools and abilities to use stealth, to being able to easily swap between COD style FPS and Gears of War 3rd person to just Rambo your way in and out.
Great Optimization
Cons
Hour and a Half campaign plus replayability with new objectives and unlocks (All progress transfers to MGS V Phantom Pain)
Being a console port Mouse and Keyboard is crude, remote works flawlessly (Use a wired X-Box Remote to circumvent compatibility issues)
Price was ridiculous at $60, $20 is far better, when it's on sale its $7 and that's unbeatable....

The Good:
(1) Dinos look pretty realistic. Their skin textures are really of high quality.
(2) Animation of dinos looks realistic, too - I'm only talking about individual dino where no interaction with other dinos or objects is involved.
(3) Guests, grass, and most of the models look nice overall. Mesozoica is a pretty game.
(4) Highly-customizable buildings and structures. I know some people hate it, but I don't, personally. Actually, I appreciate such a feature. I myself am a fan of tycoon games that involve animal breeding, so you can imagine I've played many of the kind in the genre - Zoo Tycoon series, Wildlife Park series, Jurassic Park Operation Genesis, and etc. While playing them, I've always tried to design the exhibits to be as nature-looking as possible. This is the major reason why I really dislike how the hatchers look in Jurassic Park Operation Genesis. The hatchers in JPOG to me are ugly stacks of dull grey structures rendered with grossly low-quality metal textures that as a result have a terrible visual output. They kill the entire nature aesthetic. However, in Mesozoica, I can do this: cover the hatcher with tons of rocks (and their sizes are editable!) to make it look like a cave that has a door. I also cover the floor in the hatcher with grass to a point that there's no bare area visible. Then I put trees in it, and change their sizes to fit the interior of the hatcher. When the door of the hatcher opens, it looks like the baby dino walks out from a small paddock in a cave. It would look even nicer if somebody someday makes a dino nest (with eggs in) model that I can put along with all those trees and grass in the hatcher. I really appreciate the power of freedom and customability in Mesozoica. But, you have to be careful with the rocks because rocks, as well as other objects that have collision with the dinos, can hinder dinos' movement - which means, if, for instance, you put a rock in the hatcher and unfortunately where you put it stands in the way of the baby dino walking out the hatcher, your baby dino will get stuck there right in the hatcher for all eternity until you romove that rock. This is why I've always put the rocks behind the spot where the baby dino is generated.
The Bad:
(1) Bugs. Dinos can get stuck when they get near rocks or anything that has collision with them (including dinos themselves, meh!). They can also get stuck for no reason! At times there's no "walking" animation when dinos move; instead, they simply "slip". Sometimes, dinos either can't quit eating/drinking, or never eat/drink at all. Guests move like lifeless robots coded with poor pathfinding mechanism, and walk so fast like they're in a rush - I'm saying this from a holiday standard. I mean, visitors are supposed to be on vacation, right? In my opinion, they should walk at an a-little-bit slower pace than they currently do. Onto items/objects, I have no idea why, but it seems that after a little while into the game (such as 30 or 40 mins), objects all of a sudden become uneditable. You can't change their sizes anymore. You can't change their locations or rotate them either. The deletion button as well has no effect. You can't do anything with them after placing them.
(2) Guests have poor variation. In the first Jurassic Park movie, about 40 minutes into the film, John Hammond and the visitors that he invited finished their first meal at Jurassic Park, with a message brought to him by one of his employees. On their way out the restaurant, which located on the second floor of the visitor center, Hammond said to his scientist visitors, "you four are gonna have a spot of company out in the park, spend a little time with our target audience," and then opening his arms, "kids!" cheerfully he said, ready to hug his grandchildren upon seeing them downstairs. Yes, children, are the ultimate target audience of any main theme parks. There's no child in Mesozoica. This is very strange.
(3) Animation is terrible when any interaction between two or more models is involved. So, guests don't buy anything at the store - or maybe they do, but since the animation is awful, I can't tell if they're buying; what I see is they simply stand in front of the store and do nothing. The only thing guests do, is walking. Guests don't look at the animals. In fact, they don't look at anything. They just walk, walk, and walk. It's also weird that guest always walk abreast and in pair or trio. What, are they marching or something? Dino animation is bad as well when interaction takes place. When dinos eat, you wouldn't be able to tell they're eating if not for the presence of the meat or haystacks right in front of them. Unlike Mesozoica, tech demo of Prehistoric Kingdom has had some nice animation. In Prehistoric Kingdom, you can actually see carnivorous dinos, using their mouths, rip a piece of meat off of the larger meat, throw it upward above their heads, and then devour it as it falls. In Mesozoica, carnivorous dinos look like having mild epilepsy when eating. No meat thrown, no meat devoured, what you have is just the dino doing some epileptic seizure action. Horrible animation, so unrealistic.
(4) There's basically zero interaction among dinos. If a carnivorous dino does happen to bite a herbivorous one, the interaction between the two dinos is very unreal. The victim would simply continue to do what it's been doing (such as, taking a slow walk) without any response to the attack. The attacker gets completely ignored.
(5) There isn't any kind of management in the game. No finance management, as the game doesn't even show you how your park's running financially (income, expenses, etc). No animal management, as the only thing the game allows you to do with the dinos is to either control them or kill them. You can't name your animals. You can't check their status (sex. age, mood, health, current activity, etc) and desires (hungry, thirsty, lethergic, wanting a mate, etc). You can't do anything with them except - like I said - controlling or killing them. No guest management. You can't do anything with the guests. In a zoo tycoon game or the like, you'd usually expect to be able to do quite a few things with the guests, such as naming them, picking them up, checking their status (how much money they have, what animals they like, what their opinions are about your park, etc), desires, and etc. But NO, none of these happens in Mesozoica. Due to the lack of management, Mesozoica is barely a game.
(6) There's no terraforming.
(7) There's a general lack of content and gameplay. For example, in Jurassic Park Operation Genesis, there's this "research" thing. You have to invest money and time in inventing some very crucial technologies, of which the most interesting ones (to me), are dino vaccines. Thess vaccines have a direct effect on your dinos regarding their lifespan, which then will determine how visitors view your park. If you manage your animals terribly, that they suffer greatly under your rule, your visitors can become quite toxic. Many of them will leave your park, while fewer and fewer people will come, in return, causing you a financial crisis. But no, there isn't anything like this in Mesozoica. There's no gameplay. The game doesn't even have attractions, such as a jeep tour, something major tycoon games (Zoo Tycoon series, Wildlife Park series, JPOG) all have.
These are what I've noticed thus far. Mesozoica is obviously still in development, a bit too early even for an early access game. I'm recommending this game entirely based on the expectation that the game developer will fix all the major problems and bugs eventually, that we'll see significant improvement. If the game unfortunately remains the same or gets not much improved even in later versions, buying it would be a complete waste of money, and of space on your computer.

The Magic Circle is an immaculate game where you delve into the depths of an unfinished game. You, the player are tasked with testing a game that has been stuck in development hell, however the game is nowhere near finished regardless of the multitude of years spent in development. Along your way you stumble across a being who has been stuck within the game since its inception, trapped and alone, the developers indifferent to his existence. You are given the power to shape and mold the creatures as you see fit, outfitting them with different features from various other entities within the game.
This game is well worth your time, with its fantastic story direction, and overall freedom to accomplish tasks as you please. If you've "seen it all" from the game industry, this game is for you.
Pros:
- Freedom of progression, as well as freedom to accomplish tasks in any way you see fit.
- The innate lack of a combat system for yourself, forcing you to rely upon the creatures you encounter along the way to protect you.
- Mold the games creatures any way you like to accomplish any task. Take features from specific creatures, and add them to your personal collection of modifications you can apply to anything at any time. Do you want a turtle that has a teleportation pad on its back? YOU GOT IT.
- Fantastic Story Direction, with a twist at the end I wasn't expecting whatsoever.
- Fantastic soundtrack, which made me feel as though I was actually within the game, controlling everything myself.
- Simple collectibles system.
- Return to the game world after completing the game to allow for completionists to find any missed collectibles.
Cons:
- Short game. For the price point of $20, the game is incredibly short, spanning about 5-7 hours, whilst they are incredibly enjoyable, it is a tad much for the game.
- There is an issue of glitching through the game, as well as glitching into specific objects at certain intervals.
- Clunky movement system, wherein the player hitbox seems larger than the player himself.
Overall: I would recommend this game to anyone I know, due to its completely unconventional nature in that you are the one to shape the game world and bend it to your very will.

-While controller support is great, keyboard support is non-existant (in the sense that controller 'labels' are the only option)

brings, when it comes to local versus

I enjoy the art and design ideas expressed in the game a lot, but I'm hesitant to show of this game to friends at parties (where I most often play local multiplayer games) because introducing all the mechanics is a frustrating, time-consuming process.

Ah the X Series. I haven't heard anything good about rebirth the latest installment to the series but this review isnt about that. X3: Reunion Was the game that turned me on to the whole series. In fact just thinking about it now is making me want to sink even more hours into a title i have already sank more than what would commonly be called healthy gaming. Once you get past the steep learning curve and learn how to fly and fight and trade effectively, this game suddenly turns into how you would want to live in a future that affords you your own space oddesy. Space suddenly turns into your own playground and you become immersed in a universe that is fully dynamic.
With that said i think this title, X3 Terran conflict and X3 Albion Prelude were accidental. Terran conflict takes place after the events of this title, and adds a Major graphics overhaul. And prelude again expands on the story of Terran conflict as well as this title adding features and interfaces that were touched on in this title but done poorly. It is pretty evident the beauty of this game and the other X3 titles is the immersion of the struggle you are put through to learn, and adapt to the changes that happen around you all while getting the sense of achievement from overcoming and growing from the experiences you encounter.
What these games lack is a sense of person however. You sort of create a character or take on a storyline however you rarely interact as that character. You never really see the character and the universe usually refers to you as pilot. In Reunion, the main story you play as julian brennan. working along side Elena Kho. Trying to find your place in the universe. There is an extensive storyline and it all seems to fit very well all things considered.  The other characters however offer a backstory as to why you start out where you do, and how the other races react to you in the beginning.  Ultimately it defines how difficult the game is in the beginning to get started. Once you get on a roll however and you grow all plots start and play out no matter who you play as with the exception of Julian's plot. his has a little more frosting so to speak. Otherwise its all essentially the same. Reunion is also of the three X3 games that has a main character. Terran Conflict and Prelude do not feature main plot character who playing as change the dialogue or offer any additional content.
Pros:
Dynamic Universe - Everything you do or not do effects the universe in some way.
Rich plots - The back story to each of the plots are very compelling and their rewards give a strong sense of achievement
Diverse spacecraft - Each ship has its own classification as well as strength and weaknesses. Even some that are unique and rare.
Races - Each race is unique in its own way and their ships fit the typical role the races engage in.
Fleets - You can build, or buy your own fleet and wage war against anything within the universe, ofcourse doing so will have consquences such as you may end up destroying something you want later. The good news is there is one race you can attack and murder with extreme prejudice and not have to worry about losing a future trading station.
Cons:
Voice acting - Its there but at the time this game was released other studios did it better.
Races - While each race is unique there is nothing unique among their individuals. Humans however occasionally have diversity among males and females but you will be hard pressed telling a male or female split, paranid or teladi.
No planetary exploration. The planets in each system are just there to look pretty it seems.
No station exploration. Each station you only dock at and interact with through the ship.
From what i understand Rebirth attempted at affording planetary and staion exploration however at the cost of starship diversity. Further more these features were not done well and as such losing the ability to fly and construct a diverse fleet was too great of a sacrifice against bland cookie cutter stations.
It sucked.

- as being the first game in the titular series - is one of the early examples of the dynamic change in HOGs, presenting a nonlinear environment and a decent story. The game was developed by Gogii Games in 2009, and its age does little to worn out the naive beauty of the setting and the unconventional gameplay. It still is a very good purchase.
Crown princess Isabella returns to Castle Greystone for his marriage to Prince Adam, only to find the castle in ruins, all rooms cursed and the royal family trapped in mirrors! She is quickly joined by her fairy companion to investigate the matter, while collecting pieces of mirrors to save royal family and undo the curse if possible. All witnesses speak of a vile witch visiting the castle and putting a curse over the land, yet torn pages from our mother's diary indicate another forgotten secret to be uncovered. As being a trained magician herself, Isabella travels within the castle, solving puzzles, collecting mirror fragments and lifting curses over rooms. Will you be able to face the witch and save your family in the end?
Plot explanation aside, this game is a classic for the HOG genre. Art works and character designs are a beauty, even though they've been aged in the digital era. Voice acting is more than decent, bringing a vivid side to the whole setting. The storyline is actually curious, with a nice plot twist by the end. Sadly, the Steam overlay doesn't work, and the game has no achievements or such due to its age.
Gameplay is basic HOG; collecting items and solving puzzles. Neither HOG scenes nor puzzles are actually challenging, but there is a logic presented in all HOG scenes - which was new at the time. We use most of the items we collect through HOG scenes, either for puzzles, or concocting potions to lift curses. The ending scene is unique in the HOG genre, by presenting a boss battle - a timed HOG challenge between you and the AI - which was never used in any other game aside the series in the genre. Map has a teleport function and you are declared when you complete all there is to do in a room, marking it as cleared. By the end, the game presents you 2-3 hours of clean cut fun.
Princess Isabella - aside being a bit fluffy on the tone - is a good purchase for all casual gamers and a must have for all HOG lovers. The last game of the series,
has just been remastered by Artifex Mundi, possibly upping the quality of gameplay a couple notches. I strongly recommend the series as a whole.

You pick up loot that doesnt even effect anything and you are still using the combat mechanics from zelda. You get gold drops but gold is useless and cant actually be used for anything.
The story is laughable. Its so crap. I can't imagine what the devs thought when they cobbled that mess together. Maybe it was the day before release and all the writers has hangovers so they got the janitor who played an rpg once like 20 years ago to finish the story for them.
You get a map finally during this section but nothing else happens. The boss fight here is just as lame and uninspiered as the rest.

You get beat for the first fight and your compainion dies *spoilers but who cares*. You get an airship to get to where the boss moved to because reasons, and fight in a zelda type boss fight. I can't understand how they were able to think of such an awesome concept for the game but didnt have a single good idea other than that. I pray I see this idea take shape from devs who are actually talented.

A hidden-object classic, with lush, gorgeous graphics, excellent hidden object scenes, and fun puzzles. The story is a derivative cliché, but it's lovingly presented, with delightful voice acting and animations.
The only problem is that the low resolution makes it hard, sometimes, to identify objects sometimes in hidden-object scenes. Also, it's rather short. But that's petty criticism: fans of hidden-object games would love this one!

A mindless way to relax for a few hours. Get it on sale and the cost-value makes it an apparent worthy choice if you like hidden-object puzzle games. The hidden-object elements and the puzzles are not overly complicated, and both in terms of interface and theme/plot I would rate it as a children's game. Still, even for adults it is what you might call a "cute diversion."
The audio effects are acceptable if sometimes arcade-ish, and the music score is decent if not great. The interface is simple yet functional. The graphics are about on-par with my experiences with other hidden-object games - not mindblowing, but not ugly. Functional system all around. There is a (mostly, see below) unlimited help/hint system, and the game has the feature of a map that lets you move to any area without having to transition through the various screens normally associated with travel in adventure games. Neat feature.
There is one puzzle toward the end of the game that is "real-time" action-oriented and basically an arcade-style click-fest - not my idea of fun or something I think belongs in an otherwise relaxing adventure game - but people from the console generation might not notice as out of place. I could not finish the game because of it, but as I picked this up for a dollar and for that it was a few hours of mindless entertainment, I cannot rate is as "unrecommended" because of that flaw.

TL;DR - Would highly recommend, especially as a sale on the game+DLCs. The whole thing is very good and easily worth the time and money. 9/10
A genuinely good 4X game that started off novel and interesting but a little barebones but got quite fun and fleshed out after a few expansions. The DLC feels a little like finishing the game post-release but it doesn't feel like too much of a cash grab and really fleshes out the experience. It has its flaws for sure but it has a lot more going for it that's good than bad.
Pros:
-Very solid and intuitive UI; right-clicking to exit stuff felt natural very quickly and makes flicking through menus a breeze
-Visually very pretty; it has a unique art style that it depicts very well
-Music is good, if a little unvaried after 50+ hours
-Research on the whole feels good; a lot of variety and choices in it feel meaningful, though it might rrub some people the wrong way that no research has prerequisites
-Story and setting are incredibly deep and unique, if you care to read anything beyond mission objectives
-Solid variety and number of races/factions and each is very unique (with the exception of one that's just a pallette swap)
-I've had very good load times, for the most part
Cons:
-No mini-map, which gets frustrating on larger maps
-AI can be kind of a dink about stuff (declaring war for basically no reason, killing your units just because, refusing to even consider diplomacy with you because you killed a bunch of people...), but that's nothing new to 4X games
-Some races feel blatantly more powerful than others and some are very dependent on map type and player placement, which for the most part is fairly random, causing you to remake the game in the hopes that this time you won't get screwed
-Remaking games doesn't have a button in the menu
Mixed:
-Winning with Dust is extremely easy, to the point of it happening to me twice by accident
-Combat can feel either strategic and important or tedious and frustrating; auto-resolve will work most of the time just based on army strength but you can out-tactics the AI and/or get screwed on the RNG rolls in manual fighting
-There's no backing out when you attack someone (though they can flee from you), so a bad click or poorly planned attack can ruin your day
-Super easy to breeze through missions without paying an iota of attention to the story behind them because of how comprehensibly the objectives are outlined
-The game really comes together only with DLCs
-Customizing units is neat but tedious and only having four base models per race (sort of fewer in a couple cases) really limits how much variability there really is

This game is fantastic. It is everything Civ V is and more, so much more. It has depth and flexibility that Civ is still lacking to this day (even with the release of VI, which included some features Endless Legend has had for 2+ years). The espionage system is actually really neat and includes some really useful things to help handicap other factions.
The battle system is possibly the most fun (although lengthy) part of the game. This game features unit-stacking armies which you can combine with a hero, but when battle starts it breaks all the units and lets you position them and choose their targets at your whim. This adds a great layer to strategy as certain terrain offers different bonuses, and setting up your units intelligently can make all the difference in battle. You can also equip your hero (and units) with items, upgrading them as the game goes on to further increase your power.
It truly offers unique, repeat play as each faction has unique units, bonuses, and playstyles that completely change the way the game is played. Additionally the minor factions are actually useful, each mini-faction providing you a new unit and bonus if they are assimilated into your empire. Combine that with a neat little quest system, amazing tech trees, great lore, FANTASTIC music, and you have easily the best strategy game available at the moment.
The graphics are beautiful and the ability to scroll all the way out to easily locate resources, units, and borders is a great feature as well. Honestly there are so many positive things I could go on all day. In terms of cons I would say that it is certainly a lengthy game, manually controlling the combat can really add up over time, so it certainly isn't for the faint of heart. At the same time turns generally progress quickly and you are not forced to constantly manage your units/productions so you can move the game forward fairly quickly.
