CT Special Forces is a 3rd-person shooter games released in 2005 for PS2 and PC.
The game has hybrid of stealth and action gameplay, you can choose your style doing your missions.
Pros:
- Two playable characters with good personalities each has their own gear and gadgets; different playstyle and gameplay.
- Story is alright, nothing mind-blowing though, but not a crappy one either.
- Game is fast-paced and fluid.
- Dozens of different weapons and grenades types.
- Unique gadgets and hi-tech items. Seriously there are many I've never seen before (i played tons of stealth games)
- Multiple vehicles to ride.
- For a PC port of an old game, the game is very stable and has a good launcher.
Cons:
- Many common wide-screen resolutions are not supported.
- The checkpoint system. It doesn't save before the hard parts, and sometimes there is a long distance between 2 checkpoints.
- The last boss battle is a joke. really easy and lame.
- Game runs a bit faster than normal on modern PCs (~x1.5), but not a critical issue, i had no issue with it in the whole game.
- Many level-designs are more advantageous to the enemy more than you to the point you easily get killed because of bad position.
- The A.I is random. Sometimes it's alright sometimes it's stupid.
- Unfairly hard sometimes.
- Expensive
Conclusion:
The game doesn't deserve a $10 price tag, so if you are thinking to get it, go for a sale.
For a $0.99 i say you could give the game a shot if you like old stealth games like Syphon Filter and Splinter Cell.

Metal Gear Solid V Ground Zeroes is only a taste of what the actually game is going to be like. I'm not saying it's a bad thing, it's letting us know that the full game, The Phantom Pain, is going to be much more amazing!
Basically, your missions will take place in a small military base and it's up to you to decide how you want to approch each mission objective and side mission.
The game looks gorgeous on the PC and on next gen consoles. I can't say one bad thing about it. The controls feel great & you can feel the weight of Snake, you can feel the impact of your weapons being shot. And to make this game feel more realistic, Snake can die much easier than in past games, and getting away from harm's way can be difficult too.
You can mark enemies as well to make a more tactical approach. There's also this Reflex feature that allows you to quicky kill/stun an enemy if you were seen. You can turn this feature off if you find that it makes the game easier and gain some bonus points. Personally, I think it works for this kind of game.
Plus I like how they added a Backstory section to help you catch up on the game series if you missed out on some of the spinoff and the 3rd game.
Personally, I love this game, dispite how short it can be, but what makes this game so much fun is HOW you proceed through each mission and HOW you want to get the job done which adds replay value, even if it is just a prologue. If you want to get a heads up of what the Phantom Pain is truely like, in terms of it's game mechanics of Mother Base, give MGS Piece Walker a shot. It's really fun.

Ground Zeroes is a great prolouge to the anticipated The Phantom Pain, though I can only recommend it for a heavily discounted price.
The game is simply not two hours long, in fact, I needed around 6-7 hours to complete all the side ops and go for some unlockables, clocking in still just a 33% completion. Yet the whole package is simply not worth 20€ because essentially it contains just one map with different variations.
It is a shame that Konami didn't put this title in a much better price range, because otherwise, Ground Zeroes plays extremely well both in terms of gameplay mechanics and optimization. The graphics are superb, the controls are snappy and smooth, and the framerate stays at 60 fps constantly. This is an exceptionally good port that other developers must need to take a note of. Just look at those system requirements for a game that comes out in 2015!
The only gripe I have with the game is that Kojima decided to use audio recordings instead of cutscenes to deliver more exposition and background information about the story. Sure, the previous installments of the series contained sometimes needlessly long cutscenes and verbose dialogue but at least you had the chance to watch something interesting while receiving this information. The Magic Circle is a saterical story-driven explorative game about you (the player) play testing a game being developed by an egotisical game designer who is never happy with his work. I had pretty high hopes for this game. The trailer was pretty funny and I liked the overall concept, so I preordered it while it was on sale. However, there are some major gameplay issues that have made OmniBus one of the most frustrating games I've ever purchased. (I do realize that OmniBus is *supposed* to be ridiculous and perhaps even mildly frustrating by its very nature, but there are several *unintentional* issues with the game that severely limit its enjoyability.)
First, and most importantly, are the mid-air controls. The primary challenge of OmniBus (and, theoretically, the fun) is in recovering from the wild arcs that your bus takes through the sky after it's launched to the stars by bumpers, ramps, TNT, and more. However, the way the controls are oriented makes the bus almost impossible to land safely, leaving your bus's fate up to chance. The issue lies in the fact that the left/right keys (and A/D keys) cause the bus to do a barrel roll in either direction. A more intuitive approach would be to make the aforementioned keys rotate the bus horizontally around the X-Y plane. I also recommend increasing the rate at which the bus's rotation accelerates in the direction the user chooses; right now, it's extremely difficult to influence how the bus lands.
Second, the physics engine is bizarre. I know, I know, weird things are supposed to happen in this game, but there are still obvious glitches that make no physical sense. For instance, oftentimes when my bus is on only two if its four wheels for a short period of time, it gets launched into the air without warning. Hopefully these sorts of problems are fixed relatively soon as players report them via reviews and the Google Form the devs provided along with the release.
Third, many of the levels are poorly designed. For example, the bandit level (in which you have to knock over 9 bandit vehicles before being knocked over yourself) can be won by doing absolutely nothing and just letting the bandits run into you; they often tip themselves over as they collide with you, and when *you* get tipped over, the bandits keep running into you, which turns your vehicle upright. Another example is the train robbery level, in which the bus falls straight through the train tracks that bridge various plateaus.
Fourth, the way the camera pans at the beginning of each level can be dizzying. Plus, there are often situations where skipping the camera pan offers a major strategic advantage at the beginning of a level, but there's no indication to the player that the pan is skippable (which it is by pressing the spacebar).
Most of the issues I described above are very fixable, which is nice. I'd happily give OmniBus a thumbs-up if they were fixed - it isn't far from being a highly enjoyable game.

I am a LONG time fan of turn-based 4X games. I played Civ I and II to death (never cared much for III, IV, or V though) and I still play Master of Magic and the first two Master of Orion games. As a 30 year fan of the 4X genre, I've really tried to like this game. It has some really interesting ideas as well as some stinky little quirks. I originally gave the game a thumbs down review, but I think that does it a bit of a disservice.
My biggest issue is the way the game begins. Like all 4X games that are based off of resources, building your first city near the game's special tiles (called anomolies) is really important. Unfortunately, in Endless Legend you practically HAVE to put your first city within your first turn's movement range, regardless of the terrain or the presence of any decent place to start a city. If you can't get to a decent location, you are pretty much forced to restart the game, which is complicated by the utter lack of some sort of 'restart' option. Other games of this sort often use a ctrl-n to restart with the current game settings on a new map. Another option would have been that the game would remember what the last settings were when you started a new game. For some completely inexplicable reason neither option is provided, so if you get a bad start you have to reset everything manually to start a new game with your last settings. In my first 50 hours of play time I got a grand total of two starts that were worth playing beyond the first turn. There have been many occasions when I've tried to play, but instead quit to play something else after spending a boring 15-20 minutes restarting over and over.
The second issue is the combat system, which is pretty strange. The stances are about 1/3 implemented. The Defensive stance shouldn't ever be used unless auto-resolving the battle against a superior force. Why would you do that? Battles have to be resolved within six turns, and a little randomness when calculating outcomes can allow some of your units to avoid engagement long enough to survive what would normally be a total defeat. It shouldn't ever be used in a manual fight because there's no way to tell where a unit in Defensive stance might try to go, which can really screw things up. The Aggressive stance isn't much better. Whether auto-resolving or manually fighting, it should only be used when your forces can overwhelm the enemy quickly enough to prevent any of your units from getting gravely injured or killed. The issue with the Aggressive stance is that when an aggressive unit's target is killed by another unit, it often dashes forward in bloodthirsty mindlessness to attack a different target, giving the enemy a prime opportunity to kill them. If the two forces are somewhat close in strength, you should manually fight and almost exclusively use the Hold Position stance. Units will only move where you tell them to go and they'll stay where you put them, allowing you to employ effective tactics and battle formations. Since the Hold Position stance is the only practical choice for nearly every battle, it makes you wonder why the hell the other two stances are even there.
The game map is beautiful. It has a very contemporary art style and is covered with sparkly anomolies and glittering ruins. One of the biggest strategic decisions you'll make during the game is how to best take advantage of the resources on the map while also expanding your cities in an efficient manner. City tiles will level up and become more productive if properly bounded by other city tiles. This means that there are really only a couple of efficient city configurations and the trick is how to use those configurations while also taking advantage of the most resources.
There are quite a few different races available and they all feel distinct from one another. They each have a different 'story' that is uncovered via the completion of missions. Other missions also appear regularly and are generally enjoyable, though some are so ridiculously difficult or expensive, or the reward is so meager, that you'll wonder why anybody would ever bother with them.
The tech tree is large and quite complex. Knowing when to research the technologies necessary to solve a particular problem or meet a specific objective can literally determine success or failure, though the beginning techs are so foundational that you will seldom deviate from researching them in the same order from game to game.
The way the season changes is rather unique to Endless Legend. When Winter comes, the effects are quite dramatic, lowering production rates and slowing movement on the map. If unprepared, Winter can be financially devastating, though some of the races are affected differently than others. It is an interesting mechanic, although I have to admit that I don't really like it much.
Managing the output of your empire through the manipulation of tax rates and city production is also quite complex. I can't help but compare Endless Legend to the Civilization games. In Civilization you typically have four things to juggle... food, gold, science, and production. Endless Legend has you juggling what they call FIDSI... food, industry, dust, science, and influence. It feels like it is a lot more complicated to keep everything working well in Endless Legend than it is in other 4X games, but it could be that I just need more experience with it. Both games also have a happiness mechanic but the one in Endless Legend is absolutely brutal. Unhappiness can literally bring all your growth and production to a halt, which means you have to closely manage your expansion. The pacing also feels slower in Endless Legend.
So, if you can get a game started, and you know about the uselessness of 2/3 of the combat stances, it can be quite enjoyable and satisfying. As a result, I've decided to change my original thumbs down recommendation.

I've been playing this game for long enough I feel I can give a decent recommendation.
Kings and Heroes scratches a very specific itch when it comes to dungeon crawling and loot that only a few ARPG type games can do, but Kings and Heroes is more than that.
The game is attempting to be an MMO type where you can group up with as many as 8 players to tackle dungeons at one time with loot distribution in a round robin function.  The majority of the equipment you'll find won't be an upgrade, but it can be broken down or sold to work towards crafting that perfect piece of gear you need.
Early Access in Kings and Heroes will see you disconnect / crash from the game here and there, but it doesn't take long to get back into the action.  Not all crafting materials / plans are implemented, but what is there is enough to get you started in the world.  There isn't any story to be had yet, but the devs do a weekly chat on twitch where you can keep up with what is in the pipeline.
Can't wait to update this recommendation.

This game is a dungeon runner with a twitchy combat system that makes the game very immersive during combat. It's loot based and rogue like with a D&D influence. The dev team is active and communicative.
Graphics and effects surprised me positively and the artwork is downright impressive in some areas. The game is already quite optimized with decent frame rates overall but atm it suffers from minor stutter when you change zones in the open world. This is however a minor issue that surely can and will be fixed. There is an initial asset load when entering a zone but the LOD system seems good.  I currentlly use i7, GTX1070 and 16 Gb ram
The game has a large open world area with multiple planned cities and open world dungeons. Once these are implemented they will provide the game with diversity. The open world is populated with various npc species that can be hunted for xp and loot but at the time of writing the area is still work in progress and the world map shows the scope of development which seems quite impressive.
The crafting system is good and feels like a worthwhile activity. It's neither too difficult nor too easy to master. Drop rates are "just right" and the crafting system complements the normal loot perfectly.
At the time of writing the game has no tutorial so here is a mini tutorial for new players:
1. go to the tavern and talk to the bar maid who will give you a few coins (founders get a horse by the stables at the city gates)
2. sit down at a table and set up a dungeon.
3. try to survive for as long as possible picking up loot as you go. check regularly if the stuff you got is better than what you are wearing. (founders get an auto loot stone from the demon by the statue)
4. once you get back to town sell the unused items or salvage them at a crafting station for materials used in crafting.
5. rinse and repeat ad nauseam :)

For help with crafting and other issues ask in chat. The community is helpful.

So, I don't even know if it makes sense to give this game a review - because it's basically unfinished and in Early Access, but because it is being advertised as a "playable game" despite it's ridiculously unstable state, I thought I'd write this quick "Gotcha list" to make you aware of the things you might face if and when you buy this game, and try to play it.
Keep in mind, these setbacks will fade away with future patches (hopefully) but when they'll happen is unknown and chances are if you purcase this game, you'd want to play straight away, and not wait 3 months for stability.

Bad

I can tell you now, the "bad" section of this list will get to you so much, that you'd more than likely say "f*** it! I'll just wait till more stuff comes out or they patch it some more". However, this game has a sort of addictive quality to it.

I know that it's in Early Access, but there's nothing more annoying than going through a dungeon for almost 45 mins, getting to a major boss and FREAKING CRASHING...

In a medium saturated with guns and fists, Oh...Sir!! provides a refreshing take on nonviolent combat that is well worth the asking price.  The game takes the skeleton of a typical fighting game and replaces precision reflex button presses with turn-based sentence construction.  It then surrounds this mechanic with lovely pixel art and all the absurdist humor and briticisms of Monty Python.  In fact, the direct references are so prolific that at times the game reads like an experimental sketch from the early years of the show.  And while the intentional silliness is a selling point, it does represent a missed opportunity for linguistic depth.
Oh...Sir!!’s core gameplay finds you constructing insulting sentences by linking object phrases, like “your mother”, with descriptive phrases, like “is getting fat”, and stringing those together with conjunctions, primarily “and”.  Both players alternate picking one sentence fragment at a time from a shared pool to make the best insult they can before the pool runs out and the round ends at which point they speak their respective sentences aloud and deal damage according to the sentence quality.  Further depth of play comes from incomplete descriptive phrases, like “farted on”, that require a second object for completion, and a two-phrase pool that each player has that only they can access.  But it’s the fairly nebulous concept of a sentence’s “quality” that causes confusion.
Imagine my confusion when a more logically coherent and subtly offensive sentence would give paltry damage, while a completely incoherent and irrelevant statement from the computer would win him the match.  Surely implying that my adversary’s spouse was having an incestual affair is more insulting than saying their “sense of style changes into a hovercraft”, right?  Further obfuscating the issue, I received a grammar penalty for a complex, but technically grammatically correct sentence.  It wasn't until I saw a hint on a loading screen essentially saying "funnier insults do more damage" that the nonsensical phrase options like "hovercraft" clicked into place: weirdness is a major factor contributing to the “quality” of an insult.  In this way, the subtitle of "Insult Simulator" is meant to be taken with the same irony one would expect from "walking simulator" or "Goat Simulator".  You see, while there are some systems to account for the freedom and magnitude of language (i.e. changing new phrases to match the tense and plurality of the existing sentence), the game almost never accounts for rhetoric or the full extent of english syntax.  Scoring is based on sentence length and very broad situation and character specific cues.  Combos for extra damage are strung together by including a phrase in multiple consecutive insults.  Oh...Sir!! isn’t trying to accurately simulate the refined craft of arguing exclusively with ad hominem, it’s trying to make a video game with arbitrary video game systems.  In other words, Oh..Sir!! rewards an understanding of its own invented mechanics while punishing an understanding of the underlying mechanics and creative usage of language.
This is not to say that this focus on the wackiness of randomly generated insults is a bad thing.  In fact, in many ways it is a good decision.  For example, the more universal humor of a nonsense statement broadens the appeal of the game as increased linguistic depth might’ve made the game unreasonably difficult for people who lack an affinity for writing or rhetoric.  And the endearing aesthetic of the stiff and off kilter british caricatures definitely fits with their absurd, fractured remarks.  It just means that the game sacrifices certain interesting design possibilities.  Like, what if instead of each character having a full hypothetical set of siblings, spouses, children, and parents, they each had a unique, personal family history (perhaps akin to the generational system in Rogue Legacy) and maybe an insult about a person’s gay uncle could strike a nerve with them?  Now that could really sell the fantasy of being just a real ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a silver tongue.
In any case, Oh..Sir!!: the Insult Simulator is well worth the $2.

In Oh... Sir!!, you and an opponent take turns picking words out of a pool to craft very British insults to hurl at each other. Each player also has their own small, personal pool that only they can see/select from. It sounds simple, but there is a lot of strategy to it. Some verbs stand on their own ([your face] [is dull and ugly]), and others require a second noun ([your son] [secretly adores] [elderberries]). There are only so many nouns in the pool, so don't pick a verb that requires another noun if that last noun is going to disappear before you can grab it! There's also the very valuable "and" which allows you to create longer insults, special enders ([you posh fopdoodle!]), or "..." which allows you to carry your partially crafted insult over to the next round. You can also net bonus damage by performing combos (using the same noun multiple rounds in a row.)
There are multiple playable characters, each with their own unique phrases and weaknesses (Triggers?). One character takes extra damage from fat jokes, whereas another character can't stand his sense of style being insulted. There are even two guest characters; Lo Wang from Shadow Warrior and Serious Sam.
Game modes include quick matches, a tournament mode (like arcade mode in fighters), and local and online versus mode. There's quite a bit of fun to had for the price of entry.
Oh, and your beloved auntie tells dirty jokes at funerals and donated organs for your cousin's hovercraft, and you can't deny it!

From art to music to creative interactivity The Magic Circle was a delight to play. The story had it's moments of self indulgence and occassionally came off heavy handed but considering the unique narrative experience to be found here I can forgive those moments. Short but sweet.

The Magic Circle is an experiment in control. It allows the player to control certain aspects of the game world that they find themselves in such as enemy capabilities. This is the extent of control that you get as a player but through this limited amount of control you can do almost anything you wish. It's this confinement that breeds creativity. While the writing early on can be a bit awkward the game's story really shines as you find audio logs that flesh out the characters and change logs that show the dynamic between gameplay and art. The only problem I ran into with the game itself was that it was too short, and this just stems from a desire to play more. Overall this game is an amazing look into game design and development hell that can be funny and sad at the same time.

I was able to salvage a version of this game for the Atari Jaguar. It wasn't easy getting my hands on it but.. here is my review of it.
OmniBus is a simple, fun, challenging, quirky physics game that lets you drive an unstoppable bus. There are three modes currently for the game:
First is
which features unique worlds with levels/missions that are very different from each other to complete. There are hidden levels to be found in each world, hidden hats that you can acquire in each level to customize your bus and lastly there are giant evil bosses. Each mission will sometimes provide you with a different bus to use with a unique ability for example a hovering mechanic or a jumping ability to jump across platforms. Each mission also has a ranking system. Finish a mission with the least amount of time to earn the best medal, but let me tell you, it is very challenging and will keep you on your toes trying to go for the gold.
The second mode is
this is essentially the sandbox version of the game which lets you choose any world you currently have unlocked as well as the many different unique buses with abilities you can use. You drive colliding with anything in your path while doing stunts and tricks to get a high score.
Lastly there’s
. This mode is up to 2-4 players. Players get to choose any bus that has been unlocked in story mode along with any hat that has been acquired. Once players have chosen their powerful bus of choice, they are able to select any level to be put up against each other. The objective is simple, to be the last bus standing.. on their wheels of course. It’s up to you if you want to ram other players to make them have a bad day, use the unique ability your bus has to get you back on your wheels or lead them to a bumper and launch them off the stage. The choice is yours.
This as well as finding the hidden worlds and getting every hat in story mode and freeplay mode gives this game a good amount of replayability.
I will definitely try to 100% OmniBus in completion, but in the end I had to end up getting the Steam version of this game. My Atari Jaguar bit the dust and ended up dying on me.. see?

It's been a while since I've played a game with as much charm and creativity as this one. Though the story mode might be on the short side, every level offers something different. I was surprised by just how much variety there was, with some game mechanics being created for one level only. The dialogue given to you before and after each level is very enjoyable, and the whole game has a great goofy tone to it. Nothing quite like using a propeller, a firework, a jet engine, and a soda bottle to shoot yourself to the moon.
It's not a very easy game, often taking one good hit to force you to restart a level. Fortunately, the stages are short enough and restart quick enough that this isn't really an issue. Though I must admit, having my bus almost jump up and spin around after hitting a tiny snag was frustrating on occasion. Omnibus isn't perfect, but it does have a great feel, especially when your bus of choice reaches over 100 mph.
Though it may be short, there is a lot of replay value here. Each level hides a hat to collect, and there are target scores/times to beat in each stage. Not to mention secret areas to find. Plus, free-play mode is great fun - feeling a bit like a Pro Skater game in a bus. You can even challenge up to 4 people to a split-screen bus deathmatch.
In short, if you're looking for a few solid hours of silly fun, I'd totally recommend this one.

This game is absolutely nowhere near perfect, but I'm finding it to be very entertaining.
Basically the premise is that you're Omnibus, a bus that endlessly accelerates with no brakes that must travel the world, completing challenges and helping people along the way. Yeah, everything about this game is kinda ridiculous but it's actually incredibly funny and charming as a result.
Here's the deal though, if you're not into the whole "whacky physics challenge" games like Surgeon Simulator or QWOP where part of the entire challenge is just fighting against the game, then you probably won't enjoy this much. Your bus can go flying at the drop of a hat and there's a lot of wrestling with physics and trying to keep your bus under control which can quickly go from funny to maddening. I've gotten stuck on a couple levels and felt quite frustrated, but in the end they don't take too much of your time to play and when you beat them it feels very satisfying, as a challenging game should.
Now what's crazy is how incredibly creative the devs got - so far every single level has presented a new, unique challenge from anything before it that is still very fun and interesting, whether that be driving in a top-heavy tour bus trying not to tip over and lose your passengers or driving up the side of a building to knock King Kong off the top. It's very hard but addictive, and the ridiculous stupidity of it all just makes it that much better.
With the fact that each level has a gold medal that you can shoot for and there's a local multiplayer mode that looks kinda fun, I can see this game having a ton of replay value, and I'm definitely happy with my purchase. If it looks interesting to you, I say go for it, you'll get a sense of the game pretty quick and you can easily refund if it's not your thing!

Bringing most of the unique races from AMPLITUDE's other Endless games gives this civ-style 4x game a far larger world of strategies than most games in this genre. I highly recommend this game for the interesting lore and visual designs alone. The fact that each faction plays quite differently, with many having their own unique mechanics, is why I enjoy playing multiple matches without falling into a "general strategy".
There are, however, several sticking points. The combat between armies is very slow when played manually, which under many circumstances you will want to do, as the Auto-Combat AI is nothing more than rushing the enemy troops. In fact, that can be said about the AI players as well; though, they can build and conquer efficiently. Turns in the late game can be quite lengthy as well, with sometimes 1-2 minutes required for a 6-player match.
The DLCs are a bit mixed in value and cost, but bundles for them are frequent and serveral add welcome new layers of play to the base game (especially Shadows).
Overall, an easily recommended game, and the upcoming expansion may improve upon it again.

Endless legend is a wonderfully in depth 4x strategy game set in a rich and unique fantasy universe.  There is exploration, diplomacy, city buidling, tactical combat, and so much more.  Every playable race feels very unique, albeit some more unique than others.
While Civilization may be considered king of the genre, EL is a much needed breath of fresh air as it isn't afraid to do many things differently, and not just differently, better.  For those coming from Civilization, which I expect is most of you, you should note that this is a hard core 4x game comparitavly.
Endless Legend's strength is unfortunatly its only weekness.  It has far more complexity and inovation than other titles, but it does nothing to ease players into it.  It is by no means the quagmire you might see from something like Europa Universalis, but it is fair to point out that it WILL take some work to get the hang of it.
Overall, each game plays out faster than CIV,  and the multiplayer is actually put together so much better.  While sparse on players on some days, I have never found problems on the whole of finding people to play with.  And even better, if the host has an expansion you don't, you still get to play it.
Overall if you are a fan of the genre and want an amazing breath of fresh air, this is the game to get.  It excells at just about everything it does, and even without expansions it is an incredibly solid game; altough i do recommend getting the major expansions.  The complexity and difficulty arise out of the newness of the concepts in the game and the complete lack of a competent turtorial.  But if you can get over this hump,  you won't be in for an experience on par with Civilization, you will get to play a game that I think is even better.

TL;DR: Even better than what I thought it would be, but some parts of the story are cringe worthy.
Evoland is a beautiful game, and its charm will take you back to the old age of NES, then make you travel through all the evolutions until the PS2 era. If you're born around the 90s or if you've experienced all those consoles before, this game is a must, and I can assure you that you will love playing it.
There IS a bit of grinding to do if you want to get everything at the shops, but it's not so much, when you think about it. It's a rather short game; I spent about 6 hours on it and used a guide only once so I could remember where was a certain place. Difficulty-wise, it's fairly easy; the harder parts are definitely the Action-RPG bits, but that's maybe because I'm a bit rusty. Te final boss was much harder than anticipated, but it didn't feel out of place, so all in all, I liked the curve. The random encounters were way too frequent for my taste, though (I was appy to have them when I was grinding, but that's it).
The music is really nice, it's nothing extremely fancy, but after spending 6 hours in a row listening to them, I haven't turned the volume down once.
The only downside is the lack of creativity in some parts of the story. This is not a game where I'm expecting a grandiose storyline, but sometimes it really just felt like the parody of a game I can't cite without spoiling. The name of some characters will make you facepalm pretty hard, and some plot elements will make you roll your eyes pretty wide.
Overall, though, it's a good take on the classics, and I enjoyed playing it to the end.

I've played thousands of hours with these games. I remember when all the tinkering actually had results on the field, when spending all those hours with the game made you feel good at the end, because the end result was something YOU made.
That's gone. It had been gone for years.
The previous 2 games were absolutely horrendous, and granted, FM 2017 is better than those, but it's still a mediocre game at best.
Every season, there is gonna be a point where your team starts to suck. Every player will turn into useless garbage at the exact same time. They won't follow your instructions, they won't make tackles, won't hit the goal, and every player on the opposition's team will pull something like the aliens did on
.
Blind fanboys will say to this: "Oh, you are so bad at this game, your team had just become complacent, because you are dumb!".
They won't admit that the game has a (very, very drab) system to monitor player morale, personality, and the current level of commitment, and if it tells you that everything is right, everything should be right.
What I think the real reason is the following:
This game must be
hard to balance. They have to make an AI that will result in realistic games in both semi-professional levels, and in the Champions League.
I think it has gotten away from them. They don't really have a handle on it anymore. They can't make the tiny changes to make the end result convincing, so when they've realized the AI will
be as smart as the player, they've decided to pull a blanket over your team's head every year around the same time (the second half of the season), so at least people can't say the game is too easy.
The result of this is hours of frustration, when you will feel like you don't even control the game, like it doesn't even matter what you do, and you are right.
I don't even care about the UI glitches, the animation glitches, the replay glitches, the level of graphical detail in the match engine.
I honestly have no idea what SI is calling "development" between two releases, because this is ridiculous.
So I've let this franchise go. It had been one of my favourite games, but it had lost all the intimacy, all the connection it had with the player. It's pointless now.

Something tells me they did this so you'd have to spend time finding vantage points and tagging enemies. If you had a radar this game would have been 30 minutes long.
It's dark. The story actually confronts the dark side of war and the military-industrial complex more in a single hour than almost any other war game, bar spec ops: the line. Some think it's pretentious or silly but honestly in Ground zeroes I didn't get that at all.
The Fox engine is incredible. To get such good performance even on low to mid range machines really is impressive. I have a lot of hope for the phantom pain because of this game.
I was a little lost having not played the psp MGS games (because really, who has?) The game did have text explaining the events but I think it coulld have done a bit more, maybe a cutscene or a mass-effect style digital comic or something - seeing as the whole point of the game is to get people up to speed and give them a taster, and given the price tag for 1 to 5 hours of gameplay I think they could have done more in that regard.
I have to say, it's very good for what it is, but at £16.99? I'd wait til a sale, which'll probably happen when The Phantom Pain comes out. The idea of selling a demo isn't one I'd want to catch on, either.

Awesomenauts is a highly enjoyable 2D MOBA (as it now says on the store page) which I would highly recommend to many people, not just those who are into online fighting games and other MOBAs.
It has quite a dynamic range of characters, from gangsta frogs to bodybuilding bulls to highly intelligent communist space-monkeys, which all have a wide range of unique abilities. On top of that there are in-match items to buy which can change your playstyle dramatically, allowing for a broad scope of playability for every character.
The main gamemode basics are very easy to understand but take practice to master, so don't get frustrated when you get rekt on your first game. Every character has a class which they fit into, even though it may not say on the cover, and it is important to understand these roles in order to play effectively. Working with your two other teammates is also very important in order to win games.
The steam workshop for Awesomenauts is extremely active with many creative entries of custom maps and gamemode which you can download and try.
In summary, Awesomenauts is a great team fighting game with quite a bit of depth which I would highly recommend.

7/10 as of 11/19/2016
DISCLAIMER
This game has a lot of bugs, and its not quite polished yet with new content coming in still.
I do not include my opinion and experience on this review of PvP,  matchmaking (for dungeons), storyline, mobs, classes, UI, NPCs, and questing.
-
MY THOUGHTS
As I bought this game for $10, I think its worth my $10. I've played this game for 9.7 hours (playtime of posting this review) and I can tell that this game is not perfect.
MY THOUGHTS ON DUNGEONS
The dungeon system is fair, for solo players, you're going to mostly playing on normal or easy difficulty. On easy and normal, everything seems good for a solo player. With a team of players, you'll be able to have more fun, and be able to go through these dungeons easily. I believe this game is great with friends and a group. Dungeons might be hard for new people who have just bought the game if they put it on normal. So I suggest going into easy mode at the beggining when you play.
MY OPINION ON DUNGEONS
It also makes me play more, since I get really far into these dungeons, although some people might find it repetitive (going through the same modeled levels 5 times, and getting to a new modeled level and going through that again also 5 times, etc.). But what really makes me play this game, is by getting good loot from these dungeons, and leveling up to level 50 in these dungeons. If you don't have a goal  in this game, it will be repetitive for you for sure, unless you just play to pass and waste time.
CRAFTING AND MY OPINION
Crafting scales with your level, the max craft level is 500, and the max character level as I have seen is level 50. So you would have to depend on your character's level to craft instead of your crafting level to craft stuff that you want. So this game is pretty linear and static in terms of gear progression other than RNG loot. We have armorsmithing, weaponsmithing, alchemy, leathersmith, and tailor. The other con about crafting is that you can't mutliclass crafting, if you do wish to switch to another craft, you would lose all the progression you made on that craft.
MY OPINION ON THE COMBAT SYSTEM
I love the combat system. It's on par as an "action" MMORPG in my opinion. Mostly every ability is aimed by your mouse which is quite skilled, and every skill is casted from hotkeys, and kind of more challenging to me. And a plus for me is that its in first person! If you're not good with aiming, I suggest that you play as a Champion (melee warrior).
MY THOUGHTS OF THE OPEN WORLD
Currently as of the date I post this review, there is not much in the open world outside of the starter town. Most of the mobs are high level (level ~20), and nobody has really explored it. There's not that much to do there, and I'm pretty sure that the developers will work on that in the future, as of the current point of the game is the dungeoning.
MY THOUGHTS ON GRAPHICS
The graphics look good, I honestly thought it was going to look like a mobile game when I first saw it when scrolling down on Steam. Made with the Unreal Engine 4, this game sure does look good. Nothing there to complain about, other than if you have a weak system, then you might not run this game well on the highest settings at 60fps.
TL:DR - This game is better with a group. Dungeons could become repetitive for some, if you don't have a goal. Crafting is linear, you can't have multiple crafts at once. Combat is more action, and most attacks are aimed with your mouse. The open world in this game feels empty.  Game needs more polishing (the devs are working on that), and I overall rate this a 7/10 personally.

I am REALLY enjoying this game, a real hidden gem that has been under the radar with not much exposure on Twitch or other sites, but love the way it plays and the premise of it.
It is a really nice DNDesque experience, with warriors, clerics, wizards, rogues, rangers, humans, orcs, dwarves, elves, goblins.
It plays a lot like a newer DDO imo, if you have tried that MMO before, better graphics and updated mechanics though.
The game revolves around meeting other players, hanging out in the tavern in town, forming groups and going into a dungeon together, there isn't a huge variety of dungeon types, but the dungeons are pretty huge once inside, and have a nice dungeon crawl feel to them, moving slowly from room to room and killing mages, warriors, skeletons, beasts, and getting loots, tons and tons of loot.
That being said, it is VERY VERY rough and unpolished with tons of bugs and crashes still, at level 1 I joined like 3 different groups and left the game and came back 3 different times and the dungeons wouldn't start until the 4th time I tried and it finally took me into a solo one.
Crashed on zoning more than a few times, fatal error crashes a few times in a few hours of playing, but once you're in the dungeon with some other players and trying to stay alive and struggling room to room crawlin through the dungeon, it really is a ton of fun to find the bosses and get some nice loot drops with good stats.
So if you can get past the bugged out queues, and the crashing, and needing to restart the game a lot, the dungeon crawling and group play and loot of the game are really great for what they already are, hoping they continue to develop and add more to it, that will probably require more people to buy it though, for the $10 sale price there is many hours of enjoyment in it if you love dungeon crawling action with lots of loot, especially with a few friends.

Kinda big review
For those who dislike big texts:
- Yes, I recommend this game right now IF you are well aware that its an Early Access (and everything that this implies)
- Game is good to play alone (or by making groups on the go), but its best served with a group of friends
- Last few lines of the review have a tl;dr version/recommendation; I encourage you read that at least
1: The Crystal Ball (Character Creation)
Pretty. This is something that you can see very well in the screenshots, sure, but its still noteworthy; the textures are well made, the models are good, and the spell effects are neat, albeit simple. The character creation is nice, with a fortune teller guiding you through the whole process, giving a few lore descriptions to races and classes, and the description on which attribute does what is pretty clean and objective. The first negative point being right here: you MUST roll your attributes, until you find something that doesnt outright suck (values go from 3 to 18, and you can get an all <10 roll), or that fits your class well (because you might end up with an 18 Str Mage). Its funny because the fortune teller complains every now and then if you reroll too many times, but this should (and hopefully, will) be changed into a point-buy system.
Customization is, as of now, a bit limited, although the few choices you have do make a difference. I suppose they might expand this area, but Im not holding my breath here.
2: Everdale Village (Entering the Game)
We now hit the second problem: the lack of a tutorial. The game greets you with a letter to tell you where to find the things youll need in the village, but thats about how much guidance youll receive; be it combat or crafting, youll need to find things out for yourself, which may leave some features in the shadows (ie: to run solo, choose Create Dungeon instead of Random Dungeon; the former does not queue you on matchmaking, it seems). The commands are, in general, well mapped, but may require some use to really get them, and you may end up using things you dont want to (blocking is defaulted to F, while interacting/talking is defaulted to G). The map, on the other hand, is quite useful, and makes finding what you need even easier.
3: Exploring (Game Features)
The main objective of the game is, clearly, to scratch the murderhobo itch that all RPers have: you enter a dungeon, kill stuff, pillage their corpses and chests (the wooden ones), then you get out and sell or salvage your loot to get even better equipment to do all over again, but on harder stuff to kill. No mystery here. It may get boring eventually, but this is a game best enjoyed with a few friends anyways. Bonus points that, to get into the dungeons, you have to sit on a tavern table to get your job from an NPC (tables that dont have NPCs work too). As I said before, on the dungeon interface, you have two options: Random Dungeon matches you with other players, and you can run stuff together, and Create Dungeon allows you to choose how hard and where exactly you want your run to be, without the matchmaking part, which allows for solo and closed party runs.
There is also a PvP Zone, which I havent tested yet, which uses the same table interface to take you to its options, which include Capture the Flag.
You can also pick a crafting skill from some NPCs, which are scattered all around the village. All you gotta do is talk to the Master <Profession> NPCs, and theyll ask you if you wanna learn it. Remember you can pick only one, and trying to pick a second one will clearly state that youll lose all progress on the one you had. To craft, you apparently have to stand real close to the Salvage NPC, even though the game says you need a crafting station (which would lead you into the NPCs home to look for it).
The Class NPCs are used to advance your class; with them, you buy new skills, or upgrade the ones you already had.
Speaking of Skills, some of them (but not all, apparently) require that you have certain weapons equipped, like the Champion's Bash, which use the shield.
Also of note, you can buy a horse, and even a pet demon that acts as a bank/vendor. Both are cheap, most likely because of the testing period right now.
Outside of Everdale, there is a HUGE map to explore, although my recent adventure yielded nothing, and I suppose this is something that will be added after the base experience is well adjusted and more stable.
4: Tech
First of all, I just want to remind you that its an Early Access, and Im just adding this part to the review so that you can decide wether or not you can deal with some of its problems. So far, the only big ones Ive found are that sometimes, items may fall through the ground; it IS not optimized yet, which probably will cause heavy stuttering unless your machine is way over the top; and the outside of Everdale has a few places that may trap you, requiring that you use the (already provided at start) teleporting stone. Combat works fine, although skills may sometimes not cast (mainly because you must be still to use them; attacking or walking blocks their use), and interacting with some objects mat require a double click to work.
---
5: Summary and tl;dr
I wholeheartedly think that this game is fine and fully enjoyable as of now, and advise any RPG lover to buy it. As a tabletop RPer, it did a very good job to sate my need for a fix, even though its not the same (and doesnt intend to).
However, if you arent patient, are prone to nitpicking, or if youre simply suspicious of Early Access (no judgement here, its a healthy stance nowadays), hold your money, but do follow this game, because I think it has great potential.

I have been a huge fan of FM since I started playing it a couple of years back. FM2017 is great and frustrating in equal maesure. The depth to the game is fantastic, graphics are improved and it has great replay value.
The frustrating aspects of this game will make you want to tear your hair out.
- Your goalkeepers can be great and completely incompetent in a single game.
- Your strikers are also extremely flaky, missing absolute sitters from a yard in front of the goal, hitting the goalkeeper when one-on-one with him while there is ample space to put the ball into the net .... at other times, the same stikers are almost god-like, scoring with almost every shot.
- Sports scientists, data analysts and other support staff have been added into the game but what exactly is their function and what their important attributes are has not been dealt with.
- Matches can be very frustrating with your side creating several clear cut chances but your incompetent striker (with good attributes) keeps on missing even the most basic of chances while the opposition scores with their only shot on target.
Inspite of all this, FM 2017 can be very addictive. The joy of taking an amateur club from the lower divisions, getting them promoted, winning the league and then the champions league after years of hard work cannot be matched by any other game. The joy in finding great free agents and wonderkids from distant parts of the planet and seeing them develop at the club is one of the best aspects of this game. The moment that your youth academy, was non-existent a few years ago, produces its first wonderkid is a feeling of great pride.
I would definitely recommend this game but be prepared for a lot of frustrating hours spent screaming at your goalkeeper or strikers ....

Whilst the concept is promising, and the art is attractive, Evoland fails to be anything but a bland mess. It starts off with high hopes for itself, unlocking different technologies and gameplay mechanics, but never uses these in any significantly clever way. You unlock SNES-era graphics before fighting the first boss, and 3D immediately after, without exploring any of the pre-3D game eras in any depth, reducing the "Evo" part of Evoland to a lame gimmick.
The game itself is a shallow parody of RPGs, where the only tactics you have during the Final Fantasy sections are "Clink attacks, the girl heals". There is no strategy involved, just pure grinding. Even when you get an attack spell for her, it's completely pointless, as healing will make you untouchable. The Zelda parts are better programmed, but suffer from a lot of technical issues, such as poor telegraphing of enemy attacks, camera angle issues, projectiles blending into background objects (such as fire over lava), poor telegraphing of trapdoors (that will instantly fall away when you are close to them, rather than at a distance where it is comfortable to react to them), and a lack of reach on your weapon, which barely covers one player length.
In general, the camera is too tightly shot, making the player character huge in comparison to the screen, leaving the player to feel claustrophobic even in the most cyclopean vistas. The enemies have very poor attack patterns (the red wizards in particular, whose attack comes directly after they teleport with no antipatory action, and their teleporting away comes directly after that). The final fantasy sections have the random encounters ramped way up, and with no strategy for dealing with the enemies, it becomes boring and grindy almost as soon as you realise there's no way to defeat said enemies apart from bashing them with your sword.
The Diablo area is a huge mess, using the Legend of Zelda mechanics to bitterly jab at Diablo's loot-centric and many-enemy mechanics. It is clear that the game designer doesn't like Diablo, and hasn't played for more than ten minutes. The only way to complete that area is to stay back and use the otherwise pointless combo attack, which locks you into attacking straight in front of you without invincibility frames. I would have liked to have seen a spinning attack, since the game cribs on Legend of Zelda in every other regard anyway.
The final boss is a boring slog, again, too fast and not telegraphed enough for it to feel natural playing against it.
The game had potential, but squandered it by not having any decent game mechanics, or a story that wasn't slapped together in five minutes to brainlessly parody Final Fantasy. If you watch the trailer you've practically got everything the game has to offer.
Stay away from this non-game.

Rubber Ducky and the Rainbow Gun is a fun little action/shooter game where you play as a duck who finds a rainbow gun. You might think "wow, what an awesome gun!" and you're right, it really is!
The goal for this game is to shoot the spikies. But, that's not all. There's also a nice narrative story about the different characters of this game. Like most games, it starts off slow and casual. Then...comes the twist. It didn't take long for things to become challenging and I absolutely love that! Most games have a really slow buildup to the challenging bits but the buildup in this game was acceptable and nicely done.
There are also LOTS of different guns to choose from (which you'll unlock after successfully completing a level). My personal favorites are the rainbow gun, the banana blower and the rocket blarp.
This game looks repetitive and it is BUT nonetheless it's still entertaining and absolutely fun to play. It's not a game that you can complete on the first go because the developer included secrets in each level (I think it was like the first 5 levels or something). Without finding all the secrets, you aren't able to play the remaining levels. That's a nice addition to the game and the secrets are fun to find!
-This game is suitable for all ages.
-TONS of replay value! (because you can unlock additional characters and because of the secrets)
-LOTS of guns to shoot the spikies with!
-This game is casual and you can play it while you eat or even while you're half asleep!

There aren't really any cons for this game besides the fact that it is a short game. But for the price of the game, it's definitely worth a buy!

I was gifted this game, and after trying it out, I ended up really liking this game. It's rude, it's crude, and it's fast-paced. The element this game gives is a turn-based strategy game with a time-limit. If you get stuck, you can drink tea and refill your "word quota", kinda like drawing a card in Yu-Gi-Oh. You have 15 second each turn to choose a word or a phrase to help connect to a sentence. When the sentence is finished, you get to throw it at your opponent and hopefully reduce their health. I do sorta like the grammar feature, where the game knocks you off a point for grammar mistakes, but I do know that there are some grammar rules that are different in Britain than America, and as an American playing this British game, I have been docked off points for incorrect grammar, even though the grammar is technically correct in the States.
The game has a couple problems, though. The amount of insults you can make in this game are rather limited. And not only that, but after a few minutes, the game gets dull, and you may feel like putting the game down and picking it back up later. The game needs more variety in it for the amount of insults one can make, and it needs some more creativity to make it less casual then it already is.
Even though this game has some minor problems, for the price point of $1.99, pick this game up! It's fantastic.

Excellent game! In my opinion, Ryse has one of the best video game stories I've ever witnessed. I would love to see a movie spin off of this. Beautiful graphics too! The game also runs great on my I3 Alienware Alpha, with Windows 10 and 16GB or ram (in case other Alpha owners are on the fence). This works well with the Steam Link too if anyone is curious. I have mine set up wirelessly to my Alpha.

Now that I have invested in a gaming capable desktop (after years of being on non-gaming laptops and sticking to console gaming), I am able to play a game like Ryse, so when I saw it on Steam sale for $5, I went for it.
My impression of the game is that it was fun and engaging enough that I played through the single player campaign. If I knew someone else with the game on PC interested, I would also give the online co-op mode a try. It also has an online competitive mode, but I am generally not interested in online competitive modes.
I would recommend it to anyone that casually enjoys games like God of War, and don't mind simplistic combat like you find in games like Batman Arkham series or Assassin's Creed series where enemies kind of wait for their turn to attack you, you block / dodge, and then you hit them back.
Unlike God of War, although it has some mythological aspects to story, it is largely grounded in human war, so no fantastical powers/bosses, but still you will have sense of going through some pretty large scale epic events and battles.
Ultimately it was a satisfying journey. I am glad I made it.

While some players might find the combat repetitive; I find the combat to be great. Flowing between enemies with sword attacks, deflecting attacks and rolling out of the way is so much fun. Then to top it off with a satisfying execution with great sound effects and yells makes it even better.
What I really like about the combat is its more than just looking pretty with the execution moves; there is a level of depth and strategy to be had. Depending on how quickly you pull off the execution you will get more XP, health, damage, or fill up a bar called "Focus" that stuns nearby enemies. However you can only select one of these to at a time when doing an execution, so you have to choose wisely in a matter of seconds which one would benefit you in the moment of combat.
I HIGHLY recommend playing this on the hardest difficulty that you can select when playing for the first time. The simplicity of the combat might be forgotten just because you are really trying to survive or you know that you only have so much health until you are killed.
If you don't find the combat that interesting you might find this game rather ok, since the bulk of the game is combat. The story might keep you engaged but I wouldn't count on it.
PROS:
+ High production values
+ Very well animated
+ Great acting along with face and motion capture
+ Fantastic sound effects
+ Satisfying combat
+ The game looks amazing
+ The COOP modes are very fun
CONS:
- Combat might get repetitive
- Clunky aiming with spears

There is absolutely zero sound in the entire game, I think that speaks for itself. The gameplay is completely esoteric, tedious, and for me boring. You can't progress much into the game without buying credits and premium, which is gonna cost you more than the game itself! The community of this game is consistent of either trolls, or people who invest their soul and heart into this game, there is no room for fun. I only got to play as a politician without paying 10 dollars for another character (nope), but from my experience there is nothing to do as a politican without any power, which makes the start of the game working to try to have fun eventually. Journalist and artist seem like more fun and open characters from what I have seen, except all you're going to be doing is designing articles in hopes that people will like them. One of the few positive things I can find about the game is the reason why I bought it, it's a very unique idea that could have been done well if the developers weren't in over their heads.
Final Evaluation
-----------------
Pros: Unique idea, Many mediums to interact with the community, Low price ( 99 cents as of this review ), Room for creativity, Realtime simulation
Cons: Lag, poor design, bad community, no sound, tedious, microtransactions, frankly boring

The Magic Circle is a game built in response for some of the issues the indie game scene is facing today. The game tells a story of a game development team stuck in limbo, constantly revising their project and its mechanics. It's easy to see this as an allegory made for creators, especially ones filled with self doubt about their art. The game itself is narrative driven with light puzzles that involve editing the world and its inhabitants. The most difficult part of the game is trying to figure out where you're supposed to go next.
Please don't go into this game expecting a wide explorable world. Play it for an impacting story that features a strong voice cast and a whole bunch of emotions.

Very much a one-shot kind of game with very little replayability, but I've clocked six hours, and could probably do at least two more hours if I wanted to be a completionist (too lazy, sorry). Regardless, it was incredibly entertaining; a first-person puzzler that pokes fun at the game industry as a whole (including us).

In addition, past the first few areas, the writing is god awful. It doesn't seem to follow proper grammar, and if it does, then it's doing an extremely poor job of writing in general. First few areas had funny text, but none past that.
All in all a poor game. I wouldn't reccomend spending your time or money on it.
To the dev: I hope your next game is a hell of a lot better than this.

I was gifted this game, and after trying it out, I ended up really liking this game. It's rude, it's crude, and it's fast-paced. The element this game gives is a turn-based strategy game with a time-limit. If you get stuck, you can drink tea and refill your "word quota", kinda like drawing a card in Yu-Gi-Oh. You have 15 second each turn to choose a word or a phrase to help connect to a sentence. When the sentence is finished, you get to throw it at your opponent and hopefully reduce their health. I do sorta like the grammar feature, where the game knocks you off a point for grammar mistakes, but I do know that there are some grammar rules that are different in Britain than America, and as an American playing this British game, I have been docked off points for incorrect grammar, even though the grammar is technically correct in the States.
The game has a couple problems, though. The amount of insults you can make in this game are rather limited. And not only that, but after a few minutes, the game gets dull, and you may feel like putting the game down and picking it back up later. The game needs more variety in it for the amount of insults one can make, and it needs some more creativity to make it less casual then it already is.
Even though this game has some minor problems, for the price point of $1.99, pick this game up! It's fantastic.

If you are an MGS fan then this game is for you. Not for retail price though. Picking this up on sale when its a fiver is worth it though, but THIS IS NOT A DEMO. Consider it a prequel, of sorts.
Graphically it is quite nice, however expect to get a little sick of the one base you play your missions on. Texture quality is fair, and the animations though odd at times are a significant improvement on previous MGS titles. It's a good port in that sense. There's little animation which irks me, try jumping off something high while diving, Snake will land like a cat. There is a lot of pop-in still, which I expect to be fine-tuned with the next release but if that's a sticking point then beware! Remember they have had significantly more time for MGS V: The Phantom Pain so it will probably be much smoother.
I'd recommend a controller, but you can play the game fine with mouse and keyboard. Everything is responsive and draw distance means aiming is generally suited to your weapons effective range. A quick note: don't try to shift-tab in order to chat to friends, or Snake will pop out of cover.
The main mission is short, if you know what you are doing. Collecting misc items, trying out weapons (the gunplay is solid) and collecting prisoners (all of them) significantly extends the game. Listening to tapes adds a few more hours, and they are generally worth it. Try getting S-Rank on everything, to have access to weapons at the start of missions and you will see the AI shine.
Content-wise it is good value for money (on sale) as you'll have access to lots of cassette tapes exploting the characters of the Metal Gear Solid Peace Walker who are still in The Phantom Pain. You can get Peace Walker on an emulator and knowing it is sort of necessary to appreciate the depth of the character who appear in Ground Zeroes.
The main problem with the game is the price, and Snake trying to be a cat sometimes. Getting the game on sale is wholly worth it, the engine is solid as is the gunplay and variety in misisons because of the AI not being potato (though it still has its moments). If that still isn't enough, then I would recommend watching an in-depth stream on Twitch to get the story down. I would recommend because it, as a game, stands on its feet. For a fiver. A penny more and you, good sir, have been swindled.

I really enjoyed the story. There were a few things that bothered me, but, overall it was done very well. The ending also left me satisfied. It should be said this game isn't based on real life events or history. There are characters that appear that also appear in our history, but they are not accurate to our history. Nero for example wasn't an old man. He died young in real life. Boudica as another example never left the Britain isles let alone invade Rome. If you can look past the historical inaccuracies it is pretty satisfying.
Here is where I start to have some problems with the game. I'm not really a fan of QTE's and this game has a lot of them jam packed pretty much everywhere. If you have an extreme hatred of QTEs then you might want to consider giving this game a hard pass because you won't enjoy yourself. However, with all of that said the combat IS satisfying. Pulling off complex combos to large groups of enemies is a lot of fun. The caveat is that by the end of the game it becomes a bit stale. Make no mistake, this game is not good.
It is, however, a throwback to a simpler time. Back when we didn't google for reviews and gameplay footage before we bought a game. Or we didn't buy games ourselves at all.
My mom got this game for me when I was 12. She didn't know anything about video games, but knew that I liked the ones with soldiers in them. I didn't have a point of reference for what made a good game or a bad game, having never really played any good ones at the time. So she brought this home, and I played it. And it was awesome. Sure, the graphics were crap and the voiceacting was laughable and all that, but right then, as I played it, it was the best game ever.
So I saw it on steam the other day. And I bought it, and played it again. The options-menu contains nothing of use, only resolutions that don't actually exist, no texture settings, and a very confusing key-binding section. The game is poorly optimized, and barely runs on a modern PC. The framerate is too high, which screws up the cutscenes and makes voice-clips play atop one another. The game has a cover system, but it's entirely useless since enemies die in one or two hits, and their AI is simplistic, at best. The controls are floaty and fast, and the gunplay is limp. And it's the best. It's an absolutely awesome throwback to a time where I was a kid, and games didn't have to be any good to be fun.
I don't know if you'll enjoy this one if you don't have any nostalgia for it, but if you're looking to waste a few hours with some fun, dumb, poorly made run'n'gun action, I can think of nothing better to play. It's pretty awful, and I love it for that.

I understand my testimony is not wanted here, so I'll try to make this brief.
The game is a lot of fun. The characters are unique and interesting to play as, the gameplay sessions are intense, and the upgrade system allows each character some versatility.
The AI- mostly encountered in the Bot matches, of course, and also as substitutes for when a human player leaves a game- is very impressive. Now, this might just be because I'm so god-awful at the game, but I for one found the AI to be very challenging, and that it's easy to fall victim to them in an AI match if you let your guard down. If you want to play the game, but your internet is down, this game has definitely got you covered.
The characters themselves are very interesting, unique, and, for the most part, likable. I was particularly in love with Ayla, myself. Each one is fully voice acted. The lines written for and said by these characters are very memorable, and often funny. The vocal performances for the characters are also very well-done and likable. All of them are splendidly varied in pitch and tone, and convey emotion very well; and the vast majority of them are over-the-top in some way or another to help capture the, uh...
standards of Saturday Morning voice-acting from back in the day. Interestingly, these two traits seem to go hand in hand in each character- something I for one had long thought couldn't be the case before I played the game.
The music is great, as well- it carries that campy Saturday Morning feel, yet each track, and the soundtrack as a whole, manages to be genuinely interesting, and carry its own unique feeling- and catchy tune. And of course, in tune with the theme of the game, quite a few, namely the lyricals, have a humorous element. I used to listen to the soundtrack for hours on end without getting tired of it, myself. I found it great music for those hard work days, in particular, as well as for exercise. I'd recommend anyone reading this purchase the soundtrack, also located here on Steam, and place it in their MP3 players, as well. Of course, it's worth checking out the music on Youtube if you want to taste what you're in for; Ronimo uploads a few of its own tracks.
The Dev Team and the fan community is great, as well. Open-minded, yet rightfully scrutinous. They're very supportive of the game itself as well as of each other and any new members. They defend their own, too- I said something unacceptable of one of their well-established fans, they came to the user's defense and instituted the ban I deserve.
So, in closing:
+Fun gameplay.
+Well-programmed AI.
+Interesting characters.
+Predominately good writing/voice acting
+Fantastic soundtrack.
+Great community that looks out for each other.
I'd recommend at least giving the game a try. Make the purchase, play the tutorial and a bot match or two; and let your verdict be made. I, for one, regretted maybe only a relative few sparse minutes out of the 161 hours I've played, and all of those that I remember were on account of the odd rude player or a bot name that triggered my pseudo-PTSD. This probably won't be a problem for most.
In closing, recommended.

My feels about this game shifted as I played it, but the TL;DR version of this review is that if you've played other open world LEGO games before and liked them, you'll likely feel the same about this one.
The longer version is this.
The campaign is fine. The story is no better or worse than the other LEGO games and the corny humor managed to draw a smile and even a handful of chuckles out of me even though I'm a young adult. I'm a huge superhero - and specifically a DC fan - so the settings, the lore, and the characters were fun for me to play around with.
Speaking of characters, this game has all the ones you'd want in a DC game and then some. From the A list to the Z list, there are so many characters to play as. Ever hear of Polka Dot Man? I read the comics and even I hadn't heard of him before playing this. Yet he's in and playable.
The open world was my first bit of disappointment. Gone are the days of a single space to run, fly, and drive around in to pick up quests, save citizens in peril, and unlock collectibles in. Now everything is spread out around a bunch of smaller spaces with their own flair to them. All 7 Lantern Corps home planets are their own hubs with the Batcave, Watchtower, Hall of Justice, and Legion of Doom headquarters making up the rest. It may sound good to have so much variety, but truthfully, it kind of has some drawbacks.
There's this wormhole animation that plays when you travel between hubs where you can't really do much of anything for about 15 seconds. It may not sound that bad, but when you reach the point where you've had your fun and just want to finish the game, it just feels like dead air and wastes your time. 3 of the Lantern planets look fairly similar to one another to the point where it will take a little while to distinguish them from each other mentally.
Next, the controls. Flight took some getting used to in previous LEGO games, but once you figured out how it worked, it was easy enough to complete races and get from point A to B. With this game, I struggled all the way to the last race. The spherical planet hubs are cool to look at in the beginning, but when you try to do the races, the camera will sometimes throw you off entirely which will screw up your flight path and you'll time out your race. I've had to put the game down and walk away for a few days due to getting too frustrated with the keyboard controls in races that required sharp turns. Some vehicles control better than some characters, so when they were available, I eventually found the right fit for what I need to do for the race.
Otherwise, I feel I can recommend the game. A good time for the majority of it and some neat fanservice to people who like DC.
