The story is set in 2005, six years after the events of Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake.[23] A genetically enhanced, renegade special forces unit, FOXHOUND, leads an armed uprising on a remote island in Alaska's Fox Archipelago. This island, codenamed "Shadow Moses", is the site of a nuclear weapons disposal facility.[21] The forces that seized this island, led by a mercenary known as Liquid Snake, have acquired the nuclear-capable mecha, Metal Gear REX, and are threatening the U.S government with a nuclear reprisal if they do not receive the remains of the "legendary mercenary" Big Boss within 24 hours.[24]
Solid Snake is forced out of retirement and is dispatched at the request of Colonel Roy Campbell to penetrate the terrorists' defenses and neutralize the threat.[25] Snake is also ordered to locate two hostages: DARPA Chief Donald Anderson, and ArmsTech president Kenneth Baker.[7] Colonel Campbell's daughter, at the time believed to be niece, Meryl Silverburgh, is also held captive in the facility after refusing to take part in the uprising.[26] Snake enters the facility via an air vent and eventually locates Anderson in a cell. He informs Snake of the new Metal Gear REX unit housed at the facility and how he can prevent it from being launched using a secret detonation override code, but then suddenly dies of a heart attack.[27] Meryl, who is held in an adjoining cell, manages to break out and assist Snake in escaping as enemy soldiers are alerted to his presence. Snake then locates Baker. Whilst attempting to free him, Snake is confronted by Revolver Ocelot, who challenges Snake to a gunfight, which is interrupted by a mysterious cyborg ninja who cuts off Ocelot's right hand. Baker briefs Snake on the Metal Gear project and advises him to contact Meryl, whom he gave a PAL card that could be used to prevent the launch; but, like the DARPA Chief, he suddenly dies of a heart attack.[28][29]
Snake then contacts Meryl via codec, and agrees to meet her in the base's warhead disposal area on the condition that he contacts Metal Gear's designer, Dr. Hal "Otacon" Emmerich. As he emerges onto a canyon, Snake receives an anonymous codec call. The mysterious voice calls himself "Deepthroat" and warns Snake of a tank ambush up ahead.[30] Snake is confronted by Vulcan Raven in an M1 tank, but manages to defeat the two gunners and proceeds to the warhead disposal area. Snake locates Otacon in his lab. The ninja reappears, and Snake realizes that it is actually his formerly deceased ally Gray Fox.[31] Otacon agrees to aid Snake remotely, using special camouflage to procure information and supplies while he remains invisible. Snake meets with Meryl and agrees for her to accompany him on his mission. Meryl gives Snake the PAL card Baker gave her. As they head for the underground base, Meryl becomes possessed by Psycho Mantis's mind control tune and pulls her gun on Snake. Snake disarms Meryl and defeats Psycho Mantis who, before he dies, informs Snake that he read Meryl's mind, and discovered that he has "a large place" in her heart. After they reach the underground passageway, Sniper Wolf ambushes them; wounds Meryl; and, after a brief duel, captures Snake.
While Snake is imprisoned, Liquid confirms Snake's suspicion that they are twin brothers.[32] Snake is then tortured by Ocelot,[33] and the player can choose whether or not to give in to the torture. When Snake is taken to his cell, he discovers Anderson's body lying in the corner, drained of blood and looking decomposed for days. Eventually Snake is able to escape his cell. As Snake makes his way up the facility's communications tower, he is ambushed by Liquid in a Hind-D attack helicopter, but swiftly defeats him. As he emerges from the tower onto the snowfield, he is confronted once again by Sniper Wolf. This time, however, Snake defeats and kills Wolf in front of a grief-stricken Otacon, who was infatuated with her. Nonetheless, Otacon continues to aid Snake.
Snake engaging Metal Gear REX
Snake continues on to REX's hangar, while Vulcan Raven lies in wait. Raven, having shamanistic intuition, is able to discern Snake's heritage. He can also tell that Snake is a clone, saying that he is "from another world." Snake and Raven battle it out in a freezer warehouse, which results in Raven's death. During his death scene, Raven tells Snake that the man he saw die in front of his eyes was not the DARPA Chief but Decoy Octopus, a member of FOXHOUND. Raven leaves Snake with a cryptic message of his violent future before being devoured by ravens.[34]
Infiltrating Metal Gear's hangar, Snake overhears Liquid and Ocelot preparing the launch sequence for Metal Gear REX. Thinking he is deactivating it by using the PAL card, Snake activates Metal Gear REX.[35] Liquid then reveals his true colors, having impersonated Master Miller from the beginning of the operation. Liquid informs Snake that his entire mission was manipulated by the renegades to allow the launch of the nuclear weapon.[36] Liquid explains that they are the product of the Les Enfants Terribles project, a government-sponsored effort to clone Big Boss, that was conducted during the 1970s.[37] Liquid explains that Snake received all of Big Boss' dominant genes, while he received all of the recessive genes.[38] He also reveals to Snake the government's true reason for sending him in: the reprogrammed FoxDie virus would kill all the members of FOXHOUND, allowing the government to retrieve REX undamaged.[39]
Liquid assumes control of Metal Gear REX and a battle ensues. Gray Fox suddenly appears and destroys REX's radome and dies trying to fend off the bipedal tank from Snake. Snake destroys Metal Gear REX and is challenged again by Liquid in person. He fights Liquid atop REX and defeats him after knocking him over the edge. He is then reunited with Meryl if the player succeeded in resisting the torture sequence; or Otacon if the player submitted in the torture sequence. They escape through an underground tunnel, while being chased by Liquid, in a jeep. After the two vehicles crash at the tunnel entrance, Liquid emerges and pulls a gun on Snake but suddenly dies from the FoxDie virus.[40] Colonel Campbell, briefly ousted from command of the mission, calls off a nuclear air strike intended to obliterate the evidence of the day's events and officially declares Snake killed in action to stop the US government's search for him in the future.
In a post-credits scene, Snake is revealed to be the one with recessive genes while Liquid had the dominant genes. Snake has an indeterminate amount of time left before FoxDie kills him. Ocelot is revealed to be a double agent for the President of the United States. His intention was to obtain Baker's disk containing Metal Gear's specifications and deliver it to the President, and kill whoever knew of his true motives, one reason for his "accidental" killing of the DARPA Chief.

I rarely give out reviews as it is very rare to find a game worth commenting on.
However, when I went to the store page to pre-purchase Tempest, I was astonished to see that a bunch of Chinese players, angry that the developers had removed their language mod because the mod maker itself was promoting a pirated version of the game. Honestly, I was both astonished and angry that a bunch of players would throw an outright tantrum over something like that.
The reality is that Endless Legend is a shining gem in the 4x community. It is factions that are very engaging and different from one another and a compelling narrative behind each of them. Honestly, I haven't seen factions made in such a way since Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri, which had very memorable factions and faction leaders. The game is also very interesting with the winter dynamic that comes every now and again to test your faction. The winters will continue to get heavier and longer as the game progresses, which ties into the story a bit.
So where does this game falter? Honestly, the combat leaves a bit to be desired. It's completely automated for the most part and you only really direct your armies on a very minimal level. If in-depth combat is what you're looking for, you're better off looking at Age of Wonders 3. Otherwise, it's a pretty solid addition to the 4x formula and I consider it a must have for anyone who enjoys Civilization or other 4x's. It shouldn't come as any surprise that Civ VI is borrowing a lot of the mechanics from Endless Legend given how well they worked.
But yeah, the game is amazing and is nowhere near deserving of a mixed rating. The Chinese players should suck it up and not throw a tantrum because their language mod got removed for promoting piracy. It's a risk you take when the game doesn't have the native language.

I don't know how a game that is only 2 hours long can manage to so thoroughly overstay its welcome, but Evoland achieves it with such ease that even half way through I could barely stand it anymore. The game jumps often from mechanic to mechanic, each time executing its new mechanics even worse than it did the previous ones.
Starting as a clunky, imprecise Zelda clone it swiftly shifts gears into a dull and grindy Final Fantasy Clone, switching back and fourth between the two for a couple dungeons before introducing the worst possible Diablo clone ever conceived. Finishing off, it moves to a side scrolling action sequence for the last boss. The boss itself is dull and predictable, but due to unresponsive controls, tiny hitboxes, and him having more health than god, the fight with only two phases, each only having a single attack pattern can draw out for 20 minutes.
The game wouldn't even be so bad if it were at least moderately consistant between mechanics, but it basically throws everything away when you move to a new section. The bombs and arrows you get in the zelda sequence can't be used in the Final Fantasy section, so you end up just mashing attack and waiting for everything to die. The potions, healing spells and phoenix downs you get in the Final Fantasy section can't be used in the Zelda, Diablo or Final boss sections, something that even contradicts the "plot" of the game. All the "power" you obtain before the final boss, a power which is supposed to help you defeat him, goes completely unused because none of those abilities are available outside of the Final Fantasy sections.

Evoland is game about the history of action-adventure games, with a few RPG elements mixed in.
The game starts as a simple, black and white, 8-bit adventure, but as you progress, you gain more elements such as music, color, 32-bit graphics, and overworld, turn-based-battles, and other elements of action-adventure games. This is by far my favorite part of the game, it's fun, humorous, and is reminiscent of early NES-SNES games. More things elements pile on, such as a partner, NPCs, shops, and currency.
Eventually you gain the third dimension. However, that is when I feel the game takes the most risks, and also the experience starts to dampen. The first official dungeon in the third dimension is frustrating, the combat is slow and ineffective at some points, requiring you to run away, or face having to start over the dungeon. This is probably the most frustrating part of the game, but alas, you get to the boss. The boss is unexpectedly difficult for first-time players. Afterwards, you re-emerge in a new area of the overworld, with new enemies, and HD graphics.
After this, the experience is still slowly dampening.. There is a small required side quest. If you bought an item called the "Fast CD player", this side-quest is much less time-wasting. Without it, the game creates fake loading screens that are nothing but unnecessary.  After this, you access two of my favorite areas of the game, an area where you use crystals to change from 2-D to 3-D, which works as a time puzzle. In this area you gain the bow, which is very useful here, but not anywhere else.
Afterwards, we visit an area which both parodies Diablo and useless items in video games, such as an item that grants +300% damage to walls. Around here I should mention the humor. Evoland, is a very witty game. Making lots of jokes and some of its areas are parodies of other games.  I should also mention that whenever you gain an element, a small text box appears and says a short joke, or a relating commentary of some video games.
The final boss is interesting; it uses mechanics of other games, and puts them into one boss. However, one flaw with this fight is your character's speed. At every other areas in the game, your speed is perfectly fine, but here, you sometimes make the fight too easy or too hard.
There is one minigame, Double Twin, which I find to be great fun, it is a card game, requiring you to use the cards you have found all through the game. Double Twin has around 4 levels, which are all different in their own way, with the opponent using a different deck of cards every time.
I feel lke $10 is a little much for a 4 hour game, but the creators did go for quality and humor for the entirety of Evoland. It is a fun game, I actually recently finished my second playthrough, which I felt was more of an achievement run. The game does have its flaws, but it also has its great moments. Evoland earns a 7/10.

Short, but good. As an RPG, KotOR 1 only has 20 levels, but it has a great flow when it comes to the storytelling and it gives the proper feeling/atmosphere you'd get from a Star Wars game. The class system has a lot of influence on the way you can develop you character as regards to combat and dialogue. And I loved the fact that I, at times, could get bigger bonuses, avoid combat and win people over with persuasion. Quick tip: If you hate semi-turnbased RPGs, then you should stay away from this game. The combat is quite like the combat in Witcher 1 and that means you get a cinematic feel from combat, but your immersion might just go *poof* and disappear.
The game difficulty on normal is a bit dull, if you min-max and play smart, which is why I just switched it to hard. :3
The short time you can spend on the game does leave a bit to be desired, but the plot is easy to follow due to it being a SINGULAR plot unlike fx the plots in the Empire Strikes Back and the Return of the Jedi or the plot in KotOR 2: the Sith Lords. In addition, the plot is finely crafted and was not truncated like the plot in KotOR 2, which is why you get some GREAT twists, climactic sequences and a convincing ending.

If you get the game, then you should get a good deal of single-player fun out of it, BUT BE WARNED: KotOR 2 is a different beast and assumptions that the two games are alike will only be correct on a skin-deep level.
Final words:

Interesting storyline that immerses you in the Star Wars Universe the more you play the game. The ability to upgrade and craft your own weapons and gear, as well as the choices for skill customization make this an awesome individualized experience. There are many ways to direct the story which leads you to play the game time and time again. Good stuff!
This game is a classic regardless of how outdated it is. Great story, so many options for character development, and it's cheap on Steam. If you're a Star Wars fan, then you NEED this.

Clicker games are fun, but eventually you'll get bored once you figure out exactly how to 'min/max' the game engine.. and then all the fun goes away. From reading in-game chat and looking at guides, I can tell that some players are well on their way to doing so with
(
). That's perfectly fine.. in fact, there are a couple of basic things to keep in mind in order to make each run through your quests more fruitful- even if you aren't trying to play scientifically. Some characters are great at getting extra gold, others are great at pure DPS.. I'll leave it to you to decide whether to sort it out on your own or reach out to someone in-game or a guide to figure it out. For now, I'll just say it is a lot of fun to learn how to play.
Instead of just upgrading your assets in a static menu and watching your money increase to crazy values per second,
puts a wrinkle in its presentation by creating quests that your party must complete through various environments. There are multiple areas within each quest and the characters attempt to infuse some plot by speaking to each other and the NPCs as you progress. Further still, you are in control of the party's makeup and formation in the hopes of finding the perfect interactivity to maximize both damage and gold accumulation. For example: the starting fighter Bruenor eventually unlocks a feature that allows him to increase the damage others can do in the same row as he is. Other characters increase damage of characters behind them or in other rows. There are even incentives to have characters surrounded by party members of more than a single race.. or even if anyone is in front of them. Party makeup can get pleasantly complicated.
Gameplay is otherwise pretty standard clickfare. Increase the effect of your clicking, increase the level of your characters, and unlock more characters as you acquire extra gold to do so. If you shut the game down, your party will still fight on and earn gold as long as you are in an active quest when you quit. As you progress, you'll unlock permanent bonuses to your party play through achievements. Also, there are items earned through purchased chests that are specific to equipment slots on specific characters. These chests can be purchased for real world money or through gems earned by killing bosses at certain points during quests. One of the most important things for anyone to remember as they play is the benefit of starting over when stuck. There is a mechanic in play where the multiplier of gold you earn permanently increases the further you get in previous outings. It's known as a god's "Favor" and it is imperative you increase it greatly before taking on the more difficult quests.
There are other features that make
a lot like an RPG. There are menus that allow you to track your achievements and item collections for each hero you've earned. Something else to note: if you've received a duplicate item from a chest, it simply incrementally upgrades the item's effect.. a nice touch. An item shop features the chests mentioned earlier you can unlock to receive these items. Sometimes there will be a special deal available. In a F2P like this there will always be cries of "pay to win!".. and I imagine this game is no different; considering the items in chests directly affect your party's quality. However, since there's no 'leaderboard' or PvP, I don't feel there's any harm in supporting the developers as they maintain the game if you'd like. Chatting with other players is a nice addition and there are multiple rooms to move to if you'd like.. you can also disable chat entirely. There are also News and Changelog tabs to keep you apprised of ongoing developments as well as a place to request support in the GUI within easy reach.
I'm having a lot of fun with this game. I enjoyed messing around with Adventure Capitalist but the additional strategy and lore really flesh out the experience and keep me coming back. He also enjoyed criticizing what the characters were saying inbetween levels as they are all based off of characters from the books themselves and he was very familiar with their personalities. "So-and-so would
say that!" Perhaps he could be brought in to give the script a treatment at a later date!
To sum up, I'm enjoying the experience so far. I think many of you all would too.

The characters are exaggerated and pretentious as well, but not too much. At times I was annoyed by them, and other times I appreciated the commentary the game was making. Overall the story intrigued me enough to finish the game, which only took a few hours. I say The Magic Circle is worth playing through, but I wouldn't recommend paying 20 eurobucks for it. Finished my first playthrough.
I rarely write reviews, but I just wanted to say that, in terms of depth and thoroughness, I’ve yet to play a choicescript based game that matches this one. Usually when I play a choicescript game, there’s some option I want to try, but can’t. Not with Choice of Rebels. the choices are distinct, wide-ranging, and nuanced. With only a couple of exceptions, the characters tend to be intelligent and 3-dimensional, each with unique positions on the geopolitical situation.
The choices have far-reaching and both overt and subtle effects on the storyline , the mark of a great choicescript game, and it was easy to immerse myself in the very well developed world, which was detailed without requiring an information dump and a pronunciation dictionary. (except “Xthanos”, still not sure how to pronounce that.).
Really enjoyed how the magical system worked, and it should give rise to some very interesting scenarios in the sequels.
It’s left ambiguous whether the dieties and the angels actually exist, and what side they might be on if they do, and leaves the reader to determine whether they would be good or evil forces.
Over-all, I’d rank this game as a close second behind Choice of Robots (more due to a personal preference for the subject matter rather than any objective criteria), and I think it has the potential to become #1 in my book, depending on how the sequels turn out.

Definitely one of the better Choice Of games I've played lately! The most important thing in these games is that no matter whether they actually are, your choices feel like they impact the story, and that's certainly true here. Whether I took care of problems myself, or handed them off to someone else, every victory and failure felt like my own.
The world is extremely developed. It's a little tough to get into all the terms and cultural references, but with the handy index, that wasn't too much of an issue, and the conflict starts to really live as a result.
If I'd had to name a con, it's that the characters aren't very developed. You get to know them enough to know their general archetype, but only 1 or 2 get any depth to them. As far as I discovered in my first play-through, there also aren't a lot of romance options. However, those things are clearly not the main focus of this game, as much as managing resources and strategies are. I knew the characters enough for the story to be effective, and that's what matters here.
I'll definitely buy the sequel once it comes out, can't wait!

Awesomenauts is a fast paced brawl type game you can play with up to 3 people in a 2d side scroller. The game overall is one of the most unique games i've seen yet. This game however has so many things wrong with it i just can not find anymore enjoyment. Over the amount of time i've played, i tried each character multiple times and found many things.
There are so many issues with Awesomenauts, it's horrid. There are normal complaints about the game like a typical moba would recieve, but this game gets special complaints due to it's aspect.
This game i would not reccomend if you are returning or first picking up. Please do not. Unless you want to get placed in unfair matches with people who know far more superior tactics than you, you'll be left behind spending hours upon hours just learning the game. The spawn, where you have to control a little ship to collect the currency which is called solar is fantastic, but new players have absolutely no idea what is going on. The patterns are different from map to map, but this also makes it even harder for new or returning players to pick up on. The starting solar allows you to get a what is basically worth a kill. When you die, you lose 30 solar which isn't a terrible amount, but it does really hurt. It effectively puts the enemy team ahead 160 solar ahead due to each player getting 30 solar for killing someone, then 40 extra solar to whoever killed that person, and finally the person that died loses that 30 solar which equals the 160 solar. After a couple kills, say about 5, your team is behind 800 solar. It's insanely difficult to ever come back in a game like this. Just the solar amount is so unbalanced, a single kill can honestly make or break the game.
The match making in this game is borderline OK. If it were to be any worse, i don't think this game would be playable. I'm constantly being placed in matches where people live many miles away, recieving a lot of ping. This causes host advantage. Basically if your not the host, or they aren't close, good luck. Especially with all the debuffs that can be applied to a person, you'll be so locked down, you might as well surrender. Also you can join a game where it will basically be ending. You can literally drop leagues so fast and it would be impossible to do anything about it.
The characters in this game however are fun and have their own playstyle, they're unbalanced. A lot of people disagree with this, but some characters are just a little OP. Characters like clunk, skolldir, and derpl have larger bodies so they have a larger body block potential. This makes large mass characters have a huge advantage, where as people like Vinnie, Gnaw, and Leon much harder to body block. Now i'm not saying Body mass is what makes a person OP, it's just it gives them an advantage. Some higher damage people like raelynn, leon, and froggy, all do massive amounts of damage, but some just do more in general. Vinnie has a very high damage dash that is an AOE which could effectively be x3 damage of it's base damage instead of just 1. Vinnie alone can reach insane amounts of damage. Leon is supposed to be a stealthy assassin, but he really doesn't do a whole lot of damage since almost any debuff he recieves destroys his playstyle. he heavily relys on his basic attacks which is basically leon in a nut shell, but he does about the same amount of damage with his basic attacks as a vinnie. I could honestly make a massive list of just all the unbalanced things, it'd take a long time to make.
TL;DR: Awesomenauts is unique, and fast. It's a 2d side scrolling brawl game supports up to 3 people on either team. New or returning players are heavily punished for not spending time in the game. Matchmaking, majority of the time is terrible, and no dedicated servers. Unbalanced match making, making it unfair for new and returning players to play. Unbalanced characters. A single target damage dealer does effectively 2x-3x less damage than A AOE target damage dealer

Update: Nov 18 2017 (Game just released)
The game is still unacceptably awful when it comes to loading. You watch the world, textures and objects slowly load in around you over a period of 15 seconds every time you load in to a new area
- Corpses fall through the floor preventing you from looting them
- Items fall through the floor preventing you from looting them
- Performance is awful. On medium settings, cant maintain 60 FPS in town (i7 7700, geforce 1070)
- UI still looks cheap and amatuer, especially life bars over players heads.
- Graphics still look waxy and plastic, even on ultra setting. Horrible UE4 usage. When skyrim, a game from 2011 manages to look better all around, something is wrong.
- The tooltip to loot something pops up farther away than you can actually loot the item - very frustrating - Seems to be more prevalent in 3rd person mode
- Every 10-20 attacks or so an attack (mouse click) will become unresponsive, and you wont attack at all
- Doors will sometimes visually shut, even though they are actually open
- There is no way to view info on buffs/debuffs your character gets, even long terms ones. You just see an icon showing that you have something affecting you.
- No details or tooltips on any of the games stats. "Glancing blow" does what exactly? How exactly does deflect work? etc etc.
- You dont drown in water
- Cant rebind the M key for opening the map
- No keybind at all to swim up when in water, and you sink to the bottom automatically
- Movement of enemies in the open world is jittery, often resulting in them sliding or teleporting around
- Shadows (even ultra settings) on water, look like minecraft block shadows. (seems the video "effects" setting controls this. Even on ultra it still is pretty bad looking, just less blocky)
- When headed out of town, you go from level 4 bandits and wolves, to suddenly level 18 enemies that 2 shot you
- Dwarf holding a staff - staff goes through the dwarfs body
Fire Armor should break items around you much faster. (personal peeve)
Trying to find the npc that gave you a quest, after you finish it, is a horrible pain and a huge time waste.
For the most part, the game is much more fleshed out. It feels much more playable. Performance in dungeons is good, but blows in the open world. A LOT of open world content seems to be just place holders. NPCs and locations that are completey non-interactive. The game just doesnt feel done yet, and it really shows.
Overall, the general feel is more amateur than professional game, but there is more fun to be had now, than earlier in the beta. I may leave it installed still and give it another couple hours of play before I decide to put it on the shelf for good.

After actually reading the game description, reading several reviews, and finally playing the game. I have come to the conclusion that a lot of the reviewers do not understand what EA is:
"Early access is a funding model in the video game industry by which consumers can pay for a game in the EARLY STAGES OF DEVELOPMENT and obtain access to INCOMPLETE, ALPHA OR BETA VERSIONS of the game, while the developer is able to USE THOSE FUNDS TO CONTINUE WORK ON THE GAME." Which obviously most reviewers did not read this in the description so I doubt they will read it in my review.  So to anyone considering this game I would say keep in mind, IT IS NOT A COMPLETE GAME.
This game is STILL IN DEVELOPMENT AND NEEDS WORK, in its current state I recommend it as long as you understand what you are purchasing. So if you are looking for a COMPLETED game wait for the official release.

Highly recommend Kings and Heroes.
FPS Fantasy with smooth responsive movement and sweet graphics, Character creation feels D&D based and once you log in its fast paced dungeon crawls. Town is visually appealing and the characters have a range of looks due to armor and weapons appearing different and identifiable once equiped.
Being and EA game not all future features are worked in yet. The "open world" exists out side of town with only a  few random creatures here or there, but, the vastness of the wilderness keeps me exited aobut what is to come.
The Dungeons... only four available to date but all of them are different and unique. Add to that the ability to make five sizes of dungeons and five levels of difficulty and you have the making of a great game.
The Crafting... five unique crafting skill available for you to learn. While not all the materials are in game yet, you are able to craft the highest end armors through boss dropped patterns. The system of crafting does not require complex skill but there a "range" of quality with the highest end version being hard to get.
The Developers... AWESOME!  They are highly engaged, responsive and a fun group who care about what they are producing and listen to the community.
The Community...  the best small group of players in an early access game I have had the pleasure of hanging out with. Plenty of help from high level players with answering questiosn and guiding you through dungeons and helping with leveling if you want it.
Overall I give this game a 10/10 and can't wait to see the finished product.

This has been a really fun game so far... now 3 months.
It is early access.  A lot of the other reviews have criticized the lag and fatal errors.  Those still exist, although the developers are responsive, active on the boards to understand the issues and seemed to have fixed a number of those (most??) in the last couple of weeks.  But I expected the game to still have some issues because it is EA.
Those issues aside, it is exactly what I hoped for... a first-person fantasy game that I can play with friends online.  FPS makes this different from other games that I've played.  The first few levels are HARD to solo.  But once you get the hang of it and a few gear items, it gets better... like most games.
Where the game shines is in a group.  It is face-paced romp through up to 15-20 levels of dungeons with the ability to pick your difficulty level.   It is MUCH better if you know a person or two to play with...
There is an overworld, but there isn't much in it yet.   I'm hopeful they'll be able to build that out a bit more in the future.
If you can put up with a few hiccups in gameplay while it is in development, it is worth the time to give it a try.

I don't recommend this, but only moderately. It has plenty of positives, but doesn't really offer much to the average gamer, even to the average RPG player. You would probably be better served just playing the games it copies (I say "copies" since I don't know how else to describe it, but I certainly don't mean the term negatively): The Legend of Zelda and Final Fantasy, especially. If you've played those (and Evoland mostly assumes you have), just play similar games that take themselves a little more seriously.
Of course, Evoland is not a huge time sink: the whole thing will take 3 to 6 hours, depending on whether you speed through or try to find all the hidden items. It is shorter than it seems, though: the high random battle encounter rate and the tedious level design (which often requires you to go way around scenery obstacles for really no reason) drastically inflate how long the game takes. This is especially true if you want to do the optional goals, collecting cards and stars. The card game, which pretty much just copies Triple Triad from FF8, is pretty fun, but relatively easy and lacks replayability. The stars are pointless: they have no real purpose in the game, aren't explained, do nothing; the only real reason for them being there is to make another achievement and make the game seem like it lasts longer than it does.
The MAJOR flaw with the game, though, is that it undermines its entire premise about halfway through. The "evo" part of Evoland is that you collect "upgrades" that let the game "evolve" from 8bit RPG mechanics and graphics to 3-D design and more recent mechanics. This was the most interesting part of the game, and makes the game valuable as a retrospective of the history of RPGS. About halfway through, though, you pretty much stop collecting any more upgrades. Indeed, the mimicking of other games just starts to happen randomly: the Diablo level is an example, where Diablo mechanics just show up and then go away after the level. Things stop to make much sense. Not that they do for the most part to begin with: often the sequence of upgrades makes no sense in terms of any real history of gaming "evolution." If the game would have stuck with the idea of evolution, making some of the earlier parts last longer (you move from 8bit to 3D very quickly, then get stuck in 3D for about 3 hours without the novelty of upgrades, making the story drag) and exploring the history of RPGs after FF8 (which is where it mostly stops), then it would probably be more interesting.
Lastly, the story is just pointless. At first it's interesting as a parody of older RPGs, and then just becomes absurd. It stops working as a parody and gets cliche and doesn't even really seem to try.
Since it's short, this may be worth playing if you have any interest in the history of RPGs or just like FF7. It is also a decent deal on sale. Overall, though, this is an interesting concept with woefully failed execution.

I've played about a dozen or so of the 'choose your own adventure' games/stories and this one was amongst my favorite thus far. There have been a few examples of these where to call it a 'game' or 'choose your own adventure' seems inadequate in properly describing the quality of the actual writing. This is one of those. This is very well-written, the world building is almost exhaustively thorough (although there is an in-game glossary that is very helpful) and the story is paced excellently. The biggest strength though, is game-based, and that's how well it connects with the player.
There are constant choices that mean you won't be reading pages of text without something keeping you involved in the direction of the story. You will not be told how you're feeling, or what you're thinking, or what your aspirations and desires are--a cardinal sin many CYOA games commit. You will be choosing everything and building your story around player engagement. You will feel real ownership of your character and the state and pursuit of your rebellion, which adds substantial weight to your choices. There is also a very detailed statistics page that introduces a 'reputation' stat that greatly enhanced my enjoyment of the game.
Because this is intended to be the first chapter of a series, the world-building is a very important aspect of the story on which further chapters will be built. However, there are times when an overload of terms, places, people, and colloquialisms are packed so heavily into a few paragraphs that I did not understand what I'd just read. A few minutes reviewing the in-game glossary, accessible at any time during the story, usually cleared up the confusion but was still distacting. The only other thing that bothered me was how heavily the deck is stacked against you right off the bat. It heightened the stakes but I felt it was something that could have been built more gradually. Instead it felt like the author dropped a truckload of bricks on my head the moment I set out. It didn't end up ruining anything about my very positive and enjoyable experience with "Rebels: Uprising" but I felt it was worth mentioning all the same.
I think it's important that the relatively small audience for these games support the truly great efforts that exemplify the best of the genre and this certainly fits the bill. The fact that it is also the first in a planned series makes it even more critical to ensure that we get a continuation of what is a compelling start to a unique and exciting story. Worth the money and then some, let's vote with our wallets. :)

For the first half hour to an hour this is pretty fun, as you constantly "unlock" new game mechanics and improvements, such as scrolling screens, various eras of sound and colour, turn-based battles and 3D environments. This all comes in a quick burst however, and you quickly stop discovering anything "new", leaving the remaining few hours of gameplay as a cheap Legend of Zelda clone with some Final Fantasy elements and a brief Diablo-like section.
At points the game pokes fun at the early days of video games, mentioning the shallow plots and 8-bit music. However, this seems to be a cheap shot, as (even if intended) Evoland has awful plot and music, and even the sound effects that you "unlock" are pretty terrible. As for difficulty, even the game's "completionist" achievements, collecting stars and cards, are mindlessly easy which leaves a rather empty feeling of accomplishment upon finishing everything Evoland has to offer.
If Evoland had continued on as its first hour does, and provided the promised journey through the history of early video games, there would be a bit of potential here and could even make for a quick, fun and interesting game. As it stands though, there's little here beyond the first section, and we're left with a rather boring and pointless offering. Shame that.

I got this game for next to nothing on a humble bundle. When compared to other free to play MOBAs or even the ones you pay for in this range, the game has very little to offer. Classes can get stale and a bit too simple. The community isn't as toxic as other MOBAs, but that's largely because no one really talks.
It plays and feels like a more polished flash game. More mobile than MOBA. Even the music sounds like it's a mish-mash of free sound bites. I will say that the xp progression and the rewards is simple, but it's hard to really get a feel for the game with such a barebones tutorial. It's the typical fundamentals for the people who don't understand the minions/tower mechanics. A lot of the power ups and the levelling system wasn't thoroughly explained, either. They should have explained mechanics that are unique to the game.
I think that another reason why the community isn't toxic is because of how small it is and that one person in the 3 v 3 matches can carry hard. As opposed to team based MOBAs where you are forced to work together, one person can lead you to victory. This isn't necessarily a weak point of the game - it's just the way it is. This can be good for the lucky newbie who gets a great team, otherwise it's frustrating. But the learning curve is certainly fair with balanced classes.
For a paid MOBA, the content just isn't there. It's quite bland, and plays out like a flash game. You'll play it for a half an hour like I did and just go back to SMITE.

I can't recommend this game strongly enough.
I hadn't heard of it, but it showed up in a Humble Monthly Bundle and gave it a shot. I'm feeling so, so indebted to the HB project for getting this onto the radar of more people.
This is a real creative gem. The story and gameplay are very clever and original; the voice acting is superb (aside from a bit of clunkiness from the main narrator here and there), along with the writing; the ways in which you can and must play and think are varied and interesting - breaking the fourth wall and jostling your point of view in unexpected ways; and the weirdness of clashing art styles is pure joy.
It's pretty short, even for someone who is as thorough and ♥♥♥♥-around-y of a gamer as I am, which is my only complaint. It could probably be finished in only a few hours. However, at least the developers didn't do anything to artificially pad the game to stretch it out. It's concise. Also, there's a lot of little stuff to go back and hunt for, and there's something pretty fun that gets unlocked after finishing, so you can still tack on a few hours of play after completing.
I give this one a 9.5. Buy this damn game.

: Crytek
: Crytek
==========
First released as an Xbox One exclusive launch title, Ryse: Son of Rome is a third-person action-adventure hack 'n slash game. It went through a few changes during development, originally being slated for the Xbox360 as a Kinect-only title. After a few different proto-types, however, the game was redesigned into a third-person hack 'n slash with no Kinect features.
Set in an alternate version of Rome, Ryse follows the life of the Roman centurion Marius Titus as he becomes one of the leaders in the Roman Legion. He is on a quest to murder Nero, the Roman Emperor, whose followers murdered his family. Gameplay revolves around Marius using his sword to strike enemies and shield to deflect attacks. Execution sequences are also featured in the game, which are quick-time events that serve as an extension to combat. These QTE are, however, so rampant in the game that it makes gameplay tediously repetitive.
==========
With only a sword and shield (and the occasional turret), Marius must fight his way through literal hordes and hordes of barbarians on his journey. You have quick normal attacks, performed with a quick tap, and the slower heavy attacks, performed by holding the button down. You can also do a quick shield bash, slamming your shield into your foe to stagger them and break their guard. Using a combination of these attacks, its your goal to kill every single enemy that stands in your way. And there are a LOT of them.
As you hack away at them, when they are near death a skull icon pops up over their head. Hitting the correct button at this time triggers a QTE where (if you play with a controller, like I do) you must match the color the enemy briefly flashes to the proper colored button, like yellow to the Y button, to perform a gruesome execution. This can be done for every single enemy in the game if you wish, but it isn't required. The game encourages you to do this though, to earn more points. Proper button presses and timing rewards you with more points. Points are later spent to unlock more health, upgrades, or more gruesome executions.
One other thing about executions is that there are 4 possible rewards you receive in addition to points that you get to choose before each battle (by pressing the appropriate key/button). As you complete the execution, you either get a short buff that increases your damage for a short period of time, restored health, restored Focus, or an increase of points gained from the execution.
==========
In terms of graphics, Ryse is an absolutely stunning game. The executions are by far one of the highlights of the game graphically. Kicking a barbarian in the chest, slamming your shield into his face, and then plunging your sword down his spine...That's the good stuff! The other big deals are the environments. When you start each segment I encourage you to just take in your surroundings for a moment before pressing on to slaughter barbarians. You'll be glad you did once you notice all the little details in the world around you.
==========
The soundtrack is one of the best parts of this game. As a huge fan of VGM, this game was a big surprise. It literally puts you into the streets of Rome, and I absolutely love it when a game's soundtrack manages to make you feel like you are there in the game. Here's one of my favorite tracks:
Apart from the music, the dings and clashing of swords/shields are all over the place during big battles, but those get just as repetative as the executions. They sound nice though, and that's what counts. It feels authentic.
==========
My rig (specs on my profile) was able to run this game at medium-ish settings at 60 FPS regularly, with occasional dips to the low 30's when there was too much happening on-screen. This didn't bother me much though. I played with a controller, an old Logitech F310, and didn't have any issues with it. Being a console port, it makes sense to play with some sort of controller.
==========
Ryse: Son of Rome is a stunning game that suffers from repetitiveness and lack of variety in its gameplay. It's fun for awhile, but that changes about about 30 minutes of play. This is another game I wish I could give a neutral review rating. It's not great, but it's not terrible either. I recommend playing in it occasional short bursts until you complete it, possibly 1 stage per session. That won't take long however, as the game's story mode is very short. If you really like the game there is a co-op multiplayer where you can team-up with other players to battle the barbarian hordes on dynamic maps.
I'd only recommend picking up this game on a sale. Even with it's recent permanent price drop from $39.99 to $19.99, paying full price is too much for what it offers.

Along with Choice of Robots, probably the best of the Choice of Games series. With a sprawling, well-written story and intuitive mechanics (a first for me), there's no reason not to try it out if you're even mildly interested in the premise.
[Warning: Wall of text ahead]
As someone who's studied medieval peasant revolts and especially the German Peasant War, I feel the game does an amazing job at portraying this subject in a fantasy setting. These conflicts can be encapsulated into three main struggles - class, provincialism, and religion - and the story and mechanics reflect this perfectly. There is of course the class struggle between the peasants (helots and yeomen) and the other classes (nobles, priests, and merchants) - as well as between the nobles and the priests - which drives the conflict. Then there's the provincial struggle, both between the provinces and the empire but also between the provinces themselves, which not only causes the dillemma of whether or not to collaborate with the seccessionist nobility, but also adds the problem of spreading the revolt across borders and cultures. Finally there's the religious struggle, both in the battle of religious doctrines (think the Reformation) but also the struggle against a religious system which permeates all of society and which ties the whole brutal hierarchy together. I find this whole subject immensely fascinating, and together with the writing and the mechanics it makes for an amazingly deep story that can play out in any number of ways. I can only hope that the author does more with this because he's sitting on a gold mine.
As for the rest, I can only echo what everyone else has said, but I do have to emphasise just how massive this game is. I'd say it's around 6-7 hours for a full playthrough without restarts, and this really is a game you need to play more than once. Finally I'd highly recommend reading up on the German Peasant War, it just adds a whole new layer to the story.

I reluctantly bought this game after seeing the mixed reviews. But it seems to me the design of first person dungeon crawl with some character customizations is exactly what I've wanted, so I was willing to give it a try when it has been in early access state for almost half a year.
To sum up my in-game experience: after some decent character creation with nice looking art assets, nothing in the actual game works. NOTHING! I was first treated with the option to pick a region from US or EU, which means explicitly this game is perma online. What's the point of having a Diablo-like game with online data exclusive? Whatever, but when I selected "US" it went out there to ask me again if I would like to pick "US". Nice UI design principle indeed! Then, it starts to load--presumably trying to contact server, and this went on for 10 minutes before the client lost response so I had to restart. The second attempt to connect to the server was smooth enough, except that the game had to ask me to double check AGAIN if I was willing to play in the US!
Now that I'm logged on to the server, everything showed up in the lowest possibly details as if I was playing Quake 1 in 1996, my client again froze 20 seconds to load higher spec textures/meshes. Note this is on GTX 980 TI and i7 5820K and 16G RAM. So far so good. The game defaulted res to 1080p, and when I changed to 4k res all hell broke loose, and the UI completely went nuts all buttons are overlapping with each other and blocking the actual options. When I set it to fullscreen, guess what? "Fatal Error" CTD. It also messed up my desktop so I had to restart my Windows. Nice job!
From there I tried 4 more times booting up the game, and it ended up "fatal error"ing me 4 more times, during the best case of which I played 3 minutes with incredibly blurring textures coming right out of a PS1 game (all graphical options set to Ultra) and getting one-shotted by the second mob in a randomly generated "easy" difficulty dungeon. When I respawned it went cliched "fatal error" again. This conclude my brief experiment with this pre-pre-pre-alpha title. Good luck to you volunteer QA engineers out there.
According my general experience with early access games, this might actually come out OK one day, possibly in the 2020s, if the dev doesn't act like the 90% of the early access titles' owners to cut & run at certain point. But even then I doubt I would dedicate any time to a perma-online Diablo-like game. But who knows, perhaps the developer will listen and give an option for players to run their own servers (like ARK does). Until then I'll reserve my opinion on the FINAL product and happily exercise my right to get a refund.

This is an older game, first set to showcase the latest generation of console's hardware. Definitely not worth the original $60 it sold at, I purchased this game on sale for $5 and found it phenomenal at that price point. It's exceedingly linear, not worth a replay even for the most OCD of players, but my time in game was well spent, abeit speaking from a single player experience. I can't speak to the multiplayer aspect at all, since I never tried it.
Why is it worth $5? The visuals are excellent, the motion capture is fluid and produced great (although repetitive) combat, and the voice acting is by far the best I've heard in a game in a long time. I would've purchased a movie made of just the cutscenes for the sale price of $5, as they were reminiscent of Hollywood AAA movies.
There are quite a few criticisms of the game: the linear aspect of the story, the repetitive combat, and the overuse of quick time events, especially at the finale of the game. Boss battles are all about waiting for them to attack then countering in some fashion.
Overall I'd buy this game on sale and have an enjoyable week or weekend. My time spent is 100% single player so take that as your gauge for how much time you'll spend in the game.

Yes it is short, it feels like a DEMO, but is awesome!!!!

First of all THIS IS A DEMO. Basically.
Now if you can get it for cheap (I got it for 5€), it's absolutely worth it.
It has only has one relatively small map and one story mission + side-ops you unlock after "beating the game"*(*Completing the main mission, which you can do depending on your skill and play style, in like and hour. Though probably more)
Gameplay is awesome, graphics are great and the story(though there isn't much since this is just a demo of sorts) is good.
Though WHY THE HELL they changed Snake's voice actor, I'll never understand or agree with. Sutherland is a good enough actor and all, but you can't just go and change the voice of your main character! I hate that, but I'll deal with it on account of the game being great.
Now to the many technical problems:
(I played it on a controller. Though the aiming isn't great, I think games like this play better on a controller)
- The cursor cannot be hidden(Only by moving it to my second monitor, which btw the game lets you do, so the cursor capturing isn't working properly). It does disappear for a while, but it always comes back in a few seconds.(Yes, I am sure I did not move my mouse or use the keyboard, which would explain that)
- The game sometimes randomly kicks me to the desktop, after which my PC thinks that the game still has focus, but it doesn't. (And no, I cannot change focus, meaning changing the window or forcing the game to be on top from task manger. It doesn't work). Basically you have to kill the process and restart the game.
- Also, using borderless, you cannot change focus to another window at all (Alt-tabbing not working.) Again, windows THINKS it has changed focus, but the game remains on top no matter what.
*- Randomly lost audio during gameplay once. (*Might be that something else went wrong, since I lost audio from windows completely, weird either way...)
-Also, (personal preference) the highest after effects setting forces obnoxious blur and DOF to the game. Putting it on second highest settings reduces it, but also disables screen space reflections.
(Low ---------- adds Bloom Lighting
High --------- adds Depth of Field (Blur) + FXAA
Extra High - adds Extra Depth of Field (Blur) + Screen Space Reflections) (Thanks to Harbi.)
Over all it's a great DEMO and I would recommend it if you either can get it for cheap, or are a HUGE fan. Again, IT IS a great game, but basically just a demo. Also, on account of all the problems, Im going to have to give it a negative review.

MGSV: Ground Zeroes is a third person stealth action game that is a prologue to the upcoming MGSV: Phantom Pain. In Ground Zeroes you play as Snake on a dangerous mission to extract to child PoWs from a US Blacksite in Cuba. You can approach this mission in two ways, get in and out as quietly as possible or rain hellfire upon the Cuban base, the outcome will be the same. As well as this main mission there are some side missions to complete afterwards which involve killing certain targets, finding intel etc.
Just want to point out I have very little experience with the franchise, Peace Walker (PSP) is the only MGS game I've played and I never completed it so I'm effectively new to the series.
+Amazingly good graphics
+Freedom to choose your approach to a mission
+Provides a nice introduction to Phantom Pain
+A fair few different weapons to find/unlock and use, each leading to a different playstyle
+Grabbing enemies for melee allows you not only to kill or knock them out but also to allows you to use them to attract other enemies
+The Island can be explored at any pace that you like, you can rush your objective or take your time and kill every last guard
+Stealth is very sastisfying but open combat can also be quite fun
+Several drivable vehicles
+When they work the controls are good, more on that later (Gamepad)
+Good AI that provide a challenge to remain hidden even on Normal
+Stealth mechanics are great, shadows and tall grass hide you as well as they should
+Very well optomized, my mediocre rig can run it on High at 30FPS
-Controller support is down right disgraceful. Firstly, the cursor doesn't disappear if you're using a control and it's stuck on the loading animation which gets rather distracting, I had to use a .bat file to hide it while playing which really is not acceptable. Secondly, I found that the game stopped responding to about half of the Gamepad's inputs after around 20-30 minutes of gameplay
-There isn't much story to the game and what little there is is hard to understand if you're new to the series, even with the backstory provided
-It's incredibly short, the main mission took me an hour and a half to complete (mainly because I had no clue what I was doing) and the side mission are also pretty short
-The bit at the end of the game, after you leave the Island is basically just an advert for Phantom Pain which made GZ feel more like a demo than an actual game
Worth Noting:
-There's a very disturbing cutscene that is most certainly not for the faint hearted
Verdict:
Worth Purchasing On Sale (7/10)
A good stealth action game that has amazing graphics, lots of freedom in how you play, great stealth mechanics, good AI and is very well optomized. The lack of content means anyone new to the series should definitely get it on sale but I'm sure diehard fans won't mind shelling out a little extra.

Endless Legend is a truly fun, challenging 4X game which rewards the players ability to adapt to the game.   The game's playble factions have different strengths and weaknesses; players have to know how to make the most of what they've got.  For example, Vaulters have a huge science advantage which might reward turtling and rushing to a science victory, but when your vaulters discover necrophages living in the neighborhood then you're going to switch to a military strategy or get eaten.  Endless Legend makes mid games changes not only necessary but viable.  Players need to be prepared to pivot away from established game plans to improvised ones when the AI or other players throw a curve.  The learning curve is pretty steep here since you'll have to master not just the strengths of the different factions but also combat mechanics and the game's innovative city/borough development system on top of all the other goodies you'd expect from a 4x game.
The artwork is absolutely beautiful; you won't tire of the game's art scheme.

This game was/is part of one of the latest Humble Bundles and at a first look it was one of those games which are in my library but will (probably) never be played. But then I did not know what to play this weekend and installed it - and it was really worth it!
This is actually my first review, so this fact alone might be enough to show how I enjoyed this game.
So, what do we have here? In one sentence: It's a game about fixing a game stuck in development hell for over a decade. So it's a kind of "meta game". I like meta. Whatever...
You are "The Hero" running around in an "unfinished" world and using "life force" to fix things and change the creatures in the world to your needs. The world is quite small but as open as it gets. There are several puzzles to solve and all you have for doing so is a bunch of creatures - and their abilities. You can swap around these abilities and combine them to build the "perfect" creature for solving any special puzzle.
And all this is packed in a nice story about the development cycle of said unfinished game.
It IS a
nice game. A bit short, though. As you can see I've about 10 hours on record and that was sufficient to beat the game twice (without skipping any cut scenes or dialogues) and get all achievements (including the notorious "collect all and everything" achievement). But in the end I really enjoyed it and can really recommend it. I don't know if it's worth 20 Euros, since I got it for far less, but on discount it's really worth it. And one thing I might add: I did not need to contact any devs of this game but all I read while figuring out some things showed me that they really care, keep close to the players and try to solve issues as they occur - including analysing individual save games. This - as a gamer and a software developer - I really appreciate! And this point alone may be worth the full price, just for supporting the devs.
tl;dr: 9/10 - Great gaming experience, especially for gamers from the 90's (and earlier), I think, but a bit short.

The Magic Circle wants to be a game about making games. As one of those artsy meta-games, in the game it is a “game within a game”, wherein you are a playtester for a gaming company whose game, the Magic Circle, has been in development hell for the last 20 years. You are quickly introduced to the four main characters. Ish, the pretentious game developer who seems to be riffing on a number of haughty, pretentious game designers. Coda, a fangirl new to the company who has joined the team and is responsible for creating a demo but who is deeply angry about Ish’s failure to deliver a game for so long, and extremely possessive of the game world. Haze, a pro gamer who joined the team ten years ago to try and help Ish understand gamers. And Pro, an AI trapped inside the world, the PC of the previous version of the game which was trashed ten years ago when they started over from scratch.
This game is really driven by story, but it suffers from the flaw of everyone being kind of a jerk. The “good guys” are Pro and Haze, and they’re trying to destroy the company around them. It just goes downhill from there. This makes it hard to really like any of them; they’re kind of fun to watch for a bit, but after a while, it just becomes horror heaped upon horror. Moreover, the actual character arcs are fairly limited, and unfortunately, it felt a bit inconsistent at times.
The actual gameplay isn’t very good either; in fact, I’d classify it as outright bad. While some of this is intentional meta-badness, it is genuinely not a fun game to play. The gameplay consists of pretty obvious, basic actions. It is definitely not a twitch-based game, and is really centered around solving puzzles with the tools you have.
The core of the gameplay – in fact, the ONLY gameplay in the game – is shooting a little magic circle under an enemy. You have tons of time to do this, so this isn’t really hard. Once they’re trapped in your circle, you can strip off all the abilities from the enemy or even make it into your friend so it will attack other enemies for you.
This sounds neat, but it is literally the only gameplay mechanic there is. There are a few enemies later on in the game which your dudes cannot attack easily, and which require you to kill them by getting a tractor beam ability to pull them down to be attacked, or to get the railgun ability to shoot them from range. Then, you just do the same thing.
These three things – plus the ability to ride around on the back of a fireproof turtle – solve every puzzle in the game.

The result, then, is that the gameplay mostly consists of wandering around the game world searching for collectables; you can complete the entire game in under two hours if you’re just trying to beat it, and frankly, the collectibles don’t really add all that much. The puzzles are mostly just “find ability and use it to solve the puzzle”; none of the solutions are ever particularly clever, and almost all of them basically have one or two “pieces” to them.
The gameplay is just too straightforward, without anything really to mix things up until the end of the game where you create a little mini-dungeon to send the AI through – which is really very basic and not all that fun to create.
As there is no intensity in the actual gameplay itself, and the game world is deliberately drab and ugly (and very monotonous looking after a while), there’s just not much to love here. The story is only okay, it ends up coming off as a bit too caught up in how clever it thinks it is, and the gameplay itself is pretty poor.
All in all, I can’t really recommend this. It had some vaguely interesting ideas, but ultimately, not much was done with them, and the moment-to-moment gameplay of the game is just not very engaging.

A simple, yet highly visually pleasing Sudoku game. The gameplay is very smooth, with a soft color pallete that is nice and relaxing.

+ cool customizable UI
+ 100 sudoku levels (30x easy, 30x medium, 40x hard)
+ infinite sudoku level generator
+ developer feedback & (possible) future improvements
- no options for people who would just like to keep playing easy/medium levels
- a dark/inverted UI version is not available
Basic sudoku gameplay so not much to say in this regard. You either like to play sudoku or you don't. Great looking simple UI. It actually shows that style does matter because while there are other sudoku games on Steam this one looks the best (in my opinion at least). You have options of typing the numbers 1-9 in but I like that the gameplay can be purely done with clicking on the mouse by choosing from a sub-grid that appears after left clicking. You can also mark possible options by left clicking on the space and then right clicking on the numbers you are decidng between. If you right click on the space you remove the entry there. Show only possible moves makes this even slicker but at the cost of making the game easier. So if you want the classic sudoku experience have this turned off. Each difficulty (easy, medium, hard) unlocks as you finish the previous one. After finishing all three the sudoku level generator unlocks. This is a great way of always having a reason to come back to this game. However, for people who like only easy/medium sudoku levels it might night be that great. Also it is unclear if it generates only hard difficulty or if it varies between easy/medium/hard. Achievements go up to level 73, then there is a gap between 74 to 100. The next ones that appear are for when you unlock the infinite level generator and finish 1, 10 and 25 levels in it. Unfortunately you cannot continue a started level in the generator. Every time you click on the infinite symbol from the menu a new level is generated. Still, for me it seems like the best sudoku game I have seen on Steam. But it still has some room for improvement. Developers are great though, they quickly added missing resolution options, reset button and will most probably keep improving the game where possible. Recommended!

Evoland is a game that reminisces about classic RPG and turn-based RPGs like Zelda and Final Fantasy. It is not a game trying to rip these ideas off, but rather take you back in time to look at the history of the two genres.
It starts you off in a classic 8-bit setting, standard of the early Zelda games and works your way through to evolve into more current, cartoony 3D RPGs. And this aspect of the game works.
What doesnt work is how short the game is, and how linear or unintuitive some design aspects are.
I paid £1.74 for this game, and completed it, along with all achievements in 5 hours. For the sale price, I would say its worth it. But for its full price I would not.
It was cheap fun and a nice tribute to days of old.

Everyone (at least everyone i know) knows it as a mixture of The Legend of Zelda and Final Fantasy. This game is a thoughtful throwback to video game development that should make you appreciate how far the industry has come. Evoland is unique in that it uses every cliché in a non-cliché way, and every chest sighting evokes delightful anticipation of how it will change the game next. Features such as the graphics, gameplay, music and even the loading screen will evolve as you play. It has a tendency to make fun of itself as a reflection of how much our favorite titles from back in the day influence even today's RPG-style games.
1-2 hours is all you'd need to finish the game and there's not too much replayability, but at $5.00, it's a great deal for an interesting experience.
Oh, and that friggin kid at the fountain.....

The game starts in the 8-bit world of Nintendo, and, as you play, the world evolves around you.  You find another dimension, you find cell shading, you find turn-based battles. It concentrates on nostalgia and offers little else.  It’s not challenging, and it doesn’t have a goal. You just travel through the world solving simple puzzles and unlocking new features.

Enjoyable and quirky, albeit short. Evoland is discussed as a game which will take you through a brief evolution of the RPG through gameplay. It is not a history of the RPG game, as it does not contain historical facts; you won't see fun facts or dates and numbers. The game is aimed towards those 20+ or those who are enthusiasts for retro games, as the humor is very referential. It plays more like a game belonging to the "art game" genre, rather than an RPG of its own.
The game does not have a lot of replay value. The story is very linear, and while that may be understandable for a game who is telling the evolution of the RPG it also makes me question why there is not much customization available. There are not many items or other customizable options. There are collectable stars hidden throughout the game, but they do not (immediately as far as I know) add any content to the game. There are also cards throughout the game that DO serve a purpose, as they can be used in a card mini-game -- but the card selection isn't huge. Once you've played the game, you've played the game.
Its an enjoyable short experience, but it may seem tedious to those already familiar with the experience. If you have watched a "lets play" of this game, you've basically seen it all as its a very guided experience. I would recommend it if you haven't watched/finished a "lets play", or if you happen to pick it up while its on sale (as I did in my case). It is not my cup of tea, but I would recommend it to those who are looking for the experience this game DOES deliver and provide as it intended.

Apart from the usual moba complaints (subjective issues like bad balancing, matchmaking, ranking formulas, toxicity of players, etc.) present here, which arent that big of a deal breakers to me, the game suffers because of peer to peer connection system. On top of a rather small active player base its a huge issue.
It's common to be constantly matched with players half way around the globe from you. 400 ping enemies is something you will see all the time playing this game. Not only cant you do much to prevent such players from joining your matches (region settings dont work at all, blocking a player on steam doesnt always work and is going away in a future patch it seems) but a lagging player have an upper hand when attacking you. You have to add his ping, so to speak, to all the stun, pull and knockback effects which will move you back to the place on the lagger's monitor during a fight while on your screen you are miles away from danger. The peer to peer connection system works in favour of high ping players which is really unfair to players with stable connection.

1. what is it?
awesomenauts is a "team based" moba 2D shooter, in which 2 teams of 3 players choose one hero from an "ever expanding" roster. In order to destroy the opposing teams turrets and get into their base and destroy their generator.
2. first impressionis
I went into Awesomenauts very impressed. I loved the art-style, the corny-eighties-cartoon feeling to all the characters and i found the core game mechanics to work well.
3. later impressions
The more i played of it however, the more my opinoins changed however. I quickly discovered that the "team-based" part of Awesomenauts is not all its cracked up to be. You see, the game forces you into a rank mode form the very begining, something i'm not too fond of as I usually don't play ranked. (mainly because i'm not very good) From what i can tell instead of being based on how well you completed the objectives, you move up or down the ranks based on how many kills you get, and how many times you die. So you can be the best support character in the game, constanly healing teamates and A.i but if you don't kill many enemy players you won't move up the ranks. I quickly discovered that it was not about the actual objectives or getting your team through the match and rather it was about getting
through the match whilst leeching on your other teammates. what i mean by this is the majority of other players seem to be very selfish, i hardly ever had anyone come to my aid, they would all scarper if I was being attacked by some enemies and the majority of the time i found myself being the only one to destroy turrets.
4. the DLC
My largest gripe is perhaps with the DLC, mainly because there's £155 worth of it! i've never spent that much on a single game in my entire life; and while most of it is costumes or map packs there are some DLC characters. Every time the devs update the game they always release one or two DLc characters with unique move sets the you can only unlock with money. the problem i've found with this is they are always over-powered, they'll either have some devastating unavoidable attack or a sheild that blocks your attacks. The worst thing is however (this also rings true for characters that require you to be a ceratin level to play) that you could be playing agaisnt these characters from your first match. there's no tier system which locks them to a certain rank meaning even bad players can just clean-house with them.
5. Final verdict
I wanted to like this game, i wanted to like it so badly, and I did like it when i first started playing it, and it has a lot of good things going for it, such as a good combat and upgrade system; well designed maps and an overall great concept.
I'm just so saddened that The dev's thought it necessary to try and get people to buy so much DLC and that they messed up the team aspect of a team-based moba/shooter.
saying that, i probably won't stop playing this game, it's fun in small doses and great if you've got a whole team of freinds that you can communicate with. Just don't expect it to become your go-to-game that you'll put thousands of hours into. Just read a couple of reviews of people who've put over 1000 hours into it and you'll see how dead they think it's become.
if your going to buy it, get it when it's on sale, BUT DON'T BE ONE OF THOSE f***ING♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥WHO BUYS THE DLC CHARACTERS.

I don't often review games, but this one took my by surprise...pleasantly!!!
I don't often play beat 'em ups, but I made an exception for this game as watching videos of it definitely showed potential.
Pros:
The combat:  Wow, it feels so awesome when you time blocks and initiate a rampage of combos destroying all in your path....totally awesome!!!
The story line:  Again, I don't like to watch movies when I play a game.  With that in mind, I felt totally immersed in the story line and cutscreens in this game.  So far (about 1/2 way through the game), I love the voice acting and the story and not once have I felt "ok, enough, lets get back to the combat".
Controls:  At first I hated the controls, but pretty quickly I grasped the concepts then it became really fun.  Many people have pointed out you can't customize the keyboard layout.  I didn't feel I needed to at all.  I play everything on mouse/keyboard even though I do own a joystick and joypad.  Once I got use to the basics, the colour coding was great and I had no issues.
Price:  I think I payed $5.00 for this (certainly less than 10).  Within 15 minutes I felt like I had made my money and it was money very well spent!
Cons:
Framerate:  Really the big one is the occasional framerate issues.  At times it was horrible (of course you are in the middle of a big fight and it happens at a crucial moment).  The horrible moments were maybe 3x so far, but there are other occasional slow downs.  I've utilized some of the suggestions that others have posted to get smother game play, so I could have optimized things better for sure.  Again, not an issue very often, just annoying and destroys the immersion factor for a minute.
The tutorial:
I really didn't like the tutorial aspects of the game and felt that there were 2 issues.  1)  The words often disappeared quickly and I couldn't tell what they were telling me to do.  2) At times the descriptions were too vague.
Camera angles:  At times you are fighting and you have a great streak going (50-75 hits in a row) but the camera angle for that attack doesn't let you see the MOB who's snuck up behind you hitting you once and destroying your streak.....boooooo!  Again, thankfully I don't think this happend more than a handful of times, but really annoying when it did.
Overall, for fun factor, I give this game a 10/10 (especially for the price).  If you are looking for a combat game with fairly simple controls you can jump into and OWN hundreds of baddies, this is a great option!  Keep in mind that graphically it will challenge some video cards, but if you don't mind decreasing some of the options to improve framerate, it is FUN and I highly recommend it!
