This game is a pretty good Mystery Point & Click Adventure.
The local baddies have taken all of the stairs and hidden them in their lair.
The dwarf at the local tavern tasked me to go and find where all of the stairs have been hidden. So I grab my friend and we head to the crypt to solve this mystery. We were met with 3 hallways upon entering the insidious hideout. There were a lot of baddies that we had to click on to get rid of them, because they were hindering our search for the mysterious staircases. Eventually we'd found at least 6 staircases. At this point there were so many enemies in the hallway that we had to click on, I almost thought we were playing a dungeon crawler or something. But that wouldn't stop us from solving the mystery and finding the final staircase. But boy let me tell you, that final staircase was very well hidden. There was a door we had to interact with by pressing a button rather than clicking on it to open it, and alas the final door was inside. Upon finding the final staircase, we went down to find out who had been stealing staircases. There was a very unpleasant skeleton that we had to click on a few times before he gave in and told us he would never steal another staircase again.
With all of the staircases returned to the village and the very obnoxious skeleton restored to a regular skeleton, everyone lived happily ever after.
In all seriousness, this game is almost like a first person Diablo style game. With a DnD theme. The game has pretty poor performance, though my computer needs a new CPU really bad. The devs constantly update this game getting rid of crash bugs and improving the game. I have to give a huge hand to the devs. They're handling this game very well.
As for the game itself, everything dies pretty fast from what I've been able to see so far, including yourself. Which is enjoyable. Everything feels dangerous. That being said I'm low level and have only played on easy. It wast still a very fun experience. the dungeon itself was pretty long and it got harder the further down we went. I could see this game being insanely fun with a full party on a high difficulty. As of the 2 man short easy dungeon, it was enjoyable but I cant really give you too much info off of playing on just that.

In the game, there is side information that's completely optional to find, and it tells the story of the 'developers', and I mean the ones in the game; Why did they make the game, why did they stop, what is going on in their life, and why are they okay with not finishing a product? What will you do?

I'd put this solidly somewhere from "not bad" to "pretty good." I can't say it resonated deeply with me, but I'm not a creator nor do I have an immense creative drive. Perhaps this game hits better with those who enjoy spending time making up worlds and desiging levels, or perhaps those more familiar with the fan-circle, forums, and other stereotypes.
Part of me almost wished the sci-fi elements were a whole game because the music/art style was pretty spot on, but besides that.. I dunno. This is one of those games I can't go into a lot of detail about because, I think, a lot of it is more of how you see, interpret, and pursue things. But overall I'd say I enjoyed it reasonably, even if it didn't resonate to the depths of my soul.
As much as I know everyone is still caught in the "too-popular" vs Hipster mode about it, it's not an Undertale experience. TMC takes the fourth wall down a lot sooner and faster, and in much more obvious ways, though it does toy a bit. At the end most of everything is neatly wrapped up and I don't find myself deeply emotionally moved nor attached - but that isn't necessarily bad, nor was it necessarily the designers' goal to do those things, but it's definitely different. I feel like it was maybe supposed to be a bit more "Ah!" for me, but again - I think this may just not be quite the game that really tickles the deeper fancies of someone who doesn't find the nuances of designing levels and such to be especially compelling, or perhaps someone who doesn't have direct experience with dealing with "fans" in a situation like that.
I'm really not sure.. but ultimately, I can't say that I'd strongly recommend this to everyone and anyone, it definitely is more of a niche title, but that isn't a bad thing.

Owned this game since release, and I've seen it go through many different iterations.
I can no longer recommend this game because the developers failed to deliver on multiple fronts:
- no dedicated servers, p2p matchmaking is TERRIBLE and the impacts of delay have always been horrid
- imbalanced matchmaking for higher ranks because of a dead playerbase - I was routinely in the top 300-500 players when I was active playing back in 2013, and it got to a point where, because I was solo queueing, I could not win games to save my life as they'd be against full rank 1 premades with voice comm.
- Starstorm expansion's features haven't been fully implemented, yet Ronimo had the gall to release another paid DLC for the game
- Oh, and the addition of the EXP system a few patches ago was the final nail in the coffin. Does nothing to help the snowballing problem this game has always had, in fact it makes it worse because now winning teams can snowball on two fronts - a solar lead (allows you to buy upgrades to your character's kit), AND an xp lead for additional stat increases
Somewhere along the way Ronimo forgot about delivering a quality game and attempted to cash in on what little they've managed to deliver. It's a shame because the art and character style of this game is fantastic. Hopefully one day I can recommend this game again.

I played a LOT of Crusaders of the Lost Idols on Kongregrate and really enjoyed the game, so I was super stoked to see this one available. Unfortunately, Idle Champions of the Forgotten Realms is still in very early stages, and it shows. I've been playing this one for a fair while but I still feel like I haven't made much progress because I come to a screeching halt at around stage 55 and have been stuck here for at least a week, despite resetting normally. I have a sneaking suspicion that the stalled progress may be because I haven't spent any real money on the game.
I remember very well the first runthrough of Crusaders, which required you to reach a high enough level to reset the game using one of the abilities of Nate Dragon, who gained it at level 150. Crusaders has an experience system which means that your Crusaders gain in Damage per second every 5 hours of real time. Idle Champions doesn't appear to have this ability, which seems to explain the stalled situation. The first run of Crusaders took a lot of time, but you always felt that you were making progress, however slowly.

I'd put this solidly somewhere from "not bad" to "pretty good." I can't say it resonated deeply with me, but I'm not a creator nor do I have an immense creative drive. Perhaps this game hits better with those who enjoy spending time making up worlds and desiging levels, or perhaps those more familiar with the fan-circle, forums, and other stereotypes.
Part of me almost wished the sci-fi elements were a whole game because the music/art style was pretty spot on, but besides that.. I dunno. This is one of those games I can't go into a lot of detail about because, I think, a lot of it is more of how you see, interpret, and pursue things. But overall I'd say I enjoyed it reasonably, even if it didn't resonate to the depths of my soul.
As much as I know everyone is still caught in the "too-popular" vs Hipster mode about it, it's not an Undertale experience. TMC takes the fourth wall down a lot sooner and faster, and in much more obvious ways, though it does toy a bit. At the end most of everything is neatly wrapped up and I don't find myself deeply emotionally moved nor attached - but that isn't necessarily bad, nor was it necessarily the designers' goal to do those things, but it's definitely different. I feel like it was maybe supposed to be a bit more "Ah!" for me, but again - I think this may just not be quite the game that really tickles the deeper fancies of someone who doesn't find the nuances of designing levels and such to be especially compelling, or perhaps someone who doesn't have direct experience with dealing with "fans" in a situation like that.
I'm really not sure.. but ultimately, I can't say that I'd strongly recommend this to everyone and anyone, it definitely is more of a niche title, but that isn't a bad thing.

Generally speaking, LEGO games can be categorized as either the older, completely linear games with a small hub world and a slew of levels that feature puzzle solving and beating people up, or practically empty open world games that give you a path to follow leading to, you guessed it, a slew of levels that feature puzzle solving and beating people up. There are a few missions to complete, but largely it's just a bunch of running around.
LEGO Batman 3: Beyond Gotham is neither of these. Instead of one pointlessly gigantic open world, there are several smaller open worlds (and these are quite literally worlds) that feature densely packed missions and puzzles. The worlds are essentially their own levels, the only difference being you can tackle both the worlds themselves and the missions within in any order you like. It gives the game a real sense of progression rather than being a boring trudge through sprawling New York or Gotham, while still offering more breathing room than a menu with five levels to choose from.
If you don't like LEGO games, this one probably won't sell you on the concept. But if you've never tried one before, LEGO Batman 3 is a great place to start, especially for fans of DC Comics.

I was excited to get like 7th in the world on a 2 player game!  I played almost entirely 2 player, with my kids, so it aht regard it was fun for us.  Once you master dodging the heck out of things it gets more enjoyable.  So on the one hand, enjoyable and difficult and good for 2 player Co-op.  Highlight of the game is the Epic Bosses which are extemely well done graphically and mechanically.  My hat is off to the developers in that regard.
The rest of this review is the things I didn't like:
The game relies heavily on the three (or 4) randomly generated upgrades between levels.  Some games you hit all the right stuff each board and dominate, other games you get all the wrong stuff and die off in the fourth level-quickly.  In this way, the later boards seemed more about luck, than skill.
Some upgrades are a must have (which is frustrating) in order to survive the later levels.  Battering Ram, for example, you need because it allows you several seconds of invincibility and cool down is like 6 seconds.  Without it, you just die fast.
Some of the ships are useless unless they get their ship-unique upgrades (homing), which makes it frustrating if they don't show up in the random cycle.  Wish they would make them default, or just offer them every level as an option.
The Digit ship actually has an upgrade that lowers the ships effectiveness (auto-aiming), which makes you wonder if they completely play tested them.
The hardest ship to get (and last one we unlocked) is a rail-gun shooting mistake that has nothing going for it.  We tried, we had other player carry it to later boards to make sure we got all the upgrades and it simply sucked in so many ways, weak defense, weak offense, i don't know what they were after on this.
Would like the Ultimate shots to come more often, maybe change the mechanic that drives them (like using combos to earn your ultimate meter instead of the orange orbs).
But, for all my complaining, we did get 34 hours of fun time with me and the boys as we struggled through to unlock the ships.

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is considered by many to be a prime example of what a good Western RPG is.  While it might not have the same sense of scale that something like Baldur's Gate II or Fallout does (which isn't say the game is small by any means), it matches them easily on ambition.  True to any Bioware game it is filled with characters that feel fleshed out and fit into the universe they've been carefully added to, characters you come to care about that have interesting stories of their own.  One of the things I found most interesting, playing this game again and again over the years is that it still holds up.  It still has a great story, it still looks pretty damn good (considering it is over a decade old), and it is still just flat out fun to play.
For anyone who hasn't played this game at least once in the last decade, what are you waiting for?  It is a classic in every sense of the word.

I'm kind of suprised seeing so many reviews here wholeheartedly recommending this game, seemingly blind to it's numerous flaws. I mean yeah, I can imagine this would make a great local co-op game, but how much you enjoy co-op games has less to do with the game itself and more to do with who you play with. But, seeing as I don't do local co-op, preferring online play, or just.. not doing it at my place at all, I rate it as I would any single-player game.
Simply put, do you do local co-op at all? Then buy it at a discount, since I'm almost certain there are better local co-op games out there for the same price. If you don't do local co-op, don't bother. It's not the worst game in my library, but, there are too many design decisions and flaws that range from nitpicky, like the constant PG-13 taunting from enemy drivers, to "why would they ever why", such as the goddamn camera.
I mean really, the camera might be the most formidable foe in this entire game, either artificially coercing the POV to display all of the racers as the track twists and turns (even in single-player) to follow the track and not your car, so you crash into walls and drive off cliffs, or straying so close to the ground that the field of view goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥and your own car obscures your view. You will get used to it, certainly, but it's just this unnecessary hurdle the game puts in your way, and it always seemed to find novel ways to ♥♥♥♥ with me as I progressed through the challenges.
The moment I decided that forcing me through this game would be a waste of time, however, was when I was doing laps against 3 opponents, all of which were ahead of me. Two of them crashed into each other, hurdling each other off the cliff, but I didn't get to celebrate longer than two seconds, since they then proceeded to spawn one after another in my way and on top of me respectively, hurdling
off the cliff.
So, uh, no.

When I bought this game I didn't really know what to expect. I like anime, that's one of the main reasons I bought it, and also because I know that sometimes one can find hidden gems if searched correctly. This was one of those occasions. "Are you saying that this game is so good as to consider it a hidden gem?" Yes, at least it is for me. For a long time I was keeping an eye on this game, seeing the reviews it had. It always caught my eye since it was one of the first Japanese games of its kind that was on Steam, shortly before the boom happened. It wasn't normal to see Japanese indie hack 'n' slash games in those times. Before going to the main points I'd like to mention a few things related to the technical section:
, although that applies to almost all hack 'n' slash. The game doesn't have many screen resolutions available so I at least had to play in a different resolution to the one I have and without full screen, although that didn't bother me at all. There are also game modes in which too many enemies appear, which causes that when killing them the game is slowed down by the amount of elements that are in screen. Now, let's begin.
The plot isn't very surprising, in fact it is quite short, about 20 minutes max. The trick here is that you won't be able to finish the story at first. If you get to play and finish it for the first time, I recommend that you check your "collection" to see the clues. The endings of the story also vary depending on whether we win or lose, and the time. Despite the short of the story, I can say that it's entertaining, why? The characters. Lucrezia and Francesca are really adorable. Both have distinct and very defined personalities, and although both may seem very different it's noticeable that the relationship between them is very deep. They really caught me at this point, how am I going to forget the cheerful and nice Luc, or the mature and tender Fran? Keep in mind that this was achieved by a game whose story lasts only 20 minutes, which shows how well written the characters are.
As I mentioned earlier, Croixleur Sigma is a Hack 'n' Slash. In this case, it's one of those easy to play but difficult to master game, maybe that's why I like it so much, since I don't have much experience with these types of games. Starting with the menu, when you press "Game Start" you'll realize that there aren't many options, but don't worry because the other game modes will be unlocked as you complete the game. When you enter the arena you'll see that there are 4 slots but only one has a weapon, this is because you'll unlock more weapons as you advance. All weapons have the same basic attack, their peculiarities are in their special attacks. Each weapon of each character has a different special attack, these special attacks are vital if you want to finish the game fast. When you kill enemies you'll notice that they drop coins, these coins serve to charge the "Invincible Attack", which is a special attack that makes you immortal for a brief moment. You start with 3 of these. I stopped using them over time given that they take a lot of time, but it's not a bad idea to use them in extra modes when there are hundreds of enemies surrounding you. The key to the game is to be fast, very fast, and also know how to concentrate your attacks. Only then will you complete the game at %100, which, as you can see in my playtime, can take hours. This is because the latest achievements are incredibly difficult to obtain. Of the 15 hours you can see in my playtime, 1/4 of that was dedicated to getting the last 5 achievements. If you are not achievement hunters then it is fine, but those who are prepare to suffer because the game in the end becomes very-very-very difficult and frustrating.
As you can see, the game is quite colorful. Personally I think that the artistic style is successful, it doesn't have the latest technology in realtime shadows or something like that but I quite like it, although this version could make use of some polishing. An example is that the models of the characters don't move their mouths, unlike in the PS4/PS Vita version. This version doesn't compare to the PS4/PS Vita version, released 1 year later, which has completely redesigned visuals. On the other hand, the menus are simple in design and easy to navigate. The scenarios aren't very varied because they are all the same but with different designs, although this didn't bother me much since I was more concentrated playing.
The music of Croixleur Sigma is quite good and is well used in the game sections either in the menu, during the game or when we face the bosses. Something important is that the dynamics of the game prevent the same music to repeat every so often, so it doesn't tire or frustrate. I found the music so good that I'm going to purchase the OST when I can (
Purchased! :3). The voices are not far behind. Yes, I didn't mention it before but the game has voice actors, and it's simply a delight to the ears as they do a very good job in their respective roles. As for the sound effects, I think they are well employed and blend seamlessly with the ambience and theme of the game.
In conclusion, do I recommend this game? Of course! Since this game is aimed at a very specific niche, if you have the slightest interest in it I recommend it. It was the same with me and I don't regret having bought it. I think its price is more than enough for what it offers. In addition to all this, Croixleur Sigma has given me the confidence to buy more Japanese indie games, since I could find more hidden gems like this. Although if you can, I recommend that you buy the PS4/PS Vita version, it overcomes in several the Steam version.

For the most part it is a really good game, with fresh ideas in the MOBA genre. The art style and the humor is amazing.
On the other hand it has a lot of problems. The game uses a lot of bandwidth and in most cases you play with a ping between 200-300, which is unacceptable. Lagging players may cause unforseeable effects, like standing directly before you, while you were sure they were behind you, spells hit even though you're behind an obstacle and the list goes on and on.
Then there are characters you have to pay for, and as expected they are on average more powerful than the default ones (the new patch allows to unlock them but it takes very long). Doesn't mean you can't win a game, but in some combinations it's just not possible and due to the lack of pre-selection there is nothing you can do about it.
Finally, there is the terrible match-making, where you get matched with players that have played hundreds if not thousands of hours, where your team has basically skipped the bot matches. This is partly the case, since the player base is very small (improved with new patch). Furthermore that developers see no issues with premade teams, which basically ruins the game for playing solo. It's even gotten worse in the last few weeks, where I had loss streaks 2 weeks long, not matter how good my KD-ratio was.

This game is a shell of its former self. It's not the game I loved 2 years ago. It's not the game I pitched $75 towards their kickstarter for. The balance has been lost, the netcode is as terrible as ever, the UI is confusing, and the absurd amount of paywalled content is shameful and completely against what Ronimo used to stand for. It seems like every design philosophy that made the game great has been lost. Awesomenauts was supposed to be a sort of MOBA-lite, with one resource to fight over, unique characters, and customization that was newbie-friendly but held depth and allowed for characters to be played in many ways. Maps were relatively simple and easy to understand, with gimmicks that added to gameplay but didn't take over the game. But looking back, almost all of that has changed. New characters don't have the same charm to them, and the redesigns of old models look stiff and lifeless. The new maps are complete cluster♥♥♥♥s, with confusing routes and gimmicks that take over the entire stage, and often become infuriating to navigate through. Many character upgrades have been redesigned, but often leave you asking what changed about your character.
The biggest thing that ruined this game, though, is the EXP system. I have no ♥♥♥♥ing clue what Ronimo was thinking when they added this. It ruins just about everything that made Awesomenauts great. Awesomenauts was based around fighting over one resource (solar, aka gold), where you powered up your character solely through clearly defined upgrades. Now, however, all your statistics are gradually raised through leveling up, like any other MOBA. Nothing crazy, right? Well, not only does it go against the core philosophy of Awesomenauts, but it has been completely mishandled in two ways. First of all is snowballing. Before, there was a clear way that a team who had a rough start, or were playing characters who required a lot of upgrades to shine to come back, because the only advantage they didn't have was upgrades, which were powerful enough to matter, but not so much that a superior team couldn't come back from a deficit. With XP, however, all comeback potential is lost due to the winning team getting more upgrades in addition to vastly better statistics, very quickly making them nigh unkillable. If you ever get 2 levels ahead of the enemy team, the game is essentially over. The second problem is simplicity. Before, upgrades were finely tuned to do a set amount of damage, and their power was extremely clear. But now, these upgrades scale with your level, making their effectiveness unclear and making them potentially useless, adding to the other snowballing problem. This all adds to the already unclear UI and new stage mechanics that made getting back into this game a nightmare.
Overall, Awesomenauts just makes me said. I loved every part of this game for a long time, but slowly the devs killed it, making questionable decisions and taking the game away from what it was supposed to be. I don't know why they did it, if it was meant to keep things fresh or bring in new players, but it clearly didn't work, as the user numbers are nowhere near what they used to be. Don't bother with the infuriating mess this has become. If you played this a few years back and loved it like me, mourn the loss of one of the greatest MOBA's out there.

This is a really slick little game.
But we should probably unpack that sentence, because while it's slick, it is also very, very little.
I got through the main story in about six hours. There's not much challenge, the gameplay consists of hack-and-slash fights interspersed with quick-time events, and the environments are dreadfully linear.
But what little there is happens to be put together really well. The game is beautiful to look at, and not overly taxing on your system - playing on a mid-range PC, I got a steady 40-50 FPS throughout. The animations are fluid, the arena mode offers you a bit more of a challenge. The story is a bunch of familiar set pieces strung together - in one scene, you're storming a beach like an Ancient Roman version of SAVING PRIVATE RYAN (and, indeed, the achievement for that level is called "Saving Private Marius"), and then you find yourself rescuing people from being burned in a wickerman (like in that movie, THE WICKER MAN), and then it all ends up with (duhdoy) a giant GLADIATOR reference.
I think a good litmus test of whether you'll like this game is if you can watch movies like I, FRANKENSTEIN and genuinely enjoy yourself. It's dumb fun, but it knows it's dumb, and it never tries to pretend otherwise.
I picked it up for five bucks during a sale, and I felt like it was money well spent.

CONCLUSION :
Recommended on full price, a must-have on sale price.

This is the best paid demo I have ever played. (Of course, I haven't played many payed demos. In fact, this is probably the only paid demo I've ever even heard of.) Metal Gear is back, and at it's best ever.
If you haven't played Peace Walker, I highly recommend picking it up since it's pretty much one of the best PSP games ever (and has an HD port to the PS3 if you don't have a PSP or Vita) but also because you'll be a lot better off knowing what happened in it, since it has a lot of bearing on what goes on in Ground Zeroes. If you can't, you can still get a lot of it from the walkman tapes you'll have access too, but not quite as much as if you play PW.
The controls are fantastically tight. I can't say whether or not the KB+M controls feel good or bad since I played with a controller, but everything worked great. The only quibble I have is that I wish hints for contextual actions would show up on the screen. It took me a bit to figure out how to zoom with the sniper rifle, since I assumed it would be bound to R3 (right stick click) but it was in fact not. The control schemes for gamepads are varied, and the game supports custom key bindings for KB+M.
The game does an excellent job of letting the player be the Big Boss. No obvious markers on the map for objectives, though you can interrogate enemies to get some (though not necessarily the ones you'll want.) For example, one enemy told me where I could go to pick up ammunition, one pointed out an armory, etc. The game also gives you a variety of options for how to engage the level. Want to take a direct path and risk needing to gun your way out? Want to stick to the shadows? Want to get right up in your enemies' faces and knock them out? Want to find a nice tower and pick them all off? Want to run over them in a truck? All are possible. The game does favor stealth of course (I mean, c'mon, it's Metal Gear) but still gives you a ton of options for how you want to carry stealth out.
Sound is great, and voice acting is at least on par with what we've come to expect from the series. But all of that is overshadowed by how ridiculously good looking the visuals are. No game should have the right to look this damn good. The cutscenes look like they're practically pre-rendered. I have fairly new hardware (GTX970 and an i5-4690k) but I can still run the game with minimal settings changes at 1440p without any noticeable framerate drops. It's an excellent port.
The length of the game leaves a bit to be desired (I mean, you are paying 20 dollars for what is effectively a demo) but it'll definitely scratch the MGS itch. Pick it up on sale for $10 or less and you'll be happy.

Idle Champions of the Forgotten Realms is a Dungeons-and-Dragons licensed clicker game that (wisely) takes great liberties with both.  Like Crusaders of the Lost Idols, you won't do much clicking and the game doesn't seem to take any mechanics from D&D.  Both are good things though - non-clickers avoid the pointless carpal tunnel damage, and strict D&D rules tend not to work well on screen.  This leaves us with a lot of the cosmopolitian flavour of the Forgotten realms with relatively passive idler play.  There's still plenty to do - the characters have small per-reset skill trees, formation abilties and multiplier unlocks, to say nothing of the multiple inventory slots.  Moreover there is also an unusually large number of clickables, and watching a raven's corpse bounce off the invisible wall to the left of the screen still brings a smile to my face.
While the game is very much in active development, the devs still take time to answer tickets and seem to put emphasis on keeping system load low with specific features to downclock the game in the background, etc.
All in all a very promisng Idler game.
If you like idle games and DnD settings then it's cool.

This might be my new favorite of the Lego games.  Star Wars III might still be a technically better game, thanks to those RTS-like zones, but this one had a lot of good things going for it.  And a lot of bad things, glitches etc., that particularly show up in the late game.  However, this one's got a new story, focusing more on Braniac and the various Lantern Corps, with a good bit of the classic Lego game humor, and a whole lot of homages.  And it's those homages that put this game over the edge for me.  Superman and Wonder Woman play their classic theme music when flying around, there's a secret level based on the 1966 Adam West show, complete with the sound effect cards when you hit things, and the usual assortment of DC characters ranging from classics to obscure.  All in all, a very fun game, one that I'm actually pondering picking up the DLC for.  It has provided enough hours of entertainment to justify it, and hey, more fun could be had that way.

If you know any of the previous LEGO games, you know exactly what to expect.
Graphics and sound deliver what they are expected to- surroundings and characters look fine and the music includes licensed tunes from official TV- and movie soundtracks. Nice, but nothing raelly outstanding.
The reason to play LEGO games is the gameplay and that is so addicting that you just keep coming for more. So I was really happy to see that the levels felt longer and overall better designed in this game than its predecessor.
The downside is well known: hardly anyone seems to like the multiple hub worlds. I don't see the 7 lantern planets as actual level hubs, as neither of them actually connects to any level or, any other world than the moonbase (which in turn becomes a hub for the planets). Actually, there are only two real hubs: the space station and the moonbase, with no less than 9 additional areas to explore. Sounds great, but becomes tedious as none of these areas are interconnected. All in all, a big step down from LEGO DC Superheroes and LEGO Lord of the Rings with their enormous overworlds.
On the other hand, the side quests are fun and sometimes form small story-arcs (or rather, arcletts) wich can be quite funny. The variety of the quests is great and I could have done with quite a few more.
All in all, a solid instalment of the LEGO series that offers more of the same- not yet stale, but lacking fresh ideas.

I was hesitant to purchase the title after remembering the E3 footage of a few years ago, it looked like an absolute snoozefest of QTEs, not much more than a tech demo of the ability of the then-new consoles, but I was pleasantly surprised.
You play a Roman soldier, who rises through the ranks as he seeks to avenge his slain family against the barbarian Britons. It took me an hour or so to not absolutely despise the plot itself, it seemed cliched, and the scenarios that take place are Michael Bay-esque. However, I turned around my thinking and began seeing it as modern retelling of a Modern/Greek classic or tragedy, which becomes more and more relevant as the plot progresses and some other-worldly events transpire.
The combat itself is the weakest part of the game, it's a mutton masher in the same vein as the new Batman games or Mad Max (which I purchased alongside this title, yet another flawed yet enjoyable title that plays better than it has any right to). The controls are strange, they're responsive but the layout is uncomfortable and I found myself telling my fingers what to press when it should have came naturally. You have a light and strong attack, a light and strong 'break', a parry and a dodge. For the 8 hours it took me to complete the game, I found myself fighting these controls for the entirety, perhaps its my brain still being used to LMB/RMB combat from a 30 hour Mad Max binge, but the control scheme surely doesn't aid. I didn't find out until I got stuck on the penultimate boss fight that there was such a thing as a strong break attack for breaking enemy' guard, perhaps I missed that tutorial pop up but it was never used prior or again.
I'll also mention it wasn't until I finished the game and landed at the main menu that I realised there was a second upgrade page to improve your abilities, I managed to max my 'skills' within about 30 minutes of the campaign, and was accumulating points for no good reason. I guess it's a bit late to spend them on upgrading my finishers now, but I guess that's my own fault. This could be a statement about the difficulty as well, I played on hard, and even fighting against the control scheme, and evidently playing an unlevelled character throughout, I had no real issue with the difficulty.
Now, where this game shines is in the narrative itself. It begins cliched, but the narrative quickly picks up and I found myself forcing to continue through the dull combat just to see where the game was going with its story, which I wouldn't normally do. It's not a particularly long game, about 8 hours it took me on the hardest difficulty, a good portion of that being cutscenes. It's broken up into 8 or so chapters, each taking place in a wildly different area, and lasting approximately an hour or so. From populated Rome, to the wilds of Britain, to a moonlit Scottish tribal camp.
The voice acting in the game is magnificent, very few games I can think of match it. The animations are flawless, both in the gameplay itself as well as the cutscenes, as are the visuals in general. I also noticed the direction, something I've never thought about in a game before, some of the 'shots' are very unique and I found myself viewing it as a film in parts rather than just a cutscene. Whoever is the game director or was in charge of the cutscenes did a stellar job.
The plot itself may seem far to cliche for some in the beginning, but if you stick with it, it has some interesting ideas that are well executed. Just think of it as a saga or epic, or piece of mythology where you play as the titular character. It helps explain away some of the realism issues, such as a single man being able to take on a fortress of enemies, or the over-the-top, Saving Private Ryan-inspired beach landing scene that was shown in E3 and initially turned me off to the game.
However, the cutscenes aren't without a flaw. They're pre-rendered, even on a 1080p monitor (I'm assuming the cutscenes are rendered in 1080 because they weren't horrendous), but you could still see colour blocking in the very dark and very light parts of the game, and it seemed as though the game itself looked better than the cutscenes, although they did both look amazing.

This game is the definition of perfect (but unexaggerated) space mercenary "rpg". You have a cool mothership (some may say bad things about it, but upon installing better systems it will become a masterkill tool) , and 2 fighters for the start: The "Hero" of the story (the founder of the group) and his old friend Ace. You will gain more people on the road, and you can skill them up to certain specialties. For example, you can have a wing (squad) of three fighters, of which one is the leader (who attacks), one is an AntiMissileSistem operator (protecting the mates from enemy missiles, by pew-pew-ing them down one by one), and one is a defender (prioritises targets that attack him or the squad over the squad's attack target (this tactic is good to spread damage on large masses of fighters when you can finish them in one burst, because the leader and eventually other attackers in the wing will chase the target and defenders will cover them by eliminating any incoming offense tentatives).
Of course, there are more roles, like repairman and stealth, both of which use special system targeted at their wingmates and themselves. There are also systems like this for individual use (like Troll systems, which are one use and regenerate your craft's health pretty fast - useful at the beginning, when your ships can be wrecked out very easily by a well placed plasma cannon "shell", or personal craft stealth systems - a systems that only affects the craft it is put on - the advantage of this is that by having every squad member equiped with individual stealth devices, for example, you will not need a specific fighter dedicated to cloak the squad (so you can gain an additional attacker, for example), as everyone can keep themselves shadowed).
Tip1: Whatever you do, KEEP CORSAIR. Those 50k are a little pile of credits, while that fellow is a terminator-with-missiles, assuming that you give him a bident or H... urmm... Hrimturs (later on).
Tip2 (a bit spoily):
I personally don't consider this a bug since the gains aren't that huge, and help a lot, because in the case that you don't get them, you'll pretty much won't have enough credits to buy you (finally) a badass ship, like a gunslinger or Hrimturs, assisted by some support trident(s).

Idle Champions of the Forgotten Realms is a Dungeons-and-Dragons licensed clicker game that (wisely) takes great liberties with both.  Like Crusaders of the Lost Idols, you won't do much clicking and the game doesn't seem to take any mechanics from D&D.  Both are good things though - non-clickers avoid the pointless carpal tunnel damage, and strict D&D rules tend not to work well on screen.  This leaves us with a lot of the cosmopolitian flavour of the Forgotten realms with relatively passive idler play.  There's still plenty to do - the characters have small per-reset skill trees, formation abilties and multiplier unlocks, to say nothing of the multiple inventory slots.  Moreover there is also an unusually large number of clickables, and watching a raven's corpse bounce off the invisible wall to the left of the screen still brings a smile to my face.
While the game is very much in active development, the devs still take time to answer tickets and seem to put emphasis on keeping system load low with specific features to downclock the game in the background, etc.
All in all a very promisng Idler game.

TL;DR

Endless Legend is an incredible addition to the Civ gamer's library.  The factions play wildly differently, and have several unique mechanics that make each playthrough one of a kind beyond the RNG seed.  This depth is a double edged sword though, and the game requires a couple of warmup games to really digest how to produce units and science with real speed, or how to grow as some of the more awkward Civs such as Broken Lords or Cultists.
This is compounded by the new civilizations in each expansion.  Rather than just a mild shake up, these civilizations behave completely differently -- costing rare materials, abolishing science, surviving on pillage alone--while these are welcome additions to seasoned players, you have to realize that you should not touch them for some time if you are reading this as a new or potentially new player.    Start your first game as Wild Walkers!
The last pain point is multiplayer.  Due to the depth of combat (and length, late game with multiple armies reinforcing on each side) a turn can take 15-20 minutes to actually play out.  I would not advise playing multiplayer beyond 2 player for this reason unless you have tons of patience for those who mull over every microdecision they make.
I realize this is a mostly critical review, but that's because the positives are easy to list at the end -- the presentation is spot-on, the science trees emphasize specialization over spread, and the depth of hero customization and equipment allow you to make crazy warlords or great governors as you see fit.
Just because it's not a Firaxis title doesn't mean it's not worth one more turn.

Croixleur Sigma is a game that has plenty of potential.  The combat is nice, and the character's are... Well, interesting.
There's different weapons to pick from, I actually enjoy the weapon design designs a lot. The combat is essentially a beat em up in a tower full of three monsters. Yeah, that's it. All the enemies are just recolors of the same three with a bit more health. Just copy and paste an area and then give them a bit more health, add like three more of the recolored enemy, pass it off as the next level in the tower.
The story mode is incredibly short and easy, like, I'd say around 15 minutes. Even the giant knights that look intimidating turn out to be easy. Giant creature (gotta avoid spoilers) that's been built up with suspense at end of tower? Nope, weak. You beat the story that ended up being way too short and generally uninteresting then you unlock challenges. The first thing that comes to mind is "Hey! Replayability!" Sadly, there's not too much replayability even with the selection of different weapons and challenges. The characters have a lot of potential as well, sadly they end up being boring and feel a bit 2-Dimensional. The delivery of dialogue is just a picture of a character with text to the left of them. That's it. Ocassionally they change facial expressions, but they stay in the same pose.
I wouldn't recommend that you buy it. There's one exception however. If you love playing games over and over, learning their mechanics, and constantly playing it to find the best possible ways to beat it. If you strive to master the game in the fastest way possible, easiest way, or even the hardest way. If you're one of those people, then maybe. Even if you are, there are way better games for that than this. Even when I picked this up for $3.99 at a sale, I can't recommend it at that price. It's such a shame, I was really excited to try this game when I saw it.

AWESOMENAUTS remains to be unique among them all --freshness exudes from this title (If you have never played - PLAY!). Now: Once you break through the game's lucid learning curve, combat and manuevering opens up in a new way. Your emotions become involved. Patience is the essence of Awesomenauts. This can be a curse and a boon for all players. The frustration - the desire to win - keeps you playing, however, you feel a distinct anger dyring the interaction (Depending on how deep you get into the game/how well your team is doing).
PVP: Player versus Player.
PVP is actually a young concept in the video game society, which has recently (Past 5 years), become prominent in online mutliplayer gaming. Long story short, the FPS (First Person Shooter) genre was dominated by the likes of Counterstrike, Call of Duty, Gears of War, Halo, etc. which brought upon a staple in online gaming.
Awesomenauts is special because of the balanced utiliazation of its pletora of characters through the PvP gaming concept. Coupled with the nostaligic majesty of its side scrolling, old school, you ain't a woman/man till you done played this s%!t demanor, it's a "worth it" buy.
I won't lie to you, the game is desperate for more players, and as a gamer, I too share that sentiment. But this game deserves that privilege, because of its constant updates (to make the game balanced), addition of characters (Yes, you have to buy the DLC, which is lame, but most of you have paid 60 bucks for a game), Replayability (No, that isn't a word, but this game has it. The learning curve isn't very large. In fact, all characters there are available to play have abilities that are easy to understand and wurks, thus you can figure your role quickly. The way I see this game is a turret defense MOBA (Which is probably what the develpers categorized its as). It's a 3 v 3 battle. The object is to destroy the opoosing turrets to break through to the base. when your team destroys the base, the game is won.
Seriously, if you have a fetish for 90s culture, or even remembered the culture fondly, pick the game up.
If you love multiplayer --competitive game play, pick it up
Think you have what it takes to beat me? Pick it up.

I'm pretty nostalgic over this game. It was one of my favorite WRPG's in my adolescent years. I decided to replay it recently to see if it lives up to my standards today and in my eyes it certainly did, however... the game isn't the glorious masterpiece I saw it as years ago.
First things first I feel the game had good dungeon design as the levels felt multi-layered and non-linear for the most part. However, the minus to this is that combat is VERY EASY{aside from the last boss} and hardly ever worth a challenge. At the same time though, the plot felt VERY MUCH like what the old movies felt like. Epic, fun, cheesy at times but also providing character dilemma's that reach satisfying conclusions. Even if you don't like the plot I feel that it at leasts keeps you interested.
A lot of people complain about being forced to be a jedi ruining your class choice, but in my opinion that's not true. All that does is give you force powers. You can pretty play the game as you please, with whatever weapon you desire.
The main plot has its quirks and downfalls. The Sith are laughably one-dimensional and for the most part and don't really do much to really get you to care about them. Malak, despite being a bit more interesting in the comics, is rather boring in this game. He just didn't exude the intimidation or power that someone like, say, Vader did and his only real defining moment was blowing up Taris.
On the plus side though, the planets you travel to tend to be interesting. Some are lackluster{like Kashykk} but others are great{like Manaan}. The side missions are hit and miss, but they don't feel unworthy of completing.
Overall I don't feel like I wasted my money on buying KOTOR and playing through. I dare say KOTOR II beats it HARD in all departments and it's not the most refined WRPG around but it's definitely not the worst either. Personally, I think this game is more of a big step towards the Star Wars franchise{adding in the KOTOR era} than it is to WRPGS.

Perfectly cut to size space rpg-lite, with core mechanic that of real time tactics with active pause. It is not arcade piloting, you give commands by pointing and clicking, your units will act on their own, too, if things get hot.
You're a leader of Star Wolves, mercenary unit, sporting a mothership and a squadron of fighers (up to six pilots; you start with just you and the co-founder, Ace, and pick up others along the way).
The storyline is a multiway charlie foxtrot on a galactic scale, between you, pirates, three big corporations, the Emperor, runaway crazy AI, and more. I dare you not to become chaotic / omnicidal neutral :)
If you like space games you kind of expect to like this one, too, but don't really have high expectations going in. Yet, the game exceeds any expectations you might have! Nothing is perhaps great on its own, but all the little things add up to something great.
All that with not too complicated mechanics, and fairly linear storyline, with quite streamlined intermission downtime for trading and choosing what to do next (no open roaming through the galaxy for you)
Yet, it is satisfying; you keep on upgrading your ships and unlocking perks for your pilots, and there *are* important decisions to make, to shape the story and composition of your unit (what pilots, ships, and other equipment you end up with).

I dont know how star wolves gets me. I can be completely frustrated over mission defeats or even losing a ship. The game is random to a degree of doing the same thing could result in a win when before reload was a loss. But thats is why every move and ability used counts toward success.
After beating the game at 40 hours, I sat back to reflect on the amazing graphics which get better the deeper you play, stylized effects and larger battles explode with newer colors 10x over than early game. But the antagonizing system will have even more disregard for your squad by forcing you to reload because of a miniscule errors which regularly is the game's miscalclations of movements. Thus it is a necessity to save often and in different slots. For instance, let autosave work when mission is complete, save after shopping/allocating points, choose next mission then save after every lull in combat/exploration or change of objective. My save file looked something like this: autosave, mid mish, new save, quicksave, then overwritng per mission. Major gripe is scavenging ship parts, tiny targetting. Missions range from easy to very difficult.
I come to grips  with this being not a frustration but an infatuation. I never wanted my ships to get destroyed although I could of finished the mission anyways but chose to reload instead. I carefully crafted my own experience by making sure my Star Wolves were the very best in the galaxy and won't be subject to anything less.
At the time of my original review, I was complacent being acclimated to the steady learning curve. Then, 3rd tier ships arrived and my gameplay was evolved exponentially. This respect is utterly pure and almost a forgotten art in media nowadays.
The cast of characters become family not through conversing but by manipulating them to do whats got to be done for your mission and the sake of your choices that matter throughout the game. Does a doctor know you any better after he performs surgery upon you? Well, kind of because he/she has seen parts of you that nobody else has. Guidance is the virtue that strengthens the cooperation and this is customizable by the passive abilities afforded to the player which is shared by the whole team. Don't expect any love stories or childish affection these are the consumate proffessionals, the main protagonist whom you name at the start, rarely says a peep the entire game, but I guarantee that you know him the best by the end as he is what Star Wolves is all about, strong, silent, calculating ALPHA.
There is too much to say. The music is such a driving force as it gets more intense the further you play. The soundtrack is the real star of the show. That is the player too as it seems that each instrument is a teammate, when you get your last member he is the scientist/computer hacker, the techno parts of songs really makes more sense. The game is art. Edge of your cockpit ART!

Idle Champions of the Forgotten Realms is a Dungeons-and-Dragons licensed clicker game that (wisely) takes great liberties with both.  Like Crusaders of the Lost Idols, you won't do much clicking and the game doesn't seem to take any mechanics from D&D.  Both are good things though - non-clickers avoid the pointless carpal tunnel damage, and strict D&D rules tend not to work well on screen.  This leaves us with a lot of the cosmopolitian flavour of the Forgotten realms with relatively passive idler play.  There's still plenty to do - the characters have small per-reset skill trees, formation abilties and multiplier unlocks, to say nothing of the multiple inventory slots.  Moreover there is also an unusually large number of clickables, and watching a raven's corpse bounce off the invisible wall to the left of the screen still brings a smile to my face.
While the game is very much in active development, the devs still take time to answer tickets and seem to put emphasis on keeping system load low with specific features to downclock the game in the background, etc.
All in all a very promisng Idler game.
If you like idle games and DnD settings then it's cool.

Evoland is by far one of the most unique games I've ever had the pleasure to play. It takes heavy inspiration from the Zelda and Final Fantasy series of games, among others, but introduces a very creative twist. As you progress through your awesome adventure, you frequently find charitable chests that ultimately upgrade the grand game itself with new technologies and gameplay mechanics. You start out in a limited monochrome environment, only able to move to the right, and eventually move to full-blown 3D. Don't think you'll stay there the entire time though!
As if that wasn't enough, the game is positively packed with plenty pretty pleasing parodies that promise to put prospective players in a state of near nonstop nostalgic bliss, especially when combined with the upgrades. Those more aware of the evolotuion of video games will be totally tickled at all the really retro references revealed~

There are no prizes, but as anyone can plainly see, they can inspire impressive innovations like this~

- THE CIVILIZATIONS: No one, and I mean NO ONE, can beat this game on the uniqueness of the Civs. You can’t play any of the civs the same way, it’s literally impossible, they are that different. That’s almost like having 11-games-in-1 right there. I thought Blizzard had the crown with the unique differences between the 3 factions in StarCraft, but, sorry Blizzard, Amplitude beat you good on this one. And the unique stories of each civ is the icing on the cake.
- THE GAMEPLAY: I still don’t know how they did it. So simple, but so rich. Most 4x games bombard you with hundreds of units to choose from. This game gives your civ just a couple, but you can upgrade them through various levels of gear, so it’s LIKE you have hundreds of types of units. Genius. PLUS, almost 20 “minor factions” exist on the map, and you can incorporate them into your civ and use THEIR units. That’s a wonderful mix and match to your armies that makes every play-through unique. Endless Legend’s technology tree is a unique idea in that you can pick whatever you want within an era, and slowly new eras emerge as you research a certain number. No restrictions beyond that, very clever. And Quests! You don’t just try to win the game, you go on quests and learn more lore! What a great RPG element to the game!
- THE GRAPHICS: Those screenshots are real. This game is gorgeous. And don’t be scared by the system requirements, I run this game on a laptop with a pretty crappy mobile NVIDIA graphics processor, and the game can still be run on beautiful settings with no problems. Sometimes I just scroll around the map, zooming in and out and look at all the little details. Very talented artists.
- THE MUSIC: Beautiful, fitting, unobtrusive. I often listen to the soundtrack while I am at work. Enough said.
- THE INTERFACE: I was intimidated at first, but within a few hours I was loving it. Very well designed. Has to be played with to really get it.
- THE DEVELOPERS: I admit I am not part of the Endless Legend community, but from what I have seen, the developers interact with their users like no company I have ever seen. (I believe some of the civilizations were even created by the community, someone correct me if I am wrong.) I’ve never experienced a bug, but I know they squash them pretty quickly. FOUR expansions, three add-ons, some free - I haven’t seen that many in a long time. This is a team that listens to its users and keeps delivering.
In summary, I can say this: as a father of 3 young kids, I don’t get to game that often, but somehow I have managed to squeeze in almost 120 hours into this game, more than any other game I have ever played.
Yes, it’s that good.
TL;DR - The best 4x game ever. GET THIS GAME NOW.

Rough around the edges, early access and all, but I think there's potential for a fun co-op game here. Dungeon crawling is sort of reminiscent of Diablo, but with a first person view and a lot of abilities to work with to keep things interesting as you level up. The dungeons ramp up in difficulty as you delve deeper. With a bit of a rogue-lite element it's a bit unforgiving if you die, but you're always getting more powerful so you can ramp up the difficulty or plow through as you see fit.
As it is the AI is fairly simple, something I hope will be improved upon to make the fights more interesting and to encourage teamwork in larger groups. There are a lot of things that need to be tweaked and optimized, and the groundwork for a lot of things that you can see coming in the game - as of right now it's mostly the dungeons and none of the overworld exploration.
If you're looking for a game to spend time dungeon crawling with friends, this will be the one to look for and I can recommend it right now even in its early access state, and it should only get better from here.

Kings and heroes is a ARPG in 1st person.
Its an early access, with its bugs an missing content.
In Kings and Heroes you choose between 5 heroes (more heroes in the future), Then roll dices to get your chosen hero stats D&D style.
Then you are off to conquer your first dungeon.
The dungeons are randomly generated every time, so you will never know which way to go.
You design your own dungeon or choose to join with others in their dungeon design. (though the latter rarely works because of a low player base)
When designing a dungeon, you choose:
1 Location
2 Difficulty
3 Length
Now it's up to you, to see how far you can go before you die. The deeper you get the tougher it gets, and greater rewards.
But when you die, it's over and you can't go back!
Depending on your difficult setting it can really get tough, and the content scale with your level, so the only thing that gives you an edge, is your skills and gear.
Another key aspect in conquering difficult content is communication between players, and the game offers ingame voice for real time communication without any hassle.
Since its an early access it's not a finished product, there is still some irritating bugs and alot of content missing, but what's there now, is pretty damn good. -  I have already sunken over 140 hours into it and counting.
Noteworthy bugs/optimization:
Load times - On a standard HD it will take 2-3 minutes to start up game. 30sec -1 min loading a dungeon.
Random freezes - When entering a new dungeon level or sometimes just another part of the current level, the game freezes for a few seconds.
0,5 second freezes - now and then the game will freezes for a split second, at any given time.
Thats it, thats all the bugs and bad optimization that I encounter while playing.
People that encounter dark dungeons, and low frame rate, must have some settings wrong, or not meeting the min. required hardware.
I started playing this game on a Nvidia Gtx 660, which is the lowest recommended GFX card. And with all settings around the lowest possible, the game had none frame rate issues. It wasn't pretty, but my framerate was never under 30 fps.
This game is pure quality and fun, and I predict a very bright future for this game.
With all the nonsense and crappy games that the gaming culture has to endure these days, this game comes around with its old school quality, mixed with new age technology, making this supreme gameplay.
- A much needed fu.king good game, that only getting better.! :)

I'm pretty nostalgic over this game. It was one of my favorite WRPG's in my adolescent years. I decided to replay it recently to see if it lives up to my standards today and in my eyes it certainly did, however... the game isn't the glorious masterpiece I saw it as years ago.
First things first I feel the game had good dungeon design as the levels felt multi-layered and non-linear for the most part. However, the minus to this is that combat is VERY EASY{aside from the last boss} and hardly ever worth a challenge. At the same time though, the plot felt VERY MUCH like what the old movies felt like. Epic, fun, cheesy at times but also providing character dilemma's that reach satisfying conclusions. Even if you don't like the plot I feel that it at leasts keeps you interested.
A lot of people complain about being forced to be a jedi ruining your class choice, but in my opinion that's not true. All that does is give you force powers. You can pretty play the game as you please, with whatever weapon you desire.
The main plot has its quirks and downfalls. The Sith are laughably one-dimensional and for the most part and don't really do much to really get you to care about them. Malak, despite being a bit more interesting in the comics, is rather boring in this game. He just didn't exude the intimidation or power that someone like, say, Vader did and his only real defining moment was blowing up Taris.
On the plus side though, the planets you travel to tend to be interesting. Some are lackluster{like Kashykk} but others are great{like Manaan}. The side missions are hit and miss, but they don't feel unworthy of completing.
Overall I don't feel like I wasted my money on buying KOTOR and playing through. I dare say KOTOR II beats it HARD in all departments and it's not the most refined WRPG around but it's definitely not the worst either. Personally, I think this game is more of a big step towards the Star Wars franchise{adding in the KOTOR era} than it is to WRPGS.

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, also know as "KOTOR" to fans of the series, is one of the true founding fathers of the RPG genre. This game, which produced a metascore rating of 93 out of 100, takes you into the Star Wars universe, and lets you "run free." You can choose the path you which to take, whether it be the light side or the dark side, and you can decide which planets you wish to visit. Along the way you will encounter new characters and aliens, some of whom will even join your party. KOTOR is a game for those who enjoy long, deep stories that let you truly decide who your character becomes. It has an incredible soundtrack created by Jeremy Soule, who later went on to compose the soundtrack for multiple games, including Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim of the Elder Scrolls series, and the Harry Potter video game series. If you're looking for a first person shooter or a game with intense combat, this game is not for you. The combat is primarily turn based, and can take some getting use to. However, if you are looking for an RPG that you can immerse yourself in and play for the story, then Knights of the Old Republic is the RPG for you.

First of all, if you want a critic's review, you may want to check out Total Biscuit's "WTF is..." review.
I think that TB does reviews well and that is why I will repeat what he said, and explain that while I agree with TB on the facts, I personally, as a user rather than critic, evaulate them differently, and therefore my conclusion is that I recommend the game, unlike TB.
Right at the beginning the bad. On my computer, one of the files gets replaced for some reason after a couple of runs, and the game reverts to an older version which is not fully functional (it has different menus, missing characters etc). So every now and then I have to replace the file (validating Steam install fixes this too but takes an hour). This is an annoying bug that should be fixed. It looks like it's very rare because I only found a handful of other reports like this on the internet, and if you're new, you may be confused thinking that you're doing something wrong.
The game has stunning visuals and if you have a multi-card setup, you can probably have it even more breathtaking. I have an Core-i3 6320 and R9-290, and, like TB's review, I mostly get 60 FPS with occassional drops to 50s. I use the Steam Controller and it works flawlessly, unlike many other games.
TB argues that the game is linear. Yes, it definitely is, and in some parts the game mechanics are linear not merely figuratevely but literally (you can only move forwards and backwards, can't turn or move to the side). There are only a very few situations where you can make a choice that influences how the next part plays out.
TB further argues that the fight mechanics are limited and easy to master (compared to, say Middle Earth: Shadow of Mordor). Again, I agree. You have more action possibilities in ME:SoM, and unlike in Ryse, they get more complicated as you level up, whereas in Ryse, they only get passive bonuses and visual changes. Maybe the Legendary Difficulty makes it more of a challenge (I am still on my first playthrough on Centurion Difficulty). The mechanics are more similar to Mad Max in this respect (minus the cars).
The game itself is repetitive. Most of the game is just fighting and occasional turret section or a simple commanding section.
The story TB likened to an action blockbuster movie that simply ticks all the boxes and is full of cliches. I have to agree here as well. There is nothing surprising and nothing special here.
The question however is: is that relevant for you? I guess it depends on what you expect. If you expect an emotional story, open world, variety or a progressive learning curve, you will be disappointed. I didn't expect any of those. I just wanted an action game that works fluidly and does its job well. That worked out fine for me. I got it on a sale and find it a great value for money.
5$ / 5€: worth it, not more!

This game is one unfinished pile of junk, you can't even imagine.
It's short, we all know that, but that's not the problem: if you have the audacity to release a 45 minute demo for over 20 bucks you better make god-f*cking-d*mn sure that the game is the most polished piece of software out there. But as you'd expect from a publisher like Konami these days it's not: this game is a bug ridden mess.
The savepoints are infuriating: they are invisibly scattered around the map, once you run into them you are basically stuck with this one and only point of saved progress: say for example you get spottet and sh*t's on fire and you just so happen to enter an autosafe-area; well you're dun goofed. There's no going back, if you are lucky you only wasted 10 minutes, on a bad day you are 30 minutes in and you have to restart the entire level.
The biggest joke tho is the way your gameplay IS ACTUALLY saved; you drive into an autosave with a truck? Well guess what; when you load the point you are suddenly standing in the open, close to an EMPTY truck. Even if you position yourself smart loading a savegame will 9/10 times spawn you in a completely different location (in roughly the same area) and 4 out of these 10 times that will be right in enemy line of sight; genius, GENIUS solution!
Next thing; again savepoint related. If you walk into an autosave-area 7/10 times Snake will just keep moving in the direction you were facing while entering that area. It's like a constant force pushing your character in an unwanted direction; always a nice touch in a hard-as-all-hell stealth game. In my 3 hours of play I had 6+ occasions where this happened; you have to exit to the menu-screen to get the unwanted movement unstuck.
Another issue are the controlls or rather the "next-gen" contextual actions; often Snake will just lean on a wall or stick to cover when you try to move OUT of of cover or break away from it. Since timing is essential in this game, little things like that can ruin your run and are just plain out obnoxious.
The overall character movement animations are very well done but especially when laying down the disconnect between camera and player-model is not handled very well: Snake will swivel his upper body if you ready your weapon, basically staying in position while being able to look around 180°; but as soo as you go ADS the body aligns with the line of sight and your whole character model just turns instantly, sometimes snapping out of cover without you even noticing it. AGAIN; super stupid thing in a hardcore stealth game.
I would strongly reccomend to wait until the full game comes out and see if these issues are fixed, if not I can only really reccomend it to hardcore fans of the series.

Following the Peace Walker incident, Big Boss now aims to save Chico (a child soldier in the Sandinista Liberation Front) and Paz (a young girl from Costa Rica) from a highly dangerous and guarded facility; Guantanamo Bay.
From the first few moments of the game, you are encouraged to scout the base, and understand your surroundings through the use of the binoculars and observation. Using that information the player can approach the game in many different ways, but mainly through stealth-- sneaking through the base, interrogating and eliminating silently the enemy or an all-out Commando re-enactment.
The stealth mechanics are an improved version from the ones in previous Metal Gear titles as elements such as light, dark, weather, position, and sound come into play for the detection system. Meanwhile, combat also involves the use of cover, calculating distance, and choosing the right weapons for every situation including CQC from previous Metal Gear titles.
Where the game might face some issues is the length of its main story. The game plays similarly to a single mission, and it really limits the game in terms of the time one may spend to complete the sole objective given-- it should take about two hours to complete the game's story mission alone.
However, there additional missions and there's quite a lot to explore in the open world mainly due to the level design of the base is what makes it interesting to explore. The base itself is structured realistically, and it's also well thought as to where enemy patrols, vehicles, prisoners and other elements are depending on the mission.
What comes more surprising however is the Fox Engine, and how well-optimized the game is for the PC, the game delivers its advanced graphics, physics and animations meanwhile not destroying its performance needlessly.
As a Metal Gear game goes it offers mostly everything; its scent of sci-fi, the great dialogue, some background ideologies and the cinematics that could compete with blockbuster films, but sans the Metal Gear. There's no big bad Metal Gear to fight in this game, but it plays as a plot device instead.
The game is an enjoyable experience, and albeit short, it should help to introduce the player to some ideas that have been implemented in the upcoming The Phantom Pain. However, many aspects were improved, and polished for The Phantom Pain from the ones in Ground Zeroes, so it shouldn't be used to serve as a demo or preview of how The Phantom Pain will be.
If you're a fan of Metal Gear, or just want to enjoy a game that allows plenty of replayability then it's a good idea to buy this game on sale.

Star Wolves is a well designed Russian real-time tactical RPG set within a futuristic space setting. This game was developed by talented professionals from X-Bow Software, a small company which later evolved into Ino-Co Plus (games which they have created include such titles as
,
,
and the
series). Despite being a relatively old game, Star Wolves possesses all the necessary qualities in order to leave a good impression on the player even today, 11 years after it first came out on the market.
Gameplay is the foundation of this strategic RPG. While both in-depth and intense, gameplay in Star Wolves could hardly be called original. Prior to the beginning of every assignment, the player is tasked to equip his team of mercenary pilots with ships, weapons and various systems which can be acquired on the market and are then installed on the ships. Later during the missions, the pilots operate these ships, and every piece of equipment and weaponry plays it's part in the players success. The Mothership also plays a crucial role and can also be upgraded with different weapons and systems. During in-game battles, the possible destruction of the Mothership equals mission failure, and the player thus has to protect his base ship at all costs. Every member of the team has a skill tree which develops as the player progresses in the game. There are four different branches in this skill tree all of which have different roles, both offensive and defensive. Each character in your team will have a small range of unique abilities which will also be highly important during the single player campaign, and the player must use them wisely. In-game battles are more or less predictable, and the player will often find himself reloading the game in order to prevent loss of his own fighter ships. Regardless, the way space combat is implemented in Star Wolves is interesting and full of fiery explosions, so fans of
and other space strategies will find it to their liking. During the course of their adventures, players will encounter different factions ranging from pirate scum and private military companies of mega corporations to ancient alien races and menacing robots. All of these factions possess their own unique units, and every enemy should be dealt with by means of a unique approach and strategy. Interface within the game is simple and is very easy to get used to, although sometimes the camera can be annoying due to several levels of the spacial dimension which is present in the game. For this reason, the player must learn to raise and lower the trajectory of his Mothership during missions, but this can be easily achieved and poses no problems once gotten used to. In a short summary, gameplay in Star Wolves is based on simple roleplaying elements, and better ships with good weaponry manned by experienced pilots will dominate the space. Battles usually take form of a limited scale, although as the plotline progresses, there will be certain assignments with greater sized battles.
In Star Wolves, the graphics, despite the game's age, are still very neat and pleasent to observe. While being mostly identical throughout the entire campaign, the surrounding environment will still alter somewhat from mission to mission, mainly because the player will progress throughout the plotline by doing assignments in different star systems. In game, the different variety of ships and other structures all have their unique appearance and alot of flavor text. In short, the atmosphere is very consistent and by it's quality shows that is was done with skill and attention. On the downside, the cinematics are hilarious (in a good way), even though the creators of the game obviously didn't intend them to be like that. Still, it takes special skill to make cinematic graphics, so it's no big deal. Audio is of lesser quality, although it's not terrible. Background music in Star Wolves is repetitive, but by no means annoying. The sounds themselves (lasers, explosions, etc) are run of the mill, nothing special or dynamic, but again, as stated earlier in this review, Star Wolves is about gameplay, the sound is present, and that's good enough.
As an afterword, it can be concluded with confidence, that Star Wolves is a good RPG which players will enjoy. The game does in-fact require some time getting used to, but if the player is willing to spend this time, he won't be disappointed.
Post Scriptum - Interesting fact: The future name of X-Bow Software was already present in Star Wolves, under the name of InoCo - one of the three mega corporations which struggle for space dominance. It seems that the team at X-Bow liked their own creation so much that they later decided to name their new company after it :)
