Before I start:
1. Don't be misled by my ingame-time. This is yet another game I played with a friend of mine on his Steam-account a while ago. We actually finished the game, taking turns playing it, and when this game recently was on sale, I decided to pick it up.
2. I picked this up during a sale for 4,99. My rating will be mainly based on that price
It is kinda hard for me to rate this game, because there are a few things wrong about it, while at the same time, it has quite a few strengths.
FIrst of all, the game looks really really good. Some of the scenes actually look almost like movie-scenes, and the tutorial (a big battle) looks really impressive. You will need a decent system to run the game. I don't have a dedicated gaming-PC, but on my system (i4790, 3.6 GHz, 16 gigs of ram, GTX 960 with 4 gigs), it worked great.
It has vibrant colors, tons of details and some great animations, so graphically, it deserves a high rating.
Gameplay-wise, if you have played games like Mad Max, Shadow Of Mordor,  recent AC-games or one of the Arkham-guys, you will feel right at home. The fights are about blocking, combos, hit streaks etc, and if you play with a controller, the game gives you directions (coloring your opponent in a certain color, telling you what button to hit). Finishing an enemy is pretty much a QTE... initiate the takedown, then watch the colors and hit the right buttons to kill the guy and regenerate some health.
With a tiny bit of practice, you can easily take on big groups of mobs.
By the way - someone said in his review that the game has no controller-support... I don't understand that, because I was able to play the game with an Xbox controller for Windows without any problems. The game detected the controller, no additional setup required.
There are quite a few cutscenes (which you cannot skip if you would like to do that), which are very well done.
Now, for the weaknesses:
The story is pretty cliché and rather predictable. It's ok, but nothing to write home about really.
The game is really REALLY short...I don't quite recall just how many hours it took us to complete the game, but it must have been something like 5 hrs or so.
The fighting is pretty easy. So if you care mainly about the story and play the easiest difficulty, it gets pretty dull early on, but even the harder difficulties aren't THAT challenging.
This is highly subjective, but IMO, the game tries a bit too hard to get into the vibe of the 300 movies. There are some cutscenes, for example the story of Damocles, which feel VERY inspired by 300, and for me personally, it was a bit too obvious and too cliché. Sure, the movies were fun, but this game tries a bit too hard sometimes to cash in on that with those cutscenes and the amount of gore and executions.
So basically, the game looks really really good, has a decent combat-system, and is well optimized, but also is way too short, can get repetitive very quickly, and doesn't have that much of an interesting story.
So my thumbs up ONLY counts if you can get this game on sale. For 4.99, it's quite a steal, and I don't regret picking it up at that price, even though I finished it before. However, at a higher price (I think it's 20 EUR when not on sale), I am not sure I could give this a thumbs up due to the lack of depth and the short campaign.
Verdict:
7/10 at 5 bucks, 5-6 at standard price. Great graphics and sound, nice flowing combat system with some QTE-elements, nice animations, but too short and with too much of a "here is 300 as a game"-type vibe. Pick it up while on sale.

As an old-school MMORPG player, I'm both surprised and encouraged. Kings and Heroes has lots of subtle charm and has an old-school RPG feel somewhere in a game that has little more to offer than a random dungeon generator and a friendly,  growing community.
Game design lies somewhere between a top-down DnD action-Rpg and WoW... There are hints of humor in its current build that I hope are expanded in coming updates. The MMO feel is almost there, however, until more world content arrives (promised soon) it feels very MOBA-esque as queueing for dungeons and a few crafting professions comprise game-play.
If the promise of an old-school RPG feel and a growing MMO community bring enticement then this is a great game to support while game-play elements are fleshed out and brought online. If you need more than just a succulent taste then wait for more from the developers.
For what it's worth,  my first game-play experience lasted more than 12 hours and this is the only game I've ever reviewed on Steam...

I bought this on sale and left it to idle for the cards.

My second? Actually playing it. I'm well beyond getting a refund but even paying 65 cents for it feels like an incredible waste. I've spent 25 cents on games with more content than this.
Another annoying bit: There is nothing telling you what any of the controls actually do. Only my accident did I discover I could heal myself by hitting right click. Yes. Heal...and elongate my eternal torment.

You are in a completely black-floored room with grey brick walls.
You move with asdw.
You shoot by aiming with the mouse and clicking until your finger explodes.
You open barrels by clicking on them when you're close enough.
Weird markings on the wall constantly shoot arrows across the screen.
There are several enemies. And by 'enemies', I mean 'sprites'. They all move exactly the same speed and deal the same touch damage.
Whenever you kill all the enemies in a room, you get the chance to move to the next room.
By 'the next room', I mean an identical black floor, grey brick wall square with a randomized series of arrow shooters, enemies, and barrels. No, wait, this room has BROWN walls! WHAT VARIETY.
Or maybe you find a useless shop. Not like you'll have found the gold to buy anything.
The shop is also the same 'room'.
It's entirely possible to get multiple shops in a row. Including as your FIRST EVER ROOM, when you have literally no gold. And ALSO your SECOND EVER ROOM, when you STILL have literally no gold. This did indeed happen to me.
Enemies can and will spawn practically on top of you.
If you save up for "hat", it's a big red phallic shape on your head.
And finally, the spells you have can be changed using 1234. But heal is the only useful one so why bother?

Put very simply: this game is terrible.
- There is literally only one room. The turrets, barrels, and enemies spawn in different random locations, that's the only difference.
- Tiny selection of enemies but it DOESN'T EVEN MATTER. They're just different sprites for one enemy. What do I mean? The enemy is just programmed to move towards you at a constant speed. That's it.
- Beat every level just by walking in a circle and shooting behind you.
- Only one music track, which loops, and possibly overlaps which makes it sound broken and even more irritating.
- There aren't even "levels", technically speaking. "Levels" implies some form of progression, but all that happens when you clear a room is you start another room. It may be more or less difficult, more or less populated, etc. There is only one thing you could consider progression:
- There is a shop, which is the most ridiculously thought out shop in a game that I've ever seen. To give some perspective, there are always the same 4 items to buy: health 10 gold, magic 15g, shield 20g, "hat" 50g. You usually get 0-3 gold per room, so all of these prices are pretty high, especially when you consider:
A) The health and magic potions can be collected in each room
B) You can magic up some health
C) Magic regenerates quickly
D) You can magic up a shield
E) And the "hat" is an upright red ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
- Shoot by clicking per shot, meaning you shoot as rapidly as you can click, meaning if you are a person with:
A) Fast clicking skill, every level's a piece of cake, hardly have to move
B) Slow clicking skill, or hand impairment, this game is pretty unplayable
C) Possession of rapid-click software: see point A
- Oh, and enemies often spawn inside you causing immediate hits.
- And most of the positive reviews seem completely fake. Some even lie outright, such as "get achievements", er, no?
If you're considering buying this as something to enjoy, just look elsewhere.
If you're considering buying this for the Steam cards like I did, just leave this game to run in the background, there's just no point in playing it.
P.S. Why did I write this essay? Passes the time while I wait for the Steam cards to drop, then I'll uninstall and probably never download it again. I'm actually shooting myself in the foot by writing this review, because with fewer people buying it, fewer people will get the cards to trade and fewer booster drops will occur, but this game is just so bad. Also, it's been over 3 hours now and I've only got 3 of the 4 Steam cards, pretty slow when you consider they usually drop every half hour. EDIT: took 4.5 hours in the end,
Final thoughts: One of the few games I actually regret buying. Heck, if this was a free online game, I'd have stopped playing after a handful of rooms.

Following the Peace Walker incident, Big Boss now aims to save Chico (a child soldier in the Sandinista Liberation Front) and Paz (a young girl from Costa Rica) from a highly dangerous and guarded facility; Guantanamo Bay.
From the first few moments of the game, you are encouraged to scout the base, and understand your surroundings through the use of the binoculars and observation. Using that information the player can approach the game in many different ways, but mainly through stealth-- sneaking through the base, interrogating and eliminating silently the enemy or an all-out Commando re-enactment.
The stealth mechanics are an improved version from the ones in previous Metal Gear titles as elements such as light, dark, weather, position, and sound come into play for the detection system. Meanwhile, combat also involves the use of cover, calculating distance, and choosing the right weapons for every situation including CQC from previous Metal Gear titles.
Where the game might face some issues is the length of its main story. The game plays similarly to a single mission, and it really limits the game in terms of the time one may spend to complete the sole objective given-- it should take about two hours to complete the game's story mission alone.
However, there additional missions and there's quite a lot to explore in the open world mainly due to the level design of the base is what makes it interesting to explore. The base itself is structured realistically, and it's also well thought as to where enemy patrols, vehicles, prisoners and other elements are depending on the mission.
What comes more surprising however is the Fox Engine, and how well-optimized the game is for the PC, the game delivers its advanced graphics, physics and animations meanwhile not destroying its performance needlessly.
As a Metal Gear game goes it offers mostly everything; its scent of sci-fi, the great dialogue, some background ideologies and the cinematics that could compete with blockbuster films, but sans the Metal Gear. There's no big bad Metal Gear to fight in this game, but it plays as a plot device instead.
The game is an enjoyable experience, and albeit short, it should help to introduce the player to some ideas that have been implemented in the upcoming The Phantom Pain. However, many aspects were improved, and polished for The Phantom Pain from the ones in Ground Zeroes, so it shouldn't be used to serve as a demo or preview of how The Phantom Pain will be.
If you're a fan of Metal Gear, or just want to enjoy a game that allows plenty of replayability then it's a good idea to buy this game on sale.

This game... grows on you.
It's not MGS3. Hayter is gone. No more codec banter/easter eggs.
But what it offers in return is some of the best gameplay Metal Gear Solid has ever seen.
The game itself functions as a vertical slice of MGSV. The main story is about 2 hours worth of gameplay, and if that's all you're interested in it leaves a lot to be desired. The devil, however, is in the details. The missions are surprisingly open ended, with secondary objectives and a healthy amount of collectibles. There are guard conversations to find and overhear, prisoners to find and rescue, cassette tapes littered about.
Replay value is variable. If you have trouble making your own fun in open-world sandbox games you might not immediately see the depth that is being offered here.
I highly recommend you spend some time with this during the lead-up to the release of The Phantom Pain. This is very much a prologue in terms of story content, but the gameplay is the real star IMO.

This is one of those games that really needs a "neutral opinion" option–but I lean towards negative, and here's why: it tries to get you invested in the idea of finishing and developing games, while being ceaselessly bitter and mean-spirited about the process of finishing and developing games. It also directs some vitriol against playing games, being fans of games–pretty much anything to do with games.
The writing bounces between funny and downright cool, and the voice acting is top notch all around, but it also spends a fair amount of time giving what seems like a sincerely cynical middle finger to both itself for existing and me for playing it. So the second-half message about how cool game development is and how I should give it a shot just doesn't jive, and the whole experience breaks down for me as a result. The writing doesn't kill the game by any stretch, but what I'm being told to feel and what I actually feel just don't add up.
That said, the core ability-swapping mechanic is pretty clever and the gameplay around it evolves very organically, and there were a couple of puzzles that made me feel like a genius for solving them. The final overworld puzzle was just tedious to attempt and frustrating to fail, but that was the exception to the rule. Really, pretty much everything about the gameplay is solid; if it were tied to a less bitter narrative, I'd give it an easy thumbs up. Although, at less than four hours to finish, $20 seems pretty high to me, so I'd recommend waiting on a sale regardless.
Final thoughts: as a game, it's fine. As an *experience,* I'd call it an inferior version of The Stanley Parable with great production values.

If you can get past the aged graphics and bad (very, very bad) voice acting, this game can be really fun. Playing through on normal is challenging, but not impossible. The limited resources make you choose between equipment and skills, and time the use of your abilities - which are limited in the number of times they can be used each mission.
While the game play isn't entirely story-driven, there is a story here, and it's interesting to be in the role of a supporting character/group rather than the movers and shakers. There are also moral choices you have to make during the course of the game. I don't think these have meaningful consequences other than the amount of money you have, but it does give an element of actual role-playing.
However, there are a few issues with this game. First, it does tend to crash. Second, there is a bug that causes laser fire to remain rendered and prevents most hits to ships on either side of a conflict. This bug, while annoying, is easily corrected by restarting the game. Another problem is that ships will sometimes get stuck on objects and are unable to get loose. This is largely due to the fact that the ships have to move in a straight line to the target object or location rather than coming about. Also, the ships will run straight into anything that is in their path rather than swerving to avoid a collision - sometimes causing damage to the ship in question.
While this game has some issues and drawbacks, it was really fun to play through, and I did very much enjoy the music to the game.

Basically, if you watch the trailer and think you'll like it, you will.  It's a very simple game.

Hit enemies then dash then hit enemies then dash then hit enemies then dash.
Sound boring? Well, there's SIX different enemy types for you to hit before you dash! And then after you dash, you can hit some enemies! Even more if you count the pallette swaps, which brilliantly show whether how many times you have to hit an enemy after dashing.
But what if it's one of the big enemies? Well, you can hit the spin attack button, which will lower their health enough to make hitting them and dashing feasable.

Sometimes, when you're hungry, you want a fine dining experience with huge portions and high-quality courses. Other times, you just want a pepperoni pizza.
Ryse is a pepperoni pizza. A damn good one.
The mechanics are fairly simple, the story isn't anything extraordinary, and the experience is linear overall - and that's okay. Ryse is the sort of game you play on a Saturday afternoon after a long week, when you simply want to sit back, relax, and have some fun. It's very obviously a hardware demo for the Xbox One, and it doesn't make any qualms about it. As a result, it looks utterly gorgeous, so there's a plus.
Ultimately, it's a truly enjoyable combat adventure game, plain and simple. Not every game needs to be wildly complex to be fun, and Ryse is a great argument for the value of straightforward games. There's a time and a place.

Originally, I had purchased Awesomenauts as it's colorful presentation and cartoonish designs captivated me a few years back.  Nowadays, I've seen many gripes being tossed out from the community, and while I would like to address them to provide stable criticism, I have yet to truly understand the depth of complaints.  So, as of July 8, 2016 A.D., I would like to give my two cents on the game, Awesomenauts.
Now, games with the MOBA formula generally aren't high on my expectations, (The title itself, if not amusing, is subjective, especially to those with conflicting views on MOBAs) as I dislike being bashed by a community of players who have no patience for my less than skillful shenanigans-
(Did you know that doing poorly entices death threats?  ...Of course you do, it's the Internet)
-and still do, I could ignore that, as the charm and fun that comes with this game is enough to make for any scathing remarks.  The characters are a diverse cast of interesting archetypes that increases with each update, and the visuals and theme of...  Space and fantasy, are wonderful.
I must say, while I dislike the idea of paying for skins and getting yelled at in written language, those were the two complaints that I could get around.  The first was, well, saving money, and the second, well...
The second complaint I feel is a result of matchmaking pairing me with people who are much more "serious" than I am at the game, the ones who dedicate their focus and trust in their teammates and erupt in a furious rage when they lose as a result.  Complaints for matchmaking to be fixed are upon the complaints I do see, so perhaps if that were fixed, I would no longer be paired with anyone who could not tolerate me, and play happily without a "scrub" like me messing up their vibes.
In short, Awesomenauts still holds up decently today as a good game, but the multiplayer matchmaking does need a fixer-upper.  I cannot say for certain what, but I am sure there are others who have said more than I have in the specific matter.  But, again, I enjoy this game, and look forward to continuing playing this game for as long as it holds breath.

Brave Dungeon is a roguelike shooter, similar to the likes of The Binding of Isaac or Enter the Gungeon.
I would call it a twinstick shooter, but it has no controller support (which would be nice).
First of all, you can get this game for a dollar.
So you can expect it to be lighter on content than it's more expensive counterparts.
As you start a new game, you can choose one of three difficulty settings, easy, medium or hard.
This only seems to affect the speed of the enemies or the damage they do.
In terms of gameplay, you go through random rooms, kill the monsters in the room,
dodge the flying arrows, and maybe break a few barrels.
Sometimes a shop pops up, giving you a selection of four items to buy.
That's it.
If you have watched the trailer, you have seen all this game has to offer.
You can go through as many rooms as you can survive, but there is no point.
The game doesn't keep track of the completed rooms.
You have got 4 Enemy sprites (which all have the same speed, hover towards you and damage you on touch)
About 3 sound effects (that sound more like an Atari 2600 than NES)
2 Characters (You and the shopkeeper)
1 Music Track (That loops through the whole game)
And 4 Spells (But I can't figure out how to switch them)
You can't adjust the small window this gamee launches in, let alone switch to fullscreen.
You can't rebind the controls (or even get an overview).
Your bard moves like a tank (I think they sped up the trailer)
You have to tap repeadetly to shoot.
This is not a monetizable game. This is a high school project.
In a genre that is populated by so many titles, it's essential your game adds something to the mix. Or at least meet the established standard (controller support and fullscreen, for example).
But with a price tag attached to this, I cannot recommend.
Sorry.

I'm fairly new to the shmup genre. I used to play them back in the arcade days (80s and 90s) but just recently I've started checking a few out on PC. This one looked like a lot of fun based on the procedurally generated stuff and the ship upgrades.
And it is. It moves a little too fast and it gets really hard really fast, even on easy, but I still like it. The weapons are interesting, the graphics are nice, it's not too busy that you can't tell what's going on, and the upgrade and unlock system is really cool.
[Edit] The game was crashy after 20-30 minutes but it may be that I'm using a sound card. The developer provided a fix that replaces the OpenAL DLL file and that seems to have solved the issue. I was real impressed at the quick response!
Out of the recent shmups I've picked up and started playing, so far this is the best of the bunch. The music reminds me a little of Daft Punk and it has a really slick presentation. Thumbs up!
[Edit]
Still really enjoying this game. It's fun to pick up and play and shoot a few things. The upgrade system and randomization is a blast, as well as unlocking new ships. It still gets hard pretty quick even on Easy, but it's just so smooth and fun!

First of all: The trailer on steam page is a lie.
This is perhaps what would happen during some special event tournament, but during normal gameplay you never build a base like what is seen there. You don't have access to the dragon/ape/spider creatures. You don't spend the whole game running around with dinos fighting.
The game is somewhat enjoyable, but leaves a lot to be desired. The lobby loading can take more time than playing the game for new players (you'll die within first 5 minutes of the game).
There's only two tactics to the game: 1. Run around with primitive weapons and attacking people who are: 2. Spending 90% of game time to collect resources to make a gun + handful of bullets and test your luck at the middle platform at the end.
You can tame dinosaurs but anyone with the guns will kill those before they even get close to you.
It is challenging what with the environmental events, avoiding agressive dinosaurs, and hiding from other players, but I just feel I waste a lot of time and don't get a chance to improve myself.
Example, I grind the entire 30minutes to craft a pistol and 10 bullets. I get to the end of the game, and get headshot before I can even practise aiming or attempting to shoot the enemy player.
Also there's no tutorial. If you haven't played ARK:SE then you need to watch YT video/stream first. If you have played ARK:SE then you still need to know a few quirks, such that track arrows are crafted from narco berry+arrow rather than narcotics being required, and also that the difficulty is level 1 which in fact makes it harder. If you sit on a dino and spam attack or sprint it will gain torpor ridiculously fast and possible you'll make it sleep during battle.
I hope they improve the game and balance it. They do keep updating and modifying aspects of the game. It just isn't somehing I would recommend unless you like to waste a lot of time.

The Intro to METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN.
First off, at full price, it DEFINITELY isn't worth it.  The main mission, Ground Zeroes, can be done in about 8-10 minutes if you already know what to do and skip all the cutscenes.  That's the end of the "main" game.  After that, the Side and Extra Ops are unlocked, along with extra weapons and challenges to complete, depending on how well you did.
The extra missions take place on the same island/map, only with different guard patrols, tanks and weather conditions such as a sunny day or just a normal night.  I found that only two missions really caught my interest, the INTEL OPERATIVE RESCUE, which continues from recruiting a certain person from Peace Walker, and Déjà Vu, which I also don't want to spoil too much.
You can play any mission however you want, Loud to Stealth, Stealth to Loud, Stealth, Loud, No Kill, Kill everything, extract everyone, etc,  Though No Kill Stealth is emphasised, like the other MGS games.
It runs "fine" on my old, toaster laptop at an average 40 fps with lowest settings and resolution, save for textures, texture filtering (which can't go lower than Medium) and Models being one Medium and Extra High, respectively.
If it's on sale for 75% off, it's definitely fun and worth it.  less than that, well, it's your money.

Croixleur Sigma is the game that inspired me to use the new Steam refund function, and with a 15 minute story mode, it was a decision I think most people can arrive at quickly.
As far as technical quality goes, it’s really not great, despite its simplicity. Supporting 1600 x 900 resolution but only allowing fullscreen in a smaller or larger size seemed like an arbitrary limitation, though I doubt I would have played in 1600 x 900 anyway, as when i tried to play it windowed, no 3D assets at all loaded. The 2D UI would appear on screen, sure, but the actual game was just black. Full screen in non native resolutions didn’t go over so well when using a gamepad (which they explicitly recommended) as the analog controls were all wonked up. So I had settle for windowed mode on a non-native resolution because the other options straight up did not work. Even if you select the option to unlock the FPS, it stays locked 60; that’s not really a huge issue but it does serve to show how much the developers even cared about technical quality. Honestly I was underwhelmed by this game before I even played. And yet still, I played:
When I got into the actual game, they tried to set up some kind of irrelevant narrative, I’m guessing it’s “Because that’s what real games do, r-right guys?” Instead they only raise more questions. The kingdom is ruled by a Queen who has two constituencies: the knights and the aristocrats, but it’s not really explained what the importance of that is. They throw in some poem about the struggle between the two constituencies but that ends up just being some casual contest that exists just because. The aristocrats are warriors despite the fact that those are usually the last people to ever fight in any kind of battle, and they go to their own training academies to become better fighters. The knights basically do the same, but maybe they have to earn their way in? I’m not sure, they never really say. The two characters are of different class but apparently still bathed together as children and assuming that was important dialogue and not just some♥♥♥♥♥♥tier weeb-bait trite, it felt like they were implying knights were treated the same as aristocrats, so, why the need for two classes anyway? If knights prove their worth with combat prowess, and are held to the same training standards as aristocrats, then why even conscript aristocrats into the academy to begin with when you’ll just end up wasting time training a bunch of people that don’t actually want to be trained. Seems kind of dumb. But the developers didn’t seem to care about the writing either, so I guess we shouldn’t either. I’m just saying, if you maybe did care about writing, there’s nothing of merit in this game at all in those regards, and I could go on about that even longer.
The game throws in a bunch of weapons with different special attacks, but the basic attacks are all the same. considering the game was easily beatable without the use of any special attacks, I have to question their importance. Most of them seem like extra-strong hits which would basically just kill your combo score so there’s no point in using them if you’re trying to get a high score (which is all there is to do in this game, mind you). You’re better off saving your MP for the dash anyway because it lets you get the game over with even easier, especially the final boss: just let it knock you into the air and you can just dash and attack up there and land hits on him without having to come back down, and effectively dodge all of his attacks without even trying. It’s really not that competent. Somehow spending $4 on this seems like too much for what I got, what with the levels repeating and all. The enemies got harder, as in they got more HP and that’s it, and they even managed to do that incompetently: instead of making enemies of the same strength uniform in color, they just gave random colors to whatever they felt like: purple, yellow, black, red--it was hard to tell what an enemy’s strength was based on that because there was no consistency to the color coding between enemies at all.
Yeah basically this game is a waste of time. Just don’t bother.

Kings and Heroes is pretty good for early access.
What this is in it's current state is a late 80's D&D simulator... Back when you would get 5-6 people together on a weekend, but no one wanted to be the GM - so you'd whip up a random dungeon and go lay waste to it.
No complicated storyline or quests or NPCs to fiddle with... Just brute-force dungeon crawling for the sake of EXP and loot.
That's Kings and Heroes in a nut shell - right now. Things will undoubtedly change as development progresses.
The graphics are pretty enough, with something of a cartoony flair (not a bad thing). The combat is fluid enough to keep things twitchy for the Leeeroy Jeeeenkins players out there, but still provide challenge for us tactical folks who peek around corners.
Over the last hour and a half I've played two dungeons - both on the 'small' size setting and the 'easy' difficulty. The first was a crypt and the second a sprawling cave complex. Both were well rendered and provided plenty of tense doors and corners. :)
In both cases I made it to the final "Boss" and got roflstomped, but that's okay as I got to keep all of the loot I picked up getting there - so I'm happy.

This game is like an unpolished gem. It has it strengths, it has its weaknesses, depending on what someone expects it can be a very interesting game.
+ RPG Part
Skill/Perk system is not very complex but functional, various paths can be used for skilling the characters. The different paths lead to a slightly different gameplay approach. Could be more complex, but works nice and is motivating.
+ Fighters and Equipment
During the campaign you will slowly move up the tier-ladder with your fighters and their setup as you can buy new fighters and equipment for money after every mission. Also over time the things you can purchase get better to reflect the research taking part during the story. There is a variety in all tiers (light-, heavy-, special fighters and such) and you can choose between different gear (guns, missiles, systems) for your fighters.
You also get stuff for free during the missions and you can collect leftover items after every fight. This parts can be used or sold afterwards. All in all this part of the game works well, the progression over time feels "natural".
o Combat
You would expect the space battles to be more complex and strategic, but sadly there is not much to do for this part. You can use various approches, but all in all the most battles are to easy. The only problems occur with bad luck and some mass-fights where you are heavily outnumbered.
o Story
The story is only average, but at least you have different approaches in various missions. Some decisions have consequences (like different rewards, new characters joining, etc.) and there are two endings. All in all average.
- Presentation and Controls
While the look is average and OK for such a game the presentation is terrible. The controls are overloaded, but after a while you can get away with mouse and spacebar.
- Bugs
Technical wise you can be lucky like me (no problems) or have the worst problems with alot of crashes. Seems its not tested with alot of configurations. The KI is not very good, alot of times ships get stuck or fly into each other. Another problem arises when some scripts do not trigger as you have to reload from last save then.
So, all in all I can recommend this game only for ppl who like tactical space games and when it is on sale. If you do every sidequest, scout most parts of all maps and take your time with the RPG- and loadout things you will have around 20 hours of fun, headbanging, crying, loling and various other things. Not bad for that price.

Cannot recommend this game. Sadly. It definitely took some work and have some nice aestethics at times. Yet, what a complete blunder both as a game and as a tribute to games. Can't say it any more nicely.
Now, let's start picking this game apart. It becomes obvious from the first minutes, that this game was made with sole purpose of referencing and tributing old Action-RPG games (from 8 bit up to Diablo 1, as far as I gathered). Now, that in itself isn't a bad idea and leaves some room for leniancy when judging it as a game. Still, you cannot do sloppy job here.
1) First and foremost, I personally found references to be... dull? I get what they mean, I get what they are referencing, but realization is simply uninspired. Like "hey, remember how good it was to actually have a heart healthbar in Zelda?". Well... yeah, I guess. So what? And this "so what?" remains unanswered till the very end. This is not some complete and independent game, where "tribute" serves sole purpose of Easter Egg. You built this game around the very notion of tributes. You can't simply reference the games and leave it at that. Simple reference can't replace gameplay, it can't be entertaining on its own without YOU, as a developer, MAKING it entertaining. Make witty remarks, push old mechanic to absurdity, demonstrating how flawed it was (or maybe better than modern?). Take your cues from "Bard's Tale" made in 2005. It seriously lacked in gameplay, but still kept player invested, because it provided witty remarks non-stop. It didn't simply reference "oh, in Diablo stuff drop from mobs". It referenced "hey, remember when you got your rare armor from wolf? Isn't it kinda funny how wolf actually carries something worthless to itself?". It didn't simply reference, it scrutinized, studied, demonstrated how silly and funny those things that we accepted before were (and many still are!) about Action-RPG games. Not simple notebook containing notes about old, but a full fledged monologue from developers to player, through their game. Monologue which more often than not felt like dialogue.
2) Very bland and primitive gameplay. Yes, I know, I stated above that in this case some leniency may be given. But not THAT much, as per my opinion. You reference random encounters from Final Fantasy and what not? Well, okay. But why, for the love of all that is living, are you making them so boring, so dumb, so mind numbingly NOT FUN. It is one of the most controversial points of jRPGs in itself, the boring grinding, 99% fights which don't require ANY input other than mashing single button. You didn't simply reference old games. You presented some elements in the abhorent and repulsive way. And then FORCED player to play in this framework. What the hell? You can't claim you're demonstrating how boring random encounters are when you force player through them for 1/2-3/4 of the game. It completely misses the point. Either do those mechanics in an entertaining manner or refrain from pushing them onto player for the majority of the game. Take your cues from "Cthulhu saves the world", made not too long ago by indie developer. Yes, they to reference a lot of jRPGs, mostly jRPGs. But they also bring to the table a very solid and intresting mechanic into random encounters. Moreover, they introduce "random encounter limit" for each location, when after certain number of battles you are no longer forced through those fights with those enemies. You still can farm using specific option in character menu and people don't feel punished for retracing their steps and checking every corner for secrets. This is what this game should've been about. You reference old games and present solid entertaining mechanics from them while you're at it. You cannot force down the throat mechanics, that are much worse than even those you reference in the first place. And we're talking about Final Fantasy, the mother of all "boring and uninspiring" random encounters, the epithomy of the problem both in days of old and modern age. Yet even in those games certain steps were taken to ensure at least some interest and diversity. When you introduced Babamut in your game, it was a point where you should've made him a "one-button-win-them-all" ability, which would allow to travel the world and wrap up the remaining secrets. Yet even there you introduced ~5 real minute timer. Real minute. For crying out loud... why this? What purpose does it serve? You consider that at that point ANYTHING from random encounters can actually pose a threat to player big enough that it will make fight not trivial? You're wrong, your random encounter mechanic is too flawed and too primitive from the beginning. You can't exactly make a challenging fight when your character can do only two things - hit or heal. Literally.
3) While the rest of the references and mechanics aren't AS bad as those described in second point, they are too bland and uninspired most of the time. This game, while trying to reference many others, falls flat at each and every one of the attempts. It never begins to come close to NES Zelda in terms of combat, it never begins to come close to Diablo. Puzzles and trap sections are way too primitive and boring, so much that I actually couldn't remember any of the location and basic order of rooms right after leaving it. It was THAT boring. Yet there was intresting mechanic, with time changing. If only developers focused on this mechanic, made it more pronounced and built game around it. But no, it mostly serves secondary purpose in some of the puzzles. The rest is a mesh of "hey, we tried to make X reference, but kinda stopped at the very beginning". I understand, that it would be way too hard to make many good games inside one game. Don't. Make ONE good game and shift its mechanics slightly to represent your references. You'll be surprised how much being subtle and precise will enhance your points. Consider it an uncanny valley of sort, sometimes small changes are much more pronounced because you can compare it to almost same thing.
In the end, I cannot recommend this to anyone. Two games I mentioned above, "Bard's Tale" and "Cthulhu saves the world" provide much bigger impact. And even without them this game is too bland to be both the reference book and an enjoyable game. I sincerely hope that developers will try their hand once again, but this time put much more effort in concept and basic mechanics.

Evoland is, at its core, a game about games, and the ability to enjoy the game is based heavily on a player's ability to chuckle or even laugh out loud at each reference the game makes.  It is an action RPG/RPG that switches up its mechanics to illustrate a point, a simple and barebones fight engine in whatever form it takes, and it often pokes lighthearted fun at everything that came before and is happening now.
It starts in the black and white(ish) graphics of the old Gameboy, and each treasure chest, instead of giving you equipment or items, gives you a new feature, a game instance (such as a forced battle), a slight quip, and encouragement to continue on and exploring the world.  Or a star or card, of which the game has many; they're both linked to achievements, and after obtaining them all, it sort of made me think about all the random collections games have you do for very little reward, and I realized these were also part of the game poking fun at games.
And it's all in fun.  References to the Legend of Zelda, Final Fantasy, Crystalis, Diablo and even Mario games abound, without having to be direct one-to-one examples.  More often they are not-so-subtle amalgams of the elements of those games.  And the shifting playstyles and new “Additions” to the game overall feel . . . right.  They work very well together.  This game being simple does not mean it is inferior.
However, one might feel that the battle systems are sometimes too . . . easy.  Almost like an RPG where you've leveled to 99 or a Zelda game after getting all the hearts, there is not a lot of difficulty to be found here.  But that is just as well, to me, as the game's not really about the difficulty, but where we've been.
For a fun, simple romp through an interactive history of game mechanics, I say you can't really go wrong.  My only real reservation is that I don't actually feel that the game is “worth” $10; I would suggest getting it on a sale for at least 50% off.
But other than that, the game is fun, provided you don't take yourself (or it) to seriously.

TL:DR: Should I get this game? The answer is yes if you like hack n slash, God of War type of playstyle and of course a bit of Roman history. Otherwise the answer is a no.
THE GRAPHICS
The game graphics are powered by CRYENGINE (Unofficialy known as CRYENGINE IV) and the are what you would expect. Pretty, darn, good. The lighting, textures, post-effects, everything is really great looking and I have no complains there at all.
THE STORY
The game is about a leggion leader called Marius, who is also known as the "Son of Rome". His story starts with a tragedy and ends up as a legend. It takes roughly about 6 hours, so it is by no means a long game but it still feels finished and polished yet leaves somthing to be desired, which the game fulfills in its online compartment.
THE ONLINE
This game offers single-player online experinece as well it's main CO-OP mode, where you can chose from up to 4 different game settings and over 30 different game areas to fight on. While it may seem repetitive for some I found it quite enjoyable and had plenty of hours spent in it as we speak and will probably spent some more as the rewards keep unlocking the more you play. You play from modes of arena where you have to survive the round by doing the tasks given to you in order to proceed, the survival where you have to fight hordes of enemies and gain bonus experience upon reaching certain time and endless mode where you fight to your last breath.
THE CONCLUSION
As the TL:DR section said, if you like the type of games where you slash the enemies in half, decapitate them and cut their limbs off in epic slow motion manner, with the game mechanics similar to those in God of War, then this game is definitely for you, otherwise wait for the sale and take it anyway as it's worth the money.

I highly recommend this game times infinity. If you had thoughts on purchasing this game, I highly reccomend that you do it. This game is definitely worth your money. The game starts out with you playing as the main character of an unfinished video game that has been in development for 10 or 20 years. There have been others that have tried the whole "unfinished game" within a game thing before, but The Magic Circle does this right. Another great thing about this game is the twists and turns. One minute you think the game is over, but then it turns out there is more. You could say the same thing about the whole game. Starting out, you'll think that all the game is doing is just satire of incompetent game developers and games stuck in development hell, but it turns out there is much more to it. The game has excellent gameplay and voice acting. The gameplay mainly involves editing enemies that approach while discovering hidden parts to the game. The editing gameplay mechanic can lead to whacky things at times like having a rock for an ally that moves and shoots out fire. The voice acting within the game really makes the story shine. All the characters had a great voice acting performance, my favorite characters have to Ish Gilder and The Old Pro. Both of them made the game an even more enjoyable experience. Overall this game was a great indie title that I have enjoyed and will probably play more of in the future.

The voice acting is so adeptly done that even minor artifacts, of some prattling old man dreaming ambitiously of a dark fantasy vibrate with life, The visuals are stunning, the color scheme ingenius, and only visible in a small circle around the player character. You battle your way to the top in a 15-minutes trial, fight a boss, then... that's it. You've cleared the game. Congratulations!

I wasn't expecting any sort of literary masterpiece from an independently developed action game, but Croixleur Sigma really does plumb new depths of uninspired, cliché-ridden conversation. Perhaps one or two people might enjoy the recycled lines and pointlessly sexualised references to the two main characters bathing together as children, but everyone else would be better off just skipping it entirely.
For all its flaws, Croixleur Sigma does manage to neatly toe the line of 'easy to pick up, hard to master' – a balance which many games from much larger developers simply can't seem to manage. The variety available in weaponry and gameplay modes also means there's potentially some good replay value here, although anyone who isn't a fan of time attack gameplay will probably lose interest quite quickly, and owners of the original release may only find another hour or two of new gameplay here.

I've learned so much about football since I started playing this game, and I didn't even have to start at the finest Premier or first division clubs, I started out as an unemployed journeyman manager. I applied for jobs, I learned the game and the politics of the sport in the hardest ways, consistently losing league game after game, losing star players, losing my club tons of money, signing worthless contracts, losing my job after being caught trying to find a better managing position. The learning curve is something to awe at, not be discouraged by. The level of depth and excitement that you can experience from this simulation game is tenfold more than that of other soccer games such as PES or FIFA. Every loss is a learning experience, every draw calls for a tactical change or a player swap, and every victory and subsequent goal is so rewarding and fufilling. This is nothing like any other Football game out there, this is well developed and beautiful, and the modding community is just as great. I'll give this an 11/10, and as an American I am proud to exemplify this game as the greatest Football Simulator developed as of yet!

My opinion:
I'm glad that I bought it for 5€ because now I'm sure that Metal Gear Solid V:  Phantom Pain won't be the right game for me.
However, this very game is worth 5€ in my opinion. There are nice cutscenes, there is a solid story(rescue somebody) but all in all it feels like a demo level. Maybe it's just me but I didn't feel like a special agent. More like a weak idiot who's got somehow there and has no idea what to do, how to do it and with what I could do it.
Basically it went like this: I'm starting in front of a kind of Army Base. Now I have to find prisoners. Okay won't be that hard, huh?
So I'm going around the base and searching for a way in... oh there is a door. Nice. I will open it. Well, that was easy - I'm in.
I can see bad guys, let's avoid them....sneaking around...okay. Let's check what I my equipment is about. A rifle and a pistol and granades- OH MAY GAWD! Somebody saw me checking my iPad - äh iGear-... whatever.
Pew pew pew. He's dead. Good. Another guy is running at me. Pew pew. Pew. Not fun to shoot with this rifle at all. Let's try the pistol.... bad idea. Let's run.
I FOUND THE BASE! Great - just open the right cell...done.
What's next? Bring him to the requested chopper. Let's call it first. "Hello? Please chopter lift me up at the spot with the red X, thanks in advance!"
*waiting* *waiting* *waiting* Oh, it's here finally. Here is the guy, take him. WHATTHA♥♥♥♥? I have to jump off and find another person? Nah,... I don't want....it's not fun man... okay, okay. I'll do it.
To make it short, I completed the mission(the one and only story/main mission) and it was okay - but really not my taste. I also completed another unlockable "side" mission. Was kinda same feeling.
TLTR: Get it if you want to know how the upcoming Metal Gear Solid will feel like or if you decide that 5€ are worth a one hour mission + a few smaller additional ones.
Now I know that I won't purchase the final game. Gameplay wise it wasn't fun for me at all but imho okay for the price because the overall quality is solid....tho not really entertaining.

Well, after 22 hours I'm still a bit mystified by some of the concepts of the genre, but Idle Champions is still superb fun, and has excellent Realmsian atmosphere. The list of characters available so far are a hit parade of popular names, mostly from spin-off media (such as computer games and the Force Grey webcast), but Bruenor and Jarlaxle are in there too, and more are being added. Star Wolves is surprisingly addictive game. Sometimes you'll find yourself raging after a short skirmish with the Aliens, sometimes after defeating tons of enemy ships you'll manage to steal expensive equipment - weaponry, modules, rockets, even fighters - and your evil laughter may scare the living $**T out of your neighbours. Well at least this is my experience with Star Wolves.
I really like how strategy and RPG are mixed in this game. It gives you opportunity to build your squadron to match your playstile. Star Wolves also has a decent story and some WTF moments. The graphics are not bad for a title released in 2004. Ships, weapons, stations are all well designed (coming from a sci-fi nerd) and if you're into this stuff, most of them have a description (kind of cool to read how this fighter and this gun were used in some battle not long ago). There are some bugs that may lead to unfortunate destruction of your ships (your pilots may perform excellent under fire, but when it comes to performing maneuvers near space stations...Oh dear)  - recommend to use the Save option frequently. The voice acting is awful. AWFUL. But the music and the other sound effects are OK.
I enjoyed Star Wolves. It made me angry, it made me happy, it made me intrigued. Should you buy it? In my opinion, for 5 euros you get a really nice and addictive game.
P.S. Watch out for those space stations!
Recommend

Bottom line? A good strategy space game. If you dont like strategy nor space, then maybe you should pass.
So far, I've had a really good time playing Space Wolves. There is a decent amount of ship customization, and basic character building elements change how your character plays. There is a decent variety of ships available, mixing things up. The missions arent boring and you stay engaged while playing. There are some tough choices to make occasionally, so you feel like your have a say in how the game plays out. You get to select the order you play your missions, like a real mercenary. The graphics are 2005-2007ish, which still looks decent, and it can have its beautiful moments, like when you explode the enemy capital ships.
Those are all of the good things.
There are a few bad things, but they are not so bad as to overshadow the good things done here.
Firstly, you cannot (to my knowledge) customize the controls in the game. This is an issue usually, but so many of the controls are on the mouse that it hardly makes a difference. I am sure there are ways to change the controls elsewhere, but users shouldnt have to do that.
Secondly, there a few bugs that happen occasionally which are annoying. I've only encountered one, which crashes the game when you try moving ships in your inventory. It only happened twice, and now I save more frequently, so it doesnt make much of a difference.
Lastly, the english dubbing is laughable at best. The game was obviously not made by native english speakers. Alot of the common sayings in english are absent, and it makes things sound really awkward. Also, some of the voices in the game sound like they are supposed to be robotic/computerized, but no voice modulation was made, so they sound human, which is creepy. Each time I meet a new character, I laugh at their voice acting, that's how bad it is.
All things considered, it's important to remember this game is normally $5, and I obtained it for $1 on sale.
With a price like that, this was a huge deal. I very much like this game.

A friend told me, long long time ago, that I would like this game. Sadly, I don't trust his video-game taste that much, so I ignored that...Until yesterday, I saw this game at 0,99€ because of a sale. Only an euro?! Dude, I get that back in two days by idling! So, did I like the game in the end?
Surprisingly, IT'S GOOD! Now, hear me on this one, the game is nowhere perfect. It has issues, and as usual, I will talk about the bad things of the game first, to take them out of the way.
The first, and worst issue of them all is the voice acting. HOLY MOTHER OF F#CK, THE VOICES ARE DREADFUL. They're not AS bad as games like Ride to Hell, but they're still terrible. I can understand it, since the game was made in Russia, though. Old Spanish games like Praetorians also had terrible English voice-acting...But it's still an issue in the end. The cutscenes also look really dull and outdated. Now, I know the game is old, from 2006, BUT FOR F#CK SAKE, THERE WERE GAMES LIKE HALF LIFE 2 IN 2004 ALREADY! Another problem I see with the game, is the IA. When you tell a ship to go somewhere, they try to go there in a straight line, instead of dodging anything that's on their way. I have already lost 2 ships, because they tried to go through a space-station. THEY LITERALLY DID THAT. JUST RAM INTO IT. WHAT THE F#CK, MAN?! Another pain in the♥♥♥♥♥is the resolution, I can't put the resolution I have on it, so it looks weird. It's not the first time I see something like this, though, games like Warcraft III already had that issue, because they where made for 4:3 screens, and now everything is widescreen. The last minor issue, is the music. Why is a minor issue? Well, it's really generic and dull...But you can get used to it. Or just mute it, and play something else on your computer.
Now, that being said, what's left is a weird game that's unique, or at least it was on it's time. A hybrid between space-strategy games and RPG, with bits of Rogue-like gameplay. If you want a comparison, let me just say: This game is like mixing "Knights of the Old Republic" 's chat system, "Homeworld" 's gameplay, and "FTL" 's Rogue-like and RPG elements.
You start on some sort of "Space-Burger-King", were you can read news, trade, and go into new adventures. Whatever quest you accept, will send you into a new map, with the stuff you gotta do: Escort someone, send cargo, hunt someone who was a bounty on their heads, or just plain killing spree. The more you play, the more pilots you will get to join your team, and the more you advance, the more stuff you will be able to buy.
The game's graphics might be outdated, but for a GOD DAMN EURO, this game has quite a lot to bring. If you're a fan of Homeworld, or FTL, you might like the game. If you liked them both, then there's no reason NOT to buy the game. Just get ready to get your ears blown up by bad voice acting. Oh, and if you're interested, you can get the sequels quite cheap this week as well. I think the second game was 2€, and the third one 3€. Getting them all for 6€ is quite a deal, on my opinion.

This would make for a fun battle system in a larger game like an RPG, or an extra mode in a larger action game. But on its own, Croixleur Sigma just falls short and feels like an incomplete game.
I can't really say I would recommend this at the asking price of $7.99, but for a couple of bucks on sale, or maybe grabbed in a bundle with other games, it feels more worth it.
Croixleur is basically a hack and slash game with very simple mechanics. There are no complex combos, or even intermediate ones. We're talking simplest of the simple here when chaining together attacks. It's basically button mash, dash away to dodge attacks, and once in a while throw in an "invincible" special. The arenas are all the same. Just a circle you run around in, with different colors. Someone said this feels like Bloody Palace mode in the Devil May Cry games. But that is just the thing, the Bloody Palace Mode was just a mode in a larger game, and a much deeper game at that in terms of combat.
As it stands on its own, the story mode is just too short, with literally only 3 types of bosses, with 2 of the boss types becoming standard enemies after you beat them, which can be dropped with the greatest of ease with a simple hit hit dash, rinse and repeat set of moves. As for the standard enemies there are 3 types, with a few levels of difficulty for each. It's just...wow. Lazy. Besides story mode, you can tackle a time attack, survival and challenge mode. And that's pretty much it.
There are 2 characters to play as, with 20 weapons total to use once you unlock them all. There is not much difference in any of the weapons other than attack power,  their special, and of course the weapon skins. For basic attacks they are pretty much all similar.
I have less than an hour in the game. Yes, less than an hour. But in that hour I managed to play through story mode twice. Once making it as far as the timer allowed, and the 2nd time actually completing story mode, and then to try out the other modes afterwards. I am already bored with the title.
Buy this I guess if you like repetitive score attack type action games with extremely little style and substance.

It shouldn't be a surprise that DMC-style action games have become staples in the doujin PC market. Even without expensive set pieces these games can easily get by as long as the combat system is polished. Croixleur is a good example of this as the game features 3 enemies, 3 unique bosses, and a single arena. But the gameplay is polished and that's enough to carry the experience and warrant a purchase.
Much like classic arcade titles, the focus of Croixleur is developing player skill and going for high scores. With the 8-15 minute story/arcade mode the focus of the scoring is based mostly on speed, rewarding events and the epilogue fight purely based on how efficiently the player can clear out the waves of enemies. With the Steam achievements based around completing skill-based challenges, there is quite a few hours of speedrunning fun to be had in that 10 minute story mode.
Alternative review:
If you're a fan of:
Attack - cancel into dash - cancel dash into attack - cancel into special move - cancel into dash - repeat... then you'll find a lot to love here.
Highly recommended to lovers of action games, anime girls with swords, and fans of getting carpal tunnel.

Alright, hands down my favorite Bioware rpg released ever.
A great story that allows serious plot changing options such as killing off companions or finding out their individual personal stories. Great graphics for the time period and some of the most entertaining star wars lightsaber combat, beaten only by the Star Wars Jedi Knight series. Not to mention the STELLAR voice acting.
With the recent announcement of EA purchasing the patent for KOTOR 3, this is a great item to pick up to get you into the realm of KOTOR.
But how much could they have changed compared to the realm of star wars might you say? A but ton that's what.
Ok to start with, the game takes place 4000 years before the movies and revolves around a wide spread jedi council. You are , (with as few spoilers as I can manage to describe this in) travelling across a set of 8 unique planets and locations where you can interact with tons of sidequests.
One more entertaining sidequest (Non Main Story Spoilers) on Manaan where you act as a lawyer/detective and attempt to prove a man in court either innocent or guilty. Which winds up being a lot more fun than expected due to the depth of the investigation process and the trial interactions.
However, I do have a few complaints about the game.
First, the beginning sequence is AWFUL. The first time through it is entertaining to an extent, but if you want to start a fresh playthrough, you are often discouraged due to the length and lack of interest the beginning sequence holds. Once you are off Taris(the starting planet) however, the game's pace drastically improves. (Note: However there are mods to solve this issue should you find them necessary)
Also, the main character is unvoiced, while it is kind of nice not having to hear one or two voices for all of your characters, the addition of voice and voice editor would have made the game that much better.
Let's also not forget the utter lack of animations. Let's see, the game has about 5 death animations, 2 talking animations and very ugly running animation. Leading to a severe lack of depth visually.
All other complaints I may think of are tiny things about the game that I take as a personal disliking based on taste, not anything that drastically affects the title.
Overall, pick up this game if you like RPGs. You won't be disappointed in the slightest.

There are very few games out there that I would declare 10/10 games, this is one of them. Ever since the original Star Wars trilogy ended 30 years ago we have been given lackluster successors to the trilogy in both film and video game. Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic is a game that really captures the narrative sense of adventure and good vs evil that made the original three films such joys to watch. (SPOILERS AHEAD) The characters you interact with are for the most part a very strong point of the game. Carth is a tortured character you really to have to spend a lot of time to understand. Bastilia is a gifted Jedi who is attempting to be the emotionless patient Vulcan-like Jedi we have come to known in the prequel films which makes it all the more fun to really get her angry at you. Mission Vao and Zaalbar are basically Chewbacca and Han solo if Han was a 13 year old girl. Jolee Bindo is one of the more interesting Jedi you’ll ever encounter; he’s not a member of the Jedi order and dodges any attempts you make to probe his character. Canderous Ordo is a perfect specimen of a Mandalorian (the human version of Predators) and is a combat veteran. You get two droids on your adventures, T3 who is basically R2-D2 and my favorite companion HK-47, a assassin droid who refers to all non droids as “Meatbags” and who you’ll learn is responsible for the deaths of all his previous masters. Oh and if you run into someone called “Juhani” just kill her, it saves you a lot of time. The Combat of this game is turn-based and as you gain more levels you are able to spec into a variety of different abilities which will give you new options when it comes to fighting enemies. However the calling card of this game is the story (MAJOR, GAME RUINING SPOILERS AHEAD). The game leads you to believe at first you are a Republic (insert class here) stationed on a ship orbiting Taris and it is up to save the galaxy by rescuing the Jedi leader of the ship’s expedition who was lost on the planet following an attack by the main enemy of the game Dark Malak. You then learn after you escape the planet you learn that you are gifted and can learn the powers of the Force. You take this as simply coincidence and continue on your journey to stop Malak (M. NIGHT SHAMALYAN SPOILERS AHEAD, LAST CHANCE TO TURN BACK). However in one of the greatest plot twists in video games, you learn that your character is actually “Darth Revan” the former master of Malak whose memory was changed by the Jedi Council. Now while this game is my favorite of my all time favorites it does have its faults. There are extra quests in the game that are just not do able unless you so happen to do planets in exact orders, the first two planets (Taris and Dantooine) are major drags to get through and are not the most enjoyable things to get through. Despite this, Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic is the greatest Star Wars game to exist and is easily worth the 10 dollars.

Although a blast from the past there is some seriously flawed design which is frustrating, very upsetting.  I was really looking forward to enjoying this game until my focus changed from fun to frustration.  For example, my world evolved, up until this point I could heal with my companion or potions.  Suddenly I was no longer able to heal and worse it went from several save points to none.  Everytime I died I was forced to start at the beginning.  This is a very frustrating, unecessary, and flawed design.  I went from enjoying the game to repeating the same things over and over again hoping for a little progress.  The monsters are very easy to very difficult, not much inbetween.  You can kill bats, no problem, skeletons, a reasonable challenge, then suddenly red mages that disappear and by the time you reach them to strike, they are gone, they reappear to blast you, you change directions, rush to strike them from the side, poof gone.  You end up running around avoiding blasts just swinging your sword aimlessly as they rush you against a trap or corner where you barely stand a chance.  I don't like the controls, although simple I would prefer this game on console with an actual controller.  On PC the controls, although simple, feel clunky, and worse they seem to glitch, get stuck easily.  I am very disappointed, I was really enjoying this game, now suddenly I feel like I wasted my time and money, annoyed!  If they just allowed you to heal in certain areas, gave you a save point or two, it would have been great... how could they ruin something so special with such needless little mistakes?  I will continue trying to progress and will update my post and review if I change my mind but I really doubt it because I just do not like games that make me "mad" or "annoyed" I would rather play for fun.  I don't mind a reasonable challenge but I do not like to be challenged by needless mistakes in overall design, sorry.

I really wanted to leave this game a positive review. I have been a massive fan since CM2 in the early 90s and continued to love the series through to the current Football Manager era.
I will admit that I started to become a little cynical and even skipped FM16 due to the feeling that the game was just not moving forward in the way that I wanted. I will also own up to the fact that I detested FM14 due to the removal of the sliders and the fact that I felt limited by the tactics creator. It particularly frustrated me that I did not see any indication of the instructions that I was giving to my players and I felt restricted by just giving vaguely defined roles instead.
However, I recently had a strong feeling of nostalgia and a huge desire to come back to the FM series. First of all, I tried FM15, which I already owned, and I had a blast with it for a while. With this experience in mind, I decided to try FM17 when I saw it on sale. At first, I was excited by the extra detail and thrilled by some of the new features, but sadly I feel let down by the match engine.
The major issue is that wingers/wide midfielders in this version stay far too wide defensively and you cannot keep a proper defensive shape no matter what instructions you give tactically. They never move infield to help centrally. If, for example, you are playing a 4-4-2 formation, the central midfielders will stand around holding hands in the middle while the wide players stay out as wide as possible doing nothing. The wide players refuse to help centrally even if the opposition overloads the central areas. Currently they are hard-coded to behave like this which is completely unrealistic. This is a new change for FM17 and definitely didn't happen in previous versions of the game. There are several threads on the SI Games forum if you are interested in reading more about issue:
This is one of the most recent threads on the issue:
Note the first two comments in reply to the OP (both voted as popular posts by users of the forum):
'Well, this is a huge issue for me too, in terms of the realism of the game. It ruins the playability of FM17, for me at least, and you've illustrated it very well.'
'I sincerely hope this is addressed for FM18 as I miss my Football Manager sessions, having uninstalled the game because of this very problem. It was a significant factor in why I stopped playing FM17.'
For a game that calls itself a football simulation and prides itself on realism, this defensive issue is nothing like real life. The defensive shapes in the game are nothing like anything I have ever seen in a real football match.
What I find even more frustrating is the unwillingness of SI Games to admit the problem or to talk about the issue. Many of the threads bringing up this bug have been closed by overzealous moderators. It was never this way in the old days when I was a regular poster of the forum. Also, the devs have taken the decision not to fix this bug for this version of the game. The official line seems to be that it will be looked at for a future version of Football Manager. It is incredibly disappointing.
With this in mind, I simply cannot recommend the game while it has this major match engine/tactical issue. Ultimately, if you want to play with certain formations, you are at a major disadvantage, and the match engine is just not well balanced in this version of the FM series.

This game is fun.
That is the most important part of a review, and so I will go ahead and say it first. I really love this game. A word or two of warning however: You need a powerful computer to run this, and it is not very noob-friendly. This game puts a much more strategic twist to your usual hunger-games arena, particularly in longer team battles which can last over an hour. If you have played other HG games, like the Culling, you may be used to very fast-paced, frantic, combat-heavy gameplay. ARK SotF is not that game. You are time-constrained, of course, as the circle of death closes in, but during that time you are going to be crafting weapons and armor, taming dinosaurs, and mining metal to craft powerful guns and explosives, before leading your dinosaur army to the center ring to battle against the last remaining players. There are tons of possibilities, and lots of strategies to experiment with.
For new players, this game can prove very difficult. Not only are you playing a survival game, and need to worry about food, water, and a hostile environment, but you are dropped in there with many other players, all of whom have the mission of killing you. Spears are a one-hit kill on headshots, and it is easy to be ambushed or assassinated by sneaky players if you don't watch your back. It took me 45 games before I ever won a match. If you are persistent enough to get past this initial frustration, this game is extremely fun.
Really, though, the only thing I do not like about this game is the fan-made music on the menu. I hate it. If any of the devs read these reviews, please get rid of them, or at least let me turn them off. I want to hear the contextual music in the game, but not the fan music on the menu.
In other words:
Pros:
Many strategies to experiment with.
Great balance between pvp and pve threats.
Overall a great experience in-game.
Cons:
Needs a higher-end computer to run smoothly
Steep learning curve for new players
Annoying fan-made music plays during the menu.
Summary:
Great game for those who want a more strategic hunger games experience.

This is one of those games that looks cool with blood, gore & fast paced combat but it just fails in almost every aspect at what it's trying to do & it's not even trying to do that much.  Then it slaps you in the face with it's cash shop system to add insult to injury.
-Fast paced action combat
-Stylish Executions
-Combat is repetitive
-Executions are repetitive
-Camera is god awful
-Auto Targeting System sucks
-Combat is imbalanced
-Poor upgrade system
-Spikes in Difficulty
-Game has pay2win mechanics
-Performance Issues
What story?  The story is so generic & poorly written it might as well not even exist.  You're a soldier & you kill barbarians in the name of Rome & yada yada yada nobody cares that your family was killed by invading barbarians that somehow broke into the biggest & most heavily guarded city in the world.  Also you get stalked by some glowing ghost lady who probably wants your seed.  Moving on.
The gameplay consists of timed button presses during combat. X attacks with your sword, Y attacks with your shield (for some reason you can't block with it) & A parries incoming attacks.  First thing you'll notice when playing is you can't block with your shield during combat.  You can only parry attacks.  You can roll dodge with B which is needed to avoid heavy attacks. The parry system doesn't seem like an issue except they made the combat system mostly for 1v1 but enemies will attack you in groups & you can't really parry more than one attack at a time even if they're coming from the same general direction. You can but it rarely seems to work.  So, if you got multiple incoming attacks you're pretty much forced to dodge because if you try anything else you'll take damage.  It's like they designed the combat with the Batman games as a reference except they completely neglected what made those games combat so good in the first place.
Also, no button mashing.  If you do you'll quickly realize how much fun an axe to the back can be and there will be plenty of axes to your back because the auto targeting system is god awful.  Rarely will I ever be able to target the enemy I want to attack & when I finally manage that two more enemies get behind me forcing me to roll & then the target will auto swap to something else & it just... Can't you just trust the player to target the enemies on their own?  When you manage to get the hang of this games combat it is pretty fun at first.  Later on though it just gets tiresome as the game just throws more & more enemies at you.  They get bigger & deal more damage but you for some reason don't.  And the upgrades you get don't really increase your damage by a large enough amount to help.
That's when I noticed this big difficulty spike during an escort mission.  It's one where you need to save soldiers from burning alive in cages but you can only save them when you kill torch wielders.  Why can't I just save them right away?  Because the game won't let you.  This wouldn't be a big deal if the torchers didn't sprint away from you every chance they have while every other enemy in the dozen you're fighting is keeping you off of him.  The auto targeting system is the worst part about this particular mission as it will never target the torch guys first & the camera will never show where they're hiding.  It's like playing hide & seek in a burning house & that house is also full of bandits attacking you.  This mission alone changed my view of the game from mediocre to down right negative.  It's almost like they designed this mission to be bothersome on purpose to get you to spend money on buying upgrades because no other mission thus far was designed this way.
The absolute worst part about this game is the camera.  Half the screen is always taken up by your back.  I wish I was joking.  The camera does zoom out during combat but even still I always manage to end up being attacked by someone off screen in almost every fight.  It's god dam disgraceful really.  Fricking N64 games have better cameras than this game does.
The only thing this game has going for it is executions.  These are activated when an enemy has a skull above his head.  When you activate it goes into a QTE animation filled with gory goodness.  That's really the only thing I can find in the game that I enjoy.  Everything else is abysmal or worse.
There are segments in the game where you command soldiers in a formation but it's really just a Block or Throw Spear sequence.  You block incoming arrows & throw spears when there's an opening.  That's pretty much it.
Then even worse, the game employs a cash shop system.  Sure, you can buy upgrades for points but later down the line it requires a huge chunk of points for a single upgrade.  One upgrade I bought was only 10k but the next one after that was frigging 30k.  Another jumped from 20k to 60k & I'm not even halfway up the upgrade path yet.  They obviously want you to buy this crap with real currency or something & that's just a giant middle finger to anyone who buys the game at full price.  Even the multiplayer is full of these cash shop upgrades.  This was a $60 game when it first came out on Xbone so why in the hell are you monetizing the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it like this?  If I didn't buy this game on a sale I'd refund the dam thing right now.

This is a proper expansion pack from the days when they made those sorts of things, and if you liked
, this is basically more of it with some neat stuff added. If you're someone who
more, I'd say pick it up.
There's three new weapons: an artifact that gives you powers, a double shotgun and an ersatz Gravity Gun. Said ersatz tool, the Grabber, is pretty neat. It makes fighting certain enemies pretty trivial, but I honestly don't have a problem with that because it's fun to waste the things with their own projectiles, or even use them
projectiles. The artifact is neat to use, upgradeable, and gives you more tactical options. The double shotgun is also nice to use as an opener, or to dispatch lone enemies quickly - sadly it reloads too slowly to really use through longer fights.
The story is a continuation of the base game: two years after the initial Hell invasion, the UAC, being incapable of learning from its mistakes, sends a team back to Mars to investigate a strange signal. Predictably, all Hell breaks loose and you're the only one who can deal with the problem. I appreciate that your mission control is a woman who has some agency and knows what she's doing, not to mention being able to survive the demonic invasion. Given that the only woman in the base game was literally there so you could watch her get possessed in a cutscene, I'll take it. However, the ending is kind of disappointing even if it does provide some resolution to the story.
Actual gameplay and level design are more or less the same, although there's a couple of new xenomorph-looking enemies and a higher ratio of open spaces to closed spaces than the base game, given how the expansion's a bit shorter.
Good sequel, recommend.
