First off, don’t let my current “0.3hrs on record” deter you from reading my review.  I’ve easily put 10+ hours into this game, played it thoroughly from beginning to end, and earned 100% achievements and game completion.  I am on OSX, and there is actually a known issue where logged time does not display correctly for this game.
Evoland is a tribute game to some of the best old school RPG’s that many of us grew up with.  It uses much of the same game mechanics progressing from the first generation Gameboy through 8bit, 16bit, and eventually 3D styles.  It does not take itself too seriously and there are no pretenses as to where each piece of the game was taken from…from the default hero’s name “Clink” to easily recognizable monsters, and of course to the gameplay itself.  Despite this being very much a tribute game, I found it thoroughly enjoyable and original in its own right.  Many have complained that the game is too short, and I did find myself yearning for more after having beaten it.  However, the flow for this game was just right, and unlike many of the old school RPG’s from my childhood, I did not spend endless hours grinding for XP or farming for gold/equipment as there was simply no need for it.  That was one stretch of this memory lane I wasn’t too upset about skipping.
The game progresses quickly, unlocking upgrades to all aspects of the game (graphics, music, battle system, etc.) through treasure chests that are scattered throughout each area.  There is even a section in the game where you are required to “time travel” between two game styles in order to progress through the map.  The game is charmingly simplistic and straight forward, but not at all boring.
The best part of Evoland is of course the nostalgia factor, where I feel SHIRO absolutely succeeded.  I would have liked to have seen more content in general, but they definitely touched on all of the right ideas.  The mini collectible card game was a nice touch, although it would’ve been great to include a gallery to be able to view the cards that have been collected.  The soundtrack is excellent and the graphics were true to each era.  The most critical thing I could say about this game might be in its timing on the upgrades.  You are rewarded with several upgrades right at the start of the game but towards the end after you hit 3D mode, they become very scarce.  I think the game would have been more effective if these upgrades were spaced out a little better.
I bought Evoland on sale but would happily pay the full $10 for it.  It is also worth saying that if SHIRO ever releases an Evoland 2, I would totally buy it.  I highly recommend this game to anyone that has a soft spot for old school RPG’s.

It's an amazing idle game, definitely one of the best ones out there right now, even if it can feel a bit barebones at times, but I guess you can't expect polish on an early access game. I love how there's no paywall (although there are certainly ways to boost your gameplay using real money) and just the DnD theme makes it all more enjoyable. The progress is great, you move at a decent pace throughout the game and the many different heroes/formations allow the game to really feel like your own journey (but you'll probably be using the same optimized formationas everyone else). The campaigns are  fun, light-hearted and move quickly, which is also a plus, though it's nothing deep enough to make you feel invested in the quest itself or anything, which I guess really isn't important for an idle game anyway.
Some cons though:
-It's a bit more active than other idle games, you can't really leave it idle for too long or you'll get stuck, so you only truly idle once you hit a wall
-Combat and heroes just feel so slow. Characters take several seconds to attack and move, the enemies basically crawl towards you, dialogue moves slowly, chests take fforever to open on their own,  and the gold takes awhile to be auto-looted.
-Divine favor only effects gold drop
So all in all, it's a great game and 100% worth a shot if you like idle games, just don't go in expecting it to be an actual DnD game.

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is everything that all sci-fi RPGs want to be. Playing through KOTOR, I knew that the interesting combat, prevelant dialogue choices, and memorable characters wouldn't find their way out of my mind any time near my last gameplay session. No spoilers here, but this game contains some of the most memorable plot twists in video game history and, with the rich Star Wars universe as its settings, there is no shortage of dimension when it comes to characters and plot points.
The multiple story paths as per player choice allows for some incredible replayabilty with the choice to either become one with the dark side, or toil alongside your jedi brothers and sisters. Your customly created character is mute in the story, but the player is able to choose from multiple different dialogue choices that have significant impacts on the story. You choose everything that your character communicates with the other PCs and NPCs.
I wasn't a huge fan of Star Wars before playing this game, and that was perfectly OK. The game didn't throw anything at me that only the most hardcore of Star Wars fanatics would know, though I'm sure that there were some nods to past Star Wars installments in the game's multiple settings (including the Wookie homeworld, the Sand people homeworld, and so on).
I was more impressed with this game than any other that I've played in the recent years and I would surely recommend this game to anyone- no matter whether or not they enjoy Star Wars or even RPG. This game is a must play.
My overall rating: 9.8/10 (combat could take a while to fully grasp)
This game is so amazing it`s mind boggeling, I love it and everyone who wants to enter the Star Wars Universe this is where to start.

At the same time that the disappointing 'prequel trilogy' was hitting theatres, LucasArts, back when it was still making quality games, asked Bioware to make an RPG, and gave them the freedom to set it 4,000 years before the movies. What the audience got was a big, dramatic dose of the Star Wars Expanded Universe, with all new characters, worlds, histories, and ulitmately, one of the best Computer Role Playing Games of all time.
If you liked Mass Effect, you can see this the game where Bioware's team first worked out many of the same ideas. And, I would argue, this is a far far superior game to Mass Effect, if only because it has the more cerebral turn-based combat instead of shooty action, and also by the end of this game you have played out a complete story, without necessity for sequels.
This is one of those rare games that, once I was absorbed in it, I played it beginning to end without taking a break to play something else. The turn-based DnD style combat is decent, though it can be frustrating when facing a large number of strong foes, as even when pausing every turn, it's sometimes hard to get your characters (you get your main character and pick another 2 from your party to go on missions) to do what you want them to. But the real highlight of the game is exploring the various environments and interacting with all the NPCs.
If you're playing this on Windows, download Flawless Widescreen so you can get the game in widescreen and any resolution you want. It still looks really good! The only thing that I had to turn off in the options was 'Grass', as it caused the lower half of characters to disappear.
A gem from the golden age of Bioware and Lucasarts.

text: A must-play for Star Wars or RPG fans! BioWare executes perfectly the small team (three people) tactical RPG feeling and makes the game a natural fit into the Star Wars universe. The storyline was deep and immersive, and provided plenty of interesting "grey-area" choices that had an actual impact of the world of the game. The gameplay was engaging, with the right balance of tactics and action. Pause-and-play in the BioWare style worked excellently, putting just the right level of challenge into combat. Character progression flowed very well, although I recommend looking up a little bit about some recommended character builds if you want to optimize, because it can be a little bit confusing at the beginning (even if you've played D&D 3.5 or other d20 RPGs). $10 is a bargain, and it frequently goes on sale (I got it for $2.50). If you're looking for a solid RPG that will provide you with a large amount of playtime in an engaging world, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is for you.

First things first: you really NEED a controller for this game. While I'm sure it's possible to play with a keyboard, the game plays MUCH better when played with a controller.
Besides that, this is a very well polished hack and slash / character action game. It takes a little while to get used to using the ability system while in an actual fight, but when you actually learn to perform combos with them, you'll be really glad that you did.
I'll admit that I don't play a huge amount of these kind of games, but I felt the game was fair without being over-easy on the difficulty curve, and the mixture of dashing and attacking was fast, fluid, and pretty damn fun. The game even manages to work in the classic 'Vergil'/rival/worthy opponent fight.
The story is pretty light on the ground, but what's there is good: the characters are likeable, the dialogue is actually really well translated, and the banter the two heroines share is amusing to no end*. I actually would really like to explore and see this sort of world the game is based in, if only because the dialogue suggests something greater than the game's total sum is going on outside of the game's events.
There's also quite a few modes to play around in, so even if the story is pretty quick to go, there's a decent amount of replayability, even if highscores and leaderboards aren't your cup of tea.
Over all, an enjoyable hack and slash which is pretty noob-friendly, with an amusing story and interesting setting, even if the former is light and the ground and we only get a few hints at the later. If you can, pick it up and see if there's anything for you in there.
*There's also some sub-text in there (which becomes more or less just text by the end), so if you were looking for that kind of thing...

PLOT: Lucrezia wants to take a bath with Francesca. Franny is all "NO WAY IN HELL" and runs off to a massive tower(paging Dr. Freud). Luc has to fight through a dozen or so floors of goblins, flying eyeballs, knights in shining armor, and huge beasts to drag Fran's sorry butt into the tub.
Okay I forgot the actual plot to this game. I assure you all that there is one and it's kinda-sorta-quasi-serious. But who cares about that nonsense? This is a supplemental-arcade-arena-slashemup. If you have less than 15 minutes to spare you can complete a play-through of this game. Yes, this game is a short one, but it's pretty sweet. There are no crazy mission designs, no escorting, no stealth, nothing but just slashing through hundreds of generic foes and grabbing coins.
Before the game starts you decide on your arsenal. There are 10 weapons per gal and they all have their own special moves. Basically you want a combination of weapons that suit your play-style. Special moves can be chained for more damage, and some are only effective in mid-air, or as anti-air (gotta account for the flying eyes). Don't fuss over your style rating though, this game rewards speed and efficiency above everything else. Yellow enemies drop in a single hit, blues go down in three, and reds take 4+. Once you memorize the basics all you have to worry about is dashing around and mopping everything up.
There are a variety of modes, but variety is a rather strong word when it comes to Croixleur.
Story - Kill Everything As Fast As Possible. Lots of plot and talks about baths.
Time Attack - KEAFAP in 3 minutes
Survival - KEAFA you want. Expect to see huge crowds of enemies.
Challenge - Definitely KEAFAP.
Bonus - This is the epilogue. Luc & Fran team up to bring the hurt on slightly tougher enemies. Don't forget to KEAFAP.
For the most part Croixleur Sigma is a fast-paced and satisfying slasher. The controls are fluid enough and it's fun zipping around shredding everything. However there are some issues that I have with the game.
Certain moves have weak properties. One of the specials Luc can perform is a downward stab that causes a large shockwave. However, that shockwave is mostly for looks and only hits enemies that are practically under Luc. This tends to be the case with a number of special moves. They look like they should hit because you see the flashy trails and pretty lights connect with enemies, but instead they miss completely. It's...well not really that big an issue. I mean, it's not like it's inconsistent or anything. It would be much worse if the moves hit only some of the time.
Anti-cooperative play. When Luc & Fran team up, it spells trouble...for Luc & Fran. You have to give your BFF plenty of breathing space or she will hit you with her regular and special attacks (and vice-versa). This doesn't do any damage, but it will stun you, and can throw your rhythm off as well as waste time. Maybe the developer thought it would be too easy if this wasn't the case. Luc & Fran could just throw those special moves out constantly and be a whirling dervish of destruction. I disagree. Croixleur Sigma plays up the bestest buddies element, but then implements a design-decision that causes real-world friends to fight? That is a definite head-scratcher. Also during the bonus mode the game only ends when player 1 dies. Player 2 can die as many times as they like. This is something I abused for the cheap final battle.
Croixleur Sigma is like I said, a supplemental game. You play this title alongside your "main" game, or when you absolutely must play something, and don't have much time. It's not a deep game though, not even in terms of game-design depth. If Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae complements games like Devil May Cry and Metal Gear Rising, this game is best played alongside Dynasty Warriors. When you want a dumb 5-minute slashathon, but don't want to run around huge maps and listen to a bunch of talk about Three Kingdoms and whatever whatever, then play this game.

The very first thing I want to address in my review is the negative reviews this game has received in it's first two weeks since launching on early access. I'm OK with people not liking something I like. What enjoyment a person derives from an experience and the qualities of that experience are largely subjective. That said, I'm not particularly tolerant of people blaming others for their own failings.
Absolutely every single negative review for this game at the time of this posting without exception can be summarized as: the game is still in early development and I don't like that. I can't emphasize this enough, because absolutely every single negative review has been posted by someone willing to take the time to write something negative about a game in development but completely unwilling to learn about it before purchasing. The wall of blue text on the store page, the forums, the developers YouTube channel, Twitch, and lets not forget THE VERY REVIEW PAGE THEY ARE POSTING ON all inform you that the game is still more or less in alpha. So if you wish to make your purchasing decisions based on these knuckle dragging cretins, then here's your sign, you can skip the remainder of this review.
The store page videos give you a good idea of the game experience the game is working towards. The key here is working towards, not at currently. Quite simply if you want to be part of the development of the game then I think you'll find it a rewarding experience. I have never seen devs as active and engaged as these. You can find them posting in the forums daily and every Friday they do a live stream Q&A session with the community. I think that's the key word there “community”. We're a community here working with the devs to make this game as good as possible. Now if you don't want to pay to be part of the testing and feedback phase of development, hey, that's perfectly fine. Check back every month or two and I think you'll eventually find a game in a state that you'll really enjoy.
I could write quite a bit about this game but what I think I can say that is most relevant is that it is fun.  Perhaps that is an unsurprising statement from someone who has played it for 115 hours in two weeks time, but ultimately a fun game is what we're all chasing after. Clearly I have been having a good time. What I think makes it remarkable is there are many little things here that show it is made by people who are gamers like us. They have taken some of the best qualities from a variety of RPG games and made something unique yet kind of familiar. The action focus has been a rewarding departure from the more conventional RPG style which I have enjoyed very much, making it a more skill based game than you usually find with an RPG. It's not exactly an MMO but contains the better aspects of an MMORPG while lacking some of the pitfalls. All in all I think it's a very exciting experiment for an RPG that tips the hat to classics in a way that is endearing.

Star Wolves is a hard game to describe. It's probably best described as a space battle manager where you are managing this mercenary group, Star Wolves, in performing missions for the highest bidder (but you do get to choose). You don't control the crafts directly, but you give waypoints, and attack orders, missile launches and defenses, and so on. You can configure each fighter for different roles: missile defense (jamming), support, escort, attack, and so on. The mothership is also under your command and serves as repair and rearm station for all the fighters, and it is armed with multiple turrets (albeit, it can be overwhelmed). The idea is to defeat the enemy forces without suffering losses of your own by managing your resources: the pilots and the fighters, carefully. Each pilot has his or her own skill tree and can be unlocked with experience points, which opens up special abilities that can be tapped in battle, such as better accuracy, double defense for 30 seconds, and so on.  There is also a bit of trading and salvage as you can often salvage weapons and missiles off destroyed enemy ships, and sometimes, even steal whole fighters. Plot is somewhat on the lame side, and most dialogs are in text only, but graphics are good. All in all, it depends what sort of gamer are you. If you want hands-on fly-the-ship kind this is NOT for you. But if you like giving orders and see them carried out this is good for you.

An interesting game, for many reasons. Probably best described as a diamond in the rough, this game's strengths are not immediately visible.
The initial impression might be rather unfavourable - the user interface and menus could use some work, only two resolutions are supported, controls take a bit to get used to, and the most annoying one: it's painfully evident the script-writer's English wasn't his forte (same for voice actors).
Still, once past all that the game uses a good-looking graphical engine, the combat mechanics are solid, and the game universe is not only large but also quite elaborate - historical and current events are presented with lots of detail, the various factions each have their own distinct flavours, and the story offers interesting twists and turns, as well as a fair amount of choices that affect how future events unfold.
At £9.99 Star Wolves is a bit too pricey, but a good discount will make the game a worthwhile play for fans of the genre.

This game wears out its welcome after the first fifteen minutes. It quickly jumps through the early eras of gaming, which was the only reason I bought the game, and then devolves into an insipid mishmash of poorly executed gameplay.
To break it down, the game begins with a Zelda-stlye top down action game, which, while competently executed, lacks the aesthetic beauty, creativity, or excellent design which define excellent games like Link to the Past or Minish Cap. The visuals are uninspired, and the enemy design is limited to very few, extremely repetitive octorock clones and bats. There are one or two interesting boss fights, but it remains dull and uninteresting.
After this you are hurled into a truly horrifically designed Final Fantasy clone. Lacking a mana system, it is utterly dull and a chore to grind through. Outdated principals like random encounters and a totally pointless item system makes this truly digusting. To make it worse, this takes up the majority of the games 5 or 6 hour lifespan, and the endgame is almost nothing but it.
There are a few bright spots. Sort of clever Easter Eggs are hidden in a few spots, and the Diablo style level is both challenging and a scathing mockery of the goofy loot system in such games. Overall, however, the game is disappointing, uninspired, slapdash, and dull. There is no way in hell this thing is worth 10 dollars or your time. Heartily not recommended.

text: A must-play for Star Wars or RPG fans! BioWare executes perfectly the small team (three people) tactical RPG feeling and makes the game a natural fit into the Star Wars universe. The storyline was deep and immersive, and provided plenty of interesting "grey-area" choices that had an actual impact of the world of the game. The gameplay was engaging, with the right balance of tactics and action. Pause-and-play in the BioWare style worked excellently, putting just the right level of challenge into combat. Character progression flowed very well, although I recommend looking up a little bit about some recommended character builds if you want to optimize, because it can be a little bit confusing at the beginning (even if you've played D&D 3.5 or other d20 RPGs). $10 is a bargain, and it frequently goes on sale (I got it for $2.50). If you're looking for a solid RPG that will provide you with a large amount of playtime in an engaging world, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is for you.

The community for this game is also very small, not a lot of people know about Awesomenauts, and it doesn't help that the jackasses in it just yell at new players and scare them off, bringing this game down even more. They claim to be fixing the main issues with this game, so there's still hope on the matchmaking being fixed. If you do decide to buy this game, please, stick around and help the community grow, and maybe even leave a good review to help the game appeal to potential new members of this community. Allright, for an idle game this is probably quite good.  You don't have to clickspam to play it, there's some limited thinking involved in setting up your party formation, and it tries at least half heartedly to give the illusion of RPG by having you embark on small module feeling adventures with little snippets of story telling in them.
That said, this is a horrid use of the D&D name and a lazy attempt at a quick buck in the idle games genre from WotC.
The tacticery really doesn't matter.  It is easy enough to figure out how to get a good line of dps with support behind them figured out, and once that is done the party abilities such as shields and healing matter precious little, you still need to idle and wait for those big dps upgrades to progress.
The adventures are also very poorly written.  Not an abundance of typos, but it reeks of being written by an intern with zero experience in good writing.  Predictably there is also zero RPG going on, you are just along for the ride.  Which one can say is fine I guess as this is not an RPG, but a idle clicker masquerading as one.
The monetization also feels very stiff.  After 4 hours I was given two chests, one 'silver' and one 'gold' with the first giving only some gold and 1 bad equipment piece, and the gold chest giving three gear pieces, one with higher rarity.
You can purchase gold chests with 'Gems' earned after bosses and upon completing adventures as well.  I am at something like 300 gems out of 5000 gems needed to purchase a gold chest.  There's a 10% chance to get an 'epic' item from a gold chest, and there are an extra tier of 'golden epic' items that can only be earned for real money.  This game is blatantly designed to not let you have any kind of fun unless you pay for it.
So yeah.  Not for me, and not for people wanting to play a good game.  Its greedy, RPG enthusiasts will feel sorry for Minsc and others for seeing their names on this thing, and if this as an official D&D game is supposed to draw attention to their proper RPG's, it fails spectacularily at that.
But as an idle clicker which arguably barely qualifies to be called a game, it isn't so bad I guess.  As a bonus I did get a small smirk out of imagining a player at a table rolling D20's for days when an upgraded Minsc swings for 100 trillion damage at a time.
It is a solid time killer.

I beat the game after 8.5 hours using the scout class.
I played on the highest difficulty (Ace) out of 4.
TL:DR
-It's well worth $10 especially if they are adding more content and tweaking what is already there.
Pros:
-Great ship controls, the overall gameplay mechanics feel very solid.
-Multiple classes with different playstyles.
-Solid graphics and artstyle to match what the game is going for.
-Great performance on my rig (CPU: FX-8320 ; GPU: gtx 1070) -100fps-
-Great loot system, that can only get better with future updates.
Cons:
-Loot doesn't despawn, causing massive framerate drops after extended play (reloading fixes the issue, it's not that big a problem)
-The enemies are the simplest of AI and pose no challenge.
-Highest difficulty has no difference from normal (You will one shot everything, even the final boss)
-I never went under 100% health.
-The questing is incredibly repetitive (the same exact quests over and over).
Misc:
-The story isn't so much bad as it is simple, which I have no issue with given that there were more set pieces and more of an actual campaign.(currently the story quests are no different than side quests)
-There is no crafting in the game yet, yet it lets you upgrade your crafting areas to max (just wasting money)
-The store page says there are set items in the game, I have yet to find one.
-The looting all boils down to how much precision you have (it's the only stat that changes damage for the most part)
All things said, I genuinely enjoyed the game and am happy to have come across it.
I recommend it to anyone who enjoy ARPG titles such as Diablo or want a simple space sim that will let them turn their mind off for a bit.
Honestly at $10, you won't get a better game.
Most of the issues I have will probably be patched in the following weeks. So stay tuned for an updated version.

In this DLC, the developers basically took elements from other popular FPS (gravity gun from Half-Life 2 and slow motion from Max Payne/F.E.A.R.) and added them to the mix.  It felt like the gravity gun was forced.  It was included, and in addition, most levels were filled with explosive barrels just begging to be tossed.  These were a waste of time for me, as you get plenty of ammo for your other weapons, including the best addition to the game: The double-barreled shotgun.  Lemme tell ya, you don't know firepower until you use this thing.  Like, it feels ludicrous to not dive deeper into the slow motion mechanic or the great new enemies.  But this weapon, this thing felt just so powerful.  Even on Veteran it felt like most of the game's challenges could be handled with this thing.  It sounded and felt like the ultimate detructive weapon.  To compare it to another game, remember the first time you fired the BFG in the original Doom?  That's how I felt firing this thing for the first time.  I chuckled as the enemy in front of me was torn apart in one blow.  This thing was a beast, using it was an experience all on its own.  It honestly made the DLC for me, just seeing the game drop larger and larger enemies, larger crowds, and using this thing paired with slow motion to empty an entire room.  It was a magical weapon, unlike any weapon I have used in any FPS in recent memory.  On the surface it is simply two shotgun blasts in one, but in practice it was so much more.
So yeah, if you liked main Doom 3, get this DLC just for the double shotty.

Genuinely funny in places, and profound in others, this belongs right up there with "A Beginner's Guide" when it comes to insights into the creative process, and what it's like to work on large projects, and how fan behaviour and "love" for a franchise can foul up such things. The "game" aspect of it won't last forever; it's more a taste, an idea for you to play around with, but it's a very good one: modifying the attributes and abilities of creatures is a lot of fun, while it lasts, and there are a few basic puzzles that can be solved in a variety of ways.
Put simply, if you're into "meta" humour and storytelling, you'll like this. At one point, you get to actually design a level, and one of the characters does a real-time "Let's Play" stream of it, commenting on everything from music usage to health potion placement.
Also impressive that, while the game is one big reference to its own industry and is full of visible influences from famous games, it doesn't resort to clumsy *direct* references.
Just about the only criticism I can aim at TMC is the abrupt nature of its story - it could have leaned just a little more in the direction of Portal, with more actual puzzles and gameplay, and I would have loved to hear just a little more about the characters.

I have mixed but afterwards slightly positive feelings of Evoland.
Initial concept of Evoland is interesting: you begin with very crude controls, graphics and game mechanics, to find and discover new, nicer ones along the way. This is the premise. The game play changes between Legend of Zelda like free roam fighting and associated (actually quite nice) puzzles involving arrows, bombs and "time travelling" mechanic, and Final Fantasy / Dragon Quest style game with frequent random battles. There's also a scenario where the game goes full Diablo for a short while.
While initially entertained, I grew utterly bored after a short while into the game because of its low difficulty level and the lack of story. Granted, the latter is (albeit true-to-form) introduced only later into the game and built upon for a mediocre tale heavily inspired by Zelda / FF games. The boredom only wore off after meeting the villain for the first time. With the fast-travel by airship and an in-game guy assisting with finding of the collectables I was finally enjoying myself again. I could have sworn I had fully cleared several previously visited locations but instead found some nicely hidden puzzles.
Lasting only few hours and providing mixed amounts entertainment, I'd advice getting it on a sale. You should also have played some of the early RPGs like mentioned in this review: Evoland contains loads of references you could appreciate but might find silly if uninformed.

First, get a good computer. Second, adjust the graphical and texture settings for good performance. Third, enjoy the game. P.S Lots of blood, beware.
Good game with lots of depth with simple controls, and good story telling. Although, the skill system is pretty pointless because you get enough points to unlock them all. Would have been better to have a system where you must sacrifice choices.
In terms of gameplay, the game has some performance issues with stuttering in some high graphical areas (this has been experienced with players across all computer spectrums, from low-end to high-end). That can be ignored to some extent, but quite annoying. No fix yet (since 2014).
If you are a collection or achievement type of person, the game has many collectables. It also rewards players for exploration so you will always get something other than fighting around (beware the game is still going to be combat related, treat this like a side dish rather than the big meal).
The combat is simple and elegant, unlike other fighter games where combos require multiple button setups, the game focuses on timing and usage of perks. So anyone can get into the game, learn it quickly, but hard to master.
Multiplayer, does not have many players, so do not expect getting CO-OP matches or what not quickly. But still enjoyable for playing with friends (not so much for single players unless you want to be on the leaderboards).
Music is amazing and probably made the game a lot stronger than it was. Many times the music adds a layer emotion that attaches you to the character or makes connections to yourself. (So play with headphones or a good sound system)
Visuals, I am not much of a visual type of person. But graphical setups and scenes were good and well done. The game brings you through several environments and show off the Crytek Engine like deep green jungles, the english channel, the streets of Rome, and dark dense forests. I really enjoyed the invasion scene with the boats and fighting on the streets of York.
Story, some characters were pointless in the story. The gods are a good example because they did not have any depth other than being plot to forward the story. Most of the antagonists or villains were under developed and just silly with some exceptions in good character design.
For example, Commodus, Nero and Basillius could have been any spoiled rich kid with a superiority complex. Nothing interesting about them.
Characters that were good, Boudica, King Oswald and Vitallion. Their character shines out without plot and the player can make judgements about their lives without the game giving it to you.
(On the fence with the main character, his personality goes all over the place, from loving son to revenge driven solider, to vengeful spirit and to defender of Rome.) There is no core values or spirit in the character, he is pretty empty with goals that drive him. His entire journey to fight was based on revenge from the beginning of the game until the invasion of Rome.
His character really fleshes out during the end of the game where he defends Rome with Vitallion, but other than that, there are many disconnects in his character from the beginning to the end of the game.
In other words, his character goes from a naive revenge driven son to an honourable hero of Rome within one day. That is a pretty big personality change that no real human being truly experiences. Bring it down a notch.
Overall, the game gets a 8/10 on my list.

As other reviewers noted, this game isn't so much a journey of action/adventure games so much as it is a journey of RPGs--notably the Final Fantasy and the Legend of Zelda series. Which, admittedly, still promised a lot of fun and engagement, but didn't really deliver the way I'd hoped it would.
It incorporates both old-school turn-based RPG combat and your older "hack-and-slack" style combat reminiscent of early Zelda games. However, these forms of combat alternate, so that most world-map combat is turn-based, and the majority of the dungeons and forests are subjected to the hack-and-slash that can be a little jarring in transition. The turn-based follows a familiar timer system, where you cannot attack, heal, run, etc., until it's your "time" to do so.
While it admittedly did bring me a good bit of nostalgia, the game doesn't have much to stand on beyond that. As much as I found myself enjoying the ability to "unlock" the advancements to the game such as 16-bit color or 3-D rendering, it quickly grew tedious and monotonous. There's not a lot of story or plot to keep you interested in long term play, let alone to replay the game, and it doesn't have that something special to set it apart from other games, as it seems to rely to heavily on the nostalgia to carry the game. I did like some of the puzzles that had you switching between the 16-bit era and the more modern 3-D game structure to move through them, but it wasn't enough to make the game stand out.
Furthermore, if you're looking to play this game purely through the keyboard and mouse, you'll be a bit disappointed. The space bar acts as the action key, and movement can only be achieved by your direction keys. It makes the older style combats (particularly your hack-and-slash) a bit more difficult to pull off with finesse.
In the end, I can't really say I'd recommend the game--unless you have the time and money to kill, and don't mind enduring some frustration during gameplay to do so.

When it comes to humor, gaming humor is about as low-brow as it gets, as it consists on not so much jokes or satire as it is a vapid stream of obvious and shallow references. Evoland is meant to be a tongue-in-cheek love letter to classic jRPGs. Unfortunately, as a love-letter, is is a flaccid and unflattering presentation, and as a piece of gaming humor, it doesn't do much more than ape Legend of Zelda, Final Fantasy 7 and Diablo.
One of the defining points of this game is that as you play through it, you collect systems that slowly update the game's graphics and gameplay, giving the impression of the game evolving through the ages. Unfortunately, of all the systems they aped for the gameplay, this game somehow manages to make them less compelling than the original material. From the janky hitboxes for the top-down gameplay system, the overall lack of enemy variety, the annoyingly high encounter rate for the random turn-based battle encounters, to the Diablo-style loot that does absolutely nothing. (Which completely misses the mark because almost every loot item in this type of game adds something new to the play style.) In fact, when the world opened up near the end of the game, I was so daunted and irritated by the tedious and frequent random encounters that I would have put the game down for good if if weren't for the fact that I am literally one fight away from finishing the game. There are a couple of good things I could say about the gameplay, and it involves the dimensional swapping mechanic, and the action RPG bit of the final boss. (Which is still not as exciting or compelling as the boss fights from Ys Origins, and lacks the dungeon crawling action that is often associated with them.)
The story is the weakest point of the game, which is ironic since it's supposed to be an RPG that is a love letter to RPG games of the past that had a lot of imaginative and epic stories. In fact, it is one of the most creatively bankrupt RPGs I have ever seen as far as stories go. It is very little more than copying the tropes set by classic RPGs of the past, and the fact that the title and the world is called Evoland should be indicative of this, and that isn't as bad as it gets, believe me.
The only really good point about this game is that the music is really good. On their own, they would be really fun to listen to, and I really wish that the soundtrack was more varied than it was.
So do I recommend this game? No. Even if it's on sale for less than a dollar, I cannot really recommend this game because it is not only priced more than it is worth, it is also very taxing on your patience as it does nothing with the premise that is compelling or less aggravating than it was in the old games, nor does it do anything fresh, inspiring or funny with the premise, story-wise. All it does is remind me how much I hate random encounters, and how I am glad that some modern jRPGs got rid of it for something that lets players initiate battles themselves.
Save your time and money. Use it to buy and play the actual old-school RPGs like Ys, Titan Quest, Diablo, The Elder Scrolls, Half Minute Hero, The Carpe Fulgur Collection, or even Final Fantasy. They would be far more worth your time and money than this vapid piece of gaming junk.

Evoland is the tale of two games.

All in all I really enjoyed myself but be warned - if struggling with a crappy 3D RPG is going to outweigh your enjoyment of this games central concept then you're gonna have a bad time. Also, check out DRM Quest for a similar approach to procedurally adding elements, albeit one lampooning a whole different part of gaming culture...

There's a list of phrases and each turn you and your opponent pick one to try and form a sentence to insult each other. Once you pick a phrase it's their turn, and so on.
For instance on each of your turns might pick the phrases:
1 Your mother
2 smells like
3 a mangy dog
4 and
5 makes me sick
Then you press the exclamation point button to tell the game your sentence/insult is finished. From there the sentence is read by your character, each of which has a weakness to certain types of insults, and you do Honor damage. Whoever gets their opponent to zero honor first wins. In the event of a tie a tie breaker insult round is performed.
A ton of fun to be had with goofy insults that don't really make much sense in the long run. Still a blast though.

More of the same but worse. Resurrection of Evil serves as a conclusion to the plot of Doom 3, seeing as how the main game just sort of stopped on a clumsy cliffhanger when it got bored. The expansion pack, however, is inferior in pretty much every possible way.
The encounter design is worse, using the powerup artifact it gives you as an excuse to throw powerful enemies at every alternate step and using the "jerk's first fan level" philosophy that the best way to introduce challenge is to just make the player kill a million of something.
The scares are worse, especially in the penultimate level where the spooky red filter of doom literally flashes every couple of seconds making it feel like your tram got stuck in front of one of the attractions at a haunted house ride.
And the gear is worse, taking away your chainsaw and "kill-the-thing-and-heal-me" panic button in favor of that technological marvel that keeps showing up in sci-fi games which revolutinarily replicates the powers of a working set of hands, and the previously mentioned powerup artifact that by around the two-thirds mark of the game gives you bullettime, increased damage, and invulnerability. Which sounds ridiculous, until they start contriving reasons for you to use it in the first few levels, which they eventually give up on in favor of just doing things like "lock you in a room with a dozen hellknights and mancubi" because they handed the level editor to their 13-year-old son for a few minutes, presumably.
And of course the plot is worse, in that there barely is one. For the first half of the game your job is basically just "get out of the hole you start out in," while three suped-up hellknight-ish bosses take turns to fight you before you Megaman their powers. And the second half is "get to Delta Labs so you can shoot the villain we forgot to kill in the main game in the face." Which you do by shutting down all power in the area you're in to divert the energy to teleporting you over to Delta Labs. Because walking is too hard, I guess. Also one of the things you shut down to reroute power is the reactor. I don't think the developers knew how rerouting works. And then you shoot the boss in his silly tongue-face and he dies, the end. Literally, it cuts to black right after he dies and you get one line of dialogue from mission control as the credits roll.
Boring, pointless, and literally the only reason I bothered was because I paid money for this♥♥♥♥♥♥so I might as well see it through to the end. Don't do the same.

TL:DR - What happens when the changes from Doom 3 go too far.
Full review: Unlike the base game, I find it very hard to recommend this expansion. I already went in depth with what Doom 3 does differently in its review, so I won't repeat myself here. What I will say is that Resurrection of Evil takes the great, if somewhat off-putting, changes to the formula that the base game did [Atmosphere, game pacing, ammo, etc.], and turns it into its biggest flaw, to the point that I am writing this review now, instead of when I finish. The lighting is much darker than the base game, the action and the pacing is much slower, armor and ammo distribution is much more restrictive, and the horror angle is expanded on further... yet, due to how slow the game is, rather than keep me hooked, I find myself tuning out and focusing on going from point A to B, which is the last thing you want happening in a game like this.
As far as action is concerned, ammo for your weapons are much further and farther in between than in the base game. Thankfully, you get the Grabber, a new weapon to the game, which lets you grab small props, enemies and their projectiles in the enviroment and fling them at enemies to deal damage. Already, the biggest issue with this is that you are forced to use a slow weapon, as it takes time between release and pick-up to recharge. In addition, solution 1 in my Doom 3 review for the lighting issues in the game (Installing the duct tape mod) will not work, as you'll predominatley have the grabber as your current weapon. Another problem is that this weapon fully relies on your enemies being demons, as human enemies all attack using their fists or their guns, and will be much faster, meaning that you can't get close without being hit by bullets. To remedy this, the game also gives you an artifact [don't know the name, so don't ask]; which, when activated, will let you run around, temporarily in "hell time" [bullet time, "Slow motion" for the uninitiated]. Not only does this bring the already slow gameplay down to an almost glacial pace, but the game expects you to use it at almost every oppertunity, as not only can you hold up to 3 charges, but you can refill on charges by collecting souls from the dead UAC staff, which are placed everywhere.
The most egregious example of these issues in in Erebus level 5. In an end-level segment, you have to run a gauntlet where your helmet has very limited air, so you are running and gunning, picking up air tanks along the way; something that this add-on is not meant for. In this segment, there are a few enemies that you must retaliate to using the grabber. Their projectiles fly very quickly, so you'll need to use "hell time" to slow down the game enough to be able to take care of these enemies quickly. You'll need to do this 3 times in this segment, which will use all of your artifact ammo. However, in a case of "How did they miss this bug?", Any souls that are in this sement can not be picked up, even if you walk over the body! What's worse is that once past this segment, you transistion to Erebus Level 6... and another air tank sequence! This time it's outdoors, on mars' surface, where you run out of air much faster. There are no souls to reload your artifact in between these sequences to assist you here, so you will need to run from point A to B as fast as you can, or deal with all the enemies with the limited ammo and SEVERELY limited air that you have, at full speed. Pardon my french, but that segment can go fornicate itself with an iron stick.
Really, however, I am more bored than anything else. This expansion is not technically flawed [apart from that one example above], and it controls and plays the same as the base game. However, unlike Doom 3, which had a clear goal on what it was trying to do (What if the DOOM "storyline" was played straight?), Resurrection of Evil doesn't know whether it wants to be action or horror, and thus fails at both. I don't blame you if you want to give this expansion a try anyway; beauty is in the eye of the beholder. If this expansion didn't try to mess with the delicate balance of Action and Horror in Doom 3, this could've been a great add-on. For me, however, It's just a slow, borderline-mediocre game that doesn't seem to understand what it wants to be.

Doom 3: Resurrection of Evil is an expansion pack for the base game developed by ID software. Set 2 years after the events of 'Doom 3' you play as an unamed marine trying to recover an artifact on Mars for the UAC. As your character touches the artifact, your squadmate disentegrate, and the thought long banished, return...
The Good
- 12 levels
- 6 new enemies (although a few of them are basically reskins of old ones like the flying skulls)
- 3 new weapons (basically gravity gun, artifact and double barrel shotgun)
- 4 boss fights
- Decent playtime (completed it in around 6 hours)
The Bad
- Weak plot (not really a problem as the base game didn't have such a great plot either)
- Doesn't change much from the base game
- The last boss was a pain personally (too much was going on in the battle)
- Multiplayer is dead
Although it isn't doesn't offer anything amazing from the base game, it will definitely satisfies those who want to experience more Doom 3.

First, get a good computer. Second, adjust the graphical and texture settings for good performance. Third, enjoy the game. P.S Lots of blood, beware.
Good game with lots of depth with simple controls, and good story telling. Although, the skill system is pretty pointless because you get enough points to unlock them all. Would have been better to have a system where you must sacrifice choices.
In terms of gameplay, the game has some performance issues with stuttering in some high graphical areas (this has been experienced with players across all computer spectrums, from low-end to high-end). That can be ignored to some extent, but quite annoying. No fix yet (since 2014).
If you are a collection or achievement type of person, the game has many collectables. It also rewards players for exploration so you will always get something other than fighting around (beware the game is still going to be combat related, treat this like a side dish rather than the big meal).
The combat is simple and elegant, unlike other fighter games where combos require multiple button setups, the game focuses on timing and usage of perks. So anyone can get into the game, learn it quickly, but hard to master.
Multiplayer, does not have many players, so do not expect getting CO-OP matches or what not quickly. But still enjoyable for playing with friends (not so much for single players unless you want to be on the leaderboards).
Music is amazing and probably made the game a lot stronger than it was. Many times the music adds a layer emotion that attaches you to the character or makes connections to yourself. (So play with headphones or a good sound system)
Visuals, I am not much of a visual type of person. But graphical setups and scenes were good and well done. The game brings you through several environments and show off the Crytek Engine like deep green jungles, the english channel, the streets of Rome, and dark dense forests. I really enjoyed the invasion scene with the boats and fighting on the streets of York.
Story, some characters were pointless in the story. The gods are a good example because they did not have any depth other than being plot to forward the story. Most of the antagonists or villains were under developed and just silly with some exceptions in good character design.
For example, Commodus, Nero and Basillius could have been any spoiled rich kid with a superiority complex. Nothing interesting about them.
Characters that were good, Boudica, King Oswald and Vitallion. Their character shines out without plot and the player can make judgements about their lives without the game giving it to you.
(On the fence with the main character, his personality goes all over the place, from loving son to revenge driven solider, to vengeful spirit and to defender of Rome.) There is no core values or spirit in the character, he is pretty empty with goals that drive him. His entire journey to fight was based on revenge from the beginning of the game until the invasion of Rome.
His character really fleshes out during the end of the game where he defends Rome with Vitallion, but other than that, there are many disconnects in his character from the beginning to the end of the game.
In other words, his character goes from a naive revenge driven son to an honourable hero of Rome within one day. That is a pretty big personality change that no real human being truly experiences. Bring it down a notch.
Overall, the game gets a 8/10 on my list.

Evoland is one of those games that tells you what to expect from the outset - and it does what it says it does on the tin. The graphics are suitable for the time periods of when each generation of the games it imitates are out and there's a lot of references to other games throughout the adventure. Even having not played it for several months now, I can recall references to Mario, Final Fantasy, Zelda, Diablo and others besides. The soundtrack is equally as engaging to the nostalgic senses in the brain and it feels like it enhances the experience that you get when you play through it.
Unfortunately...it doesn't quite have much of it's own two feet beyond that. The gameplay is often an imitation of it's inspiration - and often a very limited experience of what it's imitating - and has far too much crossover for any one influence (or even it's own design) to actually cement itself as an overarching gameplay foundation. For those not floating on the nostalgic waves, this can make the game feel disjoined and maybe scattered in it's design, as if a clown was juggling too many balls to do the fancy tricks other RPG games can do to greater effect.
There have also been some issues that I recall from my last experience of it (hence the 12 hours of playing) where I lost access to my airship through a world map issue and had to restart from the beginning to get full achievement completion. And where item collection doesn't become a habit of face-hugging every wall looking for that one invisible area where it might be hiding, the other time-waster is the puzzles. I will admit, the puzzles sometimes can be pretty challenging to work out and do require some measure of thought, but others bordered the line between tedium and simplistic and a few were essentially efforts to get from A to B taking as little damage as possible.
For those who remember having their chunky white Game Boys in-hand in their teenage years or loved some of the original elements of Final Fantasy, this may be worth the few second-hand DVD's you'd get instead of this game simply on the nostalgic vibes it brings, but even then it may be better to just play the games this one imitates due to the imitation being the game's only strength - and not even that strong with very limited ability set to use. For everyone else, see what the reviewers are claiming this game reminds them of, read up on the games this one imitates, play those instead: You are more likely to get an immersive experience from those than this scripted love song to them.

Evoland purports to be a journey through the history of action/adventure gaming, but ends up being a nostalgic trip through A Link to the Past, Final Fantasy VI and Diablo.  Although I selected that I'd recommend this game, I'd really say that I'm closer to a "Neutral" than anything.
Most of the game takes place either as an overly simple turn-based RPG or the beginning of a Legend of Zelda game.  Most of the mechanics are fairly simple:  In the RPG sections you attack, use items or cast magic (and there are only three magic spells in the game); in the Zelda sections you get a sword, bombs and a bow.  The few puzzles that exist are extremely simple, and the storyline is almost non-existent.
Despite it being a simple game, Evoland is reasonably fun to play.  It's fun in the beginning to unlock new graphics types and abilities.  It also doesn't overstay its welcome...by the time it becomes apparent that the scope of the game is fairly small, it's over.  This is also a negative, however, as the entire game (including all of the optional achievements and getting 100% completion) can be easily finished in 4-5 hours.
If you can get it on sale (at least 50% off), it's a fun diversion for a few hours.  Just don't expect anything mind-blowing.

When a game does this good a job of making you feel like you're in the real world, then it can safely take liberties towards the unreal while maintaining your immersion and respect. The dialogue, at times, is overly poetic, but we stay convinced because everything else is so convincing, and it's that artistic liberty that elevates the game beyond being simply pretty pictures and into a meaningful contribution to our social discussion about issues. I also know that other games in the series involve far-out technology, again, only believable if the game can make us believe the rest is real.
This game was remarkably believable for me. It references real-world events and issues, some political and controversial.
Another realistic aspect is the visuals, although they probably rely very heavily on the inherent realistic and artistic look that rain and wetness have, but are also aided by great use of depth-of-field. Unlike other games, the depth of field is not to put your focus on something dramatically, it works just like real eyes or a camera might. When the player doesn't control the view, the cinematic scenes use a virtual camera man technique, like there's a person with a camcorder taking everything in. It's obviously very deliberate, but gives a convincing performance of being almost like spontaneous home video, again, adding to the realism.
The voice acting is top-notch and again, believable. Where other games have hokey, phoney accents, or  cartoon-tier use of inflection, this game has top actors that rely on their voices natural properties and skill to give believable performances to dialogue that is otherwise too eloquent for the real world.
The gameplay is extremely polished and perfected. The camera is not tethered to the direction your character is facing, like in many third person games. Instead, you can look around very freely, no matter which way you are moving. The cover system is the most natural one I've used. Move near a wall and your character huddles next to it, but the gameplay is mostly unchanged. If you're not in cover mode, there's little punishment, and enemies aren't much more likely to see you anyway, so the cover system serves more as a visual detail. Compare this to a game where you press a button to enter a distinct cover mode with different controls and consequences. All of this contributes to an extremely "smooth" sense to the gameplay, which I think again is a realism-adding factor.
This is an extremely important game. It's the only game I know where (slight spoiler from the intro movie here) you literally go to Guantanamo Bay and free torture victims from the US government. Other parts of the story have to do with challenging the state as well. You can't measure the importance of that in hours of gameplay in the main storyline, which is admittedly short. But if it's about gameplay hours to you over style and substance, there are hours of completionist goals added to the end game. Beating the main game took me 3 hours, but I was only 6% "complete" the whole content of the game, and so far find the extra missions at the end very playable/re-playable even though they take place in the same setting as the main mission.
Unfortunately this is the only Metal Gear game I've played. It's hard to say right now how much has been "spoiled" for me now. I really look forward to catching up on this series before MGSV comes out, and I hope an HD collection will come to Steam soon. I highly recommend this game if you are willing to take the same risk I did and possibly see some spoilers.

This game is just solidly okay -- and it's pretty expensive to be okay.
Pros:
-The premise of the game is fantastic and is well executed throughout
-The voice acting is excellent
-The use of powers (i.e. the ways you fight / interact with the world) is pretty interesting throughout
-The ability to trap monsters and have them fight for you is neat (sort of Pokemon-ish)
Cons:
-The game is REALLY short. Really really short. I beat it in < 2 hours.
-The level design is atrocious. Seriously. It's worse than some early 90s FPSes. A significant amount of my playtime was spent being lost.
-It thinks it's smarter than it is. The conceit of the game (you're trapped inside a game that has been dragging on in development for 10 years) is interesting but the main characters are insufferable and a lot of the writing is overwrought.
-It is absolutely and completely without challenge. You could watch a Let's Play of the game and have nearly the same experience as playing it, albeit without the whole "getting lost" part.
-I really cannot overstate how bad the level design is.
Overall if you can buy the game for <$5 it's probably worth it. At the normal retail price it's just ridiculous. And honestly the further I get from the game the less kind I am to it. It's really profoundly mediocre which is sad as I love the idea behind it.

Idle Champions of the Forgotten Realms is an idle game where you recruit characters, upgrade them and then try to get as far as possible with different unit formations depending on the mission. You have a good amount of missions with small backstories on each of them and there is a good amount of variety in the enemies and backgrounds. Some of the backgrounds are interactable and can net you some extra gold. The dialogue and variety in missions makes the game feel slightly more rewarding, which kept me playing.
You have the option to click, but it's not too useful (especially early on when the gold gain is low). Enemies take up to two seconds to spawn so you have to wait between clicks... and sometimes you only get 1 or 2 enemies to come and die when you need to kill 25. This kind of delay makes new runs take for long. Even if you get extra gold multipliers and increased DPS, the delay will make sure that it will take up to a minute to get through one stage. Bosses have extreme amounts of health at stages 50, 55, 60, 65 and especially 70 and it feels like the game only lets you progress 5 waves per reset (around 4 hours as you have to farm the 4th or 9th stage for optimal gold gain).
At first you progress at a reasonable speed, but then the game just turns into a waiting game. Either it takes a good while to get back to where you reseted, long to even double your bonus gains (a key mechanic in many idle games) or extremely long to upgrade your only DPS character (with all the +%all damage buffs obviously) so that it can finally get rid of the new boss. Yes, most of the time you have one hero doing 99.99% of the dps in both single target and aoe damage, so the gameplay doesn't feel too balanced.
You gain access to silver chests and their decent rewards at a good pace, but you can only get around 1-2 gold chests per day with free-to-play currency and boss farming. The silver chests mostly give common and uncommon gear while gold chests give uncommon or better gear. The difference in stats is rather high. The items that you get from both of these chests are random and are automatically equipped on one of 8 different stat-boosting slots. Oh yeah, the chests have to be opened at end of each run to make optimal use of the gold bonuses found inside as the bonus gold amounts are based on the stage number.

There is a lot to like about the game, but after some time the game just gets too tedious for me.

I'm sad to add my hat to the pile of negative reviews. Awesomenauts always had a unique sort of charm to it. It's likely the first online game I invested hundreds of hours of my life playing. Ronimo were also the first developers that I really wanted to support. I followed all the streams, bought nearly all the skins as they released and gave 50 bucks to the Starstorm kickstarter.
Unfortunately it's nowhere near as charming as it used to be. The UI used to have character and life to it and the devs kept "updating" it by removing or streamlining features. The shop redesign was the first thing to make me raise an eyebrow. Awesomenauts used to display all the items in a vending machine kind of setup where you could view all the colorful artwork for each upgrade. It clearly had a lot of love put into it. The new "improved" shop system was a transluctent sci-fi styled pull out menu with much tinier icons. While I understand Ronimo wanted to expand the amount of items per row from 3 to 6, they could have just drawn more space in between. There have been many other minor UI changes but that was the most saddening to see.
On top of the life being drained from it, I have a lot of issues with the XP system they introduced back in September. That was the final straw for me. I tried for months to play the game anyway figuring it'd grow on me. It did not. I still can't fathom why Ronimo broke their own game so badly. Snowballing matches happened occasionally under the old system, but after XP was introduced they skyrocketed. The solar drops and respawn time on kills were already strong enough ways to gain advantage, but no. That wasn't enough. Now teams gain buffs to damage and health too! Ronimo also stated their intent was to speed up matches that took too long but that wasn't ever an issue to begin with. My most memorable matches were longer ones where the leading team changed back and forth. Games are way too short now and it's much harder to have a match you feel was worth the time spent.
The XP system patch also needlessly complicated other parts of the game. Ronimo multiplied all health and damage numbers by 10 to make it seem like you were doing more. The problem with this is that every number displayed now has 1 extra digit. You can imagine how much this gets in the way during gameplay. I could tell day 1 that hindering every players view of the match was in no way a good enough tradeoff for bigger numbers. Sure you adjust to it but there was really no point in changing it to begin with. Reverting it could only improve on the issue, after all.
You also used to be able to read how much damage you'd gain for taking an upgrade but the added percentage increases with the XP system make this old method impossible. Instead, every upgrade now states the increase as a percentage. This isn't user-friendly at all. In such a fast paced game where you need to be spending as little time as possible browsing the shop, it's incredibly difficult to tell at a glance how effective an upgrade will be when it's displayed as a percentage. I used to be able to see that I'd get 25 (now 250) extra damage per stage. Now your guess is as good as mine, unless you want to be bothered to calculate percentages as your turret continues to be shredded. I don't need to know the exact numbers sure, but a ballpark figure of what I'm capable of dealing would certainly be appreciated. Again with time you could memorize what does what. However, each character added to the roster makes this more and more of a headache.
I sympathize with the developers. I really do. After putting in so much time and effort on a complete overhaul to the game's mechanics, it would be a colossal waste to revert the changes. That's the issue. Ronimo has its hands tied and can't as a company justify going back to the previous system. Unfortunately the game has to suffer for it. I had many great times with Awesomenauts but I cannot recommend this game anymore.

Though I'm a pretty die-hard Doom guy, I passed on this when it was originally released. The lukewarm reception it received at the time was just enough to make me reconsider and let it slip from my radar for years. Since the release of the newest Doom I've decided to give this a chance, and when I saw it on sale I had to go for it. With that being said, only paying two and some change for this expansion is certainly an easy pill to swallow, but if I were to have paid full price back in 2005? Maybe not so much.
Maybe that's a harsh way to put it, as the expansion is still somewhat... Uh.... "Expansive" with its roughly six or so hours of new story content (among other things, more on that in just a sec).
Its the actual quality of what's there, not so much the amount. One of its biggest selling points is this new mechanic that's introduced with something eerily similar to a gun from Half-Life 2. The grabber gun (or... Something) feels awkwardly designed and not overly practical in practice, which is a total bummer considering a few sections make a point to force it on you. The level design leaves something to be desired as well. Props for opening up the playing field in a few sections but overall it feels like more of the same- just less creepy with less ambience and attention to detail.
It's not bad despite its faults- it definitely has a few key features that make it worth playing at least once. The double barreled shotgun finally makes a long awaited return and it feels completely at home in Doom 3's domain. Easily my most used weapon on any given play through. The artifact (a strange, demon heart that devours souls and does cool stuff, like slow time for everything around you so you can get strategic with your kills) is a serious contender for best new addition though, and I would've loved to have seen more of the game designed around its powers. Despite the disappointing  decision to have the game set in the same location as the previous chapter, eliminating the need for anything too vibrant and different, it does well on changing the pace up and keeping the action heavy with more enemies more frequently. A huge plus for those who prefer fast and heavy Doom as opposed to the slow approach 3 took.
All in all I'd give it a solid 7/10. It has its moments and it certainly doesn't suck, but it has a few flaws that keep it just under awesome. The elements that work really work though and make at least a play through worthwhile. But for $5 or less you can't go wrong if you're a Doom fan.

4X-Games have not been one of my favourite games genre. That changed with Amplitude's Endless series. Endless Space was a game a very muched enjoyed and it got even better with it's successor Endless Legend. I was sceptical at first because the fantasy setting wasn't a direction i was particulary happy about (as I am more of a sci-fi fanboy :') ) but the game twists the common magic/fantasy tropes: All "magic" in the game is powered by Dust, tiny nanomachines that are known to enhance literally anything and everything. Using Clarke's law (Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic) feels like a nice touch to me here.
Back to the game: It offeres
- 8 base factions, 3 available via DLC, all with diffenrent twist on the gameplay
- an interesting sci-fi/fantasy mash-up world with an intricate story, albeit told in textboxes
- gorgeous graphics and art style
- a gimmicky, but strategic combat
Biggest critique is the AI, which is not great, just ok, and, to a point, a somewhat vague tutorial. If you're new to the 4X-genre and new to Endless Legend, I'd reccomend you watch some tutorials on youtube.
Also, bring time, because you'll start a game at six in the evening, play a bit, check the clock, be surprised at the fact it's already dawn and curse yourself because you're supposed to be somewhere in three hours.
Great game with interesting different races (not like most 4X where most races just have different skins), interesting mechanics, soothing graphics and a great soundtrack to top it.

This game is a welcome breath of air into the 4X genre. Everything from the way territory is controlled, how cities are built and how factions differ from one another is thought through and presented in an interesting way. (Although Civ 6 has taken a hint and is using a similar city expansion mechanic).
Two of the most interesting aspects of the game are the summer/winter cyce and the aforementioned faction differences. In Endless Legend, the map sometimes shifts from summer to winter, which makes things generally more difficult to survive in for all in the game. The winters are longer and come more frequentlyas the game progresses, showing the planet's slow decline into inhospitability which the game is set against. It's a good way of getting the player to hurry up and plan out how they will advance, since there's a ticking time bomb in the weather.
As for the faction differences, unlike some games, the differences between the factions are rather dramatic, and seriously affect your playstyle. One race cannot research technology properly and so has to steal it from other players, one literally changes form and function depending on the seasons, one can never be at peace and needs to eat living prey (ie enemies) to make up for their bad farming and grow, one faction will only ever have one sprawling megacity but can corrupt the minor factions around the map to work for them and supply troops and resources. That's only a few of them. Amplitude put a lot of care and attention into making every group both visually and functionally unique.
The expansions are fantastic too, each adds something that spices up the game, usually a faction and a mechanic that said faction uses a lot. For example: Shadows included the new espionage system and The Forgotten faction (who need to steal research), whilst Guardians gave all factions access to massive Guardian units, and expanded on the in game quests system to include shared quests and races to complete certain objectives for rewards.

Forget the Civilization series, this is a better 4X strategy game!
Endless Legend has amazing:
- Combat. A mix of one-unit-per-tile and stack-of-doom that combines the best of both. Good mechanics for siege and reinforcement that give you plenty of space to be clever.
- Factions. Very unique playstyles. Tank all the damage as the Broken Lords, zerg rush as the Necrophages, or rain down AOE hell with the Argent Mages.
- Lore. Very rich setting. Under the fantasy lies magic-is-nanotech with super advanced aliens - but they make it work! They like to break fantasy stereotypes - e.g. their orcs are archers, their vampires are nights in shining armor, their elves are industrial builders.
- Art. Beautiful 2D graphics. Beautiful 3D graphics. They go out of their way to make each faction's look stand out from the cookie-cutter knights/dwarves/elves/etc.
- Clean UI. Veterans of other 4X games should have no problem picking it up.
One downside is no naval combat - except that's coming in the next expansion!

Oh and one more thing, Local Co-op? I don't think so. The current steam version does not contain the required Setup.exe to set the controls for Player 2, so without that you cannot play Co-op. The best way to describe this game is, shallow. It's not that it's a terrible game, but it is very lacking in a lot of areas. For starters, gameplay is pretty much only combat with absolutely nothing else. And while the combat's a little fun at first, it quickly gets very repetitive. It boils down to spaming buttons and every once in a while remembering to block, but other than that little bit of thought, you don't have to try too hard or think too much about what you're doing. In fact you could almost play the game one handed if you didn't have to walk forward. The game tries to spice up its combat with Q.T.E. finishing moves, but these also get repetitive and what's worse, you don't even have to take part in the Q.T.E.'s to pull them off. You can literally take your hands off the keyboard/controller when the sequence starts, and it'll be successful with your only consequence being not earning any extra points.
In addition to the hack and slash mechanics, there are sections in the game where you will have to make a formation with your men and take out archers, as well as other moments where you need to use projectiles to take out far away enemies. These sections are the hardest parts of the game and for all of the wrong reasons. Partially the issue is that the game doesn't explain its controls very well (despite having way too long a tutorial) and so you'll spend a lot of time just trying to figure out how to do the sequences right, but mainly the problem with these sections is aiming, which is completely stupid. Where as in most games you aim the camera to aim a projectile, in this game it's another quite time event, basically you hold down a button and release when it tells you to and your enemy goes down instantly. Besides the fact that this slows you down in a game that's clearly made to be fast paced, it also works against you since ranged enemies will throw projectiles at you while you're aiming and you aren't able to dodge and aim at the same time. This means you'll constantly be trying aim a projectile but be forced to quit just so that you can try and dodge an incoming attack.
On top of the gameplay issues, the PC port of Ryse suffers from technical issues as well. Frame rate drops are constant and unpredictable, and they get almost as bad as Arkham Night's frame rate drops somtimes. I've also experienced problems with textures every now and again. In a game like Ryse where there's not really very much going on at any given point, frame rate drops like these are unacceptable.
Many of the game's problems stem from the fact that it's overall just generic. The main character is your generic Leonidas type of character, the character models boil down to three generic models for the majority of your enemies and one generic model for the majority of your allies, and the story is about as generic as you can get. Don't go in expecting any sort of deep compeling anything with this game.
Here's my final stance on the game. Ryse; Son of Rome has some good elements in it that could have been fleshed out into a deeper and more meaningful experience, but sadly it never rises to the potential the game had. It's a shallow, mindless button masher that screams generic, and I can only really recommend it if it's on a really good sale and you just want to waste some time because it is good for that much at least. Ryse is a game best played in short spurts when you're bored, and beyond that, it doesn't have much to offer.
