Croixleur might very well be one of the shortest games I have played my entire life. That doesn’t mean that it is a bad game. Sure in most cases I related a short game being a bad game. I have finally found a game where I can’t say that about. This might also be one of the shortest reviews I will ever do. Simply because of how short the game is. Let’s get to it then shall we ?
Croixleur is an action indie game with hack and slashing at it’s core.  Simple yet effective combat. Keeping in mind I did not do the tutorial for the game as your reading this review.  When you first start you pick between Story, Time Attack, or Survival and later unlocking Challenge mode. The story mode is timed. The trick is to get to the final floor and beat the boss within the allotted 15 minute time period.  I started with story mode. It asks you which character you want to play but at that point I had only one character.  So I had no choice but to pick her, and I had only one weapon to start with.
As the first level opened there was some nice anime style artwork with text as it’s cutscenes. I for one would have loved have seen some actual animation work for the cutscenes. The story was pretty underwhelming, generic. Not bad. Just…. not good. I won’t give you many, if any spoilers in that regard. So after the cutscenes end I walk through a portal and the first real level begins. As I fight I level up which to be totally honest I am not sure it did anything at all.  As I played I also would unlock new weapons but could never figure out how to swap to them in combat. Up to 4 total at once and if I unlocked more weapons it told me I could change them at start of my next game.
Now the combat was simple but fun. Had more depth to it as noticed later on. You get your basic attack which you can chain together to kill things. A big portion of the game is to keep a high chain of attacks going without taking damage. The higher chain the better score you get at the end of the level/story.  There was a dash that you could use to escape hits which also consumed mp. I often used this to dash through bosses to hit them without having the fear of taking hits myself. Then of course you got jump. There were several flying creatures that you had to jump and attack to destroy. These I found to be very annoying… SUPER ANNOYING… Especially seeing as how they were almost always the cause of me losing my combo..err Chain.  Then you get a special attack. Seemed like it was the same no matter what weapon I had. It is possible it was the special attack for said character.  I know the info for the game says each weapon has it’s own unique attack. I guess I just never figured that out.
The controls of the game I found to be very finicky, and super annoying at times. For one if you change your controls, the on screen queues don’t change. The camera controls often didn’t work at all.  It didn’t take to much out of combat but there were a few times where I got hit from something behind me or off screen that I couldn’t see.
Ultimately you work your away against time and things trying to kill you to get to the top of the tower… Or was it the bottom… Either way you are there to learn the secrets behind the Adjuvant Trial. I saw maybe five different types of monsters the entire game. The basic melee unit, a spell caster, a flying eyeball thing, and a giant knight that looked almost mechanical.  Now the mobs would spawn with different colors showing they had different strengths based on their color. This was rather uninspired if you ask me. The game would be so much well… cooler if there were more things to kill. I honestly felt like I saw all the game had to offer in a single eleven minute run that it took me to complete the story.
As you play through the levels ever so often it gives you two ways to advance. I’m not sure how much effect this actually has on the game but I know when I got to my final boss it was a dragon. Or it looked like a dragon at least. This was undoubtedly my favorite part of the game. Mostly because of the dialogue!
The boss fight was fun. The best part of the game for sure. After beating it I unlocked Challenge mode and did a few of the other game modes. Ultimately it is just the same thing. Over and over. The price of the game is $7.99 which isn’t bad. If your someone who enjoys scoregasm action games then you might want to pick this up. I can say that the action was  fun, and it is likely that I missed a lot of the game itself by not doing the tutorial. But COME ON!! Who does those anymore!?

Idle Champions of the Forgotten Realms is an idle game where you recruit characters, upgrade them and then try to get as far as possible with different unit formations depending on the mission. You have a good amount of missions with small backstories on each of them and there is a good amount of variety in the enemies and backgrounds. Some of the backgrounds are interactable and can net you some extra gold. The dialogue and variety in missions makes the game feel slightly more rewarding, which kept me playing.
You have the option to click, but it's not too useful (especially early on when the gold gain is low). Enemies take up to two seconds to spawn so you have to wait between clicks... and sometimes you only get 1 or 2 enemies to come and die when you need to kill 25. This kind of delay makes new runs take for long. Even if you get extra gold multipliers and increased DPS, the delay will make sure that it will take up to a minute to get through one stage. Bosses have extreme amounts of health at stages 50, 55, 60, 65 and especially 70 and it feels like the game only lets you progress 5 waves per reset (around 4 hours as you have to farm the 4th or 9th stage for optimal gold gain).
At first you progress at a reasonable speed, but then the game just turns into a waiting game. Either it takes a good while to get back to where you reseted, long to even double your bonus gains (a key mechanic in many idle games) or extremely long to upgrade your only DPS character (with all the +%all damage buffs obviously) so that it can finally get rid of the new boss. Yes, most of the time you have one hero doing 99.99% of the dps in both single target and aoe damage, so the gameplay doesn't feel too balanced.
You gain access to silver chests and their decent rewards at a good pace, but you can only get around 1-2 gold chests per day with free-to-play currency and boss farming. The silver chests mostly give common and uncommon gear while gold chests give uncommon or better gear. The difference in stats is rather high. The items that you get from both of these chests are random and are automatically equipped on one of 8 different stat-boosting slots. Oh yeah, the chests have to be opened at end of each run to make optimal use of the gold bonuses found inside as the bonus gold amounts are based on the stage number.

Expansions are hard to come by these days. They're not as popular or profitable than many modern post launch support practices but roughly ten years ago as I write this they were the bread and butter for expanding a current game while working on a sequal or seperate project. Doom 3 Resurrection of Evil features a new campaign which I will be discussing in this review.
Now what did Doom 3 RoE bring to the table? Some minor new ememies to fight and two new weapons, the Grabber which is basically the Gravity Gun from Half Life 2 and the Double Barrel Shotgun AKA the Boomstick! This will be your new friend as shotgun ammo is now more plentiful, the gun is hugely powerful and enemies can often die in one or two hits with it. Honestly at times it makes all the other weapons rather useless minor a few moments here and there. I'm also a sucker for the Double Barrel Shotgun in video games, I can't help but enjoy using them. Now the story here is nothing special like the last one, after the events of the first game a new excavation team go back to Mars and explore the ruins and you activate some artifact that actually helps you in the game. It stops time at the start but you can get upgrades for it later on.
Nothing much can't be said other than some very minor tweaks. There are less enemies that unfairly leap and spawn right behind you. I forgot to mention in my review for Doom 3 that enemies would often spawn right behind you but I can only count two cases where that happens here. I felt that the game got oddly harder later on in the campaign. Not a huge difficulty spike but enough to notice that the difficulty curve skipped a beat. I think I enjoyed this a little more. The two new weapons were fun to use and the Artifact could really help you get out of some jams. If you're gonna get Doom 3 then odds are you're going to buy Resurrection of Evil in a bundle of some form so there is no harm in trying it out. I give it 6.5/10

Ahh! What is this? Kings and Heroes? Finally, a new adventure worthy of my time!
I rolled myself a fine dwarven character, a cleric named Merrygold. With a blessed hammer and a joyous beard I set forth, landing in the bustling town of Everdale. What astonishing tales awaited me? What luminous treasure anticipated my hand at the bottom of a dark dungeon?
Ready for romance and danger I walked through the buildings, smiling as I examined the many races with various professions. I found myself inside a tavern, where a handful of weary travelrs rested. Suddenly, a man burst inside, calling out on voice chat in a strange accent-
"WOULD ANYONE LIKE TO ACCOMPANY ME TO SLAY SOME MONSTERS AND♥♥♥♥♥♥"
A strange way of wording, but I decided I would answer his call nontheless. I was about to respond to his summon when someone in the back of the room called out
"SHUT THE F**K UP YOU DAMN DIRTY ELF. THIS IS AN ORC BAR."
The two then proceeded to bicker and insult each other's mothers, while a man jumped from the top of the balcony and recited what seemed like the entire speech from Helm's Deep.
Deciding my journey lied elsewhere, I ventured to the town square, where a great statue of a courageous warrior stood. Admiring its craftmanship, I was just about to further inspect it when suddenly a robed man carrying a staff appeared at the top by some sort of teleportation spell.
"I AM YOUR KING. YOU ARE ALL PEASANTS TO ME."
This he cried out, before proceeding to rain great, firey meteors down, which the good people seemed to mostly ignore.
Feeling confused but still hopeful, I finally decided to try my combatical prowess in a dungeon. Onward I went, preparing myself for what was sure to be the fight of my life. I readied my hammer and prayed to my God, opening the first door in this accursed place.

Listen up- if you've played Mass Effect, Dragon Age, or any other semi-serious Western roleplaying game, you're going to love this title.
SWKOTOR had really, really good music, very good, like it seriously stood out for me.
The characters were enjoyable, but not nearly as fleshed out as ME & DA:O. Bastilla & Carth were the only two party members who got a solid spotlight as both had direct tie-ins to the main story. I think the playthrough for this game took around 30 hours, but it was worth it and a very solid title.
This game will have significant playthrough value twice on both the light and dark side of the force. It utilizes 3rd edition D&D rules, obviously highly modified, you can play as ranged, melee, and once you get into the, (spoiler alert) Jedi stuff, a bit of a spell caster as well.
I have a few criticisms and disappointments from the game. One is the fact it's more difficult to tell when making a "hard decision" ends up being on the Dark Side when I feel you were stuck between a rock and a hard place. You need to have almost no backbone to avoid eating up dark side points, and I was in that boat as I was trying to be the champion of the boat. The second was the quick save getting corrupted after I started using Flawless Widescreen. Might have been a coincidence, maybe not. And 3rd, probably one of the more disruptive bugs of an older game, was the fact after combat ended I constantly got stuck where my movement keys stopped working. The solution? Quick Save, Quick Load. Now you know why corrupted Quick Save files could get annoying.
I highly recommend this game and I ran it using "Flawless Widescreen" to get 1920x1080 resolution. Solid game at a solid price with significant gameplay and replay value. I am not a Star Wars geek, but also not against it. If you love RPGs you'll love this. If you love Star Wars you'll love this. Enjoy, guys!! :)

Fantastic game. The atmosphere and unique traits and playstyles of each race is refreshing in the 4X genre. A must buy!

This game is a welcome breath of air into the 4X genre. Everything from the way territory is controlled, how cities are built and how factions differ from one another is thought through and presented in an interesting way. (Although Civ 6 has taken a hint and is using a similar city expansion mechanic).
Two of the most interesting aspects of the game are the summer/winter cyce and the aforementioned faction differences. In Endless Legend, the map sometimes shifts from summer to winter, which makes things generally more difficult to survive in for all in the game. The winters are longer and come more frequentlyas the game progresses, showing the planet's slow decline into inhospitability which the game is set against. It's a good way of getting the player to hurry up and plan out how they will advance, since there's a ticking time bomb in the weather.
As for the faction differences, unlike some games, the differences between the factions are rather dramatic, and seriously affect your playstyle. One race cannot research technology properly and so has to steal it from other players, one literally changes form and function depending on the seasons, one can never be at peace and needs to eat living prey (ie enemies) to make up for their bad farming and grow, one faction will only ever have one sprawling megacity but can corrupt the minor factions around the map to work for them and supply troops and resources. That's only a few of them. Amplitude put a lot of care and attention into making every group both visually and functionally unique.
The expansions are fantastic too, each adds something that spices up the game, usually a faction and a mechanic that said faction uses a lot. For example: Shadows included the new espionage system and The Forgotten faction (who need to steal research), whilst Guardians gave all factions access to massive Guardian units, and expanded on the in game quests system to include shared quests and races to complete certain objectives for rewards.

Forget the Civilization series, this is a better 4X strategy game!
Endless Legend has amazing:
- Combat. A mix of one-unit-per-tile and stack-of-doom that combines the best of both. Good mechanics for siege and reinforcement that give you plenty of space to be clever.
- Factions. Very unique playstyles. Tank all the damage as the Broken Lords, zerg rush as the Necrophages, or rain down AOE hell with the Argent Mages.
- Lore. Very rich setting. Under the fantasy lies magic-is-nanotech with super advanced aliens - but they make it work! They like to break fantasy stereotypes - e.g. their orcs are archers, their vampires are nights in shining armor, their elves are industrial builders.
- Art. Beautiful 2D graphics. Beautiful 3D graphics. They go out of their way to make each faction's look stand out from the cookie-cutter knights/dwarves/elves/etc.
- Clean UI. Veterans of other 4X games should have no problem picking it up.
One downside is no naval combat - except that's coming in the next expansion!

This game has some of the most interesting factions available in any 4x game I've encountered. Factions have abilities and restrictions that make playing as each race a different experience from the others.
The only caveat is the tactical combat. Some games allow one side to issue all of their orders at once, then you switch sides. I move unit A, attack with B, heal with C, and not it's the other team's turn. I've seen other systems which bring up turns based on a speed stat, so I move unit A, the enemy attacks with unit X, the enemy moves unit Y, I attack with unit B, and so on. Either system is fine, because you always know what is going to happen with each unit, barring RNG. This game tries to combine the systems. You issue orders to your entire team at once, but they execute those orders, along with the enemy, in order of the speed stat for the game. If the order you issues a unit becomes impossible to carry out when that unit's turn arrives (the target hex is occupied or the target unit is dead, for instance), they revert to whatever basic attack, defend, passive stance you give the whole army at the beginning of each battle. It all makes the combat feel very squishy to me. I understand the realism associated with not having complete control of units during a battle, but it doesn't feel fun in this case. I've searched in vain for a mod to change this, but I haven't found one yet.
That criticism aside, I enjoy the game immensely.

+++Reasonably complex maze design.  You actually have to think to find the way through and the solutions are nice and varied.
++Dirt cheap game
+Relaxing music (but… --music is repetitive)
+(Trading cards + easy achievements) – I suppose this is why most people buy it, but personally I think the game itself needs to be worth it, not the cards
---Handles like crap.  What I mean is that as the maze gets larger and the ball gets smaller, it still moves the same distance with each key-press.  This makes it extremely frustrating to actually move where you want to go
--Music is repetitive.  The track itself is nice, but it is far too short, so you find yourself hearing it again and again and again.  Needs a longer track or more tracks
-The game is designed to produce trading cards so the developer can make money off people selling them on the community market.  In principle I'm not opposed to this, but the problem is that the developer has not put enough time into actually polishing up the game in such a way that makes it enjoyable to play
If you enjoy mazes, then the low price means that you can get 1-2 hours of enjoyment out of it.  Otherwise don't bother getting this game.

I can not blame this expansion for the faults of the base game, but I can praise it for what the original didn't have.
Gameplay changes drastically once again - still on the same engine, but there are more enemies, more weapons and ammunition and less horror. This is as close to what people have been expecting of Doom 3 as it gets. Instead of the three-step formula of the base game (Go through corridors, go through hell, go through slightly more exciting exciting corridors), this one tips things on its head by actually making the corridors much more distinct.
The general goals are a lot less vague. In the base game it was "go fetch this, but you can't fetch this, because you can not open this thing, so to open this thing you need to go and do something else" while here it is similar, the game makes it a lot clearer and things make a lot more sense.
The Super Shotgun is back and it's a lot more fun to use than the basic thing. They also give  you a version of the Gravity Gun, and although it may be fun to use at first, it's use gets limited to throwing an enemies' fireball back at them.
Besides that, there are many gimmicks here and there, which make the experience seriously a lot more fun.
Hell levels are less diverse than in the original, but that can be excused with the improved design of the Mars base.

Hideo Kojima’s Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes is a well-crafted experience. A bit short, yes. It’s much darker than previous Metal Gear Solid titles. They kicked David Hayter as the cheesy but defining voice-actor for Snake in favor of Kiefer Sutherland from 24. It seems like Kojima goes through a transition phase personally and it shows in his games, namely this one and P.T., the excellent precursor for the new Silent Hill.
Ground Zeroes is just a taste of what’s to come in Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain and perfectly sets the tone. It’s dark and perverse; the franchise has matured in a way. Personally, I’m really deeply invested in the story of Metal Gear and can’t wait until Big Boss’ tale comes full-circle, even if it’s going to be sinister.
Although the Paz’ memos from Peace Walker are included in the game, don’t play Ground Zeroes if you haven’t finished Peace Walker yet – much of Ground Zeroes’ brilliance will be without effect if you don’t know what’s really happening.

When making a very meta game about game design, it's easy to fall into the trap of being very pretentious and long-winded (looking at you, Beginner's Guide). Luckily, The Magic Circle manages to avoid that by balancing narrative and freedom to the point where you feel like you actually get to do something in the world while still enjoying a very clear, cohesive narrative. The game is really as involved as you make it: you can manipulate the creatures in the game in all sorts of ways to figure out new solutions to the puzzles, or you can just stroll through the game like a walking simulator (and I was that term very positively - a great walking simulator is a great thing, and a rare one as well). When you get access to the level generator, the full potential and charm of the game is fully revealed. If you were ever interested in game design, or even if you just really like video games, this game's for you. It's limited, but that just amplifies the game's message of encouraging more people to get into design.
The game is a bit on the nose at times, and there are some questionable things going on with gender roles, but all in all, it's a fantastic experience. One of the best games released this year, and an important game for the ages.

I don't often write reviews, but I had an absolute BLAST with this game and whole-heartedly recommend it to anybody looking for a unique experience. The game is short, but more than worth the time you put into it. The game encourages you to break the rules and utilize your ability to manipulate elements in the game in creative ways. My only major complaint is that I wish the game was longer. I was honestly expecting a big second or third stage for the game. Replayability is high though, with various contextual comments from different characters, and a few different ways for the final stage to go.
My biggest fear when going into this game was that it would be TOO complex, and that the systems to alter and manipulate the game would be off-putting and difficult to handle. But, while a couple improvements can be made to make things flow a bit more smoothly, the system for altering the game mechanics is actually very simple and fun.
All in all, despite it's short run-time and the 20 dollar price tag, I say it's a good buy.

Well... I guess, this game deserves a short review from me, something quite uncommon. It is hard to describe it without spoiling the fun of exploring it yourself, but I will try my best at doing the first without doing the latter.
This game's focus is story first and foremost. Gameplay, while not being bad, is obviously a mere tool to the narrative. In that regard it is akin to the "The Beginner's Guide" or "The Stanley Parable", though gameplay is a little bit more complicated in this one. It is relatively unique, basically putting a limited developer editing tools at your disposal in order to "bend" the otherwise unwinnable game to your benefit. At the same time, the game itself is relatively short (as it is evident from my time played) and doesn't expand on the idea a whole lot. Aside from collectibles and some mutually exclusive achievements, there is little replayability of note in this case.
My verdict is - buy it if you're interested in a short story-driven experience. I feel it does deserve the money. Do take into account the shortness and lack of proper replayability. Maybe you'll want to wait for the sale offer, as much as my heart bleeds saying that. I genuenly believe that developers do deserve the money for this one. I also believe, that the game could do with more content and some other changes.

The Magic Circle goes above just being about making a game, it dives into the lives of perfectionist game developers and their relationship with obsessive fans.  The gameplay is an interesting take on debug mode/recycle bin and while it mostly revolves around exploring to find the right abilities, a-la zelda or metroid, it's interesting to see the world that has been built.  The characters aren't just bright-eyed developers struggling under the weight of their project, they're real people with real flaws and interpersonal conflicts which drag the game down.
The final level was an excellent culmination of all the ideas and themes up to that point, and the final scene after you finish the game may be a sobering experience for aspiring developers and for fans of games who have no idea how these things are made.

The second was the quick save getting corrupted after I started using Flawless Widescreen. Might have been a coincidence, maybe not. And 3rd, probably one of the more disruptive bugs of an older game, was the fact after combat ended I constantly got stuck where my movement keys stopped working. The solution? Quick Save, Quick Load. Now you know why corrupted Quick Save files could get annoying.
I highly recommend this game and I ran it using "Flawless Widescreen" to get 1920x1080 resolution. Solid game at a solid price with significant gameplay and replay value. I do like the central idea behind this game- travelling between different gaming eras, so to speak- but the execution is not fun to play, and the game tries WAY too hard to be clever but just winds up being an endless parade of references. Examples: The main character is named Clink and your party members are Kaeris and Sid. You get a Buster Sword replica called Claud's Blade. Random encounter monsters include tiny mushroom monsters called Zoombas and a giant turtle named A'Tuin. A woman makes an arrow to the knee reference. There is a collectible card game called Double Twin. I could go on and on, but these references aren't clever in the least, they're just not funny. As far as the gameplay goes, there's no strategy to the Final Fantasy sections (no MP means you can just spam special moves such as Heal), and the Zelda sections are really clunky and boring. Evoland would be a lot more entertaining if it was a 20-minute game you could play for free, but I've put over an hour into the game and it doesn't seem to be ending anytime soon. An hour is too long, honestly. Don't waste your money.

I woke up today, grabbed my coffee, checked my usual sites (Drudge, CoasttoCoast, Gamefaqs), went to look around the Steam forums, when suddenly, like breaking the silence in a church, my wife says, "You should play Evoland!"  She had recently played and beaten the game several days before and promised me I would enjoy it.  Well, I had a whole day to kill, let's see about this Evoland....
Seven hours later, here I am opining about this game, vindicating my wife's prediction, and feeling better about my gaming prowess.  If you grew up playing RPGs like I did, then definitely check this little gem out.  The game is literally one big reference to everything else in the genre.  If parody is the finest form of flattery, then this game swoons at the mere thought of RPGs.
Just off the top of my head you have Goombas, Cloud, Link, Aeris, Diablo, Torneko, Dragonball, Piranha Plants,  Kefka, Chocobos, Buster swords, Cid, airships, and even NPC stereotypes.  This was a very abbreviated list too.  The battles are turn based, Zelda-esque, and hack-'n-slash.  The only types of rpg they left out were first-person dungeon crawls, and strategy.  Clearly, the developers were fans.
The whole experience feels like something a fanboy with programming chops would throw together in about a day, just for the comedy of it....coincidentally, that's exactly what did happen.  This game won first place in the Lundum Dare competition.  If you are unaware of what that is, it's o.k., but you should really check out the site, and impress others with worthless knowledge.  I make a living out of doing that.

However, in aMAZE 2, the puzzles actually get painfully hard in the end. aMAZE 2 also features a very calming and relaxing soundtrack just like aMAZE 1, but I personally liked this one better than the first one. Overall, a good sequel to aMAZE 1 that really increased the difficulty and maze creation.

You may consider aMAZE 2, one of the best Steam games focusing entirely on 2D labyrinths. It’s certainly far better than its predecessor. Developed by Blender Games and released one month away from aMAZE 1, the second part is a clear improvement in terms of size and diversity.
Again, no story whatsoever. Yet I sincerely doubt you’ll be bothered by the lack of a narrative plot in a casual title about solving mazes. You wouldn’t play such games in hopes of finding anything other that what it’s being advertised to offer. And you can rest assured that if you crave for labyrinths, aMAZE 2 shall satisfy that need.
The game doesn’t name its graphics engine yet I suspect Unity 5 is powering it, same as the previous aMAZE. This time around though, you have visual diversity far beyond just backgrounds and colors. The overall shape of the maze itself, dictates the challenge. The ball doesn’t switch sizes (again, just the color) but you will have to be more patient in aMAZE 2, if you wish to complete mazes in a timely manner. It was a stable experience regardless and the game runs in your monitor's native resolution. I really hope aMAZE 3 shall sport a fully 3D engine since that's precisely the best way to improve over the existing formula.

The soundtrack is a bit better than in the first iteration, yet it’s still not on par with many similarly priced indie games I played over the last few months. Think of aMAZE 2’s sound effects as its Achilles' heel. Mute the sounds and just listen to whatever tracks you wish, if you shall play the game in long sessions.
How can you up the ante, in the case of a video game about mazes? By offering less conventional form factors, of course! Instead of just rectangles and squares, you can now guide balls through labyrinths that are hexagonal or cylindrical. Modern layouts which are an obvious step in the right direction for this series. The controls are simple enough, even if they aren’t explained (the game really lacks a proper Setting menu). Either the Arrow or Numpad directional keys and no way to rebind them. You maneuver a ball through the new maze templates until you reach a Racing Flag which signals the end of the level.
There are no time constraints, not even a timer to mark the exact duration of a single level. Subsequently, no highscore either and I think that these small gameplay features would have been more than welcome. Perhaps the developer can add them in a future update. Even mobile games use such small but significant feedback displays. Players deserve to know how efficient they have solved a particular maze level and the pressure of a timer can add some challenge to the title as well. Even if aMAZE 2 still has some of the flaws of its predecessor, the gameplay itself still offers a lot more variety with a scaling difficulty that won’t leave you wanting for more.
Being just as affordable as aMAZE 1 (better still, if bought together), this sequel doesn’t feel rushed and actually improves some previous shortcomings. If you like this type of casual games, you don’t need a lot of convincing from me. Just pick it up bundled or on Sale and give it a chance to relax and entertain you. The Achievements are surprisingly easy to obtain and the Trading Cards are like icing on the cake at this point. If mazes are your thing, aMAZE 2 won’t disappoint you one bit!
+ Decently priced.
+ 60 mazes along 3 form factors.
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards.
+ A worthy sequel to an already interesting title.
- Lacks sound variety.

There are two types of mazes depending on the way to complete them: Straight and roundabout. Most of the mazes have you going in a roundabout way, but there are occasional ones where you can go straight towards the goal. And the differing maze formations and patterns adds a lot of variety that also tricks the eye. This is certainly better than the monotonous gameplay from the first game. This was enjoyable as you get lost and miss small paths that would lead to the goal if you didn't pay attention (unless you traced the path starting from the goal). This is the type of feeling that I was looking for, where I seriously followed a dead end that I thought was the right one for minutes and finally realize that the developer should burn in the deep fiery pits of Pastafarian hell drinking warm beer while getting serviced by that male Kim Kardashian wannabe. Another maze game in the same vein as it's predecessor it is much improved, much more challenging and fun, but also still frustrating and flawed at times as well. Playtime is probably about 1-2 hours, with little replayability.
The much larger size of mazes allows them to actually be quite demanding to find the correct route, requiring you to trace through multiple branches quite deeply several times to find the right way, so that aspect of the game is hugely improved. We also don't suffer from any backgrounds quite as bad as the previous outing, while some aren't ideal to be looking at for so long, most are fine.
However while the issue of the ball dragging along walls and slowing has gone, in its place we have a ball that travels way too fast for fine control - it is probably necessary given the larger size of mazes, but means you continually overrun the exit you want (unless there is a convenient wall in the way), and every key press moves you about three times the width of a path, making certain paths very hard to get into - some took me 8 or 9 attempts to get in the right one, particularly where you have three routes and you want the middle one. I tended to find the correct route entire in my head/using my finger, and only once done start moving the ball, to minimize the amount of moving about needed.
Overall a pretty good set of mazes that were fun to find the solutions, and I would recommend it but with the caveat how much you like playing will depend heavily on your tolerance for the issues with movement.

And yea, I still had same technical smaller problems. Bodies not disintegrating properly. Lighting/shadows breaking slightly after getting to the next level. Stuttering and lag on modern hardware.
As for multiplayer, it still looks quite dead. I write this one single phrase too much, playing old games and all. Anyway, expansion pack also would increase player limit to 8 and add Capture The Flag gamemode. Oh, and Double Shotgun, yep.

The plot of this game follows that UAC didn't give up on Mars, not to mentioning that they recieved some strange signal from the dig side 1. The research is actually ran by female character about who you could learn in original Doom 3 through PDA devices, as the one to ask for UAC investigation on Dr.Betruger. Your team's job now is to investigate what is going on there, so sure thing you blow a wall up, grab artifact and let the hell break loose once again.
And now you have to go and kill the main villian, closing the main cliffhanger for Doom 4 from the Doom 3 ending, dooming us all to wait another 10 years until new Doom game. Good job.
And so begins yet another 10 or so level long adventure, coming from caverns and back to the base. This time around it feels less polished on survival horror side. Or at least it has less emphasis on this. Areas felt less greatly done in shadow/lighting, there wasn't as much of darkness. There wasn't as much of atmosphere either. Like, ambience in sounds is even more forgettable. In all honesty, I doubt that putting player into same experience as in Doom 3 would have worked, seeing how long that game lasted in the bases. And it has some interesting scenes, like zombies walking through X-Ray or very occasional spook. Still, it's still doesn't feel as special.
Yea, means no new music.
But hey, at least now it's more actiony, it doesn't take long to get into parts where you will fight few monsters that aren't just dumb melee zombies.
Not to mentioning that I like the way story was given here a bit better. It doesn't spam with as much of useless audio logs. And PDA shows email and logs that actually seemed to be written during the invasion, making it feel more immersive and interesting to me.
And just look at all those new weapons that the developers added. It's like they listened to what was cool in 2005 and putted it in.
- Double Shotgun, check. Because it was cool since Doom 2. Just like Super Shotgun in Doom 2 it's more powerful than it got to be. I mean, seeing how it can easily one-hit most of enemies and Doom 3 is all about just facing very few enemies it's a bit too much. Still awesome gun. Still menly. Well, fine, at least Expansion isn't afraid to throw more than one enemy at you in same time.
- Gravigun, check. Because Half-Life 2 made it cool. Apparently it has some long name and mainly called Grabber. Now, I was laughing at it since Doom 3 had one of the worse implented physics at that time. Enough to be there, not good enough to be actively used. And sure thing, throwing boxes and barrels was wacky at best. But actually, as it immeditly shows you in cutscene, it's made it so you could grab enemy's fireball and throw it back, which is why you have only limited time to hold object. And for fireballs it works excellent, not to mentioning that monsters often die from a single hit, so it's actually cool gun.
- Some cool-looking heart artifact that also slows time down, check. Because Max Payne made slow-mo cool. Actually it becomes more powerful as you progress, adding increased damage and invincibility, as if it wasn't enough. While it may feel annoying that when you activate it monsters spawn into room way too long and you often have to kill them all before doors are unlocked, there are so many corpses in the game with which you feed this thing that I felt that I could as well use it in almost every fight.
Yea, I felt that I was given too much firepower in this one.
It also brings out new monsters, but nothing that can bring enemy side on same level as you. The only two worth noting were much more stylish-lookings variety of imps and this new juggernaut of sorts that is like Mancubus but shoots more often. Eh, actually there isn't much new.
At least it got boss fights! And they are pretty good, even if you can just use your heart artifact on them. Actually, I think that they require you to use all these new powers you got, so enjoy, they aren't too weak. Worth noting is awesome final boss who doesn't suck this time around. Because in Doom 3 the final fight was weak and gimmicky once you realized what to do. Good conclusion.
Expansion Pack gives player of Doom 3 more of gameplay hours. It tries to amuse them by focusing on less darkness and by adding new cool toys to use. But it doesn't feel as polished by me and less special. Still cool.

I'm giving a thumbs down because the game just isn't finished enough to be sold for EA.
When I see EA I expect some reasonable level of playable content in at least a late Alpha phase.
The game is currently in early, early, early Alpha and hardly anything works.
- It takes roughly 5 minutes to actually launch the game, and that's if you don't get a critical error.
- If you do make it in game, it's another 2-3 minutes to load all the textures, and then it's a choppy slideshow for FPS.
- Voice volume slider bar doesn't work, so you will hear screaming teens with no way to mute them.
- Most graphics options don't seem to do anything in world, like AA, so you have no way to improve performance.
- The ESC menu will randomly quit on you, giving you no way to change options or even quit the game...Alt F4 is the only way at that point.
- Some keys can't be rebound, forcing an odd control scheme.
The promo videos and screenshots look great, but they're just promos. Don't expect to see the same level of detail or have the same performance while playing.
For a price tag of $30 CAD, this is no where near a playable EA state. It's definiately a title to keep your eye on, but for now wait until they get this in a more stable, playable state before forking over your cash.

Like Batman? (or just DC in general) Like Lego? If you answered yes, then you will like this game.
This game is a Lego game, so the mechanics, and gameplay is very much the same as the other games, but with this one it's different.
Lego Batman 3 brings Batman and friends along with over 50 other characters from DC, such as, Shazam, Aquaman, Super Man, etc. People might not like this because it says Batman in the title, and when you play it, it's more of a Green Lantern game with other DC things in it, but if you are willing to realise that it's not just Batman, and take it for what it is, it's probably the best Lego game out there.
There's so much to do in this game it's crazy. I will admit though that the story mode is very boring at the beginning, but once you get to the Lantern levels (spoilers?) the main campain gets much better.
After story mode is completed, there is extra missions, freeplay, Full Lantern planets (all 7) to explore, VR missions (not really), and much more.
Every character is fun to play as, and is mostly different, and every character you see in this game is playable at some point, which is amazing.
If you are willing to get past the first really boring marathon levels of the story, you will have a great time.
[Note: You will have fun if you like the standard formula for lego games, and like DC even just a little bit]

Kings and Heros:
"Do not recommend," does not mean, "will not in the future"
I usually have a policy against "early release" games. Mainly because there is always that nagging feeling of potential. Which then translates into this happy review of hopes and dreams.... That are not even in the game yet.
Let me start off by saying that Kings and Heros feels like an immersive RPG, where you group up with players, explore dungeons, and that's pretty much it. As of June 4th, much of the world is created, but there is nothing out there.
Much of the world is just empty with landscapes everywhere but nothing to do 5 feet outside or inside of town, questing begins and ends just to show you where the inn is.
It is impressive that a game can stand on it's core mechanics alone and that is the main thing I will praise this game for. The dungeons feel like something you would expect out of a skyrim or DnD. I could not imagine what it must feel like to actually have freinds with this game. Or, even the finished product.
Either way,
TL,DR: Kings and heros is a game with great potential and impressive game mechanics. But, that's where the fun begins and ends. You will be expecting so much more after playing for a few minutes. It's just not ready.

One of the things I love most about arena brawlers is how they can take simple to understand and execute mechanics, and turn them into deep satisfying combat through various systems and enemy designs. Croixleur Sigma gets at least part of this right, but leans too heavily toward simplicity to have any long lasting appeal. Its mechanics are sound but excessively basic, and the limited amount of content makes it hard to wring more than an hour or two of enjoyment out of the experience, which ultimately left me wanting.
Nothing about Croixleur could be described as especially innovative, but that's not entirely a bad thing as it builds itself upon a proven design that has persisted because it works. Dropped at the foot of a tower, you ascend floors clearing out waves of enemies, ultimately ending in a boss and maybe a new weapon. The catch is that you're on a strict time limit, which if exceeded will lot you out of the real ending or fail you all together. It's a good method for pushing you to find faster more powerful combos, but it does mean that by design the game can be beaten in about ten minutes. There are two characters each with their own unique weapons to unlock and dialog, along with some trivial challenges and hi-score modes, but despite all of this the amount of content still seems far too little.
What Croixleur does well is its blisteringly fast button mashing combat, which feels fantastic once you get the hang of using the dash ability and various special abilities inherent to different weapons. The problem though is it doesn't go further than this. While it's fun to sprint around wacking baddies over the head, it's extremely repetitive and allows virtually no room to grow once you've mastered its few mechanics. The brainless enemies (though typical of the genre) are little more than practice dummies to beat upon, and with only a handful of different varieties become tedious to fight after your first few times through the tower. I also found the way special abilities work to be rather convoluted, requiring you to both push the correct button and be on the correct plane for them to work, and even then it was hard to predict which ability was going to activate as pressing a button repeatedly cycles through all your specials instead of simply activating whichever is assigned to said button.
Croixleur Sigma isn't a bad game, in fact I had a great time with it, but it's mechanics are so shallow and its content so limited that it's hard to recommend entirely. It's amusing and colorful, satisfying to a degree, and solid enough to entertain, but just know that you are unlikely to put more than an hour or two into it before it grows stale. In the face of its many far more engaging and deeper contemporaries, it never manages to be anything more than average, but if you're just looking for a quite fix then at the very least it will satisfy your need for badass lolis that like to kick the living hell out of demons. That alone ought to count for something.

Summary: A game you'll likely play once, but enjoy every nostalgic minute of the roughly 3 hour storyline.
Hours of fun: 3 hours
Suggested Retail Value: $5
Graphics: 6/10
Voice-acting: 6/10
Music/SFX: 6/10
Uniqueness: 6/10
First Play-through Experience: 7/10
Replay Value: 5/10
Evoland is a fun game for anyone who has a love for old-school RPGs, an interest in how RPGs have changed over the last couple of decades, or just want to experience an adventure that spans several generations of RPG all in one sitting. If that's true of you then I doubt you'll regret buying it, and you can probably expect to want to talk to others about it. I doubt anyone would regret paying $5 or less for this, though there may be a small number of gamers who would feel the story was too short to justify spending more. It's likely to wake the little kid in you, and will probably make you want to play through your library of "classics", but I doubt you'll want to play through the game a second time just to find all the "Hidden Stars". But maybe that's just because I dislike collection quests, and so completely ignored that aspect of the game (which you can easily do!).

A nice homage to the likes of Zelda and Final Fantasy. The game has some issues but it is a nice dose of nostalgia if you're familiar with those series. It's mostly a parody and the entire game can be completed in about 4-6 hours. The beginning of the game is probably the best, when you're upgrading the world around you and the game is simply just fun.
One unlockable definitely should have been the ability to run or just move faster, particularly in 3D mode which is the majority of the game. The damaging unlockables were pointless; we shouldn't need to "unlock" wall-shooting fireballs that are part of the level and going to hurt us. Particularly when this is unskippable anyway. I get it, you're copying other games, but why are you drawing unnecessary attention to it? That takes away from the joke.
Constant random turn-based encounters when you're trying to revisit an area you've already beaten seems like an oversight, it was annoying and pointless. Yes, you're parodying Final Fantasy, but it's not fun when you already beat the area. The collision detection can be sketchy at times; I mean geez, after I beat the last boss my character was jittering around for no reason as if he was on ice. Also the perspective can make hitting enemies with your weapons a bigger chore than necessary as the hitbox can be rather limited.
I get what they were trying to do with the 2D/3D crystals, but c'mon. My character can CLEARLY step over those tiny little bushes. At first it was interesting and a little nostalgic, but that wore off quickly. Especially when I could shoot a fire arrow at the bush in 3D, and that did nothing. wut.
Conclusion: This game started as a Ludum Dare entry and evolved from that. You'll have the most fun if you don't take the game seriously and just try to enjoy its nods to other games.
P.S. For those looking to get 100%: for some reason beyond me, you HAVE TO enter the Noria Mines from the front entrance to get the "Dodgeball" achievement. Why in the world? If you're like me, you'll finally beat him with full health and wonder what you did wrong or if the game is simply messing with you. Pretty big oversight.

It's important to realise when playing this game that it isn't meant to be a true RPG - it's meant to be a pisstake of the RPG genre, wherein you have to unlock everything, right down to moving, saving and battling, and it does that absolutely brilliantly. I would reccomend this game to anyone who liked the old RPGs like Final Fantasy and the like - I for one found myself chuckling heartily at the little references here and there. A brilliant little stab at the RPG genre, Evoland is so deliberately generic that it's hilarious, and any retro game fan should pick it up for its nostalgic and its comedic value.

While the game is still early access and CNE will add lots of new features, there is a core problem underlying this game:
The cooldown system.  Love it or hate it the cooldown creates a mathematical problem which will require the developers to either flatten the math so every "champion" is fairly similar or let the game be one where you push from the bottom.  By that I mean the only things that will really have a significant impact on progression in the long run are DPS All gear and Divine Favour (gold find).
They'll do their best to cludge together fixes for specific problems, like abilities having no significant impact if they're not in the "buff box", or replacing starting buff characters with later unlocked characters is problematic because of how long they take to replace the "DPS All" buffing, etc.  Ultimately they cannot escape the mathematically flawed system they created.

It pains me to do this, as this was once a great game, however I have to say that in it's current state I cannot recommend this game. It seems that the developer team assigned to this just isn't that good, especially when compared to the quality of the main ARK's developers. As this game has been changed it seems to have become very unbalanced and based on RNG.
The current meta of this game is taming alot of rexs/spinos and whover has the most wins. If there are multiple groups of these at deathmatch it is whoever is attacked last that will win. Sure grenades are overpowered as hell against single rexs/spinos, but you will never be able to make enough to kill the armies people make and guns are useless against people's tames.
The current wall is just awful, it doesn't move at all at the start and then suddenly at a certain time it charges in towards the center almost at the speed that you run. This is due to them shorten the match times for all modes but FFA in an earlier update. Now they're trying to get too much done in too little time. Also despite them now shortening FFA they changed the wall to work the same way in it, so now anyone in FFA can tame a rex/spino and the good player's can tame multiple, so the tech strat still doesn't work here. Once deathmatch arrives the wall will then push to far into the ring meaning there is hardly any space to avoid the rexs/spinos and using a longneck to snipe the rex/spino riders off the saddle is impossible. Also if players also tame 1-2 brontos for deathmatch they can hit everyone in the area of the wall.
Bow fighting is currently not a fun or fair mechanic. The speed you can spam arrows is way too fast and so it becomes a match of who gets luckier shooting in roughly the right direction with multiple arrows every second when shooting fastest. Even if you are able to hit the game often won't register it as a hit due to the terrible server latency.
Other issues seem to be the fact that the devs only seem to be listening to the whining new players who can't play the game well and as such are implementing so many unpopular decisions. As a result of these the player numbers are falling, from a game that had a few thousand players average a couple of months ago it can't seem to pull above even 1000 anymore. Also the optimisation isn't great as while it can keep a decent framerate there is frequent lag spikes and the game gets laggier overtime, requiring a restart often. Also the reward system is terrible. After over 100 wins I still don't have half the uncommons and the score required to even earn the highest tier of rewards (2200+) is greater than that of even the person with the highest score in the world..... Turtles attacking your tames for 5 minutes straight is just broken and the meganura attacking you for 5 minutes for something that you didn't even kill is just dumb. Also wild dino levels just do not belong in this game and there should be an even distribution of the dinos in the first place. Also we now have cringe music as the default on the main screen.
There are a few good points about this game though, such as the graphics being great if you can run them and the concept is amazing, however it just hasn't been done properly due to a poor developer team.
TL;DR: Was once a good game but is no longer, due to a poor developer team.

Doom 3 resurrection of evil is a mediocre game. If you didn't like Doom 3, you won't like this. If you liked Doom 3, you might still not like this. While Doom 3 was a bit of a slow-paced horror shooter (or tried to be, at least), this leans more towards action, but fails to deliver.
There are two main additions to the game: A gravity gun, and an artifact that can be used to trigger bullet time. Both fail miserably.
The gravity gun is awkward to use. You can grab barrels and crates and throw them at enemies, and you can grab enemy projectiles and lob them back. However, grab an object for too long (4-5 seconds or so), and the gravity gun runs out of charge and drops it. This means you cannot use it for battle constantly because you don't always have things at hand to throw, and you can't keep an object with you for the next encounter. Even more awkward is that it occupies the same weapon slot as fists (pressing 1 switches to grav gun, then fists if you press 1 again). This is annoying because fists one-shot enemies once you get the Berserk ability (see below), and you'll have to go through the gravity gun first.
The artifact is also awkward to use. You have to switch to it (Q by default), activate it, after which you're switched back to the weapon you had before you switched to the artifact. You have a maximum of 3 artifact charges, and the charges are replenished by consuming some special red-glowing dead bodies scattered in the levels.
The artifact is leveled up every now and then after defeating certain enemies, gaining certain effects for the duration of bullet time: first berserk (greatly increased damage, fists one-shotting people) and then invulnerability.
Unlike the original Dooms (Doom 1 and 2) where most of the monsters were in the level to begin with, monsters typically spawn from thin air. You see a reddish orb at monster height, from which lightning arcs to the ground, then the monster spawns. This is a major annoyance with bullet time because you find yourself having to wait for the monsters to spawn before you can shoot them. That means standing for several seconds in front of the spawn point twiddling your thumbs. Worse, the monster spawn points block your movement, so you can't even go ahead and leave the monsters behind. You have to wait.
Couple that with monsters often spawning behind you, blocking your movement backwards. Overall the spawning mechanic is overused and means you never "clear" an area. Every time you use a computer or get a PDA/holokey you have to prepare for some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t re-sweeping of a previously swept area.
The story is bad enough that I don't remember much of it. The artifact, being from hell and all, is drawing hellish monsters to Mars or something. You're trying to return it to hell so they stop coming. To do that you need to activate and use a teleporter, for which you need to shut down some power systems to boot up, bla bla bla. The few NPCs that talk to you and give you missions are forgettable and cliched.
Combat is the same as Doom 3, which is not a great thing. I constantly ran out of ammo for some reason, and found the reload times of weapons awkward. There were many monsters in general, and most of my time in fights--when not using bullet time because it's boring--was spent reloading or switching weapons. They also retained the screen-shake effect on getting hit, which screws up your aiming and vision.
The ending sees you going back to hell to return the artifact and fighting with Demon-form Kruger from the original Doom 3. The fight is annoying as hell, and once it's done you see a dumb cutscene and the game ends.
In conclusion: If you're a diehard Doom 3 fan, get this. If you've run out of single-player FPSes to play, you can try it out. Otherwise don't bother.

This game has so much potential.  Before I go on, I recommend it if you're comfortable with Early Access games.  If you are unhappy spending money on a product that is not finished, can crash, has bugs, etc - do not buy this game.
That said, I'm having an absolute blast.  The game supports solo play, and co-op up to 8 players.  5 Classes and multiple races to choose from, and multiple character slots available allow for a lot of variability in play.  Each class does play fairly distinct from the others and are legitimate on their own.
Crafting is not fully implemented, but what is there is functional at a base level.  This is one of the areas I'm most excited for, but if you are buying this with crafting being a primary factor, be aware it is not yet complete!
I have played both solo and with groups.  Both are a ton of fun, though get enough wizards together and your screen will be so full of color that you may lose sight of the enemy.  Towns are MMO style, with up to 250 players (I think? I could be wrong there) capable of being present.  Global voice-chat is enabled, and some people's microphones are WAY louder than others.  Hopefully there will be a way to handle this in the future.
I've crashed a couple times, but overal it's been pretty solid for an Early Access experience.  Loading can take quite awhile (especially when you launch the game initially), so just be aware of that.
Classic ARPG dungeon delving, grouping, looting, crafting, leveling, buying/selling and skill purchasing are all present to varying degrees of completion.
To sum up - I'm having a blast.  If you enjoy watching games progress from unstable, feature incomplete but fun games into fully fledged products, then do pick this up and support the developers.  If you need a finished product to justify the cost of your money, feel free to wait for it to be further along or released before purchase as there is definitely a way to go for some features and stability.

I just want to say that this game used to be incredibly good. In all honesty I've played more of Awesomenauts than any other game I've played to date. This game is a MOBA like any other, but with rather simplistic mechanics compared to other MOBAs. Things like shop items are limited to a small variety that can drastically change the style of play of characters, very unique to other MOBA shop items that merely provide stat changes. Despite being a "Watered-down" MOBA, the game was very fun to play.
As the years carried on, however, the game began to quickly lose its sheen. Ronimo has failed to listen to its fanbase time and time again. The matchmaking system now is the same as it was when it was first released: Without relative skill matchmaking, so matches are often decided before they even start. No dedicated servers, so networking in the game is strictly peer-to-peer, which doesn't work well with MOBAs. All forms of hit detection are determined by the client of the attacking player, so a lagging player can easily rack up kills by exploiting his latency. Game balancing has been an issue, as the stronger characters tend to be the newer ones available through DLC, making things feel P2W at times. The community is awful; expect cancer.
Overall, this game had potential, but slowly my expectations for Ronimo to respond to player pleading faded as they continued to take the game in a direction no player wanted.

Croixleur Sigma is an action game in the lines of Devil May Cry, simplified in a lot of aspects, but still presenting a lot of depth. It's the sort of game that's easy to learn and hard to master, offering a nice difficulty curve.
You face various sets of enemies coming in continuous waves in a circular arena, and the draw here is to become more efficient at speedily dispatching them. You're transferred to consecutive arenas with different sets of enemies and increasing difficulty, until getting to the last one, where you'll face the last boss.
There's a 15 minute time limit to go through these arenas and finish the main story. Each playthrough is short, so the experience never becomes repetitive or bothersome. This pacing makes sure that the game doesn't overstay its welcome. Surpassing your previous records is the aim every time you take the challenge again.
There are also a few extra game modes and various weapons (and a character) to unlock, to help keep the experience fresh. This game offers a surprisingly concise package in the sense that, if you're a completionist, the chalenge'll increase in such a smooth manner that you'll achieve mastery of the game precisely at the time where it runs out of content. It was a satisfying experience that deserved a hearty recommendation.

Croixleur Sigma is a battle system with a rough story slapped on it.
Like a lot of these cheap Japanese imports, I can't hit recommend, but there's fun to be had.
Basically, you play as some stereotypical anime heroine who has to pass some kind of test at her weird monster battling school/religeon/cult/whatever.
You head into the test with the thought in the back of your head that maybe this is how the tutorial works.
You kill a circular room full of monsters, take a portal to another, and so on, picking up coins as you go.
Eventually you meet another girl who you're apparently competing with, and you fight a battle with her help.
Then you fight some harder enemies and then a boss.
You've passed your test! Great! Now, on to the... credits.
Game over, after about 30 minutes.
You can go back in with a different weapon, or a difficulty multiplier, but that's it. Essentially 15 or so identical rooms of hack and slash monster fighting.
What's so disappointing about Croixleur (other than the fact that you never get to hear anybody try to pronounce the name) is that the hack and slash combat is so well done. It's thoroughly enjoyable for the fleeting campaign. By all rights this should be an epic fantasy RPG with upgradeable weapons and scaling player stats and a bunch of bosses to fight. Like a GameCube or PS2 action RPG. I'd play that and love it and not care that I'm a 26 year old man (Before you judge me, know that I got this in a bundle) playing a game as a weird 13 year old anime girl because the combat is so satisfying.
Unfortunately that's not the case. You get 15 identical rooms full of maybe 4 different monsters. You get a surprisingly large variety of weapons to find and unlock, but who cares when you can only take them back to that same arena?
Controller support is a bit odd, since the buttons are either mapped wrong for the gameplay or for the menus, but never right for both. In theory there's local co-op, but I haven't tried it and I'm a bit skeptical that it'll work right.
Basically, pick this up if you like hack and slash games and have run out of other options, and you can get it for under $2. Otherwise, keep an eye out for these devs to release a much larger game with the same battle system and grab that instead.

This one is a tricky one.
On the face of it, Ground Zeroes is an exceptionally well made 'demo' for the upcoming Phantom Pain. That's its core purpose. It introduces a number of items that will be present in MGSV:TPP, and closes with a cinematic (Kojima suprise) that leads into MGSV:TPP.
The core mission itself is short. Extract two targets in a relatively small base, and get out. There are a litter of unspecified side-objectives that contribute to your overall score at the conclusion of the mission, but they aren't anything particularly major. If you're terrible like I am, it'll take you about an hour, maybe more. If you're much more practiced, then you'll be through far more quickly.
And then it finishes. Done. Ground Zeroes main story is done and dusted, just like that.
The real meat comes in later on. The 'side ops' will have you running back through the black site again, with different objectives. The one I just completed - for instance - required me to assassinate two targets. Same again with the score increasing side-objectives.
Each run through the base will have different effects in play. For instance, the Ground Zeroes mission will have you infiltrate in the night and in the rain. The assassination mission requires you to sneak through the site in broad daylight. These, coupled with some fiendishly well hidden collectibles (XOF patches) and achievement specific mission executions are what will generate the bulk of the time spent playing this game.
The core mechanics are very sound. The stealth is superb, with enemies being observant (but not unfairly so) and reacting in a believable manner.
Were you spotted for a split second? Instead of jamming their fingers on the alarm button, the guards will observe the suspicious area for a time and if nothing of note occurs, they will return to their posts.
You can intimidate, interrogate and just generally silence guards without firing a shot. Move in close, raise your weapon and they will surrender. From there, you can do with them as you please.
The game is stunning, with some beautiful weather effects coming through and superbly detailed textures. Also optimised extraordinarily well - I had no troubles with this game at all.
The only 'bug' that I really noticed was some pop-in, but that only occurred as I performed a quick 360 degree glance after restarting at a checkpoint.
Okay, the recommendation.
Should you play this? Yes. However,I feel compelled to point out that, despite the production values, this feels increasingly like a demo for the upcoming game. Is it fun and fleshed out? Absolutely. The lack of content may bother some people.
If you can get it on sale, do so.

From the very moment I pressed ‘New Game’, I fell in love with Evoland. It’s a game that integrates evolution of the action/adventure, RPG and JRPG genres in its mechanics, starting out with a GameBoy black and white Zelda-like experience and ending with a full-fledged 3D boss battle. It’s simply amazing. But.
It doesn’t really hold up as a game that well. Ironic, isn’t it? It’s a great, and, most importantly, niche experience. If you’ve played video games for the past 15-20 years at the least, or you were/are interested in a lot of old games before your time, I think you’ll find this nostalgic trip quite enjoyable. I mean, come on, you get to buy an upgrade that removes CD loading times (that were indeed put on purpose) from the PlayStation era locations. How cool is that?
But the game is very basic. It’s got mechanics from Zelda, Final Fantasy and Diablo, and they all, while present a solid foundation, don’t have much depth to them. There are clever moments, don’t get me wrong, and the part where you time travel between Old and New graphics has got to be the most enjoyable section of the game, but it doesn’t feel enough. The soundtrack is really cool though, and game-related humor is amazing.
Still, this brings up an interesting question. Does a game need to have flawless mechanics that do not get old quickly to truly enjoy it? Perhaps that’s a topic that requires a more detailed discussion later. But at least in case of Evoland, I can honestly say – no. No it doesn’t. I loved every second of it.

I remember playing the Flash demo for this about a year or so ago and getting really excited for this. It seemed quirky, had a lot of the GOOD elements from the adventure games it was parodying and displaying, and the upgrade system was really cool. Someone already wrote a review saying it, but I'm saying it again just in case the message didn't get across: the first half is awesome. Although things like the left button and such are silly, it does a pretty decent job of taking you through the early days of video games step by step between the Adventure games like Zelda and the RPGs like Final Fantasy. However, this is cut short when you get to the part where you can finally jump into the third dimension. There's some awesome puzzles around this part where you have to go back and forth between dimensions, but any time you're on the overworld it becomes a slog of random encounters and you quickly see that along with the history of these games, the developer has left in some of the worst parts of them.
It seems like to me that around the 3d stage of the game, the developer started to get lazy. The random encounters aren't balanced (or, if the point was to be just "annoying", the encounters aren't easy enough to shrug off since it will often pick a very unfair amount of enemies for your low level party that hasn't had a chance to buy healing items and the last save was FIFTEEN MINUTES AGO IN THE MIDDLE OF A DUNGEON ARRRGHHH) and it's at this point when the upgrades, which in the beginning are major graphical and audio and mechanics upgrades, start to just be "Textures" "HD Textures" "Lighting" "DYNAMIC Lighting". The last really cool area is to get the first part of an Amulet you need, but its followed up by the second part, which while being a very cool Diablo scenario, falls short by having it be a hack and slash fest with waves of enemies that are absolutely ridiculous- even by the standard of the game it's parodying. Maybe it's not really that hard, but the problem is that you're in a Diablo-esque combat setting with those clunky Zelda controls. And the boss is literally just hit and run, as compared to the first boss that actually had some strategy, and to add insult to injury you get items and fight a ton of stuff along the way that does NOTHING for you.
When you get back into the overworld, all those monsters you fought didn't give you XP (just some gil) and the items you got were all joke items, one of them even telling you to just hit and run the boss. Not to mention, it's been probably a half hour to an hour, depending on how much you've died at this part, since the last time you saw a 2d location or gotten to do any of those sorts of puzzles.
Its after this part shortly you get an airship and can travel freely around the world, and at this point I stopped. You can travel back to one of the first villages of the game and it just sort of... pops back into 2d mode. Even though it established a dimension travelling mechanic... all of a sudden it just pops you in. Maybe I have just too high expectations from the demo, but... this was just the pinnacle of laziness to me. Maybe this game can pass as a mini-history lesson about the games industry, but as anything else it falls flat on it's face and spits in the face of anyone who saw potential for this as an actual game.
Last complaints: the game's buggy as hell. It has an option for a gamepad but won't actually detect it. It also never properly explains controls or let's you rebind stuff. There are a lot of times when you'll load up a save and not have some of the powerups you picked up beforehand. Like, I actually managed to walk past the random encounters chest because of a glitch, and I probably should have counted my blessings. And the UI leaves a LOT to be desired, especially in situations like the Diablo level where everything is just suddenly different (and then changes back to the original UI for certain areas when you return to them).
Final verdict: I bought this game on sale, and it's barely worth that. I mostly wanted to help the developer because I remembered this seeming really cool, but I obviously should have read the reviews first. Hope this helps someone. Instead of buying a history lesson, just pick up one of those oldies and play it for yourself... or play one of the many other indie games that devote themselves to those mechanics and stick with it the whole way through to make an actual GAME.

Idle Champions of the Forgotten Realms is a Dungeons & Dragons based idle/clicker game that is a lot of fun. Playing around with formations and the various champion abilities is entertaining.
There is some interesting synergy going on as you assemble your team. The gear is very diverse and characters have specialization options as they level, allowing you to customize your approach in dealing with the monsters you encounter during your adventures. The art style is whimsical and the variety of monsters keeps me interested to see what my party will come against next.
Whether you are investigating a curse or trying to rescue a couple being kept apart by Lycanthropy, the storylines are entertaining enough without bogging down the serious hack and slash and backstabbing and spell blasting action.
Multiple D&D races are represented such as Half-Elf, Drow Elf, Dwarf, and Human. But there are a few with which some players may not be familiar: Tiefling (plane touched humans), Firbolg (giant kin), Dragonborn (draconic humanoids), and Aarakocra (bird-like humanoids). There is a nice diversity of available D&D champion classes too. Fighter, Cleric, Paladin, Rogue, Bard, Wizard, Ranger, Sorcerer, Warlock, Druid, and Barbarian make up the usual suspects.
The great thing for me is that when I need to do something in the, pardon my French, “real world”, I can minimize the game and check in on my group as time allows. There is a journal you can review to see any missed conversations between your characters.
The game does not require a knowledge of the Forgotten Realms. But if you have ever journeyed through its storied landscape, it is a nice little romp down memory lane--and likely places you have visited during your campaigns. I have not yet reached Waterdeep, but the City of Splendors beckons.
I am quite looking forward to what the Devs have in store as the game is updated and fleshed out in the coming months.
Update (First Event, Highharvestide):
I had a blast on the first event in October. Highharvestide was replete with creepy scarecrows, evil Necromancers, and no ordinary rabbit that’s the most foul, cruel, and bad-tempered rodent you ever set eyes upon. The event campaign included a new adventure and variants that use event tokens to activate. You could unlock a new champion and gear up your new character throughout Highharvestide. To keep everyone on equal footing, the event started with no divine favor. In this case, you earned favor for one of the eldest gods in the Forgotten Realms, Chauntea. At the end of event, we are to be given the option to convert to a different deity.
So consult the book of armaments--chapter two verses nine to twenty-one--and lobbest thou thy holy hand grenade at thy foe while collecting harvest baskets like the deranged little Faerun red riding hood we know you are.
