So, first a caveat to this game, especially considering the words of some of the negative reviews.
This is less a game and more a celebration of the earliest days of RPGs. Honestly, for most people, I think you have to hit the right age (not much younger than mid 20s or so) to really get what Evoland is all about. RPGs have evolved a lot in the past 15 years or so, and Evoland doesn't really touch too much of that. (I'd love a bigger and higher funded sequal that did though.)
To those of us who grew up playing JRPGs on the NES and SNES, who played the original Zeldas, who killed so much time with the first Diablo... This game boils all those concepts down into its one step at a time pace. It was really well done, the unlocking of various graphical, sound, and gameplay features. It brought back a lot of memories and also helped really bring into focus the build up these games have had over the years.
I think if you're into game development, it is especially a magnificent experience. To show you how things were played with, how they were built upon a step at a time to the modern games of today.
As for the game itself, it's not going to be everyone's cup of tea. I certainly suggest not paying more than five dollars for the game, as well done as it is. It's about 5 hours worth of play time (I myself bought it and beat it in a single sitting, complete with every single achievement). And if you don't like the way that JRPGs used to be, then you might want to hold off completely. Yes, there are random encounters, and yes, the encounter rate is a bit extreme. As well, the combat is super complex, and there isn't much challenge until late in the game. But that's not really the point. Nor is the quick, standard story.
It's a very hard concept to define. It's not pure nostalgia. And it's not really about gimmicky concepts. It's sort of understanding that there were and are limitations to this style of gameplay, and yet one can love it all the same. We DID love it all the same. Sure, it's frustrating in some ways, but we put up with it. We learned how it worked and we did it.
I'm rambling, so I'll get to the point. It's a sale game, for sure. But for all those who put hundreds of hours into the various RPGs we had as we were growing up, I heavily suggest it. It's a nice little aside for a few hours.

I cannot comprehend the fact that this game was sold ten euros/dollars.
I'll explain ; to me, this game is very fun at first and is a good way to learn more about how video games evolved. It's also funny in some little references to other games or persons from the video game and internet culture. Though positive points about this game end here.
First of all, as I said, the price ; for a game 3-4 hours long, ten euros is too much. For the same price you'll find games like Terraria on which you'll spend hundreds of hours. Spot the difference.
Then, what shocked me the most is the complete lack of personnality of that game ; it looks like Shiro Games wanted to put as many references as possible, so much that there is nothing in this game who makes it stand out from others, apart from the obvious fact that you evolve across history (though it IS fun and kind of addicting at first, it quickly gets completely useless). The gameplay has nothing special (since it's just a copy and paste of other games, with all the actual interesting stuff gone), the characters are plain annoying, moving around is painfully slow, and... Good lord, can this game be more boring? In fact, it feels more like a very long tutorial then an actual game, and I think that's what makes it the exact contrary of fun. Past the very first zones, you quickly start thinking "Hey, when's the true game gonna start?", and all you get is a very synthetic and really bad version of good gameplays, which you don't even have time to enjoy.
Apart from the failed gameplay, the thing that angried me the most is THE FINAL BOSS. As of now, this is the worst final boss I've ever seen, adding a huge difficulty spike right at the end for free and gratuitous rage. Three phases, all more and more horribly, ridiculously, horrendously annoying, for a disappointing end. After a game full of video game puns, you'd expect a little cutscene, something to make you feel AT LEAST like you've achieved something, even if it contains a terrible joke.. Too bad ; you get nothing but credits. Thanks for the effort.
As a rating, I won't recommend this game. Or at least not when it's at full price ; it'll keep you from extreme boredom for a few hours. Though seriously, at the same price? Read a book. You'll have more fun than in this insipid game.

Ok, so I have somewhat odd tastes when it comes to games.
One thing that usually catches my eye (ear?) is good voicework.  I'm a sucker for good voicework that helps to pull me into the game (the Legacy of Kain series comes to mind), and I have to say that this game has some of the best voicework that I've heard in a long, long time.
Another plus is the premise.  I was aware of Hack 'n Slash before this game, so I know the concept isn't totally original, but it's very well done and feels very much like being inside an incomplete game.  So far, I've just finished the trade show section and I was rolling in the floor by the end of it.
Also, I have fire-breathing parasitic teleporter pads that follow me around and do my bidding.  So yeah, that makes me happy!

Making games isn't easy. There are so many things that need to be considered from cost of development to marketing. Throw in some ego and human error and things can get really messy. So messy in fact that in The Magic Circle, the game decides to turn against its creators, with your help of course. With the ability to hack into the games code and other useful tools given to you from an old pro, you will start a twisted journey to take the power from the powers that be. Perhaps more importantly find out who they are. The Magic Circle is a somewhat of a linear story, it isn't super difficult and the puzzles are rather light. What the game does boast is quite the atmosphere, everything can change in the blink of an eye and usually does. The entire game is also somewhat satirical and humorous, poking fun at game design and developers. Hacking into objects and bending the rules is entertaining but nothing that is seriously complicated or strategic. It's just fun. I would've loved to see this expanded on more but the story is front and center here. I would say that The Magic Circle falls under the walking simulator genre, not that I feel that is a bad thing and mean this in no harmful or derisive way. The voice work is amazing and visuals match. You will sometimes hear the composer deciding what music is appropriate for the scene and this made me chuckle. In all, while it is a linear story, it is a fun story, that allows you to screw around a bit with the behaviors of things, It has style, it has charm, and is worth your time.

Kings and Heroes is an extremely promising up and coming dungeon crawler currently in early access. While it's still a bit rough around the edges at this stage, it already includes some great features and a lot of potential!
If you grew up on dungeon crawlers the likes of Might & Magic and Demise: Ascension then I'm guessing you'll love Kings & Heroes.
Dungeons are procedurally generated so you never run the same place twice. You can set the size, difficulty, loot rules and best of all take up to 7 other friends along with you for the adventure!
Outside of the starter town I've only explored a bit so far as I believe these areas are still under heavy development but looking forward to seeing them when complete!
Oh and best of all, the devs have already said there will be no more wipes so don't feel like you need to hold off because it's in early access, get into it!

Kings and Heroes is a refreshing new IP to the fantasy action RPG genre. Chose from one of 5 classes (more to come), one of 6 races, choose your level of neutrality (good or evil or anywhere in between), and roll your stats! Then, be ready for an adventure! This game is an excellent dungeon hub game with an exceptional (and likely to improve) open world as well. The open world alone is massive, and I can foresee so much more being added to it!
The real highlight of this game is the dungeons. Choose from multiple dungeon types (more likely to be added, and are also unlocked by level), select dungeon length, and select difficulty, and get ready for fun! Join up with up to 8 friends, or fly solo! This is only the beginning, but it already is a very fun game to play, especially in a group!
This game truly reminds me of old school dungeon runner games like Dungeon Runners Online. It sticks true to its genre. It gives you the freedom to build your character as you like, any weapon or armor for any class, and allows you to specialize your character how YOU want. It even adds in a lot of fun, shiny weapons, and different gear sets that actually look different (no cosmetic-only phenomena - what a concept)!
There is going to be so much more to come to this game, and you would be hurting yourself by not joining in earlier and helping make this game something we all will enjoy. Day 1 started out bumpy, but they ended up fixing all of the major performance issues in just that patch, and I can\'t wait to see what else will come!
Whether you buy it now, or buy it in a month once more patches get released, you will come to enjoy this game as a true gem that sticks true to what it is. For once, we have an indie action RPG that is being done right. With PVP coming down the line, and even more classes, dungeons, maps and content to come, the sky is truly the limit for this game!

This game is a buggy, unoptimized mess. There is no point in this being multi-player, if one wanted an MMO like this, they would already be playing World of Warcraft. This game should have been single player only, to focus on dynamic dungeons and skills.
The dungeons are the best feature of the game but I think the developers wasted time on useless grouping features that all the other games out there do better. I really don\'t see what the point of this game is, 8 people going down narrow corridors with all kinds of bright spell effects, unprecise targetting, and enemies that don\'t animate smoothly is not a recipe for fun gameplay.
As for dynamically generating dungeons, so far all of my dungeons have been exactly the same (maybe a wall or two in a different place), and the same 3 types of enemies over and over. This is just not fun! I understand this is early access but I don\'t even understand the vision behind this game. It promises a lot of things but delivers on none of them. Core combat is unsatisfying, loot is represented as popup windows when clicking on a dead body, movement in groups is confusing, dungeons look very very similar and so do monsters, and crafting does not seem to work at all for me (I am stuck at level 6 for no obvious reason, and got there before crafting anything at all).
My advice for the developers is to take the most important features they care about one by one and fix them rather than failing at 20 things simultaneously.
I will still keep an eye on this game as for me exploring dynamic dungeons in first person and getting better and better loot is what I was hoping for and would still like to experience at some point in the future.

While I wait for the ADHD Gamer segment to finish the first render, I'll get to and post my review here:
Note: I recieved my key for this game Saturday from the publisher. I still had to wait for today to have a look, but I assume that's because Steam wouldn't allow access to the server until the game released. No blood, no foul.
I cannot recommend the game in its current state, but that may change in the near future as things get rolling and some of the more pernicious bugs are executed with extreme predjudice. Some of these things could have been resolved with more extensive beta testing and a good stress test for the servers.
Had it been offered as an Open Beta, I'd have been a bit kinder to it. Early Access is a good place for it, but if you're looking at investing $30 into this game (or whatever the 4-pack is going to run), then you might want to hold off a couple of weeks to see if the bigger issues have gone.
Texture/model optimization, especially at lower settings would be a good place to start, fix the AI that was slowing things down in town, and getting the character generation procedure to make some sort of sense for a start. It looks like the base system was dragged wholesale from the 4th Edition of Dungeons and Dragons. Oh, and set the default Graphics quality to something other than "Ultra." Yes, Ultra is pretty, but my video card got a little overheated and threw a tantrum.
Having to get all the way into the hub city to get to the Options wasn't my idea of fun.
Making the NPCs around town into people as opposed to fluffy sound bites would be really nice, as well as some lore-- the background hdere is very pretty, but a long way from the rich tapestries of history and current events that make games like EverQuest, Final Fantasy XIV, and World of Warcraft the much-beloved powerhouses they are today.
I will be logging in here and there to see how you\'re coming along, and when it\'s in a more playable condition, I'll change it to Recommend. Kings and Heroes has a lot of potential, but right now it's far too rough to be in a live environment.
For the record, the devs have pushed not one but two patches in the last ten hours, and whilst it did help matters a bit, it's still not quite where it should be. We'll see what it looks like again in a few hours, but I'm not expecting miracles.
It's come to my attention that seven out of ten people have found this review unhelpful-- I'm not a fanboy, and I have no horse in the race at this point. I think it has the potential to be good, but it's not quite there now. If the concerns I have in the video are addressed, it should cross the line between a not-recommend and a recommendation.
That depends on the developer, and not the crowd that currently seems to be having a mad because I've played all of an hour and then was critical about it. Without criticism, the devs aren't going to know what they might improve upon, and that would be even worse.
I stand by my review. If it gets better, I'll amend it.

Ground Zeroes allows you to do more than ever before, and for those willing to revisit it, its unpredictable nature will never cease to impress. * You can have different forms of firing position in prone
* The idroid is so useful since you can call in some support from the MSF :3
* Guns are awesome as well
* Ai is good, and another nice additions is that they coordinate their atk based on your last known position. They even go out in groups to search you in the area.
Map & Graphics:
* Graphics is excellent; The FOX engine reallys makes the game look photo realistic :D
* There is only 1 map :( BUT it has a nice design tho theres some hidden ways to infiltrate the base
* There are some objects that can be interacted with such as cutting the power line down; Manning turrets; driving cars and tanks; breaking in supply rooms; etc.
Overall: SCORE = (8.8/10)

Of course, that won't please anyone – FM17, like its most recent predecessors, is not a game you load up for a quick blast. But developer Sports Interactive has previously addressed this issue with the addition of the FM Classic mode, for more streamlined play.
The main game is a time-eater, and feels more extensive than ever before. Player Roles finally play a... role in FM17. It's now abundantly clear that performance is reliant on effective deployment, both individually and collectively For instance, having your entire back four set to an attacking mentality spells trouble.
The coaching feedback screens have been streamlined – visually at least – and regularly relay more pertinent information. Ignore these at your peril, particularly when preparing for a game.
When you do click continue to the match, you'll be treated to more eye-candy through an improved match engine that looks and plays better than last year. The whole presentation feels slicker, beginning with players filing out of the tunnel, lining up, or warming up in smaller groups.
Though the goal celebrations are still a bit out: watching five or six players running in a straight line, sporadically clapping above their heads, feels like a potential area for improvement.
That very slight niggle aside, watching matches on FM17 is better than ever before and but you still won't believe you're watching a real fixture. Player AI is vastly improved, with fewer erratic outbursts from your team.
The animations have clearly had an awful lot of work done to them, and the level of sophistication employed here shouldn't be underestimated – the switch to a 3D match engine was one of the more controversial changes in the series' history, but it has now been emphatically justified. And, of course, the referees' magic spray has been added to the game, which fans of line-based regulations will enjoy.

Awesomenauts is a fine 2d platformer with game breaking latency issues due to non-dedicated servers and heroes that are designed with 0 ping for effectiveness. The game focuses on burst damage, a trait that is different compared to traditional MOBAs, due to small arenas to fight in. All those factors combined prevent laning heroes from being useful and allows for handicap matches to occur for those unaware of the design flaws with hero selection.
If the lag was solved, the game is worth the time to buy and play against opponents online. Bots for offline play is decent but their A.I. is predictable, making it a bit too easy after 5-6 matches of sizing the A.I. per hero choice.
It is difficult for me to choose 'not recommend' because the problems with the game is 100% based on the lack of support for stable servers if you want to play against other players. As long as you are willing to put up with cheap deaths because of lag or play offline, then get the game. The game's experience will not be smooth while online and that is sad.

Endless Enjoyment
You look up at the stars, seeking hope and answers to unspoken questions.
The planet is dying, and in her death throes she spreads harsh winters over your crops and cities, and summer takes ever so long to return life to the fields.
Soon everything will be over for the dragonkin savants, insectoid warmongers, ghoul-like remnants of the Endless, shady assassins, and scores of Auriga’s inhabitants…
But before this impending cataclysm, you build what you can, reap what you sow, and build your empire from the ground up.
Cities will stretch as far as the eye can see, over the horizon or into the clouds.
You venerate the ground you walk on, or destroy everything in your path.
Pacts are made in Dust or blood, yet your homes still need to be fortified, inwards and outwards.
Powerful magic is created, ancient elemental guardians are resurrected,  and some will even learn to prosper during the icy colds of winter.
But the end is inevitable.
Your knowledge increases, experience is amassed, and by undertaking many quests you carve out a name for yourself. And maybe, by exploring the world, by uniting factions or obliterating them, by digging deeper into Auriga’s shell, deeper into her past, you may yet find a way to survive her, to survive the future.
You look up at the stars.
This is the Endless Legend.
This… is your present.

Steam needs an "Ambiguous" review option. I want to like this game, but I can't support the mechanics of it. It's just too tedious and doesn't reward you for your time investment (your game progress resets after each adventure). It is fun for being free to play, but that length of fun really depends on your own gaming style.
I ultimately do not recommend it simply because the only viable party formation/strategy is pure damage. The game actively discourages damage mitigation builds.
+
The game can play by itself about 75% of the time. This makes it convenient as a fun distraction/diversion for doing more important life tasks.
I like that I don't have to click anything to do damage. Mouse-clicking damage is minimal, but it can stun the enemy.
-
The other 25% of the game, the boss fights at the end of stages, require level-grinding and hand-holding. The party formation is an interesting concept, but is very limiting in that the game forces you to min-max for damage output. It's counter-intuitive for the healer to not be able to heal the tank in the party formation (doing so creates a massive loss in damage and slows level progression). The entire difficulty of the game is highly dependant on how fast and how much damage you can do. Tanking and healing builds are useless.
It takes too long to get access to the roster of party members (monster kills drop gold which is used to unlock levels/party members). Even worse, the game resets your progress (level, money, unlocked party members) each time you beat an adventure "module" (the world mission). You do get to keep your items, but having to start over from scratch each time is incredibly tedious and really emphasizes the monotony of the game.

I've got nothing aginst clicker games, idle games, or the like. They can be a fun diversion or something to just have running in the background to see how the numbers you can run up.
The main problem with this game is that you can litereally waste money on it. Not the figurative "I spent some cash on it and got some fun but now I got some remorse over it" literally waste money. Because the game resets your progress after each quest you take, taking you back to just 1 character at level 1 earning 1 gold per kill. You get to keep your equipment, but all the money you got from those paid chests? Gone. Those bounty contracts you get that give you extra money upon use? They scale to what your currently earning, so they go down in value. The money that comes out of the paid chest themselves do this as well so you get 700ish for opening one early and millions for opening them later in the quest.. but it all goes away, and so does your money.
People will defend it saying that after you finish a quest, the total gold you got translates into bonus gold find. The problem is there is no clear indication if the money you get from the paid chests actually counts towards the "earned" gold, and my own experiences with the game make me doubt that they do. Add in said gold find didn't seem to really do much.. It takes forever to accumlate a gold find that results in any noticible increase. Eventually that 1 monster that gave you one gold will give you 3! I only had to drop 11 hours into the game to get a very meager increase.
The idle part is also very.. It's not untrue, but you also won't get very far. There is no autobuy feature so you will have to keep coming back to tend to things if you want to get anywhere. Really at the start of any reset your looking at spending at least an hour minding it to get your character to a place they can actually idle and grind anywhere worthwhile. It's not wrong to say its an idle game as it will progress while your not playing.. it just really needs a lot of babysitting if you want to get anywhere.
Okay so what about if you don't drop any money on the game? It's free so it can't be that bad right?
Well.. its free, but its free with paid chests and.. it seems obviously scaled towards the gear you get out of those chests. There was a promotion to get a 700% weapon with any purchase and with that extra 700% damage on my main character I seemed to just barely be doing enough damage to make killing normal enemies smooth. Mind you at this point I was doing BILLIONS of damage per hit with just one character. Eventually you will be doing multiple trillians or quintillions of damage with any one character and barely be able to keep up with killing imps, rats, or cows.
you CAN eventually earn ONE of the paid chests through just playing the game.. 11 hours of actively having the thing running and baby sitting it I just barely managed to get enough gems
to get a gold chest. So theres that.
Its just not scaled or really set up in a way I can recommend. Maybe it's still appealing to someone but I'm going to say give it a pass. It's a shame because I really like Forgotten Realms but this seems like another case of WotC wanting just a bit too much for what they are giving you.
[update] For an example of how bad the scaling on this game gets if you do not put cash into it, they recently actived a limited time seasonal event. This event uses it's own currency and own cash multiplier meaning you start back at square 1 other than your chest found equipment.
Even with the equipment I got from the chests I did purchase, and the chests that I had earned via letting the game idle, I still was unable to complete the very first board using just Brueno and Celest, the only two champions you can easily get when your starting out fresh. They simply got swarmed and killed. Had i had more gold chest equipment I'm sure I would have been fine, but simply with what I had it was not enough, and the heroes jump in cost from 50 gold for Celest to 1k for Jamiah, a level of ingame currency your not going to be able to obtain when you cannot kill 25 first level bandits without getting swarmed and dying.

Others have pointed out that this is not a game in and of itself, but most of them fail to mention that it's basically nothing at all. I knew what was inside of the download. A news feed, an interactive map of the verse, videos, pictures and a social network-like mini-game of collecting cards. What I didn't know was that almost all of that was locked.
The point of this not-a-game is to earn BP(Brownie Points) that will be turned into in-game money when Firefly Online(FFO) launches. Currently, the only free way to earn BP is your daily log-in reward, referring friends, looking at news and the one-time social media connecting. I uninstalled the game, so I won't see what the daily log-in is, but I assume 25BP or less. Referrals earn you 100BP. Each news item, of which there are only 20 over the last couple years of development, earn you 10BP each. And connecting your facebook, twitter and Youtube well net you 25BP each.
Now, what about that Map of the verse and the Trading Post card game? That looks like fun, right? Well, it does look like fun, but you can't access it. You have to buy one of their packs (which even if you wanted to, they have removed from the store, more on that in a minute) to unlock them. The Big Damn Hero Pack is $5 and will get you access to the mini-games inside this not-a-game which will let you earn more BP, and tbh, looks like a little bit of fun. The problem is, the game packs have all been removed and can no longer be purchased.
The devs have stated the removal of the game pack sales is due to server complications, and that they are so nice, they would rather you have smoother gameplay than earn extra money. Nevermind that owning one of those pack(s) is the only way to get any gameplay in the first place.
Honestly, I just learned about this game today, and I am already depressed. I feel so bad for anyone who backed them and have been waiting the last couple years. This game is getting pushed back and has horrible developer communication. If it wasn't for the fact that these guys got all of the original cast to come back and do voice over work, I would have written this off as dead, and I still think it might be dead even so.
In short, you can't play this game anymore, there are no game packs to unlock anything that can even be remotely close to a game in it. And even if you just wanted to watch the interviews and read the dialogue from the Map, you can't. Hell, they set the vimeo videos to private in the news section. It minimizes the game and tries to take you directly to vimeo, which is a hassle, but would at least be decent if they worked. The videos are no longer viewable, at least for me.
TL;DR
You have to pay $5 to play any of the game parts in it.
You can no longer buy the game packs even if you wanted to pay $5.

Outdated: Astounding piece of kit - and absolutely integral to any game artist or aspiring game artist. I've used this software for a fair while now and my only gripe... and the singular reason in me not giving this software a recommended review is the stability issues.
I'm somewhat on the fence review wise - after careful consideration I've fallen on the not recommend side . The last major crash which saw 4 hours work lost pushed me over the edge. Ideally - as I sit at 55/45 - I'd love to be able to write a review that would be 'neutral' - not recommend/not recommend
Before I delve into a more indepth reason as to why - here is my initial feedback on the software.
Pros:
- Wide range of PBR techniques to work with
- Wide range of content available with the base version - presets, masks etc.
- Lots of community created items available for purchase or for free download (smart materials, masks etc)
- Easy to navigate viewport and HuD ( does take some getting used to)
- Very compatible with current generation game engines.
- Exceptional community support.
Cons:
- Lack of a stable recovery file system ( save on crash) - I've had this option appear once.
- Smaller material preset choice compared to Quixels dDo ( ! though over dDo2, I would recommend this hands down)
Back to why I can not wholy recommend this in its current state:
I've had dozens of crashes working with higher resolution projects, and losing 1-5 hours of work is an absolute farce. The software does not offer an autosave feature, and any save on crash features that are present are very hit and miss.  I've had upwards of a dozen crashes, and only had the recovery save option appear once. Collectively I've lost upwards of 20  hours work, which as a freelancer - is really very frustrating as well as  extremely expensive.
I am aware that one rebuttle would of course be to manually save more often - but I am not used to that routine ( most other software I use for work has an autosave function)
I am also aware that due to the manner in which the software is built - an autosave/backup system is difficult to implement. I would quite happily settle for a little pop up reminder every 20-30 minutes - asking me to save progress. There are plenty of fixes for a small problem, but one which can so easily turn out to be a major issue.
I'll continue using the product, and continue supporting it when newer versions come out - but the lack of any reasonable save file function - in this industry ... in 2017 ... is somewhat falling short for me.
TLDR: awesome piece of kit, can not recommend until the stability is improved - and a better crash/error handling system included.
UPDATE:
Previous updates have fixed some of the issues , namely autosave functions which have been extremely useful.

Beautiful graphics, a fantasy setting, and 4X. If you like those three things, then that is what you will get with this game.  Is it the best 4X game?  No.  But is it a good game?  Yes, yes it is.  And in my opinion a very fun game.
I'm not going to wax lyrical about pros and cons as there are already much better examples posted and with far more eloquence.  That being said, I will offer this advice:  If you wish to get the most out of this game, then take advantage of the different races and victory paths by playing as many of them as you want however and whenever you want.  What I mean by this, is don't get locked into one playthrough long past the point when it has become redundant.
The strength of this game is not in its endgame.  It is in its variety and richness of races and play styles.  I stopped hating this game the moment I realized that and started having fun.
With that in mind, I also recommend buying this game on sale.  You really won't have to wait long with as frequent as the Steam sales typically are.  And if you buy it on sale, you are much less likely to become frustrated in those tedious end stages I just mentioned.
If you are a hardcore 4x player, this game may not be for you.  But if you're like me, and it's as much the fantasy aspect as the strategy part of the game that calls to you the most, then I say have at it!

The only other 4X game I've played is Civ 5, so my review will largely be from comparing my experiences of the games.
I bought this game after seeing the plethora of great reviews, but after playing it, I have to say it is massively overrated. I bought this game on sale through the Humble Store and I completely regret the purchase.
Pros
+ Beautiful map
+ Minor factions assimilation
+ Decent diplomacy options
+ Quests give you something to do
+ Nice music
+ Unique factions
Cons
- Barely anything to do
- Never enough armies
- Some factions are just better
- AI accepts your compliment the first turn you meet them, then immediately engages you for no reason
- Attempting to trade with AI is difficult
- Cities take forever to get anything done
- Combat is a massive chore that feigns depth, but really doesn't need you to do anything at all; it is not the tactics minigame it pretends to be
- Combat AI runs around like a headless chicken
- Massive power gaps arise between units for no apparent reason
- Ugly units when viewed up close
- Winter slows everything down further
- No voice acting
- Turn sequence is similar to hybrid mode in Civ, but ENEMY units can move at the same time as you
- Quests don't mesh well and often give impossible objectives
- Poor character diversity (of the three factions I played, all 9 heroes were female with long dark hair and all 3 leaders were too); you can customize just about every aspect of a faction except for its appearance in the custom faction editor the game provides
One of my games involved me crushing a nearby enemy faction's army very early on and taking one of their cities. The next time I found their army about 50 turns later, their hero had 3 times the health mine did and their army's units were far stronger than mine, despite being the basic unit (units can be upgraded, but I don't understand how they managed to grow their cities, army size, army quality, and hero strength beyond my own after I set them back as much as I did).
Maybe I just don't know how to play the game, the tutorial goes over the basics, but gives no indication of what a good way to growing your nation is.
Before this game, I had never googled how to enjoy a game. I have now and it didn't help.
Maybe multiplayer offers a better experience.
I would rate Civ 5 a solid 8.5/10 (not paid for review 8.5/10, but a legitimate 8.5/10 as it was actually engaging).
I give this game 3/10. The pros don't really mean anything when the game just feels fundamentally broken.

I had great hopes for this game, it looked great and while I still feel I got my $70 out of it, I feel its "replayability" is pretty limited.  Overall I'd give it a C-.
One little tip I learned (didn't see this posted anywhere):
You don't automatically get your enemies' stuff when you take them out, but after you take your enemy's last territory, you can truce them and take ALL their tech in exchange for offering the truce.  For some reason they don't like letting go of resources in this situation, but you can often get a few of those as well.  The beginning of the next turn they're out of the game and (especially on the harder levels) you'll usually jump one or two tech eras due to the sudden influx of technology.
Anyway...
Pros:
1. Nice graphics
2. Interesting quests/storylines (the first time)
3. Customizable units
4. Decent mechanics for exploration, movement, fog-of-war, and city building
5. Alternate victory scenarios beyond elimination/supremacy over your opponents (e.g., quest victories)
Cons:
1.  The AI is terrible.  Winning at any level beyond normal is simply a matter of grinding and surviving to the later stages where you can amass a strong enough force to start rolling over your neighbors, taking 1-2 territories at a time.  Increasing game "difficulty" simply boosts the computer-controlled production (to the point of ridiculousness beyond the "serious" level).  The AI seems totally unaware/incapable of any strategic movement.  For example, you can surround another empire's capital city with armies and it doesn't even seem to notice, it just waits for you to kill it.  In the games I've played, once you've amassed a decent military the computer-controlled empires didn't attack at all, they just waited to be taken over.
2.  Tactical combat is tedious.  The combat area is small, the tactics you can employ are limited, and the initiative-based combat system coupled with the poor AI often leads units to behave inexplicably.  Even on the "fastest" setting the turns still aren't terribly fast.  The "automatic" combat (especially at the early stages of the game at higher levels of difficulty) can't be trusted, so you're faced with either (1) playing out each of a large number of combats manually or (2) losing units you're replacing at a 1:10 ratio with the competing computer-controlled units.
3.  Slow turns and Late-game lag for large maps.  My desktop is 2 years old and had no problem displaying the graphics at the highest level, but the turns still take 10+ seconds to complete at the very early stages.  After 150 turns or so, the game turns into a complete resource hog, and memory and processor utilization goes through the roof to the point where it's almost unplayable (i.e., 60+ second turns).  I can't imagine playing a multiplayer game with a large map.
4.  The quests just repeat and there is little or no variety in them.  After you've learned the sequence for a faction quest, you can alter your game play in anticipation of the tasks you know you'll need to fulfill.

A fairly interesting take on the Idle game genre.
You take up to 9 heroes on self contained 'adventures' that have unique requirements, monsters, and challenges. It's pretty fun, but so far the game probably could be beaten within a week. I've played it for about 3 days and have been able to reach up to area 85 on various adventures in free play.
You arrange your heroes/champions (i'll use that interchangably) in a 3x3 grid. This is of strategic importance to gain benefits to dps and/or other abilities from different champions. Say, you've got a hero that buffs the column that he resides in, you'll want to arrange your heroes to take advantage of that. The game doesn't have rpg stats like the D&D liscence suggests, and is broken down into 3 parts, Health, DPS, and Abilities. Health is how much HP the hero has, when they lose all of it, they will no longer provide any benefits to the team or attack monsters, they will also 'fade' and allow any monsters to approach the other members. DPS is how much damage you deal per second, each hero has its own damage and cooldown (say, an attack every 4.5 seconds), DPS is the combined total of all of these without consideration to 'multiple attacks' (say, a hero can 'cleave' which may hit 3-5 enemies near their attack area). Abilities are skills and buffs that you gain upon 'leveling' a hero, you level up a hero with gold that you earn on and during adventures. These abilities can increase DPS for one or multiple heroes at once and may have conditions, some abilities or skills are called 'ultimate abilities' which have a period cooldown and are of strategic use. After each adventure you 'complete' or 'reset' and this will give you a number of 'faith tokens?' based on how much gold you earned, which add up and give you a bonus to gold find for the next adventure. Reseting will clear leveling progress for your heroes but you'll be able to keep Items found and Equipment earned from chests. Chests are random loot you find on bosses, and can also be bought with gems which is an ingame currency that is also found on bosses. More info on these can be found in the game description.
I like the 'variants' to the adventures which give different types of challenges, whether it's escorting chickens, or being attacked by invulnerable beings of energy. They add some interesting aspects to the game.
Overall I've enjoyed this game a bit. Hope you do too.

Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes is probably one of the most jarring games I've played. Without spoiling the plot, the Ground Zeroes acts as a prelude to Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain and continues off where Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker ends. MGSV:GZ has a darker feel to it, so if you're a fan of that silly action movie like Metal Gear Solid charm, this game's main plot doesn't have much of that. I feel that because the more serious turn, the story, although short, is very compelling and it really makes you start to understand Snake's transformation from who he was during the MGS3, Portable Ops, and Peace Walker.
Outside the story, the game is incredibly smooth running. It runs on nearly max specs on my laptop (Purchased in 2012, has a dedicated Radeon 7400 HD graphics card)
The game feels really great to play, (a better feel than MGS3)
The biggest problem is that the main story takes place in one mission. The main mission is about an hour long. I feel as if the $20 retail price is definitely worth paying, especially if you're a Metal Gear fan.

If you're looking for a fun and continuously entertaining LEGO game, this is an excellent choice.  While it lacks an open world to explore like the previous installment and the recent Marvel Superheroes game, it still delivers a satisying LEGO experience.  Gameplaywise, not much has changed.  The LEGO game format is in full use, but still manages to be fun enough to push you through the story.  You break bricks to build with bricks, and pummel enemies with your vast array of characters given in each level.  This game elaborates on the tool specific costumes from previous LEGO Batman games, adding more suits for Batman, Robin and other characters.  The story is pretty light, but is entertaining enough to keep you playing.  As LEGO games always are, the story is childish; there are many instances of cringe-worthy jokes being littered through each scene.  But, as LEGO stories go, it's good enough for an original tale.

UPDATE May 2017
The bad news is, if you didn't take my advice and buy the game last year, you're out of luck on your Princess Crown. In the past year, everything has improved.  The devs have been very busy and the game is smoothing out beautifully.  Having missed almost all of the past year, I returned to the game to find combat more fun, dungeons better balanced, crafting improved and the overworld enabled.  That's a lot of work put into the game.
The world is beautifully rendered.  Dungeons provide the basic leveling experience, with different kinds becoming available as you level up.  Dungeons also provide your only source of gold and main source of crafting materials, either as drops or by salvaging equipment found.
Crafting is a key part of the game, with an RNG that can crit your crafted items at any crafting level to any rarity of dropped gear in the game.
If you enjoy dungeon crawling, breaking and smashing everything in sight, challenging dungeon boss fights and carrying the loot home for after battle crafting, this may just be your game.

EDITED REVIEW (6/4/2016)
.
All right, so I'm editing this review to further explain some things.
So, first off, this is (at the time of writing) an early access game; a lot of games on Steam labeled as "Early Access" are either already almost 100% completed, or are barely even assembled enough to be considered a game. To put things bluntly, this game is not lying when they say "Early Access"; the game is not finished and still needs coats of polish, but the concept and mechanics are absolutely there.
.
Here's the quick and dirty rundown:
.
PROS
- Up to 8 players in a single dungeon/party
- Game runs pretty smoothly in the dungeons
.
CONS
- The inventory system isn't perfect (No trashing items, can't move items from page to page) [At least to my knowledge]
- Graphical issues plaguing AMD users
- Lighting is kind of wonky sometimes or overly bright and reflective
- Myriad of bugs typical of games still in development
.
Yes there's more cons than pros in the above, however I still would recommend the game, provided it's further down the line in development and some of the more pressing issues have been fixed (such as dungeon tiles not snapping properly, making the boss of a dungeon inaccessible). The game's concept and core mechanics however are solid and clearly there's a diamond in the rough here, but only time will reveal how polished that diamond really is. I really want this game to become great, as I play with a group of friends that can go from anywhere from 2 players to 6 or sometimes even 7, so a game that allows more than 4 or 5 would be a godsend. I recommend this game, but I also recommend waiting for a bit further into its overall development.
.
.
.
.
TL;DR: "Wait and see" kind of game, if you're into dungeon delvers and play games with more than 3 other friends, KEEP YOUR EYES ON THIS GAME, but don't necessarily buy it just yet (at time of writing).
.
For AMD Users: Don't buy the game until the graphical issues are fixed. At present weapons that have a frost or frost/blight effect (held by either players OR enemies) will turn your entire screen into a starburst of rainbow light vomit.

I wouldn't normally play idle clickers but the Forgotten Realms setting drew me to this one. The Baldur’s Gate series is one of my favourite gaming series with its engrossing stories and characters, its enjoyable tactical combat and its huge worlds to explore. Other than the superficial, Idle Champions of the Forgotten Realms shares nothing with the Black Isle titles I remember so well, as you can see in my first impressions video.
There appears to be little in the way of story and character development (your own and NPCs) and the gameplay is almost none existent. In fact you can let the game play in the background with the more basic mobs, which is why I guess they call this an idle clicker. The presentation is alright and if you’re a fan of this shallow genre you might get something out of it, but to me this is just a huge waste of a great license.

Reluctant Recommendation:
On my phone I play pretty much 99% idle games and clickers, and pc around 30% (or as something catches my eye) so speaking from clicker/idle game experience, putting a namebrand logo on any game, doesn't make it great, especially if the name brand is not implemented into the game itself. Sadly this is the case of ICFR.  I does however, grab lots of cool ideas from other games (cept D&D) and mashes nicely into this one. Yet, at the end of the day, it is simply another cookie clicker clone - well it comes off more of a TAP TITAN game (or keeping with steam, a TAP ADVENTURE).
I am NOT giving it a "thumbs down" as the game as it stands is great, and it's FREE, Just nothing out fo the oridary. If you like Tap Titans, you'll like this. Give it a shot.

My Bite Sized Review - Ryse: Son of Rome
The Good:
+Great looking game
+Runs well enough on my old comp
+Executions look cool
+Colour coded gameplay elements means less hud markers are needed (yellow = Y, blue = X, red = B, etc.)
+Environments are detailed and look great
+Story gets better near the end
+New and interesting take on multiplayer (**Note below however)
The Bad:
-Repeated enimies, no new ones introduced after the first 30 minutes of game (you kill barbarians and evil centureons)
-Gameplay doesn't really evolve past the first 30 minutes (execute enemies, press Y on objects)
-Environments are linear, no real choice, one path
-Story doesn't make sense in spots (Enemies want the same thing as you, yet you kill them?)
-Main Character is about as interesting as a sack of potatoes
-No new weapons to use or unlock in single player - you have a sword and shield and spear, they never change
-**Multiplayer is pretty much died
The Verdict:

Short version: The Magic Circle is an ambitious, original game with a great premise that it doesn't quite manage to fully deliver. Even so, I had a blast.
Long version:
So, the idea is that this is supposedly an eagerly anticipated sequel that's been in development hell for something like 20 years and is still a long way from finished. There's cut content that you can restore, mechanics that were planned but never implemented (or axed right in front of you), change logs scattered throughout, the developers drop in and have conversations with each other and with you (assuming you're a tester), etc. It's a great idea and unfortunately, The Magic Circle just doesn't quite manage to sell it. It's not large enough or layered enough with older versions (and logs, etc) to genuinely feel like a project that longrunning and embattled. It's more of a broad overview of what something like that might look like, on a macro scale. It's probably fine in the long run - this is an indie game made by a small team on a small budget, and it's not really fair to expect anything quite as elaborate as the premise suggests. But it does undercut the illusion a bit.
Similarly, the writing definitely gives a broad, parodic sense of the sort of personalities and conflicts that might go into a debacle of that sort and the clashing priorities at work, but because they're so broad, they never quite feel like real people and the commentary on gaming culture and development is pretty surface level. But hey, it's funny and it works well enough in context, just don't expect deep insider insights.
Those are really my main complaints, though. The game itself is brilliant, with a core mechanic in the main section that lends itself to a huge range of solutions to problems and a sort of anarchic tinkering with the game structure that is really enjoyable and beautifully realized, right down to visual representation on literally every editable object of all the different traits they can be assigned. And while the game isn't particularly large, that overworld has plenty of nooks and crannies to hide logs and other collectibles and special creatures and such. Heck, I'm still missing a couple and I could swear I've scoured everywhere. And while the scope undercuts the simulation a bit, there's some neat tricks with desktop simulation and such that help sell it. There are also a couple of later segments that are fun (if a little didactic) in other ways and while they're not as original or massively appealing as the core conceit, they're still well done with a bunch of scope for doing your own thing. All in all, I thoroughly enjoyed my time with TMC and definitely recommend it.

The Magic Circle is an anti-game. Instead of a fourth wall, The Magic Circle has a mirror.
This is a game that rewards you for finding the seams in the world. It's impossible to know what's intentional and what's a level design oversight or a glitch in the code, and it doesn't matter. The game will tell you what you can't do before forcing you to figure out that you can. It doesn't hold your hand or force you into a decision. And then it does, in occasional moments of brutally self-aware beauty.
Exploration, exploitation and some seriously out-of-the-box thinking are punctuated by fragments of an overrarching narrative. Most of which is hiding around dark corners or on thin ledges, but all relating a story devoid of violence, romance, magic or politics. For most of the game the player doesn't even seem to have much role or influence in the story. Despite The Magic Circle's lack of clear antagonists, absence of typical game themes and incoherent storytelling, by the end I found myself strangely moved by emotions that few games ever even touch.
If you've ever been curious about game development or if you've ever spent time in a game trying to get to a place you shouldn't be able to or getting NPCs to kill each other, you NEED to play this game. Everyone, though, should give this a go.
The Magic Circle lets you play around in an unfinished game full of glitchy inconsistencies and somehow makes it feel compelling and gratifying. It's unique, brilliant and impossible to describe.
Good for people who are up to date with gaming politics and enjoy satire. Go in blind and enjoy yourself. 7/10.

Finally, another Metal Gear Solid comes to PC, this time back to its routes of being a stealthy tactical title which is a far cry from the type of game REVENGEANCE was.
The stealthy aspect of Ground Zeroes does everything right. It's something that the whole series does well, so it should be expected though. As I have only had the experience with MGS 1, 2, Snake Eater and Revengeance, the melee controls seem fluid and faultless. All in all, the combat system and stealth are amazing, and I wouldn't change anything about them.
Now, I seem to be saying this every time I review a big AAA game, but these are some absolutely gorgeous graphics, whack all the settings up to full and you are looking at an actual piece of artwork. I couldn't believe how real the world looks in here. The character models, faces, everything, this game really shows off the power of PC gaming.
Ground Zeroes is the prologue for a future MGS title, Phantom Pane, although I understand Phantom Pane is going to be a much bigger title, I still felt a little miffed off that I was paying £16,99 for a game that only lasted two hours, and that's with doing the extra missions at the end. The actual main story can be completed in less than an hour if you know what you are doing....this to me was the only negative point from this release.
I had no technical issues at all, it's quite surprising to see a developer who mainly makes games for consoles, push out such a well-made port. A nice, steady, 60 fps the whole time playing.
The final verdict on Ground Zeroes; I would recommend it, but maybe wait until it drops on sale so you don't feeling the same as I did with regards to the game's length. If it wasn't for that, I'd say this is a must buy and a great game to test your rigs on.

This game is really good. It's far more ambitious than other 4X games, and it does so very well, but it still has its fair share of issues. An Endless Legend 2 has the possibility of being the best 4X game ever.
+Cool lore
+All victory types are more or less equally attainable
+Decently expansive diplomacy, very expansive AI diplomatic states (when civ would have five states, neutral, friendly, guarded, hostile, and afraid, Endless Legend has at least 10, with things like envious, mildly envious, terrified, indifferent, or dismissive)
+Fleshed out espionage
+Well put-together war, with mechanics like high-defense cities giving more health to the garrison, sieging cities to decrease fortification and cripple the city, privateer armies that can fight without a flag to attack other civs or even allies without any repercussions
+DLC is all worth it even at full price
+cool devs
+Only the server host has to have DLC for all the players in a multiplayer game to use it
+UI is very efficient and effective
-Combat, the community seems to be split in half for whether or not the combat is any good, so I'll try to explain it and you decide for yourself.
One army (group of several units) attacks another, and an area of about 15 hexes by 15 is fenced out, and the each army's units are sent out to the battlefield. You can set your units position on your half of this area before any combat starts. Once you're ready, you can give your units orders. You can right-click where you want your units to go or who you want them to attack, or where you want them to go and then attack, and you can set a stance, where if that unit can't complete its orders it will either A. attack if an enemy is in range or B. do nothing if an enemy is in range, or you can set it to stay where it is and not attack unless it's counter-attacking. Once they have orders, all the units on the board move in one turn, in the order of which units have the highest "Initiative" stat. Also, other armies can join at the beginning of each planning stage, at two tiles (two units per turn) marked with a flag. This can be upgraded to four if certain criteria are met.
-UI is meh in appearance
-Worlds feel claustrophobic due to empire's expansion and the number of empires compared to the size of the world
-AI compusively makes units which makes performance go from great at the beginning of a game to abysmal by the end.
-AI is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and needs massive bonuses to compete with a real player on higher difficulties.
-Few factions make replayability lower, because every game has the same factions, but it's balanced by the fact that playing as each faction is essentially a whole new game
-No local multiplayer (Devs say it would be impossible because of the way the game is structured, and I'm inclined to believe them because of their reputation and what I've seen so far in the game)

This is one of those situations where the a-typical steam system of "Thumbs up or thumbs down" doesn't really work. This game isn't made badly, and I would recommend it to some people. But overall, this game was vastly overblown and overrated, at least from a strategic point of view.
1. Graphics were ok, but not great. I did really like the artwork and the way the world looked, but it has a lot of tearing and graphical issues. Nothing so sevre it will ruin the game, but enough to note.
2. Music was actually pretty cool. It's always nice to hear a new soundtrack instead of hearing songs I know I heard on my PS2 games. This was easily the best part of the game.
3. Story for the game, while well written, is delivered poorly. It's 2016; time to actually record voice tracks and make cut scenes, not just constantly throw text boxes at us. This is a common complaint in multiple genres, and it outright confuses me why this games community is so forgiving. The bland delivery prevents any of the stories from feeling different.
4. Gameplay is a strange thing to me. I WANTED to enjoy it. I put effort into learning this game and really tried to see the joy, but every campaign ultimate leads to the same place. Difficulty settings have huge curves between them. Easy is boring, normal is unforgiving. After hours of research, I found that most who are good at this game A. Copied someone elses strategy and B. Save scummed to hell. The difficulty is not provided by clever AI who utilize the rules of this game and world, but rather they get military and economic buffs.
I ran two campaigns that had a 6th faction (I was playing against 5 comps) screw everything. The game was actually fun for the bulk of the campaign. I had cool wars, overcame adversity, and when I was almost crushed outright, I managed to claw my way back and win. It was a blast... until I encountered the bug faction. They had not warred with anyone, yet had higher level troops. They had NONE of the higher end resources (not even tier 1), so how they controlled so much and could have so many while producing so little was beyond me. By the end of the campaign, he overran us with much larger armies (this faction got 14 per army to all the rest of us having 8) and crushed the campaign. It wasn't fun or interesting, it was aggitating. I don't mind losing to a strong opponent. But this is supposed to be a strategy game, how does having no resources or battles result in better armies? This is evidence that tactics and actual strategy do not come into play here. Resource domination and harassment is a very common tactic in games and even IRL, so why it is almost meaningless in this game is beyond me.
5. Combat is TERRIBLE. The battle system is a bad minigame by any other games standards. If you have ever played Sid Meir's Pirates and invaded a city, you experienced a better battle system. Most mobile games are better. The strategies are all based on bad mechanics, and the AI will exploit these bad mechanics to force troops to follow them in a mosh pit style circle. Almost anything would have been better than this.
Honestly? I did have some fun with this game. But the last third of every campaign I played turned an otherwise enjoyable game for me into a burden or a chore. I WANT to like this, and I want to recommend it. That's ultimately what frustrated me so bad about this game. My desire to enjoy it was smothered by bad campaign structure.
And I would actually recommend this to people of a certain taste. I have friends who love games that are extremely time consuming and daunting, and I'm sure they would enjoy it. But for gamers of my taste and desire, this game is not going to provide you the tactical planning and strategic objectives you're looking for.
In closing, I know this review will be receiving a 0% helpfulness rating. For some strange reason, the X4 genre can produce pure garbage (not nessicarily this game, but I'm referring to others) and never receive an ounce of criticism. It's a strange enigma, that's for sure.
I wrote this review as best I could to avoid complaining and simply try to warn gamers of my taste not to buy it because it will not provide an experience they will enjoy. Right now, I'm sure there's someone like me who's more about tactics > micromanagement looking at purchasing this game, and the reviews for this game are extremely misleading in this regard. Do yourself a favor if you're looking at this game, do more research than you would for the average video game, because this game isn't a clear cut case of universal appeal.
In the end I will resist rating this by Good/Bad or by 1-10/10. It's not that simple. It's actually a good game that's well constructed, I just think it's being marketed to a vast number of people who are just not going to like it. I'd like to help those individuals spend their money on something they will actually enjoy.

I remember the day my father brought home an Xbox and a copy of Knights of the Old Republic. If that day had turned out any differently, I doubt my life would look anything like it does now. I can vividly recall waking up on Saturday mornings throughout elementary school, creaking over old floorboards to wake up my dad (and avoid waking up my mother) in order to play this game before my sisters woke up and took the TV to watch their Saturday cartoons. At first, it was my father who did all the playing. Later, I took control for walking and conversations while he handled combat. By the time we beat the game several years later, I was the one holding the controller and my father was along for the amazing and immersive story.
We were both terrible at video games. Wandering the vast, hypnotic, and alien landscapes and cities this game offers felt genuinely dangerous and adventurous. Each fight, down to the smallest skirmish, took several failed attempts, each involving fitzing around with the pauseable real-time combat that my grade school brain had such a hard time wrapping itself around. We spent countless hours walking back and forth, navigating menus, and deliberating every choice. Playing this game in two hour bursts every week, this journey felt like a lifetime of adventure and discovery. And, for me, it was.
I distinctly remember the moment we discovered KOTOR's seminal game-changing twist. If you still don't know, for the love of God, don't go looking for it. I remember laughing with my father at HK47, long before I knew he was a beloved character. To me, Bastila Shan, Darth Malek, Carth Onasi, and everyone else weren't just characters in a game. They were part of a universe I desperately wanted to escape to.
Coming back and playing this game again after so long, what struck me is how enjoyable it is today. It's impossible for me to completely remove my nostalgia goggles for a game as important to me as this, but I can confidently recommend this game to anyone who's remotely interested in it. And I hope some father boots up this game with his son and shares this amazing experience with him.

As to be expected, the DLC characters have beefier stats than the base characters. This is simply because if there was no true incentive to buy the DLC, then there would be no need to stray from the free characters you get in the first place.
This happens all the times in games with DLC characters such as League of Legends. However, League of Legends demand for a new character is often due to his/her new and unique playstyle rather than pure stats. You can still very much outplay some one with a DLC character but they have more leeway with making mistakes and their stats. However, even talking with some experienced players in the top 100, they say their stats are unbalanced but can still be overcome.
This goes back to the first issue however. If a more advanced players uses a DLC character, they have the advantage of the stats and skill over just skill itself as it should be.
This is a minor issue to be honest but an issue non the less.
Unlike a lot of other games, this game hosts games VIA Peer to Peer server hosting, or client to client hosting.
A majority of my games are met with having 400-600 ping (On average, even connecting to someone in the UK from California, I'll have 80 ping at the most!!) and if the host is on the other team, his moves will register just fine while yours will have a delay. This makes skill shot characters almost useless. Some people as hosts can abuse this with something called Lag Switching: A simple program you can set up to purposely put a heavier load on your Modem, giving you higher latency.
Also on the rise recently, I have been in a few games that a host has forced others to disconnect through a hangup program or a DDP (Direct Distruption Program) that forces other IPs or connections to disconnect from them (The Host). Ironically, these are the games I have had the best ping with (24-50). I have reported both cases and one has resulted in a VAC ban so at least this problem is being taken care of... at a snail's pace.
This ONLY happens with a Client Side hosting system such as in this game. These hackers would haft to DDoS them which is more difficult to do if the game had its own servers.

Idle Champions (and Crusaders of the Lost Idols) are one of the most unique idle games I have played. I definitely enjoy idle games and this game adds many features that other games like it don't have allowing for each player to play differently and still get to the same objective. Each player has the ability to place their heroes into different spots within a formation to increase their dps, gold find, etc and the gear that you get for each hero can also play a role in which ones you choose. This allows for more variation between resets. Also instead of continuously resetting and replaying the same exact game loop, Idle Champions uses objectives that alter formation structure and gameplay. This variation  adds more content to keep you engaged.
Also, let's not forget that it's a Dungeons and Dragons idle game!!! My two favorite things! XD
The devs based it off of the D&D 5e system, so grab your monster manual.. It may just save your life. :P
Yes, this is an idle/clicker game so if you have never played one before you may want to see what you are getting yourself into. I have easily played (not including idle time) over 10,000 hours of idle games in my lifetime. This genre of games definitely leave you wanting more.
I began playing Idle Champions while it was in closed alpha where I could see how much the developers care and worked to make the game. They continually work with the community to design new and interesting updates allowing for a nice change in meta. The developers are always around in chat talking and helping out fellow players!
Idle Champions defintely has the potential to one of the best idle/clicker games I have ever played/seen. At this time, it is currently in early access and many components of the game have not been implemented yet, but with the developers who are constantly working with the community to help make the game the best it can be I definitely have high hopes.
If you have not yet, I highly recommend getting Idle Champions!

Requires love for the sport.

This game and the entire FM series is fantastic. It is something of an outlier in gaming. It's for a semi-niche, if not very niche, audience, But if you are that audience, then this is one of the best franchises in existence.
Do you like football/soccer?
Do you like Microsoft Excel?
Then FM is for you!
Seriously though, you need to be really into staring at stats and numbers. You also need to be really into tactics. I actually have never understood people who download workshop tactics, since that's like, a major portion of the game. And to get the most out of this game, you need to be an anal retentive micro manager. Sure, you can delegate things to staff, but I've always been a "Handle all tasks myself" guy.
If you have never played FM, you might spend a given hour of playtime doing anything from chastising your U-18s for not training hard enough, to negotiating contracts, to forecasting how you'll meet the homegrown quota next year now that you've qualified for the UCL and making transfer notes for your next window. Oh and eventually you will manage some games.
There are many ways to watch your games. Personally, I don't use the full engine per say, as I watch all 90 minutes (at high speed) of every single game, but in 2D so I can see the team's shape better. I only watch the true graphical engine on goal replays. That's how I have done it for years.
Anyways, I suppose the true beauty of the game, is that it gets one very important thing right, which all great simulation games get right: it makes you feel like if you were the manager of the club, what you achieved in the game is what you could have done in real life. So, yes, if they had appointed me at Newcastle United this season, in 2019 we would have blitzed Bayern in a UCL semi-final 6-0 with our brilliant tiki-taka possession play.
Obviously that's not true, but the game will make you feel like it is. I'll actually brag to my wife (I cannot begin to tell you how little she cares) about some games I win. I yell at the little dots on my screen like they are real people during the games.
Finally, for everyone who gives negative reviews based on the "it's the same as last year" argument - yes, it is. And that is a good thing. I only require my FM to be a little bit better each year. If the game stayed exactly the same I would buy it every year anyways just for the updated official database.
Anyways, thousands and thousands of hours across FM games for many years, just thought I should finally leave a review.

First, this game is absolutely gorgeous on Ultra settings. I can't count the amount of times I was completely blown away by the different settings you make your way through. From dark and dismal forests, to the streets of Rome, to the assault on the shores of Britain, the game does not skimp on visual detail.
Sadly the combat is incredibly basic with no depth, the entire game is a very long quick time event. Mash X for light attacks, Y for heavy attacks, A for dodgeroll, or B for stun followed by a QTE to kill them. That's it. The bosses in the game aren't hard and the patterns for beating them are recognized and mastered very quickly but good god if you don't have to muster through a solid 5-10 minutes of the same boring pattern with marginal mixups. It's a mindless button-mashing fest but I managed to have fun with it overall.
The Co-op horde-esque modes are mindless fun with a friend but don't have a lot of staying power. I feel I got as much out of it as I could in around 2 hours and haven't felt the need to really go back to it.
The story is very bare bones and you see the resolution coming from a mile away. I think I beat the main story at around 6 hours or so.
Overall the game is an amazing visual experience but not much else. I'd recommend picking it up when it's heavily on sale, I think I paid $10 USD and was happy with it, otherwise I can't recommend it for the full price.

BEST EVER PROGRAM

Substance Painter is quite simply the best texturing software available right now.
Easy to use, fast and highly customizable. Plus, it's a really good baking tool too.

Well.... I think it’s the best, for me atleast. That's the thing about opinions, they are all subjective and unless you do a case study with like 10,000 people it’s all just personal opinions based on your past experiences which can be said for just about any kind of product or brand ever. Base line: Whatever works, works.
Now I've used a lot of different Painting/ Texturing/ Baking programs over my time, starting with basic stuff like photoshop, websites like CGTextures (now Textures. com) for Texture sourcing and xNormals for baking different High to Low geometry maps. When PBR came around programs like Quixels nDo 2 & dDo came out first and yeah they are still neck and neck with Substance Painter in terms of functionality and power. I used Substance Painter 1 for 32 hours, textured a few assets but was not really impressed as I was already using dDo which as I understood better thus going back to dDo rendered me better results.
In Comes Substance Painter 2 and I thought to myself "ok, let’s give it a real shot this time around" 150 hours and atleast 20-30 textured assets later it’s my program of choice right now. I've gone back to dDo every once in a while for specific assets and just to brush up but Substance Painter 2 is my go-to tool. Not only for PBR Painting either! There baking tools are flawless and I'm getting better results using the inbuilt baking tool with less errors then I would with xNormals which was unexpected as xNormals has been the industry standard for a long while.
On to the main features though, The Texture Painting. Defiantly the most powerful of all software’s I've used. PBR Materials & Smart Materials are a great base to work from and provide a lot of different filters, masks and affects you can alter to your liking or add/create from scratch. Everything works in layers like photoshop with masks that you can also edit directly with brushes without having to go back and forth like dDo. You can even undo your mask changes! CRAZY RIGHT.
You can create normal map decals in photoshop and import them into substance to then paint directly onto your mesh in 3D or 2D views. There are a few different particle brushes which give some nice but sometimes unexpected results that might not work as you expect depending on the asset, its size and both mesh/normal map angles. The Normal map painting works as expected, you set your decal, scale it and add where you want. Works great, good for adding lots of quick details really quick that would normally take a long time to do in 3D modelling.
Some of the achievements are still bugged and have been since Painter 1 was released. Secondly the software is so damn stable I can't even do the report bugs achievement unless I just send them messages like "hey, your program is pretty neat. Keep it up ;)"
If you are going to add achievements to your product because steam offers the support for them please make them atleast function... Yes this might not be considered a game but as both and artist and a gamer I try to get the most out of my products, achievements included.

Update May 2017: Substance Painter will no longer receive regular updates, but transfer to a $75 a year subscription model for "Indie Licence" holders. This makes the lack of comprehensive UDIM support all the more disagreeable and makes this a 'Not recommended' for people who are not making their own models.
Original review:
Pretty solid; it takes a couple of hours to get to grips with, but has a lot of functionality. It's probably not going to be your one-stop solution to all your texturing needs, but it goes a long way. There could always be more materials, bruses, generators, tools, and the like but the standard package is a good place to start.
However - if you are going to be working with existing models that you cannot alter (in case of modding, rendering etc.) you will inevitably run in to the severely lacking UDIM support, lacking support for multiple textures per model, etc. In that case, Substance Painter is very hit or miss, and will probably not be a reliable part of your workflow.
Get everything that has "Allegorithmic" mark on it.
Even you are newbie, you can make great things by great tutorials. it is Unity 3D friendly like other substance products.

First things first: A very, very big THANK YOU to Allegorithmic! It isn't an exaggeration to say that I couldn't function without Substance Painter 2, and imho, the world's a better place because this software exists.
Next: my usage time isn't accurate. I used the trial version for the entire 1-month time period; then, I purchased the Indie pack (SP, SD, B2M3), used that for however many hours I've clocked on my Steam account. Then, I downloaded the 2.3.0 standalone version from the Allegorithmic website because I want to control which version I use, and Steam forces you to use the latest version, which isn't good under a controlled workflow. So, I've used SP2 religiously for the last five'ish months.
When I first used SP2, I didn't like it. There was not at all wrong with it, I just hadn't taken the time to learn how to use it (wanted instant results, zero effort, but reality doesn't work that way). A learning curve exists, but it is minimal. It was mostly down me not having a clear picture in my head of what I was aiming at, and without that clarity, I ended up bumbling around for a few weeks (whilst the software patiently humoured my attempts at 'art').
Computer specs: Intel i7-4770 @ 3.4 GHz, 16GB RAM, Windows 7 Pro 64 bit SP1, non-SSD drives. My GPU is a single NVIDIA GTX760 with 2GB of VRAM, and it's fine with SP2 (granted, after using countless multi-channel layers on a model, SP2 does slow down, which is a no-brainer on a two-year-old GPU running industry standard software).
I could re-hash the praise of other reviewers, but I think it all boils down to this: if you are a 3D artist, buy this software, watch all the SP2 tutorials on YouTube, then take the time to learn the software (unless you're a pro, learning SP2 will not happen overnight).
Everything ever made is limited. The trick is to learn those limits, and then how to work around them.
11/10: would totally rant on Steam again about software I love :)

Completely recommend. I am a long time ARK: Survival Evolved player, and have been playing Survival of the Fittest since before the standalone release. I can say definitively, this is one of my favorite competitive games for the time being.
What this game is, in summary: Hunger Games configuration with crafting, hunting, gathering, and most importantly, taming and riding wild dinosaurs.
You will start by decending from the sky onto a ring that is raised off the rest of the map. Here, you have two options - run for the center and hope to get lucky with the many boxes that spawn there at the beginning, or head straight into the wild.
Once in the wild, you will attempt to craft yourself armor, weapons, tranquilizing arrows, and perhaps shelter, all while being hunted by the other players. Over time, the map will get smaller, forcing the remaining players to the middle for a battle royale.
The Good:
-Quick games (1/2 player tribe options)
-Variable play styles (relatively balanced)
-No "pay to win" mechanic (everyone starts the round exactly the same, except cosmetically)
-Ranked system
-Dinosaurs!
The Bad:
-Still needs better optimization (runs fine on my computer, though I turn almost every setting to low to be more competitive with no ground clutter and the like)
