If you are fan of games like Final Fantasy (Sakaguchi era), Legend of Zelda or Dragon Quest and you would like to take few hours and reminisce about these gaming gems Evoland is the game you want to play.
Main essence of this game is unlocking various upgrades for the game itself. So instead of finding a treasure with new equipment you might find a new view perspective or resolution upgrade. Other than that Evoland is constantly switching it's gameplay mechanics between Zelda-like adventure and classic turn-based JRPG with a few minigames and puzzles here and there. Lore of the game is not so original yet interesting and fun. The story, characters and locations are all paying an ultimate homage to the Zelda and Final Fantasy (VI and VII) games and everything is presented in very genuine and entertaining way. If you haven't played any of those games I wouldn't recommend the game to you since the references are main source of amusement for players.
Gameplay is very casual and the game takes between 4-6 hours to beat and complete so don't expect to get engulfed to the long story with evolving characters. This game is no way an RPG on it's own. But if you don't have the time to go through those old Japanese masterpieces again but you want to bring up some quick nostalgia - pick up Evoland.

Awesomenauts,
A fun, casual & cartoonish MOBA that is a blast to play alone and even better with friends. However, the game has a few MAJOR flaws that almost ruin the entire game and cannot be ignored.
Cons:
-	LOW player base. In a game which is entirely against online players it literally becomes unplayable in non-peak times.
-	NO dedicated servers. Causes many lag problems which is further complicated by the game being advantageous towards higher ping.
-	UNBALANCED. Many balancing problems, especially every time a DLC is released. Also bad map designs and other problems such as snowballing.
-	LATE JOINING. Yes, you heard me right, it is very possible to join a game literally seconds before your team loses.
-	All the above problems have turned a once polite player base to salt.
Pros:
-	When you actually find a game with reasonable ping and non-salty players it can be quite enjoyable.
-	Interesting cast of Nauts, no two are the same.
-	Music and voice lines are very entertaining and enjoyable.
-	Lots of replay-ability, assuming of course you can actually find games.
Verdict:
A fun, interesting game brought down some rather large problems should have been resolved YEARS ago. If they made the game free and upped the price of DLC the player base would grow and solve the most major problem of being unable to play the game.
I cannot recommend this game in it's current state although with a few small changes they could fix the large problems and create a more "awesome" game.
Worth getting on sale or if it does go free, if you are in any way serious about MOBAs steer clear.

In The Magic Circle you’re a playtester of a game that’s been in development for 20 years, with no end in sight. The project director seems out of touch with the people he works with, as their conversations break down into drama and backstabbing, with no consensus on what the game should be. The project has become the most important thing in his life, but he can’t decide on what it’s supposed to be. Over the long development a part of the game seems to have gained sentience, and wants you the player to take over and finish the game yourself.
You explore an unfinished world, full of half done or abandoned designs, reaching back to the early 90s. The older designs look like System Shock 1, while the new one is a fantasy adventure. You solve puzzles by capturing creatures and objects, and modifying their properties. Even though the game is broken, your method of interacting with it is quite nice! This game was made by Jordan Thomas, best known for making The Cradle in Thief 3, Fort Frolic in Bioshock, and then as Creative Designer on Bioshock 2. By now he knows how to make a game, and The Magic Circle feels like a game made by an expert. There’s no newbie design mistakes, and the game does all it can to make the experience as smooth as possible, without sacrificing complexity. There’s often several solutions to puzzles, so you’re unlikely to get stuck anywhere.
To make a game as meta as this requires the developers be smarty pants. And so they were, invoking authenticity in all the dialog and notes you come across. The references in the game clearly come from Looking Glass, Irrational Games, Ion Storm, and Origin. The closest comparison to this would be The Stanley Parable and Portal 2, but it’s more ambitious than either of them. It only dawned on me after I’d finished it just how much this games does, and how well it succeeds in all it tries to do. If you like to read behind the scenes stuff about game development, The Magic Circle will be a treat.
While the game is fun in many ways (Stanley Parable kind), the overall amount of gameplay is very little.

Endless Legend is an interesting beast, in many ways.
First of all, each faction is unique. If you're used to Civilization factions, which have maybe a unique unit or two and some kind of resource boost, you may have to take some time to readjust.
Each faction has powers and mechanics that render them VERY different from each other. For example, one faction relies entirely on money for its population growth. Another has such diplomatic mastery that it can force treaties through. One can only build one city, and relies on converting minor factions for resources and military.
Secondly, the seasons. While writing this I only have the Guardians expansion installed, and there's another expansion that deals with seasons, so keep that in mind.
Auriga has two seasons: summer and winter. At first, winter is simply a minor inconvenience, lowering resource production and movement for a few turns. However, Auriga is a dying world, and winter comes more and more frequently as the game drags on, and becomes more and more harsh.
Preparing for winter becomes incredibly important, as an empire that does not have the proper means of dealing with it will fall behind.
While I mainly find winter to be a bit of a nuisance, grinding the game to a halt when it gets bad, it does offer a lot of strategic depth to the game.
Then there's combat. I honestly find the system a bit unwieldly, and recommend simply using auto-resolve for fights, but there's certainly room for tactics if one wishes it. Overall, however, it is much more important to keep your armies up to date and packed with the right units to counter your opponents.
4X is generally about macro more than micro.
Heroes. You start with one, they help your armies out, some locations require them to be interacted with. But don't just storm off exploring! Consider setting your hero up as governor of a city, gaining experience every turn and providing benefits. Come winter, you'll be glad to have one to keep your city from becoming completely snowed in.
Then there's quests. These can be ignored if you want to, but each faction has a story to explore, and minor quests crop up all over the map. Quests do grant you valuable resources and items, so they're definitely worth pursuing if you can spare the units.
Lastly, city building. Alright, listen up, this is important: you expand you city by building burroughs. Any tiles adjacent to or under a burrough grants you its listed income of science, food, industry, dust(money), and influence. But you don't want to stretch your city out too much, because tightly built cities get bonuses. So, when settling, judging your options for expansion is important.
Furthermore, the strategic resources available depend on the region you settle in, rather than proximity to your city. As long as the resource is within the regional border, you can build an extractor on it.
Overall, this game is a great little timesink, and one I recommend for fans of the genre. It looks great, sounds great, and plays great. Just be aware that it's not a game that ends quickly.

1. The collectible card system runs on the Coupon Collector's Dilemma. When I pointed this out to developers, the response I got was basically, "it's optional; people don't *have* to do it." Which is accurate, but a cynical approach to the idea of cultivating a loyal fandom.
2. At one point, the Cortex was getting regular updates. Currently, my feed is showing the "latest news" was back in September. I've seen a few additional posts outside the Cortex. Maybe they've abandoned that in favor of their Facebook Feed. Which negates the whole idea of the BDH drive (which was supposed to be the "inside track" for in game news and updates.)
3. It's been years since this game was announced. But, like George RR Martin books, the release dates are vague and keep getting moved. I'm no longer confident it will be released.
So, I don't think it's unreasonable of me, at this time, to be disappointed and disillusioned. Your opinion may differ. Which is fine. You can keep waiting for that train.

If you don't like 4X games, this probably wouldn't be the game to change your mind, but it's a delightful entry into the genre with an exceedingly well-designed UI overlaying a veritable trove of imagination.
Strange as it may sound, I'd put the UI as the standout feature of the game; other studios really should pay attention to just how well designed and thought through it is.
The game itself is a 4X with a few twists to the genre: RPG-lite elements for heroes; tactical combat; quests to find and complete; winter rolling around every so often, and so on.  The factions are also something of a star feature.  They don't have the writing behind them that the SMAC factions did, but mechanically and visually, they're much more diverse than the SMAC factions ever were.  City building is much more interesting than in Civ and most other 4Xs, but it seems that Civ6 is copying the city expansion system from this game.
Combat's a mixed bag; it can be quite frustrating, at least until you learn how it all works, and then becomes rather too easy.  Of course, on higher difficulties, that gets balanced out a bit, but I'd still put the combat as a weak spot.  On the other hand, it's still enormously more satisfying than combat in Civ
The artwork is reasonably polished with a highly coherent aesthetic, but looking through other reviews, it's clear the aesthetic is not to everyone's taste.  Personally I like it, and find it gets across all the information I need to understand things very well.
One annoyance is, well, it's a sci-fi fantasy, and that means it comes with strange names for resources.  Gold?  Makes you richer, yes.  Spices, inmproves food production, of course. Pixie Blood?  I guess I know what that is, but I've no idea what it would be useful for just from the name.  Palladian?  Huh, what?  This comes with the territory I guess, but is still much less clear than mechanically equivalent resources in less exotic games.
All in all, this is well worth the asking price and is exceedingly well-designed.

Just finished playing, and all I can say: amazing.
First, the characters: fantastic job, both in the writing and the delivery. Stephen Russel, especially, is a joy to listen to (which is great as you'll hear plenty of him), bringin his near-trademark "no-nonsense down-to-earth" style to his role. Regardless,
The writing, too, is great, with each character's dialogue showing enough content to give me a sense of their basic motivations (creator wants to make the game perfect, lead actress wants the thing to be over with and move on, etc), but as you play, you find enough information to elivate them from *just* characitures and sterotypes into actual people. In the end, I found myself fealing sorry for the villian of the piece despite him having brought it on himself.
Second, the gameplay: It's a nice twist on puzzle gaming (for the most part) where you're going around rewriting and editing the world around you - in a very literal fashion - to suit your wims. This gives all the puzzles a very non-linear feal, giving me the real sense that I could find new answers to every puzzle I faced.
Not that these are "puzzles" in the traditional sense, no no no - no Hanoi Towers here. Similar to the likes of Myst, this game uses the world itself as your obstacle, with your motivation being exploration and self-challenge. All too often, I would just sit there, wracking my brain over how to use what I'd collected so far to get across some barrier to the goodie that awaited me.
Third, the gmae's style: even though the point is that the game is very "unfinished", I actually do like the black-and-white overall theme of everything. It makes the use of what sparse color there is in the game VERY striking, even jarring, which is exactly what the creative team probably wanted.
Of course, the style of "unfinished" extends everywhere, from the creatures you meet all the way to the music itself, which somehow manages to sound great despite the composer/sound designers intentionally flubbing their parts to make it sound very rough draft.
The humor's good, too. I found myself laughing at several moments in the game, when I wasn't ♥♥♥♥ling with glee, at any rate. And the subtlties of this game's story are near critical mass. I won't spoil them for you save to say this: collect everything you can. Leave no stone untunred, mess with everything you get access to, and explore all those hard-to-reach and out-of-the-way places. You will find the effort well worth it.
This game does have some flaws. The end game puzzle, while EXTREMELY satisfying, felt a bit buggy - and funnily enough, that's not intentional here. Too often, I'd be unable to take some actions because the game wouldn't let me despite my having what I needed to do so. If it's not a bug, then I would recommend some better indication of what it takes to use things properly here, to avoid needless confusion.
Is the game short? Sure, I beat it in 7 hours without 100%ing it, and I imagine it would take about 10 for me to get what I missed. But that's not a bad thing here, as it's not about qunatity, but quality. This game is as long as it needs to be. No more, no less, and for that, it's extremely satisfying without being daunting.
I recommend this to anyone who's interested in the game industry in any capacity besides just "but game, play game, trade it back in", especially to those who are looking for some snark and fun gameplay to go with thei commentary.
And to answer the creators' urging at the end of this game: yes, I'm interested in making something of my own now. What form that will be is unclear. But the spark has been lit.

I have now completed this game and have no intent of playing it again for a while.
Considering its length I am glad I bought it on sale.
However, the contents within this package (wrapped between two Kojima-length cutscenes) are quite good.
We have a small sandbox consisting of a military base one could sneak around in for days, unlocking all the weapons and finding all the little details. But that does not really interest me.
The story is short and simple; sneak around and complete some objectives + listen to overdone dialogue. Which is quite enjoyable, since the stealthing is well done and the AI dumb/smart enough to facilitate getting away with being caught unless you're dumb enough to trigger all of them at once. ..or so I thought until I successfully attempted running across a fully lit parking lot with 10 guys firing at me, with a hostage on my back, and surviving.
The graphics are approaching too good to be true (at least for my obsolete graphics card), and seamlessly switch from cutscene to gameplay. The game also runs smoother than diarrhea. I played on pretty high settings and had no frame dropping what-so-ever. Thumbs up for that.
If you don't thing you'd enjoy what's basically a proof-of-concept, wait for METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN TRADEMARK VERY SUBTLE TRAILER AT THE END OF THIS GAME. As for me, I think it would be cool to see this foundation fleshed out in a full game. You got me sold on The Phantom Pain, Kojima. But you don't got me sold on another short proof-of-concept game.

Gameplay Elements
Story:
Starting off, the story in the game is pretty middle of the road. If you are particularly fond of revenge stories with predictable plot points you will enjoy the story of this game.
I, however, prefer a little bit deeper of a story. With all of the money they spent on making the game GORGEOUS, I feel like some of that portion of the budget could have been put to better use in the writer's room.
The best moment in the story is when you realize that the red liquid pouring from the eyes of the statue in the opening cinematic is from Nero's son.
The consistency of the story isn't really great in it's elements. Early on in the game the protagonist Marius tells Nero that the gods don't care about taking an active interest in the world of men, and then proceeds to witness the gods taking an active interest in the world of men. It is especially frustrating because the opening actually follows after the events of the storyline.
With the poor execution of the combat system(get to that soon) the game could have been at it's strongest if it was more story oriented. It tells a frequently turned out tale, without any room for customization or player choice or freedom. It feels as though someone on the development team played through one of the TellTale games, and thought it would be cool to make a story based game with none of the choices.
Combat:
Without a doubt the weakest part of the game, in my opinion. I played the game on the toughest difficulty they allow you on your first playthrough, but it seems like an artificial difficulty increase. The enemies themselves are not very tough, mostly it is the clunkiness of combat and the inoptimization of the system that makes it tough. The animations are repetitive to the point where you always know what mouse button to press to get a perfect execution, and very little variation to enemy types.
When you press a key that isn't your left or right mouse button, your character stops and spins his sword in his hand, which would be 90s action movie cool, if it didn't get you killed all the time. If you go to pick up some spears from the ground so you can fight off some archers, you better do it at just the right angle or you will be standing there spinning your sword around while you turn into a ♥♥♥♥ing pincushion. Attempting to jump down ledges also causes some good ol' pincushioning at time too.
The game follows your standard Assassin's Creed or Arkham Batman style combat, where you stand amongst a group of enemies and you wait to press space bar in order to block and counter attack the enemy. It is not difficult to master, but the system is, as mentioned, not quite intuitive either. Subpar to most other hacknslash wave of enemy games out there.
The "skill tree" offers very little in any true rpg elements even at the farthest stretches of the definition. It completely consists of % based increases on the monotonous nothingness that the combat system offers.
NO KEYREBINDING, WHICH IS A MUST HAVE IN THIS DAY AND AGE.
Aesthetics:
The game is beautiful, no doubt about it. Probably the strongest feature of the game is the visuals and the sound. The music is excellent, and the voice acting is very strong. Other things to consider:
I am unsure about other people, but I have a pretty high end rig, and this game constantly froze up on me. Sometimes the game would stall and the sound would loop for a good 5 minutes before returning to normal, if at all. After exactly 17 of these experiences and a bunch of troubleshooting, I realized it wasn't anything on my end. I could not figure out how to solve the problem. So, even though it persisted, I trudged onward.
I played this through family sharing with a buddy of mine. If this game is one that you think you would enjoy, I would advise not paying more than 4.99 for it. If you can help it, use family sharing to bum it off someone else's library so you don't need to spend the cash.
At the end of the game, I can honestly say my favorite part was the revelation of the statue's bloody tears. Other than that, it is very forgettable. Plagued with crashes and freeze ups, as well as very lackluster story and combat mechanics I can't say I am surprised at how far Crytech has fallen in recent years. It is a shame to behold, given how fantastic Crysis 1 and 2 were, as well as the original Far Cry.
I tried to be as objective as possible, but honestly it boggles my mind how the game has so many positive reviews.
Thanks for taking the time to read, I hope this review helps you make an informed decision on whether or not this game is worth playing.

Right. Out of curiosity, I spent an hour reading the reviews of FM17. Most of them are downright pathetic and are filled with total BS. As you can see, I’ve spent quite a lot of time playing this year’s game. Is it perfect? No, but show me a video game (especially a sports one) that is. If you want an honest and genuine review, keep reading.
Let’s get this out of the way; I’m not a fanboy. For what it’s worth, I wasn’t a fan of FM16 alright? So put the ‘I was payed to type this’ theory away.
Let’s start with the match engine. Is it pretty? Heck no, but that’s not the focus of this game. If you want a game that looks pretty, go play PES or FIFA. These two games cannot be compared to FM. They’re totally different, obviously, so if a review compares them, automatically disregard it. The major focus of FM is coding the variables that determine matches, player interactions, player development, and so on. So please, spare me with the graphics complaints.
Football Manager is meant for the addicts. The diehards. The football obsessive. The people who know the game and how it works. 99% of the negative reviews are filled with people who basically don’t have a friggen clue about football manager. I won’t call them noobs because it sounds trashy, but these people haven’t spent enough time to really understand the game and how it works. They see black and white. For example, I saw someone complain that they received 40 million at Arsenal and that it isn’t even enough to buy a decent CB. Reality check: you can get about 4 or 5 if you know anything about the game. These people expect that because they’re a big club, everything should be easy and straightforward.
Another frequent complaint is that they always lose when they’re the better side. Admittedly, almost every game I lose in my saves are undeserved, but that’s because my teams are really good and rarely get smashed. You can’t win every game. This season (in reality), Liverpool were 3-1 up at Bournemouth in the 64th minute. Bournemouth roared back and won 4-3 on a last minute goal. The evidence is there. Your team will bottle games. It happens. If you’re a good player, you know how to bounce back and not let this frustrate you. The people who complain feel like they should automatically win every game against a weaker opponent. Don’t fall for the BS. It’s not the game’s fault. It’s the players who don’t get it and the players who whine and complain when they are the problem the entire time. Notice how they blame the game for everything and that it’s never their fault.
Now, as an experienced player and an addict, I’ve came across some strange things that I find odd. For example, I’ve noticed that after I win a match with the score line of 4-0, my teams struggle in the next 3-4 games and rarely win. It’s strange and hence why I say the game isn’t perfect. But you know what? I look for ways to get around it instead of raging and calling the game ‘bad’ or ‘stupid’. Another thing that frustrates me is that when I’m playing in a playoff final at Wembley, many of my key players have left for international duty and are ineligible. Again, I’ve realized this is my fault, as I have the option to block them from leaving when I receive the “players chosen for international duty” e-mail. However, I would like game to realize that these players are in a final and block their move automatically. My complaints are small and reasonable. People calling the game ‘dumb’ and ‘stupid’ and criticizing everything are pathetic. I hope SI don’t cave in to the basic casual players and stick to their target audience: the people who learn from mistakes and figure out how to build a squad and how to build the best tactic. The addicts. The diehards. Not the babies that expect to win every game.
(EDIT): Upon reflection, I've noticed that this is mainly a rant against awful and laughable reviews based on pathetic reasons rather than an actual game review. Is this game perfect? Again, No, but the problems people cite as legitmate reasons caused SOLELY by the game are flat out false (see the Arsenal example above).
Undeserved losses are incredibly tough to swallow especially if they cost you a cup final or the league....I...I don't want to talk about it.
We've all been there. We rant at our computer screens multiple times. "How tf do they have 2 shots on target and 2 goals while we have 10 shots on target and can't even get a friggen highlight?" The mouse goes flying across the room. Your day is ruined. The whole nine right?
Take it from me. As someone who lead Tenerife to a quintople, won the champions league, had a player win back-to-back player of the year awards all while using the best tactic I've ever built and used, there is a solution to almost every problem in FM.
If you lose a game undeservingly, it generally means 2 things.
1. Your team is actually really good and will hardly ever get smashed. Not everyone can be the invincibles, so the losses will pretty much be all undeserved.
2. Something in your tactics is off. It's up to you to figure out what it is. It could be a striker in a slump, your backline is too deep or too high, you don't instruct your players to close down wingers to stop crosses, etc.
It just seems to me that the people who can't accept blame go to the reviews and blast everything about the game. If you're debating about wether to buy the game or not, my best advice would be to go on YouTube to find a more detailed review. Not in these Steam reviews where people take out their frustration and complain about crazy things.

A short but sweet love letter to the RPGs you grew up with... assuming you grew up playing RPGs primarily in the late 80s to early 00s. I fear a lot of the game's more clever moments might be lost on anyone outside of that age group, but I'd recommend it nonetheless... so long as you've at least played Final Fantasy VII, haha.
It's clunky at times, combat is often dull and just there to be there, but when the game has a good idea it's usually a great idea. I don't want to say too much, but one dungeon threw me a curve I was absolutely not expecting and I loved every minute of it.
Standout points to me: the game's absolutely gorgeous 3D art, as it evolves through various styles reminiscent of 32-bit RPGs, to something more Dreamcast/PS2-like in its conclusion, and a very clever, very satisfying final boss battle that reminded me more than a little of Brave Fencer Musashi in some ways.

Evoland is a fun game for those who have roots and a deep love for JRPGs. It cleverly starts off from the 'dark ages', in 8-bit, allowing only the most basic movement. It, however, eventually becomes an action RPG with elements of the classic, turn-based RPG. It even has a card game VERY similar to Triple Triad. I will say one negative thing about this game. Though I am recommending it, people who aren't huge fans or have deep roots of the genre, be wary. The game is very short and, unless you enjoy this kind of genre, will feel lacking and making you want more.

I love Dungeons and Dragons and Forgotten Realms, but unfortunately this game currently fails to deliver pretty much everywhere:
- Story: it's next to non-existent, which is dramatic since this game is a clicker and it should be all about the story. Most successful clickers offer other kind of eye rewards (mainly naked ladies), but since you cannot stick naked elves in a d&d game you would AT least expect a good story..

- Balance: If you are a fanboy and you play JUST because there is your favorite Forgotten Realms hero you'll be sorely disappointed. After you unlock most of heroes only a handful prove to be useful in the formation DPS. Most of heroes just buff others to do more damage and you end up having only ONE hero (currently Minsc)  doing 95% of the party damage. So sad. Heroes who don't buff end up doing 1-2% of damage even if they are supposed to be powerful characters, like Jarlaxle.
Idle Champions of Forgotten Realms fail when D&D needed the most a good videogame. You cannot keep living of the enhanced versions of old games like Baldur's Gate. You need something new, but WotC is incapable to strike a good deal with a game house even after the failure of Sword Coast Legends. You would believe they would learn from their mistakes. Instead they invested into an idle clicker when people craved for a 5e turn based rpg.. And this idle clicker is probably one of the worst of its kind.

The Firefly Online Cortex was a nice distraction, for a time.
Intended as a companion app for the forthcoming release of Firefly Online.
There are some nice banjo tunes, reminiscient of the Firefly series.
You're given the opportunity to spent some money, in support of
the team, developing Firefly Online. For 5$ you'll get to be a
"Big Damn Hero".
Sounds shiny. For your money, you'll be able the access a devblog,
which has rather been neglected, if not desserted. When there is
a post, its saddly more fluff, than any real information.
Also you'll get access to a map of 'The Verse', where you are able
to do Trade Runs. Meaning clicking on three planets on the map,
to get a loot box. In this box are cards, with pictures from the series.
Collecting these cards rewards you some in-game fluff for the game.
One run gets you 50 Brownie Points, the in-app currency. The random
generator hates everyone the same, as the devs pointed out. So you
can get as high as 500.000 Brownie Points, or higher, and still be
left wanting for some cards, to finish your set.
But you'll also presented with the oppurtunity to buy card packs,
in different price categories. If you're easy to be enraged, you
should be careful, as these packs also can tend to give you
duplicates of cards you'll already have.
The game, Firefly Online, for which this is the companion app,
has been delayed, from a release in 2013, to 2014 and has now
been stated to be back in alpha stages. Beta TBA. Release TBA.
As mentioned, the APP is a nice distraction, no harm in trying it
out, or even spending the 5$, if you're not expecting too much.
The official, and only, channel of communication from the Devs,
is their Facebook page. The page is managed by a 'community
manager', not related to the development process, posting
in-character as a Ship's Mech, which may be entertaining
for the first dozen posts of mostly evasive nature.
There has been some unrest, whether the devs are capable of
finishing what they started. Support tickets are going unanswered
for months. Inconvenient threads and posts encountered a
tendency to be deleted. If this is still the case, or has
changed, due to backlash, I'm not able to say, as I ceased
visiting the page. Facebook as official channel is another thing.
This review is a thumbs down, as for the way communication and the
'transparent development' is handled by Spark Plug Interactive and QMx.
As of August 2014 all official channels of information have been closed
down, or are laying bare. The official page is down. The publisher, Qmx,
is not listing the Firefly Online project anymore on their company page.
Inquiries about FFO are completely ignored from the publisher side.
The developer, SPG, has been confirmed to state, that they are
not allowed to comment on the situation. There have been
several attempts by people to contact Fox for comment, but
to no avail. Which is maybe not all too surprising, looking at the
track record of Fox and their handling of the Firefly Franchise.
More and more, Qmx gives the impression to be not much
better than Fox. There have been a growing number of folks
stating, that there is a blatant disregard for their customers.
Also, the deletion of critical inquiries have been reported.
While still maintaining hope, one might say, it is
looking rather dim.

I initially posted a negative review of this, but I dislike the idea of leaving a negative on a free game that isn't offensive in some way. The STEAM review system is really weak unless you absolutely love or despise a game, and there are many games that are perfectly fine, but just don't keep my interest. Sometimes it's the game's fault, sometime it's mine, and sometimes it's just a mismatch in tastes.
This game falls into that last category. I really like the idea of idle / offline play in an RPG, but I'm wanting to find one that's serious in style, that combines idle gameplay with a strong story. This game was too casual for me. It's cartoony, mostly silly, and makes little pretense at telling an actual story; you just fight through a series of screens that are only connected by the loosest of narrative until you defeat the last boss, at which point your party is reset for the next leg of the adventure.
It's not to my taste, but there's a fair amount of depth and attention to detail, and it delivers what it promises in the teaser videos. It's a fine casual game. All those things deserve a thumbs-up, so I'm giving one and moving on. Best of luck to the Devs.

As someone who has never dug into an idle game before, but someone who is madly in love with the D&D brand, Idle Champions is an amazing game for what it's worth. The gamplay is simple, but stylish - you control a party of D&D characters, most of which are historic figures from the game's Forgotten Realms campaign setting, and some of whom are tie-ins for an ongoing D&D webseries known as Force Grey. The party starts with a single character, who attacks enemies as they pop up from the opposite side of the screen. Every enemy slain drops gold, and gold can be spent to upgrade your characters and add new ones to the party. You start with one character available to unlock, and each subsequent unlock grants you another character. You can also conserve your gold to skip ahead in the lineup, should you decide you don't want a particular character in your party.
Each time you upgrade a character, their stats increase multiplicatively. Every few levels (anywhere from 5-25 levels) they receive a bonus upgrade. The bonus upgrades are character-specific, very diverse, and eventually even branch off into multiple paths based on decisions you make as you select them. Some are flat damage increases for the character, some increase the damage of your entire party, and every character has an Ultimate ability that they unlock in the 50-100 range that deals a ton of damage on a long cooldown, usually including additional effects (like knocking targets back, fully healing your party, and stunning enemies to prevent them from moving or attacking).
You and your party march through hordes of monsters, moving forward or backward in stage levels as you kill them (usually in multiples of 25 kills per stage). There's a bit of strategy in sticking around a level to actively farm, but a lot of your money will come from your AFK time while the game is closed. After leveling and upgrading as desired, there are boss levels to fight at every 5th stage. The bosses are considerably tougher, but drop more money, as well as a bag that contains a variety of rewards. Boss stages are farmable as well, so if the first level of a new stage is too much for you you can backpedal and beat up bosses again to catch up to a better point.
Numbers scale like crazy in this game. For those who aren't familiar with idle games, you start by dealing about 20 damage a hit at the very first level, and there is generally no upper limit to how much damage you can put out (highest I've seen is in the quadrillions). Health and gold scale as proportionately, both ally and enemy. Each stage you progress makes the numbers climb higher and higher, and it can generally be very satisfying to watch characters scale out of control.
Finishing a quest (which is a bundle of stages) will give you gems (the cash shop currency) and divine favor (which is a bonus to the amount of gold you gain in subsequent quests). Your divine favor is based on how much money you earned during your quest, though it might not be advisable to spend too long farming if you're looking to be totally efficient in this game. Stacking lots of gold find does make the game easier on subsequent quests, and helps with that crazy numerical scaling mentioned earlier.
You can repeat finished quests, and finishing quests unlocks harder ones with restrictions and challenges that alter the playthrough. Repeating quests rewards Divine Favor, but the gem rewards seem to be once per quest (a shame, probably the only downside to the game really).
As mindless as it sounds, there's a lot of strategy and micromanagement to be had. The party's formation matters, as they're arranged in a rhombus-shape with multiple rows and columns. The rank and file of your party matters, as characters have both damage-boosting auras and effects like healing and shields. Your cleric needs to be adjacent as many people as possible to increase their damage, and anybody in the row in front of her is healed every few seconds. The bard has to be at least 2 rows from your frontline to give them temporary hit points when they're damaged. This is especially important during the midgame of most quests, as bosses tend to get so tough that they have to engage one of your champs, but with enough health, healing, and shields your frontline won't give to a boss. It's kind of hard to read all the buffs (they show up underneath the characters a little icons, and mousing over them gives a pop-up but it's unreliable and hard to read with so much going on on the screen), but arranging your party in the right formation and giving them the right buffs is essential to progression. The rogue wants the space ahead of him to be unoccupied, which means he needs to be up front, so make sure you have a suitable tank to help soak some of the damage he would take for being frontline (it's worth it, I promise).
Besides formation, the cash shop offers chests, which come in two varieties - silver chests, which occasionally drop from enemies and can be purchased with the gems earned from quests; And gold chests, which are purchased with real money and have substantially better rewards. Every chest drops 3(silver) or 5(gold) items that apply to champs you've unlocked, increasing their stats and improving their special abilities. Opening duplicates of the same item after the first increases the base item's effect by 1%, up to 10 times for a 105 increase. It remains to be seen if you can pull additional copies of equipment after pulling the 10th, but I'd hope not, as that'd make chests pretty poor to open after a point. Items come in a variety of rarities, and every champ has the same number of equipment slots. Equipment auto-improves as you find better stuff, and auto-equips when you first find it. Chests also contain items that can buff your party our your own capabilities (you have a self-clicker, but it's paltry and mostly unnecessary - only level it if you have money to spend but nobody to upgrade, it won't make much of a difference), and though they mostly serve as filler, you will probably find a use for them. I've yet to fill an inventory with them, so that's a good sign as to their efficacy.
---
All in all, f you've never played an idle game I don't know if I can recommend it just because it looks like a D&D game. It's unique in its execution, and the mechanics are great, but it only borrows as much of the D&D image as it can to make it appeal to longtime fans. The mechanics make for a great game, but somebody who's only played D&D since it came out in the mid-late 70's probably won't get as excited about it as I evidently am. Upper limits are a pipe dream in this game, you can invest or as much or as little time as you want and the game will do the rest. If you want to farm it out and upgrade your champs to the max, more power to you.
I can recommend it for everything else, though. I don't feel burdened into paying for gold chests with microtransactions (you can buy a single gold chest for 500 gems, which is inadvisable if you need to equip your party, but still provides an option after silver chests begin to fail you). I like watching my characters slam people for quadrillions of damage. I like clicking a button and watching an Ultimate ability decimate waves of enemies. I like picking whether or not I want Jarlaxle Baenrae or Minsc and Boo to join the party, or to level Bruenor Battlehammer up to level 500 (which might be the level cap? I've yet to hit it, but there's an achivement for doing so). I like that there's no immediate endgame, and that I can progress in the game by closing it and doing other things, then coming back to see how much AFK gold I earned. I like watching the numbers climb to ridiculous proportions, opening chests and popping potions, all of it feels good. Does it feel like a D&D game? It does to me, but I can't speak for every fan of the game, long-time or otherwise. In summation, I'm very much in love with this game, and would suggest giving it a try.

Right off the bat I'll say YES YES YES this is an AWESOME game.
It's a sidescrolling MOBA -- basically this is how it works:
There's a red and blue team. The ultimate goal is to get to their base and destroy it, located on the far left and far right of the map. But the base is defended by several turrets which you have to destroy first. And they fight back really hard. So, each team makes AI-controlled "droids" (robots), which walk up to the turrets and distract them so that you can attack the turrets safely. The main fighting is between the Awesomenauts which are player-controlled. There are many different characters to choose from with different traits, attacks, and upgrades.
This game is NOT p2w. Though there are DLC which give you exclusive characters, these characters are not more OP than the vanilla ones.
There is one thing about the game which I don't like: playing multiplayer with strangers. I wouldn't recommend this as if the other team are in a call, they will crush you, and laggy players/ragequitting players mess up the game. So play single player or custom matches with your friends.

Pros :
- Insanely fun with a extreme amount of replay ability.

Cons :

- Leveling system is annoying, either it means nothing or its the singlehanded thing why one other team wins.
- Lag issues are huge, I have been lagged to death on towers on certain occasions and been hit across the map by a projectile that I clearly dodged.

Over all thought this game is great, if you want a game where you can chill out and be awesome, Awesomenauts is a good game for you. Before judging Painter 2, I should go with Painter 1 first.
Substance Painter is a great tool for texturing your models. Traditionally, artists use photoshop to draw directly onto UV'ed texture maps. It worked as how you wanted. Then 3D applications like 3ds Max, Zbrush, and ect. supporting mesh or polygon paint come out. It works better and you can fix the seams along the UV shells. However, the problem still remains, players or audiences want better visual presentation, artists pursue more realistic result. So you don't just paint a texture map. Instead, you have to make an accurate material. It is where Substance Painter suits the need best.
With Substance Designer, you can paint material directly onto your models. It has 2D + 3D viewport making it very useful to  monitor the result during the process. Moreover, it supports PBR and IBL by default which is currently an industrial standard.
For people who are familiar with photoshop, don't worry, Substance Painter is simple to use and ease to comprehend. It supports alpha, brush, layer, erase, and things you can find in photoshop. So after few hours of playing it, you will get yourself into it.
Another benefit is that you can use both Substance Designer and Painter at the same time, you can make some procedural textures in Designer and imported into Painter and then paint your custom details. It is a great combo.
Also, a sweet thing is that you can bake your maps inside Painter. It saves your time and you don't need to swap applications to get your baked map into texturing process and you can always rebake and adjust them.
So let's get back to Painter 2. It is a newer version of 1 with some fixes and improvements. From my experience, I noticed that 3D viewport has been improved, and thanks to Nvidia and Allegorithmic, they integrated Nvidia's Iray GPU render into Painter 2 after they've done it with Designer 5. This is a powerful render engine and you can get a photo-real result inside viewport and no need to load your texture and mesh into 3D application and make a render. Also, this make Painter even a competitor to Marmoset Toolbag 2 when presenting 3D assets.
Next thing is paint and erase go physical, it provides magical result to your asset if you choose the right way, but sometimes it is difficult to control and the results don't look good.
Particles works a lot better, leak and burn are matching more the way in real world. New smudge tool and clone tool are just like what you use in photoshop.
The most important thing is I don't think Allegorithmic will continue updating Painter 1, so Painter 2 will be the future for them to improve. And Allegorithmic is trying their best to build an environment. Even if some features you expect don't show in Painter 2, I believe in them, Allegorithmic will make Painter 2 better in next years. Also, I got 50% off since I own Painter 1, and if you bought painter 1 after Feb 1st, you will get Painter 2 for free. So if you need a texture tool, just buy it, if you want future upgrade, buy it and even though you are comfortable with Painter 1, with Painter 2 grows you will buy it sooner or later, so just buy it now.

Why on earth are the recent reviews mixed? On any other game, that would set off red flags for me as a potential buyer, and that's terrible.
Endless Legend is a beautiful 4x strategy game, making terrific use of procedural generation for its terrain and ensuring a fairly unique experience for each game. The writing and "story" of the game are fantastic and I find myself drawn far into the Endless lore. It also gives plenty of customization and modding support, which is practically a must-have for indies nowadays. Even in the vanilla game, you can tweak values in the map generator and turn off/on victory conditions if you aren't fond of some. You can also create your own faction, with its own traits, in case you aren't fond of the original ones.
Amplitude seems to care a lot for updating the game's content. I hear there's an expansion coming out soon that will - finally - add naval warfare to the game, which is one of the few things Endless Legend lacks.
Honestly, if you're into 4x strategies and like detailed, pretty world-building, this game is a must-have.

Fm has become extremely disappointing, which is rather sad for a football game that has few replacements, if any. The only reason I bought it is because of a few reviews defending the game, and criticising the whiney fans who cry every time they lose a game. But this isn't about how you react to losing, it's about the manner in which you lose... a bit too often, that makes the game experience so utterly implausible and unfair, that you feel like stopping it instantly. From an ardent fan, who gave it more than a few chances, you hope and wish that the age old method of tactical experimentation to figure out a working formula will eventually yield results and see you win games that you deserve to win. But when in a hard fought game where you are winning against the odds, out of sheer tactical diligence and great performances, you end up losing through a quickfire set piece brace, you tend to get frustrated. That happens once. Twice. Thrice. Till you start getting the feeling like the game is conspiring against you.
I also noticed a rather disturbing trend where I was squeezing out results by confounding the game engine by making frivolous tactical changes every few minutes to delay the game into victory. Once I realised the lenghts to which I was going to get back the few wins I felt I deserved, I realised that NOTHING about this game felt authentic anymore. And that's when FM lost its most unique property that makes you feel like playing the game season after season — how it makes you feel like a real football manager. But when results, players, tactics, decisions all seem so dubious, and the only effort the gamemakers make to introduce a sense of reality into the game is social media feeds and image read manager models, this is not even close to the real deal it was 4-5 years ago. This apart from every other legitimate criticism that has been offered constructively by the fans over the years, that have been clearly ignored all this while. HIGHLY DISAPPOINTED. Don't waste your money or time on this.

If you have a solid computer, a 360/Xbox One controller, and can get this for $5 or less, I might recommend it.
Gameplay is pretty repetitive, but the game isn't long enough for this to REALLY ruin it. The history, however inaccurate, is an interesting setting. Similar to God of War in terms of settings and reliance on mythology. The difference (aside from Roman vs Greek mythology) is that the Roman gods are very minor background characters that only appear a small handful of times, even if they may be driving the plot.
The bulk of the game is very pretty Roman settings and quick time events. The quick time events are "well done" relatively speaking, but they're still QTEs. You basically play the relatively simple combat (parry, shield bash/break, regular attacks) until the enemy is hurt enough to perform a QTE execution. You have a few different bonuses you can level with your experience, and whatever bonus is currently selected will trigger once completing a QTE excecution. For example, you can have increased damage, or heal some health back.
The plot is fine. Not amazing. The relatively unique setting (for a AAA action game) is helpful, but it's a pretty standard revenge story that will probably remind you of Gladiator.
No idea how good the multiplayer is, but I'm going to go out on a limb and say "who cares?" and "no one is playing it in any significant numbers anyway."
Again, $5 or less. And a good computer with an xbox controller. And some interest/tolerance of ancient Roman settings. Then and only then should you buy this.

For a long a time, I had a positive review up for the Firefly Online Cortex.
Alas, over the last month, the communication of the developer has died down to a crawl.
That the official channel is a Facebook page doesnt't help things. At the moment, people
are waiting months for answers on support tickets, known issues aren't being adressed.
What was intended as a supporting app for coming Firefly Online, has degraded into
a pseudo card collecting clicker app. One where the chances are inherently stacked
against you. Even with being card packs, and not a few of them, your chances are dim,
to gain those fun perks of collecting 10 duplicates of every of the over 100 cards.
The 'VIP' information, that you can get for buying the 'Big Damn Hero' perk from
inside the app, fail to provide substantial information, for where the development
is at, if it will be anywhere near release or if the studio, which has been developing
Match 3 and other mobile games for the last years, will be pushin the release for
another year. This has the feeling of history repeating.
In the last days critical voices have been banned and deleted form the official
facebook page. Whereas no new information has been derived from the developers.
At the same time, the dev has a kickstarter funding game in the making, an action
runner game, which has been delayed multiple times too, including about half a
year of radio silence. The devs tend to visit an inofficial fan community, where
they share talk about the state of the Cortex and FFO. It sounds all shiny and well.
They can sure talk the talk, but there's growing distrust if they can walk the walk.
The last, inofficial and unverified, news, is that Firefly Online is apparently on
hold, as per a post from the developer on a closed community fan page.
Update August 2016
No news on the situation. No comment from the publisher Qmx. Or from Fox.
This paints a bleak picture for Firefly Online. There's still hope. But official
information would go a long way. Several people tried contacting Qmx and
Fox. But to no avail. :(
Update January 2017
No news. Official content taken offline. No sign of life from the
developer, or support on any of their self published products.
Update May 2017
No news. Official inquiries are ignored. There are rumours
abound about a gag order in place preventing involved
parties to release information. No confirmation for
these rumours are to be found. There is no activity
on any product or page from the developer. All support
has been dropped. There is no sign that the developer
does exist in more then name only at this point in time.

- not so large, but very believable map (U.S. mil-base on Cuba)
- nice atmosphere and overall setting
- countless approaches to finish each mission
- possibility to turn off any "augmentation" on your HUD and make game feel more real (also much more harder :))
- high replayability - i didn't trust this one and also i was thinking "but i don't want game which has one map and going there again and again" - well, i must admit how wrong i was, game is more and more fun with every replay
Cons:
- you will get an explanation for basic moves of Snake, but rest of special movements, CQC etc. you need to figure yourself (or search it on the web, anyway someone remembers i.e. nice training camp in Splinter Cell 1 where one could get used with every Sam's move?)
- more and more i am into game (i.e. after 10-12 hours of playing) i see some small objects and NPCs pop-ins
- really unballanced AI - explanation is bellow
On the one hand overall (or global) feeling of AI is nice:
- they can see you and they can hear you. Blowing something up (throwing an grenade, shooting an barrell, using C4 etc.) draws their attention, same with unsilenced gunshots. And they will go investigate, even if there is last soldier standing in opposite corner of base
- if some NPC thinks he sees something suspicious there is possibility he will go investigate, but guards on towers will call for someone else go to investigate meanwhile they cover any area from above
But in on the other hand - at local scale they can be reall dumb and limited:
- AI can't climb small buildings or/and structures, can't climb/jump over obstacles, same with crawling under obstacles, they not even able to check places where you can hide crawling (under some structures and buildings). I think when AI sees you on roof of some small building and he reports via radio he is going to check it it is just stupid to see him going around you away saying "nothing found" instead of he simply could get up to roof same as id did with Snake.
- another example - you have possibility to turn off electricity for certain area in game. CP sends guard or two to investigate main distribution/fuses rack in area. They will find it. You will knock them or kill them. CP will send one more to investigate. Get rid of him/them and you are fine, no more checking why are all cameras and all lights out, no matter there are tens of another guards in base
- final example - you can plant C4 around whole base, but no NPC will notice/report/try to disarm them, not even if they are standing in front of it and looking on it, no matter there is BIG RED light flashing with loud BEEP, BEEP ;)
Conclusion
Even MGSV:GZ can sometimes look unballanced when it comes to sort of "game realism" (i.e. you have realistic gun silencer which worns out, fine, on the other way you have sometimes stupidly acting AI), but still is a must play for every stealth fan. If you don't like hiding "for ever" waiting for right moment, observing your surroundings and carefuly planning your mission approach - go play some other game. This game is not about being sort of John Rambo running through all mission in total havoc and complaining "hey, i finished game in one hour". Yes, you can do it, but it is nonsense as game offers tons of ways to have fun with stealth.
I played series/games like Thief (old series and new one), Splinter Cell, Far Cry and Assassins Creed, Dishonored etc. and loved them all, every game has its own stealth mechanics or possibilities. But what you can do and see in such let's say "stealth sandbox" like MGSV:GZ is - this is just fantastic. And if you do hear people complaining about short play time don't listen them. Game is presented like "teaser" and showing off new MGS series possibilities to be fully shown in upcoming Phantom Pain. And i take it as it is beautiful presentation with ballanced fun and level of realism. And everything in game feels and works perfect.
Conclusion v2:
Can't wait for Phantom Pain. And ended up with just downloaded MGS1 :).

Ssenkrad_II is a reviewer that falsifies how this game's mechanics works as well as blocks any comments that bring out the blatant lies the "reviewer" makes. It is possible to win the game through diplomacy, quest, supremacy, etc. This is coming from some one that has the achievements for winning the game multiple ways and has almost the same amount of hours as the reviewer claiming that supremacy is the only way to win.
The false review mentioned found here:
Do not trust any reviews from the previously mentioned Steam user as they simply do not go in-depth or even allow people to question the credibility of their claims when they try to paint the game in a light that implies a mechanic is broken.
The actual game itself does not have a hard learning curve if you've played previous turn based strategy games. The diplomacy system is straightforward and shows you whether or not the trade will be agreed. Diplomacy is basic to the point that complimenting an empire for a handful of turns can make a hostile empire more friendly to the point that you can eventually ally them.
Endless Legend is a great game that is an easy pick up for anyone wanting to get into the 4x, turn based strategy genre. Factions are easy to learn and the game allows you to partake in an interesting campaign if you decide to try the quest victory. The AI can also present a challenge at higher difficulties as they are given modifiers to their economy, the handicap for the player will increase as the difficulty increases.
Settling cities is also an easy task depending on how you prioritize your city, where you place your city, and whether or not the city has a hero assigned to it. If you have a city focused on production you can dish out settlers to expand quickly but will have to sacrifice turns in doing so vs. building up that city to become a dust farm (gold).
This game also has a wonderful modding community for anyone that is interested in expanding the game through user-created content.

Evoland is a brilliant sendup of the entire history of 2D action-adventure games and of JRPGs. It's so good that I'm voluntarily recommending it because I think more people need to play it. It's clever, and it's fun on its own merits.

Evoland is a unique game is every way, sane for its gameplay. Now, this might sound like a strange way to describe the game, but allow me to elaborate further.
Evoland is a game wherein you start with a basic, black and white, 8-bit adventure game where you can only move right. While, like other Adventure games, you must unlock items to progress, you must also progress by unlocking game features. From features as banal as breaking pots, to as important as having a health bar, many gameplay elements which are nowadays considering traditional and mandatory, must be discovered.
And this is why you WILL enjoy Evoland if you have a taste for nostalgia. The game is a clear salute to classics like Final Fantasy, Legend of Zelda, Monster Quest, and even Diablo. If you like any of those games, you'll notice at least half a dozen references and nods made to those games throughout the game. However, these are Duke Nukem style of references - heavy handed and not sly in the slightest.
It's an interesting premise, and seeing the game evolve from original Gameboy graphics to a 3D cartoony style fitting for any modern indie game is rewarding in its own merit. As long as you're unlocking new things, you'll be having a blast, and chuckling when the game offers sarcastic or tongue-in-cheek humor at the expense of tropes common of old-school games.
While this is all well and good, the "combat" is dull as a doornail. As stated earlier, the game takes inspiration from LoZ, Final Fantasy, and Diablo. There are three different "combat" systems that activate in specific areas, all of which are a copy of other game's combat systems, without the same depth or complexity.
The Final Fantasy combat system doesn't have nearly as many party members, spells, options, or items. It doesn't even have an MP system, so you can spam spells as much as you want, making the game dreadfully easy.
The LoZ combat system offers a sword that can only be swung (no charing, spinning, or anything fancy), unlimited bombs (though only one can be shot at a time), and arrows.
The Diablo combat system has NO active abilities, no level ups, no meaningful looting (obsesive looting is treated as a joke in these sections, instead of as a gameplay mechanic) and not even a mana bar.
These "combat systems" also suffer from two more fatal flaws. For one, you don't get to choose what combat system you use. If an area is a Diablo combat area, you can't run through the area again with the Final Fantasy combat system. Secondly, the game is just too easy. I only died once in the entire game, and that's simply because I didn't figure out the solution to the final boss fight before he killed me.
Speaking of the final boss -- if you need a good story, don't get involved. The game is a nostalgia trip, and it plays old games having bad and cliche stories as a joke.
With all the negatives aside, I will say this. Evoland is a unique, and genuinely funny experience. While the game's combat is dull, seeing what gameplay element you will unlock next pushes you through until the very end. If you need a good nostalgia hit for the days of the SNES and Genesis, look no further.

I beat the game in 2-3 hours using an x360 controller. It is neat to start out with b&w 2d graphics and slowly watch them become better, but the feeling runs dry in the first hour. The game is completely linear and serves mostly as a tech demo for all the different puzzles, playstyles, and visuals that the many adventure games of the past have already done.
Any type of major puzzle used to block progress that you can think of has probably been used. Burn down saplings so that they don't block your path when you teleport to the future (Oracle of Ages/Seasons.) Find the right path to walk across a room or you will fall through the floor (Link to the Past.) Bomb through cracked walls. Find all switches. Push blocks to make a path. And so on.
Most combat is in 2d Zelda format, followed by turn-based, FF style battles, and some light ARPG style combat. Evoland is not unpleasant, but with no real story, it's not exactly memorable either.

When I went into this game, I was really looking forward to it. A nostolgia trip that takes you through the best of top down adventure, RPG and turn based battles. What is actually here is a brief parody game poking fun at itself and tropes across two decades of game genres and technological advances.
To my dismay, Evoland bluntly tells you, you're in this era of RPGs. I guess its meant for comedy, but I just didn't care for it. You'll unlock different eras of games and different technologies, such as sound effects, music, 16 bit graphics, high definition textures, 3D battle systems and so on. Its all part of the joke. You'll see all the stereotypes and tropes here and the game will be quick to point them out to you so that you'll understand its a joke.
Evoland has great graphics, and some gameplay elements that would make for a great game. This feels like a good tech demo since every era is so brief with no depth. I can understand paying $5 if they use this engine to make a real full fledged game, but you'll breeze through this game with no challenge. I would say its the perfect game for kids, but with so much hinging on nostalgia, kids might not understand.
You'll play in top down Zelda segments, using a sword to cut down grass, bombs to blow up walls and arrows to transfer fire between lit and unlit candles. Eventually that top down will turn into a 3D version of itself which you can switch between using crystals. Its a nice system that I would have liked to see a lot more of if not be its own game. There are Final Fantasy 2 style towns, random battles and turn based combat, but there is no depth to combat. Its all turn based fighting where your main character has no skills. The secondary character has spells, but nothing lost for using the spells like a traditional turn based RPG would have. Eventually the old school RPG updates itself to be 3D later on in the game.
Eventually, you'll find a Final Fantasy 8 style town. After that you'll find a Diablo styled dungeon with gold, health orbs and loot dropping on the ground for you to collect. It felt like a button mashing chore to get through it. Nothing intelligent to the gameplay, just button mashing.
In the game you'll collect gold, cards and stars, but other than that, there's not much going on. There is little need for gold since there is barely anything to buy. The stars just go to an achievement. The cards lead to a Final Fantasy 8 inspired mini game that is nice to play where your cards have numbers on each of the four sides of the cards and you lay them down in a grid of 3 by 3 to determine who has the most cards once you've thrown down. It is a great feature to have and they went the extra mile to include it.
With that said, the game just feels so hollow, all style, no substance. There is no storyline twist, such as an evil wizard devolves the land once you've easily breezed through the evolutionary eras. I knew how far I had progressed based on what evolutionary stage I was on. It just felt disappointing. Since there is no depth, the combat is really just tedium if not button mashing. The focus was on making the game feel like the other games we know and love.
As a comedy game it missed its mark with me in the 3 hours it took to complete it. There were definitely highs and boring lows. If it was more difficult the game wouldn't be fun after the laughs wear off. I've gone through it twice now and disliked it more the second time.

It's hard to judge a free game honestly. Clearly a lot of work went into this adventure game, and it has some interesting visuals and interesting puzzles. Unfortunately there are some elements that stopped it from being as good as it could hav been. My main complaint is that there are no subtitles or volume options - perhaps it's meant to be played with headphones, I was playing it on a 5.1 room stereo. The music/ambient noise overwhelmed the dialogue, and between that and his accent I frequently couldn't understand what Vinny was saying, which prevented me from completing one of the puzzles based entirely around hearing what he says.
This probably ties into my other main complaint. I found the story to be pretty much incomprehensible. It's perhaps supposed to have a dreamlike quality but they seem to be trying to communicate some sort of plot, I just couldn't really get what it was or why the things that were happening were moving it forward. The ending didn't do much to tie it all together, it just left me with as many questions as I started with.
A couple of other issues I had - your character uses the f- slur to insult someone and I thought that was pretty unnecessary. FInally, the thing I was frustrated with most happened in the Basement level - specifically the part of the puzzle where you have to lower a door then run up the stairs and jump over it before it blocks you off again (with a pretty small margin of error). Doing that the first time is fine, but later it's incorporated into a bit where you'll probably die a few times (or at least I did) and you'll have to do it every single time. I have no idea why the switch on the other side of that door doesn't just open it permanently, but it wasn't much fun.
I think the bones of a good game are here but it fell a little bit short for me, ultimately. Again, though, it was free and I don't regret trying it.

As someone who has never dug into an idle game before, but someone who is madly in love with the D&D brand, Idle Champions is an amazing game for what it's worth. The gamplay is simple, but stylish - you control a party of D&D characters, most of which are historic figures from the game's Forgotten Realms campaign setting, and some of whom are tie-ins for an ongoing D&D webseries known as Force Grey. The party starts with a single character, who attacks enemies as they pop up from the opposite side of the screen. Every enemy slain drops gold, and gold can be spent to upgrade your characters and add new ones to the party. You start with one character available to unlock, and each subsequent unlock grants you another character. You can also conserve your gold to skip ahead in the lineup, should you decide you don't want a particular character in your party.
Each time you upgrade a character, their stats increase multiplicatively. Every few levels (anywhere from 5-25 levels) they receive a bonus upgrade. The bonus upgrades are character-specific, very diverse, and eventually even branch off into multiple paths based on decisions you make as you select them. Some are flat damage increases for the character, some increase the damage of your entire party, and every character has an Ultimate ability that they unlock in the 50-100 range that deals a ton of damage on a long cooldown, usually including additional effects (like knocking targets back, fully healing your party, and stunning enemies to prevent them from moving or attacking).
You and your party march through hordes of monsters, moving forward or backward in stage levels as you kill them (usually in multiples of 25 kills per stage). There's a bit of strategy in sticking around a level to actively farm, but a lot of your money will come from your AFK time while the game is closed. After leveling and upgrading as desired, there are boss levels to fight at every 5th stage. The bosses are considerably tougher, but drop more money, as well as a bag that contains a variety of rewards. Boss stages are farmable as well, so if the first level of a new stage is too much for you you can backpedal and beat up bosses again to catch up to a better point.
Numbers scale like crazy in this game. For those who aren't familiar with idle games, you start by dealing about 20 damage a hit at the very first level, and there is generally no upper limit to how much damage you can put out (highest I've seen is in the quadrillions). Health and gold scale as proportionately, both ally and enemy. Each stage you progress makes the numbers climb higher and higher, and it can generally be very satisfying to watch characters scale out of control.
Finishing a quest (which is a bundle of stages) will give you gems (the cash shop currency) and divine favor (which is a bonus to the amount of gold you gain in subsequent quests). Your divine favor is based on how much money you earned during your quest, though it might not be advisable to spend too long farming if you're looking to be totally efficient in this game. Stacking lots of gold find does make the game easier on subsequent quests, and helps with that crazy numerical scaling mentioned earlier.
You can repeat finished quests, and finishing quests unlocks harder ones with restrictions and challenges that alter the playthrough. Repeating quests rewards Divine Favor, but the gem rewards seem to be once per quest (a shame, probably the only downside to the game really).
As mindless as it sounds, there's a lot of strategy and micromanagement to be had. The party's formation matters, as they're arranged in a rhombus-shape with multiple rows and columns. The rank and file of your party matters, as characters have both damage-boosting auras and effects like healing and shields. Your cleric needs to be adjacent as many people as possible to increase their damage, and anybody in the row in front of her is healed every few seconds. The bard has to be at least 2 rows from your frontline to give them temporary hit points when they're damaged. This is especially important during the midgame of most quests, as bosses tend to get so tough that they have to engage one of your champs, but with enough health, healing, and shields your frontline won't give to a boss. It's kind of hard to read all the buffs (they show up underneath the characters a little icons, and mousing over them gives a pop-up but it's unreliable and hard to read with so much going on on the screen), but arranging your party in the right formation and giving them the right buffs is essential to progression. The rogue wants the space ahead of him to be unoccupied, which means he needs to be up front, so make sure you have a suitable tank to help soak some of the damage he would take for being frontline (it's worth it, I promise).
Besides formation, the cash shop offers chests, which come in two varieties - silver chests, which occasionally drop from enemies and can be purchased with the gems earned from quests; And gold chests, which are purchased with real money and have substantially better rewards. Every chest drops 3(silver) or 5(gold) items that apply to champs you've unlocked, increasing their stats and improving their special abilities. Opening duplicates of the same item after the first increases the base item's effect by 1%, up to 10 times for a 105 increase. It remains to be seen if you can pull additional copies of equipment after pulling the 10th, but I'd hope not, as that'd make chests pretty poor to open after a point. Items come in a variety of rarities, and every champ has the same number of equipment slots. Equipment auto-improves as you find better stuff, and auto-equips when you first find it. Chests also contain items that can buff your party our your own capabilities (you have a self-clicker, but it's paltry and mostly unnecessary - only level it if you have money to spend but nobody to upgrade, it won't make much of a difference), and though they mostly serve as filler, you will probably find a use for them. I've yet to fill an inventory with them, so that's a good sign as to their efficacy.
---
All in all, f you've never played an idle game I don't know if I can recommend it just because it looks like a D&D game. It's unique in its execution, and the mechanics are great, but it only borrows as much of the D&D image as it can to make it appeal to longtime fans. The mechanics make for a great game, but somebody who's only played D&D since it came out in the mid-late 70's probably won't get as excited about it as I evidently am. Upper limits are a pipe dream in this game, you can invest or as much or as little time as you want and the game will do the rest. If you want to farm it out and upgrade your champs to the max, more power to you.
I can recommend it for everything else, though. I don't feel burdened into paying for gold chests with microtransactions (you can buy a single gold chest for 500 gems, which is inadvisable if you need to equip your party, but still provides an option after silver chests begin to fail you). I like watching my characters slam people for quadrillions of damage. I like clicking a button and watching an Ultimate ability decimate waves of enemies. I like picking whether or not I want Jarlaxle Baenrae or Minsc and Boo to join the party, or to level Bruenor Battlehammer up to level 500 (which might be the level cap? I've yet to hit it, but there's an achivement for doing so). I like that there's no immediate endgame, and that I can progress in the game by closing it and doing other things, then coming back to see how much AFK gold I earned. I like watching the numbers climb to ridiculous proportions, opening chests and popping potions, all of it feels good. Does it feel like a D&D game? It does to me, but I can't speak for every fan of the game, long-time or otherwise. In summation, I'm very much in love with this game, and would suggest giving it a try.
