For everyone with a decent graphics card, I did some testing for the Devs for things that need improving. For starters, when you start the game, every time chose "no sky". Then when its up, go to options and: Turn all shadows to low, post processing on low, view distance on medium, world title buffers on high, textures on medium. Then disable bloom, high quality VFX, light shafts, distance field shadowing, and motion blur. Also disable "view camera bob" and turn "camera shake scale" all the way down. Then turn "sky quality" and "ground clutter" all the way down. And there ya go, game should run pretty darn well. Enjoy killing people and dinosaurs! :D

The potential is there however with a hunger games style brawl with dinosaurs and a great crafting system to work with. Unfortunetely however the game still has two major gameplay flaws. The time to load into the game itself afterward is set at 5 minutes (every single game) which is painfully long when the majority of players die within the first five minutes anyway from contesting the center or running into each other at the start with spears. However the few games you do happen to survive past the five minute mark are great and leave a lasting impression. Hopefully as the game gets improved and more popular the down time will be decreased and the game won't murder older machines so heavily.
Ultimately I would love to see this game succeed, but with the current down time and quality on my three year old laptop i could only stomach one or two nights of this game before I just get sick of waiting in a lobby for equal amount of time as i was playing in a match. I'll leave this game an upvote, but only because I assume these problems will be fixed eventually with patches and popularity.

This game is more of a dissapointment than most simply because it is so close to being good.
There are many things it does right. The district based city building is fun and influences your city positioning. The custom civ builder is simple but an option rarely seen to completion in other 4x games. Among many other things the game has/had a lot of potential.
However, I feel in Endless Legend's rush to be different it abandoned many of the estabalished good things about other 4x titles. The multitude of layered gameplay makes the entire game feel crowded and each turn quickly feels like more of a chore than a few thought provoking choices. The questline mechanics has the game pulling you in directions you very well might not want and the sheer array of victory options makes the end-game more of a race to a specific tile than a strategic finale built on your own play.
All in all, Endless Legend provides a whole heap of new or newish mechanics that other 4X games haven't even thought about. But unfortunately they are all tied very loosely together and the game suffers for it. In my experience I have yet to see any of my friends give anything more positive than a 'meh' about this game at best.
Regretfully I give this game a 4/10

Map is beautiful as its pleasing to just look at, the music is immersive as its soothing, the gameplay just excells with varied minor faction units that can be conquered, assimilated and produced for an always different variety on every new gameplay, that on top of the fact that heroes and units can be equipped with different armors/weapons/accessories. However I wish they would have some different color schemes.
Everything is beautifully crafted, quests are simple and entertaining, combat is quite straightfoward and usually automatic even on manual mode, mostly the stronger army will win and after the first battles you'll see yourself using the auto mode pretty much every battle or spectator mode just to enjoy the slaughter, even so tactical decisions as using high ground/forests/manneuver the enemy for aoe/line attacks could turn the tide when armies may seem balanced. Factions are loyal to their lore and the unique traits adds massively to the replayability.
I currently don't see any major negative aspects on this game, some people claim that the A.I is a bit weak combat wise, but so far i've only played on normal difficulties so I'll comment on that later on. Also, it must be noted the fact that some factions ares focused on economy/expansion/research/etc wise, meaning they will pursuit said ways of winning the match instead of pure elimination of the other empires.
Easily 9/10

Each race feels unique compared to each other, the only downside is there isn't a great deal of unique units per faction, however this is made up by unit customisation and the additional units incorporated by assimilating minor factions into your empire. The art style is great and reminds me heavily of magic the gathering. Lots of sci-fi elements with a fantasy veneer makes the game quite appealing to me. I've recently bought some of the DLC during the steam sale and found a whole new life to the game, the DLC is good but certainly not mandatory.
I enjoy playing games like total war, CK2 and Civ but for me this game has really replaced Civ, I can't wait for the next installment.

A great game with the understanding that it is strictly vocabulary based. 400 words is enough to get you started learning a language. With that said, if you are learning a non-latin based character system (as in, your language does not using letters "abc" but instead uses Chinese or Russian "letters"), you will need to learn that on your own, as this game does not teach this to you. I purchased the Russian starter pack, and luckily for me, I already learned the Russian "alphabet" before purchasing.
I like how relaxed the environment is in the game, and that you can interact with virtually anything within the environment. It's fun to learn, and effective. I'm planning on picking up a French and Danish language pack soon.
For $10.00, it's definitly worth the purchase. It really does help you learn solid vocab. I hope the developer continues working on this game, because this could really help a lot of people truly learn a language. I would definitely support this project. Now for some recommendations: I wish the game could have extended its boundaries to an outside world, such as a playground, a school, etc. It would have been nice to get more than roughly 400 words, and to be able to learn grammar. Maybe an interactive story where you practice grammar? The possibilities are endless.

This does not teach grammar and sentance structure.
This is a tool to increase your vocabulary with verb, Adjective, and Nouns.
This is a lot better than using picture flashcards.
Whilst Influent and Duolingo may not necessarily be the best tools for language learning, using both of them together is pretty effective, and I recommend Influent for using alongside Duolingo.

Good game for all the reasons the other reviews point out. I'd just like to add the warning to be mindfull of what you click on because it can get mighty frustrating when you get to the last 10 words & you thought you had clicked on everything only to find out you haven't. This is a vocabulary learning tool only, so just from this game alone you definitely won't master a language. All it does is give you 420 basic words of things found in an apartment. If you learn best through visualization, this game is for you. You will still need to use other tools alongside it, for example Duolingo or Quizlet, and you'll need to learn grammar rules from somewhere else. But to start with, it's a really useful tool.
Also for the people who leave negative reviews bc they expected more than just vocab - don't blame the game for you not reading the description. Nowhere does it say anything about grammar, it clearly states it's about vocab and pronunciation.
If you want to learn a language but need to build up some basic vocabulary first, I recommend you get this.

Football Manager 2017 follows in the footsteps of the previous versions. It's safe to say that if you have liked any of the previous versions of Football Manager, this is the game for you. If you are looking for a FIFA like game then you are at the wrong game. This is a simulation game, through and through.
The game revolves around the role of Manager or Head Coach of a football team, that's association football aka soccer, not the American version. You are put into the life of a manager of a club of your choice. Want to start at the best clubs with the best players? Go ahead. Want to start unemployed and work your way up to the biggest clubs? No problem. Want to start at your favourite club located in the middle of the football pyramid? Sure. You can pick and choose clubs as you want at the start, but be prepared; The fans will be more demanding for results in the bigger clubs, just as you are as a fan in real life.
The biggest strength of the game is the amazing database of players all over the world. Scouted and rated far better than any other game. If you have a friend playing in the sunday league, he could be in their database. This creates a very real world to play with and players can often immerse themselves into the game due to this.
That being said, the game is a virtual spreadsheet with an engine processing your input. You as the manager cannot control the players with other than general instructions. You cannot control a player as you would in FIFA or other similar games.
If you like simulations and football, this is the best choice, but it's very hard to master. But that's football isn't it?

The annoyingly bad in match AI make this game not worth playing. Here is an example of the latest annoyance that has forced me to stop bothering.
My team (Newcastle going for promotion) is well set up with most players playing to 6.5 -7.5 rating or above consistently.   No one in my first eleven has a lower average than 6.8 after the first 6 matches.
Expectations are that we should storm the league.
6 matches in a row, all is fine .. some players play badly in individual matches , some well, as you would expect ... making tactical changes & substitutions seem to work & the team are unbeaten with 3 home & 1 away win &  2 away draws.
Now we play QPR away ... who are in 17th in the championship & have conceeded 2 or more goals in 4 of their 5 matches & have only won one match at home. The press prediction is that we are going to slaughter them.
Right from the off, QPR dominate the match ... they slice through my back 4 & 2 defensive midfielders like a knife through butter. Any setting between overload attacking & contain defending makes no difference.
Within 5 minutes they are 2 nil up ... one worldie from outside the box & for the second my goal keeper suddenly forgets how to catch an easy crossed ball & lets it drop to one of 3 QPR players unmarked inside my box as my defenders are having a laze about somewhere up the pitch instead of running back to defend.
25 minutes played & we are 3 nil down. The highest rated player on my side is a forward at 6.6. The average rating is 5.5.
I substitute 2 central defenders & my left wing back. With 65 minutes gone we are 3 nil down still, but under constant attack & the substitutes are playing as badly as the players they replaced.
So, I restored the game to before the match & out of interest replayed it with exactly the same players in the same line up as before.  This time I won 6 - 1 !  My Main striker got a hat trick & midfield general got a 8.2 rating!
I carried on playing & the pattern repeats .... every so often (I would guess 6 - 10 matches) the game suddenly decides that every player on your team is going to play like a 12 year old girl for the next match, regardless of what you do.
This obviously takes away most of the skill & pleasure from the game. I can guarantee this will spoil the game for you & if you are like me have you almost screaming at your players about how useless they are!
Other annoyances include:
The game seems to determine a players rating before the match begins & whatever you do or say will make no difference.
So if you have a player who starts off playing badly, they will never improve, so if it's a defender, you have to substitute them after 5 or 10 minutes or suffer leaked goals.
Playing away matches, you can dominate the game for 70 minutes & be 5 or more goals up with your opponents barely touching the ball. But around this time, the home team will suddenly start to increase thier possession & unless you then switch to a defensive formation ... (at times I have had to put 2 defensive midfielders in front of a back 5, telling the wing backs to only defend & setting to "contain") ... the other side will start scoring & continue nearly every attack until you switch to defensive mode. This is the same even with careful use of your substitutes & against teams much weaker than yours.
For example, I was 7 nil up after 75 minutes playing as a very attacking Liverpool side against Middlesborough & as an experiment kept on attacking. I kept an eye of the fitness levels of both sides & mine were way above the opposition's.
They started getting a bit of possession & this built until they had practically 100% possession in my half. They scored on 78, 82, 84, 84 minutes. I then kept the team exactly as it was but switched to "contain" from "attack". They didn't score again but I scored in the 89th & 93rd minute!
When you play cup matches, it suddenly becomes about 75% harder to score. If you are the big team in the tie playing minnows, you will have the lions share of posession & totally dominate, but your forwards will hit the bar, miss penalties, sky sitters way over , hit the corner flag, etc .... their goal keeper will turn into Gordan Banks for the day ... anything the game engine can conjure up to stop you scoring will happen.
Basically, the game seems very driven by it's own internal algorythms, to the extent that you feel that anything you do will not alter things when they start going wrong.
The flip side to this is it is possible to find a formation & combination of players that suit your squad & the game becomes impossibly easy. For instance I played as Liverpool & had mixed results until I hit upon two formations ... one for playing weaker teams & one for "top 6" & above teams.
I then went the rest of the season unbeaten, winning the FA cup & league. The next season I won the league (unbeaten with 1 away draw 1-1 to Arsenal the rest wins), the FA & EFL cup, Charity shield & Champions Cup. I then won the world club championship, etc & gave up as there was no point in going on. This is not due to any skill on my part, just by hitting on the correct formations & playing them every match unchanged.
Players are almost imposible to manage... they will ask for a new contract & will drop morale unless you agree to negotiate. If they are on say £100,000 a week the agent will ask for £275,000 & will walk away if you try to negotiate much below £250,000!
The player will then have bad morale because they count it as you breaking your promise to negotiate & will threaten to take it public, etc. This will spread through your team.
You can praise a player after a match who got say 9.0 rating & sometimes they will get annoyed & tell you to leave them alone as they didnt think they played well. The next match, the same player gets 7.5 & accepts your praise with thanks!
The pre & post match interviews are very boringly scripted & the same stuff is trotted out again & again. The game also has no concept of squad rotation, even if you give players the "rotation" status the interviewer will make a big thing about you "dropping" players when you rotate them. It assumes you have a starting eleven & stick to it with no rotation.
Lower league (Championship & below) players are astonsishingly bad in some respects. I played at local Sunday league level & I was far better than the match model shows aspects of these players.
In particular, forwards regularily miss open gaols from a few yards out, nearly hitting the corner flag, etc. Defenders will run and leave the ball behind. Goal keepers will catch the ball, stand still for a moment then drop it, sometimes into their own net... they will let the easiest of shots past them & have you tearing your hair out in frustration. Even Premier League keepers regularily drop the ball when they try to kick it out of their hands.
Even premier league players will regularily chest the ball down, trap it, stand still  then run off leaving the ball stationary behind them!
After a while, you get to know exactly what any player in a particular situation will do, yet you are powerless to stop it.... e.g. wingers will hold on to the ball, even when instructed to not run with it & pass quickly... eventually the winger will be surrounded by 2 or more players who will take the ball off him & 6 times out of ten score on the break. You groan as soon as the winger starts his move, because you know what is going to happen but cannot prevent it.
As an experiment, I created the best left defender possible with the in game editor  & put him up against a run of the mill premier league winger. The defender never stopped the winger once & every cross went in. I have come to the conclusion that you cannot stop crosses once a winger is facing a full back.
So don't say you were not warned if you buy this game.

I have to say: Ryse: Son of Rome seems like the game that was made for me. I'm a huge fan of hack and slash games and couldn't resist buying this game when it was on sale.
Pros:
- amazing visuals, not surprising considering it's a launch title intended to showcase the graphical capabilities of the new console generation
- well optimized. My R9 280X can run this game at a solid 60fps on ultra high graphics settings (with VSync off of course)
- pretty engaging storyline. It's nothing amazing, but it gets the job done.
- good voice acting. Good acting in general really.
Cons:
- repetitive gameplay. You'll eventually get used to the same execution animations over and over.
- lack of variety. You get hack and slash segments followed by turret sections. You can see the developers attempting some variety, but it's not really enough
I can easily see why someone might not like Ryse, but I personally couldn't put the game down while I was playing it and constantly wished it wouldn't end.

Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes is a beautiful representation of what to expect in the highly anticipated Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain.
Arguably the biggest complaints of this game are the lack of length and lack of David Hayter.
However, the length of this game can be greatly expanded if the player puts in the time to really milk the game for all of its content. Yes, that may seem like an arduous thing to do and may seem unrealistic, but it is a remedy for the lack of face value gameplay that the game offers to a more casual audience of the series.
To the highly invested, "hardcore" for lack of a better word, fans of the series, full completion of this game feels much more rewarding than it does a chore.
Gameplay wise, this installment of the MGS series takes a very different, yet very familiar approach to the iconic gameplay from games past.
Keeping true to the stealth genre, Ground Zeroes takes what the players already know, and polishes it to the point where every last mistake, alert, and ranking is solely placed on the actions of the player. Unlike previous games, the camera is in full control of the player and situational awareness is emphasized to no end. There is no room for recklessness. Unless, of course, that is the playstyle the player chooses. Not just the stealth in this game is polished, but the combat is seriously improved to the point where it is on par, if not better, than some triple-A third person shooters available on the market.
For serious fans of Metal Gear, yes this game is short, but for a lowered price and seriously considering this as only a demo/prologue for the Phantom Pain, it is absolutely worth the $20 (or the $10 I got it for on sale). Doing everything this game has to offer, and even goofing around in the sandbox that it is will give you the full contents worth of your money. Metal Gear fans should absolutely play this and I recommend it wholeheartedly.
To those who know little to nothing about the series, go pick up the Metal Gear Solid Legacy collection on consoles and playthrough those (otherwise, you'll be missing out on arguably one of the greatest games series ever created).
Side note:
The fans of the Metal Gear series have complained about replacing David Hayter with Kiefer Sutherland for the voice of Big Boss. While the fact remains that David Hayter has given an iconic performance for Snake for the last decade or so, the series itself is headed in a darker direction that is in need of a more subtle, dare say more mature voice that Sutherland offers. Change is not always a bad thing, and with word from Kojima that Big Boss will be more of a silent-protagonist, I'm sure that what Sutherland brings to the table will be worthwile and his work in MGSV will in no way overshadow what Hayter has done in the past.
SUPPORT MGSV; BUY THIS GAME.

This game has received an incredible amount of backlash for the lack of content in the game given the price. Unfortunately, despite having enjoyed this game and being a huge fan of the franchise and even owning another copy on the PS3 from when it had come out earlier on consoles, I find myself unable to defend this.
This game does so many things right and I'm gonna mostly just focus on the features that have been added in this title. The design of the level is very open, allowing for numerous tactics on how to accomplish your objectives and you can even do them in whatever order you choose. The CQC first introduced in MGS3: Snake Eater is given a huge boost with new techniques while keeping all the old and is the best it's ever been, what with the ability to grab enemies from behind cover, deal with numerous enemies at once, stealing weapons, and coercing them to call over additional to help so you can set traps like leaving C4 on the soldier's back. The vehicles handle pretty well. And the stealth has been given a more free feel, like adding the ability to sprint and jump which sounds like no big deal but if you've played the other titles in the series, you'll probably appreciate it more. The visual presentation of this game is beautiful. I think these guys did a great job with the FOX Engine. The landscapes and lighting are incredibly detailed and the characer animations are very lifelike and smooth. And the big one that only MGS fans were really bothered by was the replacement of David Hayter with Kiefer Sutherland as the voice of Big Boss/Naked Snake. I honestly don't even wanna talk about this because the outrage is just kinda silly to me. Yes, I love Hayter. His goofy, gruff voice gave a certain cheesy, action movie charm to the character of Solid Snake. But, even when Snake Eater first came out in 2004 and they had decided to make a game focusing on the career and arc of Big Boss, I still thought it was rather off putting that they had used the same voice actor, considering they are rather different characters in terms of personality and beliefs. When Kojima has stated that he was going to be making Sutherland the voice of Big Boss as a way of matching up with the new, darker tone of MGS5, I was curious and in favor. It sounded like an interesting idea and, in my opinion (for whatever it's worth), I thought he did a pretty good job and I'm looking forward to seeing more of his performance in Phantom Pain. And finally, the story left a lot of intrigue at the end, what with everything you worked for in Peace Walker being destroyed by a new, mysterious foe. It was a major cliff hanger and I can't wait to see the next part.
Now the problems with the game. FIrstly, the story left a lot intrigue at the end, what with everything you worked for in Peace Walker being destroyed by a new, mysterious foe. No, I didn't type that twice on accident. This was just both a good and a VERY bad thing. Despite having what I felt was a good amount of replay value, it just didn't deliver enough of the story. Originally, Ground Zeroes and Phantom Pain were both going to be released as the same game, with Ground Zeroes being the prologue. But, probably due to the ungodly long amount of development time that was going into the latter project, Kojima Productions decided to release this game with a total of 2-3 hours of legitimate content, only about 20 minutes of that being a continuation of Big Boss's story, and charged $20-$40. This is a really fun game, but if this had been some small, virtual teaser release for, at the most, $10 I would probably be more inclined to speak up for it. Maybe if they had decided to release even a low brow version of MGS: Online or promised discount DLC missions. But for what they delivered, only as a 17 year Metal Gear Solid fan was I able to get as much appreciation out of this title as I could. However, not everyone is a fan of this series. And as a interesting guy who re-releases his games a lot and keeps saying he would like more people to get into the series, this was just a big fumble on Kojima's part that only the die hard fanboys seem to make any attempt to defend.
If you're willing to spend the full amount on Steam or it goes on sale, I would definetely say give it a try. It's an incredibly well made game for what it has. But if you pass it up, I won't blame you.

Its great. I mean, what can I say that hasn't already been said about it in various reviews? It is a game that takes a wonderful mix of puzzle like planning and assessment of levels with the action packed and skill based movement of running games - especially at the later levels.
Overall, the game I think succeeds because of its general simplicity of design and concept, but in a way that makes complexity able to be built into the level design itself. It may take an hour just working on one level, coming up with one strategy and testing it over and over until you find its a deadend and you need a new route and having to work back with a new strategy, and once you find that working path you want to take, it can take many of attempts before you finally get that strategy down and finish it out.
What makes the game fun is this mix. Alone, the puzzles themselves may seem rather simple or the movement around the levels to be rather monotonous, but together it creates a meshed fluid machine of play where every movement to the next has to be precise and calculated while you think about the next step you need to take and the overall path you should follow to beat any one level. It leads to its own kind of fun with taking on every new challenge as they are thrown at you.
The only downside there might be for this game, would be that there is a rather...dramatic difficulty spike for the last few levels. The game overall eases you in very slowly to how the tiles function without any sort of annoying tutorial, just showing you how they work by putting them together and letting you figure it out as a player. I will also say that the last few levels are the most fun levels in the game just because of each of the individual challenges each provides, but the last few do take quite a bit of skill and thinking to pull off compared to most of the easier levels.
Albeit, this small complaint is rather lessened when you take that there are quite a few player created levels to practice on, ranging in difficulty from beginner level easy all the way up to beyond even the last levels of the game, and even a few artsy levels with pixel art of various things made in tiles that you have to clear.
Overall, this is a fun game to spend time with, and for the hours of time ive gotten out of it, I will definately say it was worth the cost. As soon as it had released, I sent of two copies to friends I knew would enjoy the game. It is certainly not for everyone, but if you are interested in puzzle games or just flexing that good ol hand eye coordination, this is certainly a good pickup.

So I bought the game today and played it to completion. I'm really split as to whether I should recommend it or not.
On the one hand, it does have a very nice story and I found it addictive (while it lasted), and reminds of Portal in that regard. The voice acting is brilliant and [SPOILER ALERT]
[\SPOILER ALERT] is refreshing.
However, it lacks puzzles or challenges. It lacks much of a world to explore. I simply don't expect to be able to finish a game in 4 hours, not when it costs £13/$20. There is the option to 'level up' in the game, but its simply unnecessary. You can do everything by just walking without thought and pressing buttons as they come up (I got 90% of the hidden messages this way).
The game has lots of options for creative solutions, but these are not needed as there are basically no problems to be solved. Which I think is the dissapointing thing about this game.
To summarise, the game feels like a short, odd sci-fi/fantasy book. The story keeps you going, and when you finally put it down you feel slightly uneasy about what's just happened. Unfortunately, I don't think that's quite enough for me to recommend it as a game.

I, like many others, believe that the update where the exp system was introduced has ruined the game.
Whilst it does speed up games, stopping them from lasting as long and makes upgrades at the shop less overpowering, it brings more negatives than posities.
With this system there is almost no chance of being able to win a game you have previously been losing because of the level differences they gain from being on the winning team. This makes the first few minuits of the game determine who will win as once you start to level more than the other team, as you can easily overwhelm them throughout the rest of the game.
Another problem with this system is that newer players struggle against players with expainsion packs, giving stronger characters, and more experienced players. This is beacuse people can't be 'carried' by their team members as they give not only solar, but now exp to the other team which again causes this overwhelming effect further.
While I understand this update would have taken a lot of time to create and put into the game, and not all players dislike the new exp system, but I don't think Ronimo games should have kept this system implemented whith all the negetive feedback it has been getting. Maybe they should consider making a second game with the exp system and keeping the original as it is, or maybe giving a vote in game as to whether the games they play should use the exp system or not? creating both original games and games using the exp system.
Overall the new exp system has almost destroyed this game for me, as I barely get as much enjoyment out of it as I used to when the update wasn't around.
I'll not be recommending this game to anybody while the update is in place as I believe the update makes it increasingly harder for new players to join, and the money can be spent buying a less broken game.

I’ll start with the bugs, and to be honest there are a fair amount. Most if which have been around since the games release. There’s dismemberment, random clothing loss, and invisible obstructions. All of which have been around forever, I can recall these from playing shortly after the original release. Some of the newer ones involve blank screens on loading saves and complete crashes on video loads. And while my research shows a lot more issues with simply getting the game to run on Windows 7, I had no issues in that regard with Vista.
While I did have the loading bug every time I started playing, I had notother major or minor bug issues for the first 20 hours of playtime. I did experience the video crash once, but otherwise had a perfect play. With my research to various forums and gaming sites I can say its not bug free. It would appear to me that it’s more of a crap shoot with your current system as to whether or not you’ll be dealing with them, and to what degree.
In Knights of the Old Republic you play as a Republic solider, who eventually becomes a Jedi. In starting the game you choose to be either male or female, and have about ten faces to choose from. While a little more in character customization would have been nice, its certainly not major flaw. You pick one of three starting classes; Solider, Scoundrel, or Smuggler. Once passing the Jedi trials you pick your sub-class; Jedi Guardian, Jedi Consular, or Jedi Sentinel, which are just Jedi’d versions of their main counterpart. While some weapons and armor are upgradeable, all the upgrades are predetermined. Armor and melee weapons get two upgrades and ranged can get four. The only thing you can really upgrade or customize is your lightsaber. There are only three types in the game, all the hilts look alike, but blade color can be altered. Red crystals will be what you find the most of, but blue, green, yellow, purple, and even a couple special colors are there to pick from. You can also find Power Crystals. There are several of these throughout the game each with different stats, you are however limited to two for each lightsaber.
The story is, simply put, excellent. It compares only with the great Star Wars novels. Giving you a perfect blend of drama, suspense, and comedy. All the while keeping you on your feet wondering what’s coming around the bend. And on top of the main storyline, there are many small ones and sub-plots. Each of your companions has a back story of their own, as well as many NPC’s you meet in your travels.  While these short stories wrap nicely, I was often left wondering what would happen next to these people. Sure their immediate problems have been solved, but what other woes will they find in their plight?  It takes a special level of writing to bring about this kind of character interest.  Sure this is common for the main cast, wondering where everyone ends up after the games finale.  But to have these thoughts with small roles from simple side quests is another level of depth that the writing holds.  And there is always the great, possibly greatest, surprise twist.  Which many publications still, to this day list as one of the greatest moments in videogame stories.
Gameplay seems to be the place where KotOR gets the most heat.  Although most major publications give it raving reviews across the board, when you look past these at the players opinions, you get a different story.  While I think most that complain about this game do so because they didn’t know what they were getting ready to play.  Or just expected something completely different.  It is an RPG after all.  The combat is turn-based.  But it doesn’t look it, which I think it what throws players off.  The mechanics of the combat and how it all works was taken straight from the Star Wars Roleplaying Game, which is derived from the Dungeons & Dragons rule book.  What this means is this is basically a tabletop game on a computer with pretty visuals.  All the combat, and in fact everything you do, is based on the d20 system.  While the game handles all of these dice rolls and modifiers in the background, you can view all the information in a menu.  The beauty of this system is that each turn is a predetermined about time, but the actual action is played together on screen.  The combat looks beautiful, as you strike with your lightsaber and they actually block the blow.  The only time things aren’t perfect is when you have multiple attackers.  The defender is only animated to defend against one foe.  This same d20 system is all throughout the game.  From picking locks, repairing droids, persuading information, and lying.  Everything has a roll and a check.  Sometimes you get it sometimes you don’t.
Knights of the Old Republic is a beautiful game, that could use some texture improvements.  It has a flawless story that only keeps you guessing and wondering more after.  The real-time turn-based combat makes you feel like you’re playing a 3rd-person shooter.  It’s full of memorable characters that are so loved they’ve been incorporated into other pieces of Star Wars cannon.  It’s a game that oozes excellence.  It’s unfortunate it has the bugs that it does, mainly the ones it’s had forever, I can’t excuse those.  If you are able to get it to run, which odds are you will.  I highly recommend you play it.  From start to finish, then play it again.

Endless Legend is a fantastic 4X Strategy games. Playing it has been a breath of fresh air in a genre that has grown stale lately. Recommend this to any strategy fan, espcially to people who love managing empires.

Currently my favorite 4X game (although Stelaris is a close second). Zoomable detail levels on the map are particularly well handled (and the art assets are really nice). I played an absurd number of hours of Civ II when it first came out and this is the first one that has merited a second playthrough.
My only grump is that I wish there was a more consistent set of hot keys (clicking through notifications that you just want a quick look at gets tedious by turn 400).
This game is truly a hidden gem
A masterful and unique take on a 4X game. I enjoyed this more than the last Civilization game. Hard to put down, with imaginative character design and satisfying tactical and strategic layers.

The issue I've always had with Civ is that research and technology always follow a predictable path based on established real world history which is boring to me. I've always wondered what it would be like if you have offshoots, like never inventing gunpowder and creating a contemporary medieval society with modern alloys and plastics, or keep improving steam engines for a steampunk based society.
Endless Legend looks like it could scratch the "not boring" itch. Initial impressions from the tutorial promised the familiar addictive gameplay with the addition of a fine tuned combat system and a sleek UI (as a graphic designer by trade, I really appreciate a good UI) that had me excited to play further.
Setting up a new game, I was a little disappointed to find there was no campaign. Having no basis on which to judge all the factions as a new player it seems a campaign would be a great way to introduce them slowly so as to not feel overwhelmed by choice. But the lack of one was not a deal breaker, I figured: it's an indie dev, I guess it's better to have a game that's polished and works well than spread themselves too thin.
I resolved to feel my own way through the factions by setting up a hotseat game and play a few at once, at least for the first era or two, get a feel for how they play and what appeals to me. Then, later I might see if my wife wants to try a game.
It took a few minutes of fussing with the settings before I realised:
A quick search later and I find it isn't even an upcoming feature. The devs have categorically stated it isn't planned, and likely never will be due to the difficultly incorporating it into a system with simultaneous turns. While this is a fair point I'd be willing to concede, the lack of LAN play gives me further pause. The cynic in me suspects they'd rather every player have to purchase a copy of the game, so of course it's a low priority. However the fact that there's no mods to add either of these gameplay modes despite workshop support leads me to believe it may in fact be too hard to change their existing system.
This does mean I cannot recommend the game though, and I've requested a refund. Hotseat is the way I get most enjoyment out of games of this ilk, so as much as the world and factions intrigue me, without a hotseat mode it's simply not for me.

The first thing Legend does right is that it disregards genre tropes in favor of injecting its own unique lore into a fully realized and lush game world. One can't help but compare Auriga with Brian Reynolds' sentient planet Chiron in the 4X classic Alpha Centauri. Though perhaps not quite as epic as Firaxis' earliest and most grand creations, Legend's universe and the inhabitants of Auriga are no less captivating.
The turn-based gameplay is similar to that of Sid Meier's Civilization series, but brings a number of innovative features and improvements to the table that I've been crying for since Civilization II. Legend also borrows from other classic and highly regarded strategy franchises like Heroes of Might & Magic and Age of Wonders. The wealth of options available to the player for directing the evolution of his faction is staggering. I don't think I'll ever have enough time to explore every single nook and cranny of this game. With all of the expansions, there is a huge amount of content here.
The in-game tutorial is adequate for getting your feet wet, but ends rather abruptly, leaving quite a few important gameplay elements untouched upon. Thankfully the UI and comprehensive tooltip systems do a great job of filling in many of the blanks. If you've ever played a strategy game like this before, you'll acclimate quickly.
Highly recommended for veterans of the genre, and friendly enough to keep from scaring away interested newcomers too. The developers of Civilization 6 would be well-advised to take a look at some of the unique mechanics in Endless Legend; and perhaps take a few notes while they're at it.

Clear interface and a lot to discover. Very interesting tech tree to explore, in which you are encouraged to follow a route of specialisation rather than knowing everything.
There apears to be little unit variarty untill you find that the weapons you equip change the unit in a fundemental way. Complement your nation's weakness by asimilating a minor faction into your empire, thus getting their unit.
A very interesting battle map which has a very intriguing way of auto resolving. It actually plays the battle out as if the AI was commanding your army.
All of the factions are asymetric. They'll overlap with on some areas but still do them in different ways. All factions have a unique city athstetic on a beautifully crafted map. Wild Walkers with their angular elf like structures that are almost always inside forests, Cultists have one huge city whose districs make a circle, always putting the emphasis (giving worship) to the city centre.
The lore! The main questline of the major factions unlock unique technologies that are otherwise unatainable, and give you insight into the lore of a faction. After playing one faction for some time you can dream their lore, but for me it remains fun to read it every time. Minor factions will also offer questlines in return for the ocasional resource, technology and pacification (they join the city in their province, giving a population).
(possible negatives)
The combat map/system takes quite a bit of getting used to. It seems extremely counter intuitive at first and doesn't change much in single player after unlocking the 3 basic unit types and understanding what the differences types of equipment give and take from a unit. It also doesn't help that there is no way to understand the intricacies of control without manualy controling battles for a long time, while you will be tempted at first to just manualy resolve everything.
You need to love experimenting.
This is a 4X game and you have to love the core formulae beyond "I once played a Civ game and didn't hate it". Find out how all the different factions play out, try to change your playstyle when you find yourself doing the same thing over and over again. It's okay to have a favourite faction, but try a new one every once in a while.
The game heavily accelerates around turn 100, ussualy ending between 160 and 180 with the last 20 turns being extremely slow to the point where I think newer or more casual players will quickly lose focus. (But I am neither so what do I know D: ) Experiment with a difficulty setting that works for you, but keep in mind that higher on the AI will cheat heavily. (The Budget way to increase difficulty in strategygames !)
Despite my earlier praise of the battle system, in late turns they do come down to biggest number wins. Heavily depending on your (RNG) success in questing, you will not see a change in unit setup after the midgame. Just better equipment and larger armies.
You can of course, try experimenting with a strange unit setup to try and suprise/confuse the AI. A super tanky support unit that the AI likes to focus so much? Or maybe your Hero's abilities are now making your ranged units to shoot from an extra tiles away. There is still room to experiment, but the AI doesn't always make this required.

Mostly by people not inherently understanding of the 4X genre or skill level concerns. Many people seemed to want to give the game a 'moderate' score rather than positive or negative (as they end up doing).
To each their own of course. Keep in mind that you need to like exploring the game, finding out how to challange yourself or what works for you. Read the lore of the factions, find how they all work.
In conclusion, I love this game. Havn't loved a 4X game this much for a long time and I cannot wait to see what the company has learned going forward into Endless Space 2.

Dear Wildcard Studio
Since I did a negative review of Survival Evolved I feel like I have to review this one as well. I've been playing this game for some weeks now, with 180 hours approx. on a Mac OS X El Capitan 3,2 GHz Intel Core i5, 16 GB 1600 MHz DDR3 and NVIDIA GeForce GTX 675MX 1024 MB.
This one runs just fine on low settings ( still looking really good) and the main problem is about lag and sync. Sometimes I feel like I have what I like to call " Lag Radar". When someone is around me or I look in the direction of some player it starts dropping FPS so I know I have to run the other way until we're 5 left, but that's fun because is what this game is all about, right? Being the Fittest with what you have. In PvP I experienced some really bad moments, like the bow just going useless in the sense that it doesn't even drag the arrow back to fire, and sometimes in PvE. But anyway the game itself it's just great. The idea, the development and the " Free to Play" thing, for what I'm thankful.
I guess some improvements can be made for the lag problem, maybe the crafting system could be the cause or simply my bad peruvian average internet connection.
Talking about the game mechanics, I think the whole Tame following system should be improved because I lost hundreds of good dinos in the forest and had pretty nice armies decimated by rocks and trees, specially in my first matches. I still remember a match in which I had this Sarco stuck on a rock that was 2 meters away and blocked my other tames while I was pushed by the Ring of Death and I had to just leave them all. Since I started it improved, but I'm totally sure you can do even better. Another thing that I think would be appreciated by the most is a hit feedback on the HUD when you actually hit a player. Sometimes you feel like you're hitting somebody with your arrows or spears and run for a final charge just to realize you actually didn't and you're running to death.
In the end, this is one of the best competitive games I've ever played, I have a lot of fun playing it and I absolutely recommend it for any player! It takes time and practice and specially to be focused on what you're doing.

An effective and fun practice tool for common object recognition in many languages.

I picked this up to supplement Duolingo. I like that several languages are supported, so you can live those polyglot dreams.
There are frustrating points though, mainly the controls. You are tested by finding objects in your apartment, sometimes it's hard to get over to the thing you want in time. Clicking the fridge when you meant to click the butter *barely* taller than its shelf or trying to click something really small while feeling rushed by the timer. There are no other people to interact with and you are stuck in your house.
It also doesn't teach you to use the language so much as builds your vocabulary of household objects. Despite these shortcomings, it's a great way to break up the routine of learning. Don't expect it to be all you need, but a nice diversion in the right direction.

At the time of writing this review, I've mastered all 420 words the game has to offer, and completed all the tasks on the 'To Do' list. I played the English version of the game, so that's the one I'll be reviewing. I also own the Japanese pack, but I haven't completed that one yet.
One thing I'd like to start with is that 'Influent' never advertises, nor does it claim to make one fluent in any of the languages available here (and I double checked this). The description of the game here on the store page clearly states that it is a game focused on VOCABULARY ACQUISITION and PRONUNCIATION. It never claims to teach one grammar, syntax, conversation, or any other facet of language. I feel like a lot of people thought 'Influent' was a full-blown language learning tool, which it is not. The negative reviews here are unnecessary and uncalled for. Having addressed that, let's move on to the actual thing.
The setting of the game is limited to the main character's apartment. You can explore his room, the bathroom, living room, and the kitchen. The point of the game is simple: as you explore, you're expected to click on various items that you encounter and collect vocabulary. Upon clicking on an item, you hear the word as it's spoken by a native speaker, and you can find more information about it such as its word class, phonetic transcription, synonyms, or you can just add it into your vocab list. In total, there are 420 words to collect — but in reality — there's "only" 284 items that you physically come across in the game. These items mostly consist of normal household articles, but there are some small surprises here and there like a cat nestled on the chair of the protagonist. As of now, there are no other locations available, and the words are very basic in nature — so don't expect to turn into a walking dictionary just by playing this. The game WILL equip you with a very nice elementary vocab though.
One thing that I particularly liked was the fact that certain words feature synonyms, and the player has the ability to switch between them (e.g. you can decide whether you want to call soft drink a "soda" or a "pop" as both are commonly used in the U.S., although "soda" is preferred in the West Coast). I thought this was a nice touch. Another thing that I really liked was the whole unlocking system which allows the player to acquire new words in the form of adjectives and verbs that are usually applicable to the nouns connected with them — "usually" being the key word here as some choices seemed extremely random (e.g. "beer" is apparently "disgusting"). Another thing of note is that 'Influent' teaches American English, and there's no option to switch to British English. The vocabulary and the pronunciation reflect that. So, this may put off students of British English, even though it shouldn't bother them that much.
Speaking of pronunciation, the game uses the IPA (International Phonetic Alphabet) to transcribe English words in order to show how they're really pronounced. That's all neat and great, but there are some truly odd transcriptions for many of the words featured  in the game. Not wrong, just a tad nonstandard. In some cases, I thought the transcriptions in the game actually reflect how the words sound in real life much better than what you usually find in dictionaries. For instance: calendar, magazine, and milk were transcribed as [ˈkæl-ɛn-dəɹ], [mei-ɡə-ˈzin], and [mɪəlk] instead of the more traditional [ˈkæl-ən-dəɹ], [mæ-ɡə-ˈzin], [mɪlk]. However, the /ɔ/ vowel is frequently confused with the /oʊ/ diphthong, and so you get funny transcriptions like ['fɔ-tʌ-gɹæf] for "photograph," [pɪlɔ] for "pillow," and even ['skeit-bɔʊɹd] for "skateboard." Some transcriptions left me puzzled - for example:  [ˈkæɹ-pɪt] for "carpet," [ˈwɑʊ-lɪt] for "wallet," and [ˈbʌl-ə-'tɛn-bɔɹd] for "bulletin board." There are also words in which the stress mark is often placed on the wrong syllable, e.g. [pɪk'tʃʊɹ] or [flʌ-'fi]. I'm honestly quite surprised nobody's pointed this out yet. So, this might get a bit annoying — especially if you're already accustomed to different transcriptions.
All in all, I thought 'Influent' was an extremely auspicious effort — one that could potentially become one of the best language learning tools out there. It'd be great to see new content and locations added into the game, and something tells me that we will. There's certainly a lot of room for improvement, but the groundwork had been laid and it is very solid. While it won't make one fluent, it is a brilliant supplement to, say, an elementary level textbook.

The game is by no means perfect and it has its fair share of bugs, but if you want to shut off your brain and enjoy a beautiful game with an ok none historically accurate story it's a good time.
Pros
-Lighting and Texturing is Master class this game is pretty unrivaled in terms of looks
-Combat feels fluid and fun, especially the in formation sequences
-Pacing feels pretty good, story never really bogs down to a crawl
-Difficulty curve feels fair without being punishing
-Combat finishers are both satisfying and upgradeable
Cons
-Poor performance all around I had to monkey with a lot of stuff to get a consistent 30 fps without frame drops
-A lot of QTE's so if you aren't a fan of god of war style Finishers could be a turn off
-Not HIstorically accurate at all, I don't know why we don't have a game set in a historically accurate Rome
-The story while functional often makes very little sense, with character motivations being brought into question a lot
-Game is really short I beat it no problem in 5 hours so if you are looking for a long experience you won't find it here.
-Combat while fun can be drawn out too much in huge sequences involving you fighting 10 or more men that take a freaking beating before going down.
BottomLine
While the game is fun and exciting to play at times, it falls very short in terms of story. I really like the setting of Rome and a proper plot set around the Political schemeings of the inner workings of the city would be very interesting. If you're looking for a few hours of fun with a competant brawler, and this game is on sale you could do a lot worse with your time.

This might possibly be the worst videogame ever made. I'm going to try and explain what this unplayable abomination is about, but to be perfectly honest I have no idea. The game starts with the protagonist visiting somebody's house for a party, and then waking up in a bedroom. After the lamest hallucination in videogame history, he winds up in a new part of the house with a radio yelling at him. What you'll soon discover is that all the dialogue in the game is a poorly blended mixture of misplaced philosophical brilliance, and random bursts of immature filth. The main character only has one of these.
I guess you can call the game a very lacklustre Saw reimagining, with the mystery ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ giving the repulsive protagonist very non-threatening tasks to proceed through the house. Based on a choice you're given early on, the game proceeds down two linear and equally rubbish storylines. In one, the radio keeps giving you lacklustre tasks even as the world turns into an ugly and nonsensical fantasy. In the other, he tries to murder you and you escape through a musty building in the wilderness.
I'll be honest, this game is as bad as it gets. I'd be happy with a well-made walking simulator, but Only If fancies itself as more of a cinematic puzzle/action game. It fails magnificently with slow and buggy controls matched with frustrating and unclear design. Still, it's hard to decide if the gameplay is the worst part of the experience. The concept of the game, as far as I can tell from the incomprehensible dialogue, is being trapped in a confusing situation and being drugged by your captors so you can't tell what is real. The best thing I can say is that the design of the more realistic areas isn't bad for what it is, but it's bogged down with some very ugly and poorly realised sequences and a script that would make Jimmy Screamerclause proud.
I'm fine with fiction portraying what would make a horrible reality, art should be free to be as twisted as it needs to be. But all the decisions made in this game only serve to make the story unpleasant and the characters unlikeable.
This game is bad. Play it if you must, but take my word for it that it won't be worth your time.

I could write an essay about this game, it feels like the all writers are writers trope in a video game except being the first game to have used it makes it feel fresh. It really feels like the developers have taken the 7 years since bioshock and tried earnestly to build an entire game dedicated to answering the central conceit and the most remarkable thing is it just about succeeds.
It poses a lot of smart questions about how different generations of game deveopers operate and the value of each from the auteurs of the 90's like Peter Molyneux, Warren Spector and Richard Garriot to their proteges in the naughties who were roundly bludgend by big buisness into impotence and went of to seek their fortunes on their own to the new age of crowd funding and nostalgia games of the latest generation. It really is Game as Art like you've never seen before (instead of art in games).

The Magic Circle is as much an allegory about the games industry as much as it is a game in and of itself. In the game you are a player character that is trapped inside a game that will never be finished. Your goal? Well that is not quite clear in the beginning. Exploration of the world, and who you are, are the main driving forces early on. As the story develops you begin to learn the fate of the people who were working on the game, and where everything went wrong.
The game likes to play with your expectations and uses the fact that you are in a broken, unfinished game, to play with the idea of bugs and glitches. That is why when the game crashed on me one time, I thought it was part of the game.
Overall I have enjoyed my time with The Magic Circle. With a unique mash-up of art styles, witty and funny characters, and a combat system more like Pokemon than a first person action game, The Magic Circle is a game that anyone can enjoy.

For full disclosure, I bought this game purely because James Urbaniak is in it. But when I began playing it, I realized it's one of the most unique and entertaining games I've played in a long, long time. Its story and its ideas are so strange it's hard to explain, but that is not a bad thing.

I’ll start with the bugs, and to be honest there are a fair amount. Most if which have been around since the games release. There’s dismemberment, random clothing loss, and invisible obstructions. All of which have been around forever, I can recall these from playing shortly after the original release. Some of the newer ones involve blank screens on loading saves and complete crashes on video loads. And while my research shows a lot more issues with simply getting the game to run on Windows 7, I had no issues in that regard with Vista.
While I did have the loading bug every time I started playing, I had notother major or minor bug issues for the first 20 hours of playtime. I did experience the video crash once, but otherwise had a perfect play. With my research to various forums and gaming sites I can say its not bug free. It would appear to me that it’s more of a crap shoot with your current system as to whether or not you’ll be dealing with them, and to what degree.
In Knights of the Old Republic you play as a Republic solider, who eventually becomes a Jedi. In starting the game you choose to be either male or female, and have about ten faces to choose from. While a little more in character customization would have been nice, its certainly not major flaw. You pick one of three starting classes; Solider, Scoundrel, or Smuggler. Once passing the Jedi trials you pick your sub-class; Jedi Guardian, Jedi Consular, or Jedi Sentinel, which are just Jedi’d versions of their main counterpart. While some weapons and armor are upgradeable, all the upgrades are predetermined. Armor and melee weapons get two upgrades and ranged can get four. The only thing you can really upgrade or customize is your lightsaber. There are only three types in the game, all the hilts look alike, but blade color can be altered. Red crystals will be what you find the most of, but blue, green, yellow, purple, and even a couple special colors are there to pick from. You can also find Power Crystals. There are several of these throughout the game each with different stats, you are however limited to two for each lightsaber.
The story is, simply put, excellent. It compares only with the great Star Wars novels. Giving you a perfect blend of drama, suspense, and comedy. All the while keeping you on your feet wondering what’s coming around the bend. And on top of the main storyline, there are many small ones and sub-plots. Each of your companions has a back story of their own, as well as many NPC’s you meet in your travels.  While these short stories wrap nicely, I was often left wondering what would happen next to these people. Sure their immediate problems have been solved, but what other woes will they find in their plight?  It takes a special level of writing to bring about this kind of character interest.  Sure this is common for the main cast, wondering where everyone ends up after the games finale.  But to have these thoughts with small roles from simple side quests is another level of depth that the writing holds.  And there is always the great, possibly greatest, surprise twist.  Which many publications still, to this day list as one of the greatest moments in videogame stories.
Gameplay seems to be the place where KotOR gets the most heat.  Although most major publications give it raving reviews across the board, when you look past these at the players opinions, you get a different story.  While I think most that complain about this game do so because they didn’t know what they were getting ready to play.  Or just expected something completely different.  It is an RPG after all.  The combat is turn-based.  But it doesn’t look it, which I think it what throws players off.  The mechanics of the combat and how it all works was taken straight from the Star Wars Roleplaying Game, which is derived from the Dungeons & Dragons rule book.  What this means is this is basically a tabletop game on a computer with pretty visuals.  All the combat, and in fact everything you do, is based on the d20 system.  While the game handles all of these dice rolls and modifiers in the background, you can view all the information in a menu.  The beauty of this system is that each turn is a predetermined about time, but the actual action is played together on screen.  The combat looks beautiful, as you strike with your lightsaber and they actually block the blow.  The only time things aren’t perfect is when you have multiple attackers.  The defender is only animated to defend against one foe.  This same d20 system is all throughout the game.  From picking locks, repairing droids, persuading information, and lying.  Everything has a roll and a check.  Sometimes you get it sometimes you don’t.
Knights of the Old Republic is a beautiful game, that could use some texture improvements.  It has a flawless story that only keeps you guessing and wondering more after.  The real-time turn-based combat makes you feel like you’re playing a 3rd-person shooter.  It’s full of memorable characters that are so loved they’ve been incorporated into other pieces of Star Wars cannon.  It’s a game that oozes excellence.  It’s unfortunate it has the bugs that it does, mainly the ones it’s had forever, I can’t excuse those.  If you are able to get it to run, which odds are you will.  I highly recommend you play it.  From start to finish, then play it again.

Typically I feel worrisome in recommending any game, as one's opinion and/or preference can be composed of anything, and because of how fearful I am of leading one to buying anything with a result of disappointment, though I will do so with this game largely so I can strike a check for the Pillar of Community Steam badge, and perhaps contribute somewhat to one's efforts in discovering an enjoyable experience in this video game.
Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic was developed and released by Bioware for Windows in 2003, when the company wasn't tainted by the tyrannical Electronic Arts, commonly known as EA. This package of entertainment's story was written by Drew Karpyshyn, who is also the writer of Mass Effect One and Two's stories, as well as the author of the three Darth Bane novels. Taking place 4,000 years before the official six Star Wars movies, it is free of any plot limitations from the events of the six films, and other stories pertaining to the same timeline. Granted by such space, Karpyshyn weaved a tale which is not disgracefully stupid yet, suitably complex and even surprising; plot twists are present, one of which may grab your jaw and yank it downward before it can drop. I found learning of this Star Wars era enjoyable, with its intriguing events and circumstances, charismatic and sometimes lovable characters, original designs and concepts, and amounts of new and expanded Star Wars universe knowledge only a nerd such as myself can favor. This game can teach a player more about the Jedi, the Sith, the Force, and the remaining aspects of the Star Wars universe than the six movies can. Despite that, it remains to feel, seem, and exist as something residing in the Star Wars universe; familiar, if not similar, species, devices, and planets are omnipresent throughout the game.
Being an RPG, one can customize the playable characters' attributes and abilities, and shape his or her destiny. Options of things to customize include physical abilities and appearance, fighting styles, choice among various tools of combat, and allies. To side with the Light or the Dark is one's decision to be made by the selection of responses to certain situations and/or characters. Combat and enemies can prove to be resilient and ferocious enough to require planning and strategy to defeat; weapon employment, ally roles, and positions are some things to consider in order to overcome powerful opponents in a classical RPG fighting style.
Many consider this game a classic in today's age; some have reported of this to be the greatest game they've ever played. While I may not hold an identical opinion, I do understand why they do. When I began playing for the first occasion, I was addicted; I had an urge to progress through the game's story, uncover its secrets, gain more strength, and enjoy heated battles. I do deem this to be a game shining among the dull slabs of this time, though I understand such a conviction is merely an opinion. Please, do not decide to buy this game-as cheap as it is on Steam now-after reading this unsuitable and poorly-written recommendation. I suggest researching more before making a conclusion, perhaps by consulting professional reviews and watching gameplay videos.

I have played many CS games before, but I mainly played CS:S and CS:GO. And this game is nothing like CS. If you think CS:GO is nothing like CS, just look at this.
Graphics:
The graphics are borrowed from a game from 1999. Graphics in a game don't matter, but it does help if you do manage to UPDATE THEM? There is no excuse to use graphics from 1999, considering this is a game from 2014, but at least the graphics are bearable.
Grade: D-
Animations:
The animations are borrowed from CS 1.6, which would be fine, but this is a tense, action packed game. The slow reload animations meant for a tactical, slow-paced FPS doesn't fit in the game. Sometimes, the animations don't even work, and I'll think the gun broke, only to realize it just didn't display and manage to waste a round into a wall. The death animations for the zombies don't make sense. Most of them are just kneeling to the ground, rising, and falling again. I'm not a master in physics, but I'm pretty sure getting shot by an AWP, a .308 winchester rifle, would at least throw back the zombies instead of forcing them to kneel. CS 1.6 managed to make different animations for getting killed in different place (shot in stomach, shot in head, shot in back etc.) and THAT was made in 1999, so why not this?
Grade: F-
Gameplay:
Terrible. This is nothing like CS. This is fast-paced and action packed, unlike CS' slow-paced, tactical action. The weapons feel too powerful, as even a gun weak like the Glock 17 can kill a zombie in 1 or 2 hits. The start screen is pretty, but user-UNfriendly. I accidently joined a game trying to join a normal game. There are way too many zombies in the co-op game heading at you, and even though I set my gun as the AUG, I still get the machine gun that empties in 5 seconds. Despite it being action-packed, I often got very bored.
Grade: F--
Sound:
Can't really judge this, as the game borrowed many, many sounds from CS 1.6, but the music is very loud. I often couldn't  hear anything when music played.
Grade: F
Verdict:
The game is a cluster♥♥♥♥ of zombies coming at you, with loud music and animations that don't help the game. It doesn't deserve to have "Counter Strike" in the title. Fans of counter strike, this is not your game. I suggest any CS game but this.
Grade: F-

For a begginer in a second language I have found this game to be helpful in that it is a small stepping stone on my way to learning words.
To clarify this, I am learning High German primarily from one fluent speaking friend, a couple of phone apps (which I find underwhelming), and this ... The only thing I could do to improve my rate of learning is take a German course and then immerse myself in the country.
But as I say, it is a small stepping stone, I do appreciate that it is devoloped by a single person (last time I checked), and that this person (or persons) has many other languages to update.
Where this falls down;
*No option to choose gender.
*Gendered items of level solely male. (knowing what to call a wallet does not help me when I carry a purse)
*Items, such as milk in the refrigerator, whilst when clicked are pronounced "milch", still read "milk" on the carton, this breaks much of the immersion. -
- I feel that when learning a language it is best not to translate object names, simply to hold it up and give it the correct name in that language, otherwise the association between terms will be forever referenced back to the first language and create a mental lag.
*Despite a female character being shown on the cover, she never makes an appearance, the player never gets to choose to play as her in her appartment.
*No character interaction so as to learn grammar and how to use the words we learn in a sentence.
German has around four words for "the", they are each gendered, and may be used in a non gendered way to indicate plural items or people, In-Fluent will not teach you this. -
- Rather than striving to, it could simply mention what it does not teach so as to make the user aware they will need to pick that up elsewhere.
*Character movement is clunky, to move around either mouse button must be clicked and dragged around.
*It is not readily apparent to a player (well, at least me), that items once clicked then need to have their corresponding word below clicked so as to catalog them.
*Some items are far too small and may wreck the experience of challenge mode, i.e trying to click on keys and clicking the bench they sit on is a constant problem.
*This is a game that could benefit from the use of phonetics.
This game will teach you many household items, there are at least 200 words to catalog before learning other names for the same item depending on how it may be used in a sentence.
For the dedicated player I would say suppliment this with a lot of postit notes around the house of what objects are called in the language you are attempting to learn. -
- If you pronounce these as the game has been pronouncing these, you will likely be ever so slightly off with the accent, however walking about the house and saying the name of an item every time you interact with it will help your pronunciation alongside learning.
Although a lot of work has been put into this game I would suggest best to pick it up on Steam sale due to its current limitations.

If this game was more than just a room and it evetually lead to higher level grammar learning they could have charged WAY more. Otherwise for what they charged it is fair for what you get.
I was embarrassed at how despite taking French from Kindegarten to Grade 11 and living in Canada (where you have bilingual labelling) at how at first, quite bad, I was at recognizing the labels. Within two hours though I had covered a lot of ground due to my prior langauge learning.
As said if this game was not limited to just the apartment you live in then it be a far more valuable reasource than what it claims to be.

A loving homage to classic RPG tropes from games such as Final Fantasy to Legend of Zelda to Diablo, 'Evoland' is both a clever deconstruction and fun game in it's own right. Over the course of it's short but fun 3-5 hour campaign you'll go from blocky sprites to HD rendered 3D, charting the chronology and evolution of the genre and tipping its hat to everything from Chocobo's and Cid to minimap's and hidden chests. Collectibles extend the challenge for completionists but don't let the short length put you off as this is one game every RPG fan should play.

If you've heard of Evoland, then you already know that it's designed to be a love letter to RPGs and action-adventure games, most notably the Legend of Zelda series and Final Fantasy series, but also Super Mario Bros., Dragon Quest, Diablo, and who knows what else. The beginning, where you get the different features, is very smartly implemented, and the game has a nice sense of humor. Once you get all of the different features about 40% of the way through the game, it slows down and loses all its novelty.
The game itself at this point alternates between a bad Final Fantasy homage and a bad Legend of Zelda homage, as other Steam reviewers have pointed out. Combat and movement are stiff, the world is tiny, the encouter rate in the overworld is ridiculous, the random battles themselves are completely devoid of challenge or purpose, and some of the stars and cards are pretty difficult to find without help.
On the plus side, again, it has a sense of humor, it's short enough to not overstay its welcome, and it features its own clone of FFVIII's Triple Triad. It's worth playing once, but you should absolutely not pay the full price for it.
